en: "One should meditate upon this syllable *om* as the *udgītha*. For one begins the *udgītha* chant with *om*; [now follows] its detailed exposition.

(1) One should meditate upon this syllable *om* as the *udgītha*. This syllable *om* is the closest designation of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); for when it is employed, He becomes pleased, just as people in the world are pleased when their own dear names are mentioned. Here, however, because it is used preceded by the particle *iti*, it is distinguished from its status as a designator and is understood merely as the form of the word itself. Thus, like an image or other such objects, it becomes a representative symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self.

Thus, it is understood from all the Vedāntas that this [syllable] is the most excellent means for the meditation upon the Supreme Self (paramātman), both as its name and as its symbol (pratīka); its excellence is well-known from its frequent employment in the rites of recitation (japa), at the beginning and end of Vedic study (svādhyāya), and so forth. Therefore, one should meditate upon this very syllable—which consists of phonemes and is denoted by the word "udgītha" because it is a constituent part of the udgītha chant—namely, one should maintain a steady and one-pointed mental focus upon the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the ritual action and serves as the symbol of the Supreme Self.

The Śruti itself states the reason why the syllable *oṃ* is denoted by the word *udgītha*: "For one sings [the udgītha] with 'om'; since, having begun with 'om', one sings [it], therefore the syllable *oṃ* is the *udgītha*. Regarding its further explanation (*upavyākhyāna*): the further explanation of that syllable is the statement that its worship is such-and-such, its power is such-and-such, and its fruit is such-and-such; thus the explanation proceeds.

The supplementary statement: Of these beings, the earth is the essence; of the earth, water is the essence; of water, plants are the essence; of plants, man is the essence; of man, speech is the essence; of speech, the *Ṛk* is the essence; of the *Ṛk*, the *Sāman* is the essence; of the *Sāman*, the *Udgītha* is the essence. 2. (2)

Of these beings, both moving and stationary, the earth is the essence (*rasa*), the goal, the ultimate resort, and the support. Of the earth, water is the essence—for the earth is woven like warp and woof within the waters; therefore, they are the essence of the earth. Of the waters, plants are the essence, because plants are a transformation of water. Of those [plants], man is the essence, because man is a transformation of food. And of that man, speech is the essence—for among the limbs of man, speech is the most essential; therefore, speech is called the essence of man.

Of that speech, the *ṛc* is the essence, the most substantial part; of the *ṛc*, the *sāman* is the essence, the more substantial part; and of that *sāman*, because it is the subject under discussion, the *udgītha*—that is, the syllable *oṃ*—is the most substantial part.
This very *udgītha* is the essence of essences, the supreme, the highest, the eighth, which is the *udgītha*. 3.

Thus—this very syllable *om*, known as the *udgītha*, is the *rasatama* (the most excellent essence) among the successive essences beginning with the elements; it is *parama* (supreme), because it is a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self; it is *parārdhya*—"*ardha*" means a place, and "that which is beyond the highest" (*para*) is *parārdha*; that which deserves such a place is *parārdhya*—meaning it is worthy of the station of the Supreme Self, because it is to be meditated upon (*upāsya*) like the Supreme Self itself; it is the "eighth," in the enumeration of the essences beginning with the earth; it is the *udgītha*, that which is the *udgītha*.

"What is what? Which Ṛc? Which Sāman? Which Udgītha?"—thus it is investigated. (4) It has been stated that "the essence of the Ṛc is speech"; so, which is that Ṛc? Which is that Sāman? Or which is that Udgītha? The repetition "which... which" (*katamā katamā*) is for the sake of emphasis. Now, one might object: "The suffix *-tamac* is prescribed when there is an inquiry regarding the specific type among many (*bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne*); however, there is no multiplicity of types of Ṛcs here. How, then, is the use of *-tamac* appropriate? This is not a fault.

The compound *jātiparipraśnaḥ* is analyzed as *jātau paripraśnaḥ*—"an inquiry regarding a genus"—because in this analysis, the multiplicity of individual instances (*vyakti*) within the genus is logically established; it is not, however, analyzed as *jāteḥ paripraśnaḥ*—"an inquiry about the genus. [Objection: But if it were analyzed as *jāteḥ paripraśnaḥ*, then examples such as "Which Kaṭha? would be appropriate; however, they are not suitable for the analysis *jātau paripraśnaḥ*. [Response: Even in that case, there is no fault, because the inquiry is directed toward the genus itself—such as the Kaṭhas—with the intention of referring to the multiplicity of its individual instances.

If the question were regarding the genus (*jāti*), then a supplementary rule would have to be made for cases such as "Which one? Which one? [to account for the singular form]. "It has been deliberated upon" means that the investigation has been performed. Speech is the *ṛc*, breath is the *sāman*, and this syllable "Om" is the *udgītha*. Now, this is a couple: speech and breath, and the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. 5. (5) ————

For when an inquiry has been made, the statement of a reply is appropriate: "Speech indeed is the *ṛc*, breath is the *sāman*, and this syllable 'Om' is the *udgītha*. Even though speech and the *ṛc* are one, there is no contradiction regarding its being the eighth, because it belongs to a different preceding sentence; for the purpose of establishing the quality of attainment (*āpti*), it is said that "this syllable 'Om' is the *udgītha*. Since speech and breath are the sources of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, it is stated that "speech indeed is the *ṛc* and breath is the *sāman*."

For by the sequential grasping of speech and breath as the sources of the *ṛc* and *sāman*, there would be the inclusion of all *ṛcs* and all *sāmans*; and with the inclusion of all *ṛcs* and *sāmans*, there would be the inclusion of all rites accomplished by means of the *ṛc* and *sāman*; and with their inclusion, all desires would be included. By the statement "The syllable 'Om' is the *udgītha*," the suspicion that this is merely a figurative application (*bhakti*) is removed. By the phrase "That indeed is this," the couple is indicated.

"What is that couple? he asks. He replies: "Speech and breath, which are the causes of all *ṛc*s and *sāman*s, constitute the couple. The meaning is that *ṛc* and *sāman*—as the causes of *ṛc* and *sāman*—are what are designated by the terms *ṛc* and *sāman*; it is not that *ṛc* and *sāman* themselves independently form the couple. For otherwise, there would be two separate couples—one consisting of speech and breath, and another consisting of *ṛc* and *sāman*—and in that case, the singular designation "this is indeed that couple" (*tad vā etan mithunam*) would be untenable.
Therefore, the state of being a couple belongs only to speech and breath, which are the sources of *ṛc* and *sāman*.

This very couple is merged in this syllable *oṃ*. Indeed, when a couple comes together, they fulfill each other's desire. This couple, characterized in this way, is merged in this syllable *oṃ*. Thus, since the couple—distinguished by the quality of attaining all desires—is found merged in the *oṃ* syllable, it is established that the *oṃ* syllable possesses the quality of attaining all desires. Furthermore, the *oṃ* syllable consists of speech (*vāṅmaya*), is produced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and is merged with the couple.

Since it is well known that a couple is the fulfiller of desires, an illustration is given: just as in the world when a couple—that is, the male and female components of a pair—come together and unite through sexual intercourse, they then fulfill, that is, provide for each other's mutual desire; in the same way, the fact that the syllable *oṃ* possesses the quality of attaining all desires by means of the couple entered into its own self is established. He says this so that the Udgātṛ priest who worships it also comes to possess those qualities: He who knows thus becomes the fulfiller of the desires of his own people, both those born of his loins and those acquired through marriage. And he who hates him, and he whom he hates, fail to attain their desires. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.13.1–2) The meaning is that he who knows thus becomes the fulfiller of the desires of his own people, both those born of his loins (*aurasa*) and those acquired through marriage (*sāmnājya*). Furthermore, he who hates him and he whom he hates both fail to attain their desires. Thus, the Udgātṛ priest who knows this becomes the fulfiller of the desires of his own people, both those born of his loins and those acquired through marriage. And he who hates him, and he whom he hates, fail to attain their desires. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.13.1–2) Therefore, one should know this very syllable *oṃ*. One should meditate upon it as the highest, as the greatest, as the most plenteous, as the best, as the most excellent, as the most agreeable, as the most beautiful, as the most true, and as the most immortal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.1) One should know this very syllable *oṃ*. One should meditate upon it as the highest, as the greatest, as the most plenteous, as the best, as the most excellent, as the most agreeable, as the most beautiful, as the most true, and as the most immortal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.1) Now, the highest is heaven; the greatest is the sun; the most plenteous is food; the best is the mind; the most excellent is the breath; the most agreeable is love; the most beautiful is sight; the most true is speech; and the most immortal is the ear. These are the eight forms of Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.2) Now, the highest is heaven; the greatest is the sun; the most plenteous is food; the best is the mind; the most excellent is the breath; the most agreeable is love; the most beautiful is sight; the most true is speech; and the most immortal is the ear. These are the eight forms of Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.2) One who meditates upon these [eight] as the forms of Brahman becomes the highest, the greatest, the most plenteous, the best, the most excellent, the most agreeable, the most beautiful, the most true, and the most immortal among his own people. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.3) One who meditates upon these [eight] as the forms of Brahman becomes the highest, the greatest, the most plenteous, the best, the most excellent, the most agreeable, the most beautiful, the most true, and the most immortal among his own people. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.3) Furthermore, whatever he desires from these [eight], that he obtains. Therefore, one should meditate upon them as the forms of Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.4) Furthermore, whatever he desires from these [eight], that he obtains. Therefore, one should meditate upon them as the forms of Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.4) Now, one should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* as the threefold knowledge (*trayi vidyā*). The syllable *a* is the Ṛgveda; the syllable *u* is the Yajurveda; and the syllable *m* is the Sāmaveda. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.1) Now, one should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* as the threefold knowledge (*trayi vidyā*). The syllable *a* is the Ṛgveda; the syllable *u* is the Yajurveda; and the syllable *m* is the Sāmaveda. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.1) The sound that follows is the Atharvaveda and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa. What is uttered as *oṃ* is the threefold knowledge. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters the threefold knowledge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.2) The sound that follows is the Atharvaveda and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa. What is uttered as *oṃ* is the threefold knowledge. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters the threefold knowledge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.2) When the Adhvaryu priest gives the command with *oṃ*, when the Hotṛ priest recites, and when the Udgātṛ priest sings, he utters the threefold knowledge. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters the threefold knowledge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.3) When the Adhvaryu priest gives the command with *oṃ*, when the Hotṛ priest recites, and when the Udgātṛ priest sings, he utters the threefold knowledge. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters the threefold knowledge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.3) When one utters *oṃ* at the beginning, one utters the threefold knowledge. When one utters *oṃ* at the end, one utters the threefold knowledge. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters the threefold knowledge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.4) When one utters *oṃ* at the beginning, one utters the threefold knowledge. When one utters *oṃ* at the end, one utters the threefold knowledge. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters the threefold knowledge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.25.4) Now, one should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* as the three worlds. The syllable *a* is this world; the syllable *u* is the intermediate space; and the syllable *m* is that world. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.26.1) Now, one should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* as the three worlds. The syllable *a* is this world; the syllable *u* is the intermediate space; and the syllable *m* is that world. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.26.1) What is uttered as *oṃ* is these three worlds. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters these three worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.26.2) What is uttered as *oṃ* is these three worlds. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters these three worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.26.2) When the Adhvaryu priest gives the command with *oṃ*, when the Hotṛ priest recites, and when the Udgātṛ priest sings, he utters these three worlds. Therefore, when one utters *oṃ*, one utters these three worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.26.3) When the Adhvaryu priest gives the command with *oṃ*, when the Hotṛ priest recites, and when the Udgātṛ priest sings, he utters these
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable *akṣara* as the *udgītha*, indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires.

That is to say, he who meditates upon this syllable as the *udgītha* endowed with the quality of attainment (*āpti*) becomes the fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer; the meaning is that for him there is the aforementioned fruit, according to the Vedic text: "In whatever way one meditates upon it, that very thing one becomes."

This very syllable is indeed the syllable of assent; for whatever one assents to, one says "Om" to that. This assent is indeed prosperity; for he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha, becomes a fulfiller of desires.

And the syllable *oṃ* possesses the quality of prosperity. How so? This very subject under discussion is the "syllable of permission" (*anujñākṣara*); it is both permission (*anujñā*) and a syllable (*akṣara*). Permission means consent; the meaning is the syllable *oṃ*. How is it permission? The scripture itself says: whatever knowledge or wealth one grants permission for—whether a learned man or a wealthy man gives his consent therein—he says simply "oṃ. Likewise, in the Veda: "Thirty-three [deities]," "Oṃ," he said, and so forth.

And likewise in common worldly usage, when someone says, "I take this wealth of yours," one simply replies, "Om. Therefore, this very thing is indeed prosperity (*samṛddhi*); that which is consent (*anujñā*) is prosperity, because consent has its root in prosperity—for one who is prosperous gives consent by saying "Om. Thus, the meaning is that the syllable *Oṃ* possesses the quality of prosperity. Because he is a worshipper of the quality of prosperity, being endowed with that attribute, he becomes a fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer;
"he who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha," and so forth, as explained previously.

Therefore, this triple knowledge proceeds: one causes the announcement with "Om," one recites the praise with "Om," and one sings the Udgītha with "Om"; it is for the sake of honoring this very syllable, by its greatness and its essence. 9.

Now, he praises the Imperishable (akṣara) for the sake of its being an object of meditation and for the purpose of generating enthusiasm. How so? By means of that aforementioned Imperishable, this triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā)—meaning the ritual action prescribed by the triple knowledge, characterized by the Ṛgveda and the others—it is not as if the triple knowledge itself proceeds through the calls of *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth; rather, it is well known that the ritual action proceeds in such a manner. How? "Saying 'Om,' one makes the call; saying 'Om,' one recites; saying 'Om,' one sings the *udgītha*. From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that this refers to the Soma sacrifice.

And that ritual action is for the sake of honoring—that is, for the purpose of worshiping—this very Imperishable (akṣara); for it is a symbol (pratīka) of the Supreme Self, and the honoring of that [symbol] would indeed be the honoring of the Supreme Self itself, according to the Smṛti: "By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. Furthermore, it is by the majesty—the greatness—of this very Imperishable, meaning by the vital breaths of the officiating priests and the sacrificer; likewise, it is by the essence of this very Imperishable, meaning by the oblation produced from the essence of rice, barley, and so forth.

Sacrifices, oblations, and so forth are performed by means of the Imperishable (akṣara); that [Imperishable] rises as the sun; from that, through the sequence beginning with rain, vital breath (prāṇa) and food (anna) are produced; and by means of the vital breaths and food, the sacrifice is extended. Therefore it is said: "by the greatness and the essence of the Imperishable. In this regard, he raises an objection against the established position that one who possesses knowledge of the Imperishable must perform ritual action:

Therefore, both perform [the ritual]: he who knows it thus, and he who does not know it. But knowledge and ignorance are distinct; for what one performs with knowledge, faith, and the *upaniṣad* becomes more powerful. This indeed is the further explanation of this very syllable. Thus ends the first section. (10) — 1 — 10 —

By means of that syllable, both perform [the rite]: he who knows this syllable as it has been explained, and he who knows merely the ritual action but does not know the true nature of the syllable; both of them perform the action, and the fruit would arise from the power of the action alone—what then is the use of the knowledge of the true nature of the syllable? For it is observed in the world that when two people eat a *harītakī* fruit, the purgative effect occurs for both—the one who knows its taste and the other who does not—it is not so [in this case].

Because knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are indeed different—for knowledge and ignorance are distinct—the word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the previous position. It is not that the mere knowledge of the *oṃkāra* as a subsidiary part of ritual action is the same as the knowledge characterized by the qualities of being the "most savory," "attainment," and "prosperity"; rather, it is superior to that. Therefore, the intention is that because of this superiority of the means (*aṅga*), a superiority of the result is logical. For it is observed in the world that between a merchant and a forest-dweller (*śabara*) selling rubies and other gems, the merchant’s superiority of knowledge results in a superiority of profit.

Therefore, whatever action one performs while endowed with knowledge (*vidyā*) and realization (*vijñāna*), being possessed of faith (*śraddhā*) and full of conviction, and being joined with the *upaniṣad*—that is to say, with yoga—that very action becomes more powerful than the action of the ignorant, meaning it yields a superior fruit. By the statement that the action of the knower is more powerful, the intention is that even the action of the ignorant is indeed powerful.

Nor is there a lack of qualification for ritual action on the part of the ignorant, since the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) is seen to be performed by the ignorant as well in the section concerning Upastya. "The syllable is the most savory, the attainment, and the prosperity"—this is one meditation, because no other effort is observed in between; for indeed, this very syllable under discussion, known as the *udgītha*, is the subject of this detailed exposition (*upavyākhyāna*), since it is to be meditated upon in many ways through its various attributes.
Thus ends the commentary on the first section.

When the gods and the Asuras, both of whom were offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another, the gods then took up the Udgītha, thinking, "By this we shall overcome them. The "gods and Asuras" (*devāsurāḥ*) refers to the gods and the Asuras. The "gods" (*devāḥ*)—derived from the root *div*, meaning "to shine"—are the functions of the senses illuminated by the scriptures. The "Asuras" are the opposite of those; they are the natural functions of the senses consisting of darkness (*tamas*), so called because they delight (*ramanāt*) in their own vital breaths (*asu*) which are directed toward various sense-objects. The particles *ha vai* are indeclinables that indicate a past event.

In whatever cause—characterized by the mutual seizure of each other's domains—they contended; since the verb *yat* preceded by the prefix *sam* has the meaning of "battle," the sense is that they engaged in combat.

The natural functions of the senses, which consist of darkness (*tamas*) and are engaged in suppressing the scriptural light, are the *asuras*; likewise, their opposites—the gods (*devas*), whose nature is the light of discrimination regarding the subject matter of the scriptures—are engaged in suppressing the *asuras* who consist of natural darkness. Thus, like a battle characterized by mutual suppression and emergence, the battle between the gods and the *asuras* proceeds within every body of all living beings from time immemorial; this is the intended meaning.

This is recounted here by the Śruti in the form of a narrative for the purpose of discerning the arising of dharma and adharma, being intended as an injunction for the knowledge of the purification of the vital breaths (prāṇas). Therefore, both the gods and the asuras are "prājāpatyas," meaning offspring of Prajāpati—Prajāpati being the person (puruṣa) authorized for action and knowledge, according to another Śruti passage: "The Puruṣa alone is the Uktha; he indeed is the Great Prajāpati."

For his ritual and natural functions of the organs are opposed to one another like children, because they arise from the same source. Therefore, for that reason—characterized by excellence and deficiency—the gods took up (*ājahruḥ*), that is, brought forth, the *udgītha*, meaning the sacrificial act of the Udgātṛ priest indicated by the *udgītha* portion; the intention is that since it is impossible to bring forth that alone, they brought forth the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices.
For what purpose did they take them up? It is said: with the intention, "By means of this rite we shall overcome these Asuras. Thus they were minded.

And when they desired to take up that Udgītha rite, they then meditated upon the breath of the nose as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, one smells both the fragrant and the foul with it, for it has been pierced by evil. 2.

Those gods meditated upon the nasal breath—the conscious sense of smell located in the nose—as the Udgātṛ, the performer of the Udgītha, by means of the Udgītha-portion [of the Sāman]; that is to say, they meditated upon the syllable Om, known as the Udgītha, through the vision of the nasal breath. For in this way, there would be neither an abandonment of the subject under discussion nor an introduction of an irrelevant subject; for the syllable Om is indeed the subject introduced here by the words, "Of this very syllable... and so forth.

[Objection: You have stated that they brought back the ritual action characterized by the *udgītha*; how is it now that you say they meditated upon the syllable *oṃ*, called the *udgītha*, through the vision of the nasal breath (*nāsikya-prāṇa*)? [Response: This is not a fault. For within the very ritual of the *udgītha*, the syllable *oṃ*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*-chant—is intended as the object of meditation through the vision of its agent, the deity Breath (*prāṇa*), and not as something independent. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to say that they brought back the ritual for the sake of that [meditation].

When the Udgātṛ had been thus chosen by the gods, the Asuras—whose nature consists of ignorance—pierced that deity, the Prāṇa located in the nose, who is of the form of light, with their own evil, which consists of attachment to unrighteousness; that is to say, they contaminated him. For that Prāṇa in the nose had become one whose discriminative knowledge was overcome by attachment to the conceit of perceiving pleasant odors; through that defect, he became associated with evil.

This is what was stated: "The Asuras pierced it with evil. Because it was pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the vital breath (prāṇa), impelled by that evil, is the grasper of foul odors for living beings. Therefore, by means of that [evil], people smell both—the fragrant and the foul—for it is indeed pierced by evil. The mention of "both" is not intended to be restrictive, just as in the case of the statement, "Whose two oblations both meet with disaster";
this is because of the scriptural passage in the same context: "Whatever foul odor one smells here... [which refers only to the unpleasant].

Then, indeed, they meditated upon speech as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, one speaks both the true and the untrue by means of it, for it has been pierced by evil. Then, indeed, they meditated upon the mind as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, one forms both the formable and the unformable by means of it, for it has been pierced by evil.

(6) This inquiry was initiated by the Śruti for the purpose of experiencing the purity of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) so that it may become an object of meditation. Therefore, after examining the deities of the eye and the other senses in succession, they are set aside on the grounds that they have been pierced by the evil of Asura. The rest is the same—as in the passage beginning, "Then indeed, speech, the eye, the ear, the mind," and so forth. Other deities not explicitly mentioned, such as those of the skin, the tongue, and others, are also to be understood, based on another scriptural text which states: "In this very way, these deities were [pierced] by evils."

Then, indeed, they meditated upon that very vital breath which is principal (*mukhya*) as the *udgītha*. When the Asuras reached it, they were shattered, just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a solid stone.

Because they were pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the deities beginning with the vital breath were cast aside; immediately thereafter, they meditated upon that well-known vital breath which exists in the mouth (*mukhya*) as the *udgītha*. When the Asuras reached it—as before—they were shattered and destroyed merely by their intention, without having accomplished anything against the vital breath.

Regarding the question "How are they destroyed?", he provides an illustration here: just as in the world, an *ākhaṇa*—a stone that cannot be dug up even with spades and the like, nor can it be split with chisels—is called *akhana*; *ākhaṇa* is simply another term for *akhana*. Having struck such a stone (*ṛtvā*), by implication, a clod of earth or a lump of dust thrown at it with the intention of breaking the stone would, without doing anything at all to that stone, itself shatter and crumble away. Thus [it is].

The meaning is: "they shall shatter. Thus, Prāṇa is pure because it cannot be overcome by the Asuras. Just as [the stones] shatter after striking a stone that is a mere flake, even so he indeed shatters who desires evil against one who knows this, and he who seeks to harm him; for such a person is like a flake of stone. 8. (8) ————-

He states the result for one who knows thus and has become the self of the vital breath (prāṇa) with the words, "Just as a stone... This is the very illustration: in this very way he is shattered and destroyed. Who is he? He says: whoever desires—that is, wishes—to do evil, which is unworthy, toward one who knows thus, that is, toward one who knows the vital breath as described; and whoever also seeks to injure him—that is, harms the knower of the vital breath by employing abuse, beating, and so forth—he too is shattered in this very same way. Such is the meaning.

Because he is a knower of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and by virtue of being the vital breath itself, he is "unpierced by stones" (*aśmākhaṇa*)—meaning he is invincible. Now, one might object: the nasal breath is also of the nature of air, just like the principal breath; yet that nasal breath was pierced by evil—even while being the vital breath, it was not the principal one. How so? This is not a fault; for the nasal breath, though also of the nature of air, was pierced by evil by the Asuras due to a deficiency in its location and the organs of articulation.

But because that [primary sense] is impossible [in this context], and because the deity of the location is stronger, it is appropriately stated that [the nose] is not pierced—just as axes and other tools perform their specific functions when held by a skilled person, but not when in the hands of another; likewise, because it is associated with a defective sense, it is the deity of the nose that is pierced, not the primary one. "By this [breath], he does not perceive what is fragrant nor what is foul-smelling, for he is free from evil. Therefore, whatever he eats and whatever he drinks, by that he sustains the other vital breaths. Having finally reached this very one, he departs; thus, at the end, he simply opens his mouth. (9) (9) ————-The primary [breath] is not pierced because of the impossibility of that [piercing] and because the deity residing in its location is more powerful—it is fittingly said that it is not pierced. Just as tools such as axes perform a specific function when held by a person who has received training, but not when in the hands of another, so too, because it is associated with a defective nose, it is the deity of the nose that is pierced, not the primary one.
