Just

Because the principal [breath] was not pierced by the Asuras, therefore the world does not perceive either fragrance or foul odor through it; rather, one perceives both of those through the sense of smell alone. And because the effects of evil are not seen in it, it is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*); that is, evil has been struck away, destroyed, and removed from it—thus it is "free from evil," meaning it is pure. Furthermore, while the breaths such as the sense of smell are "self-supporting" (*ātmaṃbhari*) due to their attachment to pleasant things and the like, the principal breath is not self-supporting in that way.

What then? It has all things as its object. How so? It is said: by that which the world eats and drinks through that principal [breath], it protects—that is, sustains—the other vital breaths, such as smell and the rest; for by means of that, their maintenance occurs. Therefore, the breath is the sustainer of all; hence, it is pure.

But how is it understood that the subsistence of the others [the sense-organs] depends primarily on eating and drinking? It is said: having failed to obtain—that is, not finding—this very primary breath (mukhya-prāṇa), which is the function of the primary breath, namely food and drink, at the end—that is, at the time of death—the aggregate of the breaths such as the sense of smell and so forth departs. For one who is without breath is unable to eat or drink; thus, the departure of the collection of the sense of smell and the rest is well known.

For the desire to eat is observed in the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since one indeed "opens wide" (*vyādadāti*)—that is to say, one makes a gaping of the mouth; for that is the sign of the breath having departed when food is not obtained. Then Aṅgiras meditated upon the *udgītha*; they consider him alone to be Aṅgiras, because he is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*). 10.

"Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras indeed meditated upon that principal breath (mukhya prāṇa) as the Udgītha possessing such qualities; this is connected with what will be said later, "Baka Dālbhya. Similarly, some have made the connection that Baka meditated upon it as Bṛhaspati and as Āyāsya—on account of the statement: "They consider this very Prāṇa to be Aṅgirasa, Bṛhaspati, and Āyāsya. This is certainly so when the literal sense [of the names] is not possible.

However, it is possible that even in the case of the injunction of the sages (*ṛṣicodanā*), it may be according to what is heard—just as in another scriptural passage: "Therefore, they call him by the name 'the hundred-versed ones,' though he is this very one"; likewise, the scripture brings about the sages themselves, such as Mādhyma, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, and so forth, as Prāṇa. Similarly, for the sake of realizing non-difference, it makes even those sages who were practitioners of the meditation on Prāṇa—namely Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Āyāsya, and others—into Prāṇa itself, [stating]: "Prāṇa is indeed the father, Prāṇa is the mother."

And so on. Therefore, the seer named Aṅgirā, being the vital breath (prāṇa) itself, meditated upon himself as the vital breath, as Aṅgirā, as the Udgītha. Because he, being the vital breath of the limbs (aṅga), is their essence (rasa), he is called Aṅgirasa.
By that [name], Bṛhaspati meditated upon him as the Udgītha. They consider him indeed to be Bṛhaspati, for speech (vāk) is the Great One (bṛhatī), and he is its lord (pati).
By that [name], Ayāsya meditated upon him as the Udgītha. They consider him indeed to be Ayāsya, because he moves (ayate) from the mouth (āsya).
(11) Likewise, he is the lord of the Bṛhatī meter; therefore, he is Bṛhaspati.

(12) Likewise, because he goes forth (*ayate*) from this mouth, he is Āyāsya; the meaning is that the seer is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Similarly, another worshipper as well should meditate upon the self—the *udgītha*—as the vital breath endowed with qualities such as being the descendant of Aṅgiras.
By means of that [knowledge], Baka Dālbhya came to know it. He became the *udgātṛ* priest for the residents of Naimiṣa, and he used to sing forth all their desires for them. 13.

(13) Not only did Aṅgiras and the others perform worship [of this Prāṇa]; Baka by name, the son of Dalbha—known as Dālbhya—came to know that Prāṇa exactly as it had been shown; having known it, he became the Udgātṛ priest for those performing the sacrificial session at Naimiṣa. And by the power of his knowledge of Prāṇa, he used to sing forth desires for these people of Naimiṣa—that is to say, he indeed sang them forth. "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Imperishable as the Udgītha, becomes a singer of desires"—this refers to the meditation with respect to the body (ādhyātmam). (14)

Thus ends the second section. (14) Likewise, there is another result for the Udgātṛ priest: he indeed becomes a bringer of desires. For one who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable *akṣara* as the Udgītha characterized by the aforementioned qualities, this aforementioned visible fruit belongs to him; however, his invisible fruit is the state of becoming the Self of Breath (*prāṇātma-bhāva*). The intention is that this is already established by the conclusion of the scripture: "Having become a god, he goes to the gods."

"Thus with reference to the self"—this is the conclusion of what has been said regarding this meditation on the *udgītha* having the Self as its object; it serves to focus the mind for the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*) which is about to be described.

This concludes the commentary on the second section. Now, with reference to the deities: one should meditate upon that very sun which shines there as the *udgītha*. Rising indeed, he sings the *udgītha* for the sake of all creatures. Rising, he drives away darkness and fear. He who knows this becomes indeed a driver-away of fear and darkness. (1)

(1) — Now, immediately thereafter, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*), that is, concerning the divine realm, is introduced; this is because the *udgītha* is to be meditated upon in many ways. "That which is yonder sun that shines—one should meditate on it as the *udgītha*" means that one should meditate on the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the sun.

Regarding the term *udgītha*: since the word *udgītha* denotes a syllable, how can it apply to the sun? It is explained as follows: rising, indeed, this [sun] sings forth (*udgāyati*) for the sake of creatures—that is, for the purpose of producing food for creatures. For if he were not to rise, there would be no production of rice and other crops. Therefore, he "sings forth" as it were—just as a singer (*udgātṛ*) sings for the sake of food. Thus, the meaning is that the sun is the *udgītha*.

Furthermore, as it rises, the sun destroys the nocturnal darkness and the fear born from it for living beings. He who knows the Sun as possessing such qualities becomes, indeed, the destroyer—the dispeller—of fear characterized by birth and death, as well as of the darkness that is its cause, namely ignorance. Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the Sun appear as if distinct due to the difference in their locations, nevertheless, there is no difference in their essential reality (*tattva*). How so?

This breath here and that sun yonder are indeed the same. This is warm, and that is warm; this is called *svara* (sound), and that is called *svara*. They call this one *pratyāsvara* (echo), and that one *asvara*. Therefore, one should meditate upon this breath here and that sun yonder as the *udgītha*.

The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed equal and identical to the Sun (Savitṛ) in its qualities, and the Sun is identical to the vital breath; for this vital breath is warm, and that Sun is also warm. Furthermore, they call this vital breath "Svara" (the Sounder), and likewise they call that Sun "Svara" and "Pratyāsvara" (the Returner); because the vital breath merely sounds forth and, once dead, does not return, whereas the Sun, having set, returns again day after day, and is therefore called "Pratyāsvara."

In terms of both their qualities and their names, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the sun are identical to one another. Therefore, because there is no difference in their true nature, one should meditate upon this *prāṇa* and that sun as the *udgītha*. Now, indeed, one should meditate upon the *vyāna* itself as the *udgītha*: that which one breathes out is *prāṇa*, and that which one breathes in is *apāna*. Now, the junction of *prāṇa* and *apāna* is *vyāna*; and what is *vyāna* is speech (*vāk*). Therefore, even while not breathing out or breathing in, one utters speech. 3. (3) ————-

Now, indeed, worship of the *udgītha* is being stated by way of another method: one should worship the *vyāna*—which will be defined by its characteristics—as a particular function of the *prāṇa* itself, as the *udgītha*. Now its true nature is being determined: that which a person breathes out (*prāṇiti*), expelling air from the mouth and nose, is the specific function of the wind called *prāṇa*; that which one breathes in (*apāniti*), drawing air inward through those same [orifices], is the *apāna*, the function known as *apāna*.

To the question "What follows from that?", it is said: Now, that junction of the prāṇa and apāna—which have been described by their characteristics—namely, the specific mode of activity between them, is vyāna. This is not the same as the vyāna well-known in the Sāṃkhya and other systems of philosophy, because the Śruti provides a specific definition [of its nature]. Why, then, is the meditation on vyāna alone enjoined with great effort, setting aside prāṇa and apāna? Because it is the cause of powerful (vīryavat) action.

How is it that speech has its cause in the action of *vīrya* (vital energy)? He says: That which is *vyāna* is speech, because speech is the effect of *vyāna*. Since speech is brought about by *vyāna*, therefore, without breathing in (*aprāṇan*) or breathing out (*anapānan*), that is, without performing the functions of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the world utters—that is, pronounces—speech. Whatever is speech is *ṛc*; therefore, without breathing in or breathing out, one utters the *ṛc*. Whatever is *ṛc* is *sāman*; therefore, without breathing in or breathing out, one sings the *sāman*. Whatever is *sāman* is *udgītha*; therefore, without breathing in or breathing out, one chants the *udgītha*. 4. (4) ————-

The intention is this: one performs a specific verse of the *Ṛgveda*, the *Sāman* residing within that verse, and the *Udgītha* which is a constituent part of the *Sāman*, by means of the *vyāna* alone, without breathing out or breathing in.

Therefore, whatever other powerful actions there are—such as the churning of fire, the running in a race, or the drawing of a firm bow—one performs them without breathing out or breathing in; for this reason, one should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the *vyāna* itself. 5.

It is not only the utterance of speech and so forth; therefore, other powerful actions as well—those which are accomplished through a greater degree of effort, such as the churning of fire, running the course of a race, or the drawing of a firm bow—he performs while neither breathing out nor breathing in. Thus, vyāna is distinguished from the functions of prāṇa and the others. Meditation upon that which is distinguished is superior because it bears fruit, just like the worship of a king.

For this reason, for this cause, one should meditate upon the *vyāna* alone as the *udgītha*, and not on any other function. The fruit is that one's ritual action becomes more powerful. Now, indeed, one should meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*: "Ud-gī-tha. *Ut* is breath (*prāṇa*), for by means of breath one rises up; *gī* is speech (*vāc*), for they call speech *gī*; *tha* is food (*anna*), for in food all this is established. 6. (6) ————

Now, one should indeed meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*, lest they be taken merely as the syllables of the word "bhakti" (devotion). To this end, he specifies: "the *udgītha*"; that is to say, the syllables of the name *udgītha*. Even when meditating on the syllables of a name, it becomes meditation on the possessor of the name itself, just as in the case of [addressing someone] as "Amukamiśra. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is "ut. One should view the vital breath in the syllable "ut. How is the vital breath "ut"? He says: for by means of the vital breath everyone rises (*uttiṣṭhati*), since we observe the collapse of one who is without breath.

Therefore, there is a commonality between *ud* and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Speech is *gīḥ*, for the learned call speech "giraḥ. Likewise, food is *tham*, for everything here is established (*sthita*) in food; therefore, there is a commonality between food and the syllable *tha*.
These are the commonalities among the three as stated by the scripture; they should be understood to apply to the remaining [syllables] as well, according to their corresponding nature.

The *ud* is heaven, the *gī* is the intermediate space, and the *tha* is the earth; the *ud* is the sun, the *gī* is the wind, and the *tha* is fire; the *ud* is the Sāmaveda, the *gī* is the Yajurveda, and the *tha* is the Ṛgveda. Speech yields its milk for him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon these syllables of the *udgītha* as "ud-gī-tha"—the milk of speech, which is the milk of speech itself. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. 7. (7)

The sky alone is "ut" because of its high position; the intermediate space is "gīḥ" because it swallows (girana) the worlds; the earth is "tham" because it is the place where living beings stand. The sun alone is "ut" because of its upwardness; the wind is "gīḥ" because it swallows fire and the others; fire is "tham" because it is the locus of sacrificial rites. The Sāmaveda alone is "ut" because it is praised as heaven; the Yajurveda is "gīḥ" because the oblation offered with the *yajus* formulas is swallowed by the deities; the Ṛgveda is "tham" because the Sāmaveda is supported upon the Ṛgveda.

The fruit of the meditation on the syllables of the *udgītha* is now stated: it "milks" (*dugdhe*), that is, it yields for this practitioner. What is it that milks? Speech (*vāk*). What does it milk? The "milk" (*doha*). As to what that milk is, he says: "the milk of speech"—the intended meaning is the fruit accomplished by the words of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; that milk of speech, speech itself milks, that is, it milks its own self.

Furthermore, one becomes possessed of food (*annavān*), having abundant food, and an eater of food (*annāda*), with a kindled digestive fire (*dīptāgni*), who, being a knower, meditates thus upon these aforementioned syllables of the *udgītha* according to their described qualities, thinking, "This is the *udgītha*."
Now, one should worship with the thought, "May there be fulfillment of blessings, success, and approaches"; one should meditate upon that *sāman* with which one intends to chant the praise.

Now, therefore, "the fulfillment of blessings" (*āśīḥsamṛddhiḥ*)—that is, the fulfillment of one's desires as they may come to pass; this is the remainder of the sentence. "Approaches" (*upasaraṇāni*) means those things which are to be approached, to be resorted to, or meditated upon. How so? One should worship thus: one should worship in this manner. For example, whichever specific *sāman* with which the Udgātṛ priest intends to praise—that is, will perform the hymn—he should approach that *sāman*, resort to it, and contemplate it through its origin and other characteristics.

In whichever ṛc [he intends to recite], he should run toward that ṛc; toward whichever seer it belongs to, he should run toward that seer; and toward whichever deity he is about to praise, he should run toward that deity. 9.

One should meditate upon that *ṛc* in which the *sāman* is based, by means of its deity and other attributes; one should meditate upon that *ṛṣi* from whom the *sāman* was derived; one should meditate upon that deity whom one intends to praise;
one should meditate upon that *chandas* (meter) with which one will praise; and one should meditate upon that *stoma* (hymn-form) with which one is about to praise. 10. (10)

One should meditate upon that *chandas* (meter), such as the *gāyatrī*, by which one intends to praise; one should meditate upon that *stoma* (hymn-form) with which one is about to praise—using the middle voice (*stoṣyamāṇa*) because the fruit of the constituent parts of the *stoma* accrues to the agent—and one should meditate upon that direction toward which one intends to praise. 11.
In whichever direction one intends to praise, one should run toward that direction with the presiding deities and so forth.

Having finally approached the Self, one should praise while meditating on the desired object, being vigilant; for that desire which one praises with will surely be fulfilled for him quickly—whatever desire one may have when praising, whatever desire one may have when praising. 12. Thus ends the third section. 3.

(12) — The Udgātṛ priest should praise himself—his own form through his lineage, name, and so forth—the Sāmans and others in due order, and finally himself at the end; he should praise while meditating on his desire, remaining vigilant and not making any error regarding the vowels, sibilants, consonants, and other elements of the chant. Then, it is near—at hand—indeed, that for one who knows thus, that desire shall be fulfilled, shall reach completion. What is that? It is "whatever desire" (*yatkāmaḥ*) he may have; being possessed of that desire, he should praise.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the commentary on the third section.
"Om"—this syllable is the Udgītha; one should meditate upon it as such, for with "Om" one sings the Udgītha. Here follows its detailed exposition.

The repetition of the syllable *om* and so forth, which was introduced at the beginning, is for the purpose of ensuring that the subject matter does not shift elsewhere by being interrupted by other meditations on the syllables of the *udgītha*. This is the commencement [of the section] intended to enjoin meditation on the very same syllable previously mentioned, as characterized by the qualities of immortality and fearlessness. The passage beginning with "Om" has already been explained.

"The gods, indeed, fearing death, entered the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). They covered themselves with the meters (*chandas*). Because they covered themselves with these, that is the 'metrical' nature (*chandastva*) of the meters. (2) (2) —-

It is said what the gods did when they were afraid of death, the destroyer: they entered the threefold knowledge—that is, the ritual action prescribed by the three Vedas; the meaning is that they commenced Vedic rites, considering them to be protection from death. Furthermore, performing recitations, oblations, and so forth with the *chandasaḥ*—the mantras not employed in [specific] rituals—they concealed themselves within other actions; that is, they covered themselves.

Because they covered [themselves] with these mantras, therefore, from the act of covering (*chādana*) by means of the meters (*chandas*), the nature of being meters for the mantras is well-established.

Death then watched them there, just as one might watch a fish in water, [watching] in the *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*. Having discovered this, they ascended above the *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus* and entered into the very *Svara* (the tone). 3.

There, Mṛtyu beheld those gods devoted to ritual action, just as in this world a fisherman might see a fish in water that is not very deep, considering it capable of being caught by means of a hook and a net. Thus he looked upon them; the meaning is that Mṛtyu regarded the gods as beings who could be overcome through the means of exhausting their ritual actions. Where did he see these gods? It is said: "In the Ṛg, the Sāman, and the Yajus"—that is, in the rituals associated with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

Those gods, having been purified by Vedic ritual and being of pure soul, came to know what Death intended to do; and having known it, they turned away—meaning they rose up from their works, that is, from the rituals connected with the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus.

Because of that action, being hopeless regarding the removal of the fear of death, they abandoned that [world] and entered—indeed, they had already entered—the imperishable *svara*, which is designated by the word *svara* and possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness; that is, they became devoted to the meditation on the syllable *Oṃ*. The word "eva" (indeed) has the sense of restriction and serves to exclude other possibilities, meaning that they became solely devoted to its meditation. But how can the imperishable (*akṣara*) be denoted by the word *svara*? It is said in reply:

Whenever one encounters a *ṛc*, one utters "Om" as a transcendental accent (*atisvara*); likewise for the *sāman* and likewise for the *yajus*. This very syllable is that accent. What is it? It is this syllable, which is immortal and fearless. Having entered into that, the gods became immortal and fearless. Whenever one encounters a *ṛc*, one utters "Om" as a transcendental accent; likewise for the *sāman* and likewise for the *yajus*. This indeed is the accent. What is it? It is this syllable, which is immortal and fearless. Having entered into that—just as they were by nature—the gods became immortal and fearless.
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. This sun, verily, is the Udgītha; this is the Praṇava, for he goes along sounding "Om.

Now, that which is the *udgītha* for the Bahvṛcas is the *praṇava*, and that which is their *praṇava* is indeed the very same thing designated by the word *udgītha* in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. "Yonder sun is the *udgītha*; he is the *praṇava*"; even that which is designated by the word *praṇava* for the Bahvṛcas is that very same one, and no other. How is the sun the *udgītha*? The syllable called *udgītha* is this "Om. For he (the sun), while sounding (*svaran*)—since roots have multiple meanings—or else while moving (*gacchan*) while sounding (*svaran*), goes (*eti*).
Therefore, yonder Savitṛ is the *udgītha*.

"It was to this very one that I directed my speech; therefore, you are my only son," thus said Kauṣītaki to his son. "Worship the rays [of the sun]; many sons indeed shall be yours. This is with respect to the deities. 2. (2)

"I have indeed approached this very one," that is, I have meditated upon it by making no distinction between the rays and the sun—this is the meaning. "Therefore, you are my only son"—thus did Kauṣītaki, the descendant of Kuṣītaka, say to his son. For this reason, "you should turn them around, you should turn them around," that is, you should differentiate the rays and the sun through your yoga.
In this way, many indeed will be your sons; thus [ends] the section concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*).
Now, with reference to the self: one should meditate upon that which is this principal vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*, for it moves along sounding "Om.

Next, the internal [meditation] is described. One should meditate upon that which is this very principal *prāṇa* as the *udgītha*, and so forth, as before. Likewise, "for this *prāṇa* also goes sounding 'Om'; the meaning is that it proceeds for the sake of the functioning of speech and the other organs, as if granting permission by saying "Om. For indeed, those standing near a person about to die at the time of death do not hear the *prāṇa* uttering the syllable "Om. On account of this similarity, the utterance of "Om" in the case of the sun should also be understood as a mere granting of permission.

"I meditated upon this very one; therefore, you are my only son," so said Kauṣītaki to his son. "Meditate upon the Prāṇas as abundance; then indeed many sons will be born to me. (4) The passage beginning with "I meditated upon this very one" is to be understood as before. Therefore, perceiving the Udgītha—consisting of speech and the other organs as well as the principal Prāṇa—as distinguished by the quality of multiplicity, one should meditate upon it as abundance (*bhūman*) with the mind; the meaning is that one should repeat it as before. The intention is: "In this way, many sons will indeed be born to me."

Since the view that identifies the *prāṇa* and the sun as the *udgītha* has been set aside due to the defect of yielding the fruit of having only one son, this section enjoins the practice of viewing the rays and the vital breaths as distinct, for the sake of obtaining the fruit of having many sons.

"Now, indeed, that which is the *udgītha* is the *praṇava*; that which is the *praṇava* is the *udgītha*. Even from the Hotṛ’s seat, he rectifies what was poorly sung; he rectifies it. Thus ends the fifth section. (5) ———— 5 ————

Now, regarding that which was stated as "the Udgītha," etc., concerning the vision of the identity between the *praṇava* and the Udgītha, its fruit is being declared: from the *hotṛṣadana*. The *hotṛṣadana* is that place where the *hotṛ* priest, being stationed, recites; the meaning is "from the ritual act of the *hotṛ* when it is correctly performed. For a result cannot be brought forth merely from a location. What is that [result]? Indeed, even if the *udgīta*—that is, the singing (*udgāna*) performed by the *udgātṛ*—is badly sung (*durudgīta*), meaning it has been executed defectively, causing a flaw in his own ritual duty; [even so, he obtains this fruit].
"He brings them together" means he connects them—just as medical treatment restores the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) when they have become unbalanced.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth section.

This very earth is the *ṛc*, fire is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. This [earth] is *sā*, and fire is *ama*; that makes *sāma*. 1.

(1) This very earth is the *ṛc*; one should form the vision of the earth within the *ṛc*. Likewise, fire is the *sāman*; one should form the vision of fire within the *sāman*. How is it that the earth and fire possess the nature of *ṛc* and *sāman*? It is said: this *sāman*, called fire, is "rested upon" (*adhyūḍha*)—meaning it is situated above and supported by—this *ṛc* which is the earth; it is like the *sāman* resting upon the *ṛc*. For this very reason, even now, the *sāman* is sung by the chanters of the *Sāmaveda* as being rested upon the *ṛc*.

And just as the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are not absolutely different from one another, so too are these two, earth and fire. How so? This very earth is that which is denoted by the word "half" (*sāman*) of the name *Sāman*; the other half, denoted by the word "ama," is fire (*agni*). Thus, this pair of earth and fire, having attained the state of being designated by the single term *Sāman*, is the *Sāman*. Therefore, the pair of earth and fire is not different from one another, being eternally joined like the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*. And for this reason, the meaning is that earth and fire possess the nature of the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*.
Some say that this very [Ṛk] is "Sā" and Agni is "Ama," for the purpose of enjoining the visualization of Earth and Fire upon the Ṛk and the Sāman respectively.

The intermediate space itself is the Ṛk and Vāyu is the Sāman; thus, this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛk. Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛk. The intermediate space itself is "Sā" and Vāyu is "Ama"—that is the Sāman.
The intermediate space itself is the *ṛc*, and the wind is the *sāman*, and so forth as before.

The sky itself is the *ṛc*, and the sun is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The sky is the *sā* and the sun is the *ama*; that is the *sāman*. 3.
(3) — [No commentary provided for this verse.]

The stars are the *ṛc* and the moon is the *sāman*. This very *sāman* rests upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as resting upon the *ṛc*. The stars are indeed the *sā*, and the moon is the *ama*; that is the *sāman*. (4) — The moon is the lord of the stars; therefore, it is the *sāman*.

Now, that which is the white light of the sun is the *Ṛg*, and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is the *Sāman*. This *Sāman* is supported upon this *Ṛg*; therefore, the *Sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *Ṛg*.

(5) Now, that which is the white light—the white radiance—of the sun is the *Ṛg*. And that which is the blue, the exceedingly black—that is, the extreme darkness—within the sun is the *Sāman*. For it is seen by one whose vision is perfectly concentrated.

Now, that which is the white light of the sun is indeed this [Ṛgveda]; and that which is the blue, the ultra-black, is the Yajurveda; and that is the Sāmaveda. And as for this golden person who is seen within the sun, with a golden beard and golden hair, golden even to the very tips of his nails—entirely of gold—he is that.

These two are indeed the two splendors: the white and the black. And that [white] is the *Ṛc*, and this [black] is the *Sāman*. Now, that which is within the sun—within the interior, in the middle of the sun—is golden; it is "golden" because it is as if made of gold. For it is not possible for the Divine to be a modification of actual gold, since that would be incompatible with its being the essence of the *Ṛc* and *Sāman*, and with its being free from evil. Indeed, there can be no possibility of evil or the like reaching a material object made of gold, such that it would need to be denied; furthermore, it is not perceived by the eye.

Therefore, the word *hiraṇmaya* is indeed an elided simile, meaning "consisting of light" (*jyotirmaya*). The same application [of this interpretation] holds for the subsequent [epithets] as well. He is called *puruṣa* because he dwells in the city (*puri śayanāt*) or because he fills (*pūrayati*) the world with his own self. He is seen by those whose eyes have turned away [from sense objects], whose minds are concentrated, and who depend on such means as celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Since even those possessing brilliance may have black beards, hair, and so forth, he specifies: "golden-bearded, golden-haired"; the meaning is that his beard and hair consist of nothing but light.

"Down to the very tips of the nails"—that is, including the nails and the tips of the nails, he is entirely like gold; the meaning is that his form is pure light. "His eyes are like a lotus flower that is as bright as a monkey's buttocks. His name is "Ut" (the Risen); for he has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils. 7. (7) ————-The final answer is: Down to the very tips of the nails—that is, including the nails and the tips of the nails, he is entirely like gold; the meaning is that his form is pure light. "His eyes are like a lotus flower that is as bright as a monkey's buttocks. His name is "Ut" (the Risen); for he has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils. 7. (7) ————-

Even though he is thus golden-colored in every respect, there is a distinction regarding his eyes. How so? His "kapyāsa" (monkey-dung) refers to the seat (*āsa*) of a monkey (*kapi*); the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the instrument for the action of sitting (*āsi*). It is the part on the back of a monkey where it sits. A lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) like a "kapyāsa" is exceedingly brilliant; such are the eyes of the Lord. Because this is a comparison using a comparison, it is not a "low comparison. This name, "Udita," belongs to him who is distinguished by such qualities and is used figuratively.

How is this figurative? This very deity has "risen" (*uditaḥ*)—that is, gone out (*ut-itaḥ*), emerged—from all evils (*sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ*), meaning from evil and its effects; as he will later state: "The Self which is free from evil," and so forth. Therefore, his name is "Ud" (the Risen). He who knows that one endowed with such qualities, named Ud, in the manner described, likewise rises—that is, goes out—from all evils. The two particles *ha* and *vai* are used for emphasis; the meaning is: he certainly rises.

The *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are his two joints (*geṣṇau*). Therefore he is the *Udgītha*, and for that very reason the *Udgātṛ* priest [is so called], for he is its singer. He rules over those worlds which are beyond that [sun] and over the desires of the gods. This is with respect to the divine realm (*adhidaivata*). Thus ends the sixth section. Intending to explain how this deity possesses the nature of the *Udgītha*, just as the sun and others do, [the text] says: "The *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are his two joints. The joints are the parts characterized as earth and so forth, as previously described. For the deity is the Self of all; because he is the ruler of the worlds both higher and lower and of their desires, it is appropriate that he has the earth, fire, and so forth as his *Ṛk* and *Sāman* joints, since he is the source of all.

Since he is thus named *Unnāman* and has the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* for his song (*geṣṇa*), therefore, although the state of having the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* for his song is already established, the status of being the *Udgītha* is stated by means of a cryptic term (*parokṣeṇa*), because the God is fond of the cryptic; hence he is called the *Udgītha*. And for that very reason, he is the *Udgātṛ*, because he sings forth (*udaṃ gāyati*) this [prāṇa] of the aforementioned name *Unnāman*; thus, the well-known designation of the *Udgātṛ* as "Udgātṛ" is logically justified.

This very deity is Unnāma (the High-named). He rules over those worlds which are beyond that Āditya, the worlds that go upward from the upward-moving [sun]. It is not merely that he is the ruler; because of the word "and" (*ca*), he also sustains them, as stated in the Vedic mantra: "He upheld the earth and this heaven," and so forth. Furthermore, he rules over the desires of the gods. Thus has been described the nature of the divine Udgītha with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*). This concludes the commentary on the sixth section.

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): speech itself is the *ṛc*, and breath is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. Speech itself is *sā*, and breath is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. (1) Now, what follows is explained with respect to the self: speech alone is the *ṛc*, and breath is the *sāman*, because of the commonality of their respective positions—lower and upper. "Breath" here refers to the sense of smell together with the vital air (*vāyu*). "Speech itself is *sā*, breath is *ama*" and so forth, as explained previously.

The eye indeed is the *ṛc*, and the self is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is superposed upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being superposed upon the *ṛc*. The eye indeed is the *sā*, and the self is the *aman*; thus it is *sāman*.
(2) — The eye indeed is the *ṛc*, and the self is the *sāman*. By "self" is meant the shadow-self (*chāyātman*), for the *sāman* resides within it.

The ear is indeed the *ṛc* and the mind is the *sāman*; thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The ear is indeed the *sā*, the mind is the *ama*; that is the *sāman*.
(3) — The ear is indeed the *ṛc* and the mind is the *sāman*; because the ear is the presiding principle, the mind possesses the nature of the *sāman*.

Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *ṛc*; that which is the blue-black beyond it is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*, and thus the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. Furthermore, that which is the white light of the eye is indeed the *sāman*; and that which is the blue-black beyond it is the *ṛc*. Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *ṛc*; and that which is the blue-black beyond it—like the sun, the locus of the power of sight—is the *sāman*.

Now, this person who is seen within the eye—he is indeed the Ṛg, he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha, he is the Yajus, he is the Brahman. Whatever is the form of that [celestial sun], that is the form of this one; whatever are the two songs (geṣṇau) of that, those are the two songs of this one; whatever is the name of that, that is the name of this one. 5.

(5) Now, as before, that person who is seen within the eye—he is indeed the *ṛc*, both as speech and so forth with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), and as the earth and so forth with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*); and the well-known *ṛc* consists of syllables bound into quarters. Likewise is the *sāman*; because of its association with the *uktha*, the *sāman* is the chant, while the *ṛc* is the recitation (*śastra*) other than the *uktha*. Similarly, the *yajus*—everything consisting of "svāhā," "svadhā," "vaṣaṭ," and so forth—is speech, and that is he. For we have already stated that this is so because he is the self of all and the source of all.

Because of the context of the *Ṛg* and other Vedas, "that" refers to Brahman; thus, "the *ṛc*s" means the Vedas. The form of this very person of the eye is extended [to the solar person] by way of analogy. What is that? It is that which was described with respect to the deity—the solar person—as "golden" and so forth; as for his two joints (*geṣṇau*), those same two are the joints of this person of the eye as well; and what is his name—"Ut" and "Udgītha"—that indeed is his name.

If it is argued that there is a difference between the solar deity and the ocular deity because of the difference in location, the transfer of qualities, names, and the designation of different spheres of sovereignty, we say no; for it is impossible for a single entity to attain the nature of both "by means of that" and "by means of this. If it is argued that this is possible through a twofold manifestation—since the scripture will later state, "He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold," and so on—we say no; for a single conscious being cannot undergo such division because it is partless. Therefore, there is indeed identity between the internal (ādhyātmika) and the celestial (ādhidaivika) aspects.

As for what you said regarding the transfer of form (*rūpa*) and so forth as a cause for differentiation—that was not for the sake of understanding a difference [in essence]; rather, it was for the purpose of ensuring that no suspicion of difference arises from the difference in location.
"He is the lord of those worlds which are below this one, and of the desires of men. Therefore, when these people sing on the lute, they sing of him; hence they are winners of wealth.

This very person who is in the eye rules over those worlds that are internal to this self and are situated below it, as well as over the desires connected with human beings. Therefore, when singers sing on the lute, they sing of him alone. Because they sing of the Lord, they are "winners of wealth"—that is to say, they are possessed of wealth.
Now, he who, knowing it thus, sings the Sāman, sings of both; by means of that [upper sun], he obtains those worlds which are beyond it and the desires of the gods.

(7) Now, he who, knowing this thus—knowing the deity Udgītha as described—sings the Sāman, sings both the one belonging to the eye and the one belonging to the sun. The fruit for such a knower is stated: by means of that very sun, he attains those worlds which are beyond it, having become the deity residing within the sun; and he attains the desires of the gods. Furthermore, by means of this [earthly] one, he attains those worlds which are below it and the desires of men. Therefore, an Udgātṛ priest who knows this should say: ... 8 ...

(8–9) — Now, by means of this very visual [power], he attains those worlds which are on this side of it, as well as the desires of human beings—meaning, having become visual. Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows thus should say to the sacrificer: "What desired object (*kāma*) of yours shall I obtain for you by singing? For this reason, because this Udgātṛ is able—that is, capable—of accomplishing a desire through the singing of the *udgītha*, he is so called. Who is he? He who, knowing thus, sings the *sāman*. The repetition is intended to mark the conclusion of the meditation (*upāsana*). Thus ends the commentary on the seventh section.

"What desire shall I obtain for you by singing? [he asks]. For he alone is capable of obtaining desires through his song who, knowing this, sings the Sāman—he sings the Sāman. Thus ends the seventh section.

Furthermore, by means of this very eye, he attains those worlds which are on this side of it, as well as the desires of men—meaning, having become the eye. Therefore, an Udgātṛ priest who knows this should say to the sacrificer: "What desired object (*kāma*) of yours shall I obtain for you by singing? For this reason, this Udgātṛ is able—that is, capable—of accomplishing a desire through his singing of the *udgītha*. Who is he? He who, knowing thus, sings the *sāman*. The repetition [of the concluding statement] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the meditation. Thus ends the commentary on the seventh section of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*.

There were three who were skilled in the Udgītha: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali. They said, "We are indeed skilled in the Udgītha; come, let us have a discussion on the Udgītha. 1.

Because the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be meditated upon in many ways, the text introduces another meditation with the fruit of the quality of being "higher than the high" (parovarīyas) by means of a different method. The historical narrative (itihāsa), however, is for the purpose of easy comprehension. "Three" means numbering three; "ha" indicates a traditional report; they were "skilled" (kuśalāḥ)—that is, proficient—regarding the Udgītha, meaning with respect to the knowledge of the Udgītha. The intention is that they were so when they had gathered together at a certain place, time, or occasion. For it is not the case that only three people in the entire world possess proficiency in the knowledge of the Udgītha and so forth.

Indeed, Uṣasti, Jānaśruti, Kaikeya, and others are heard of as being almost omniscient. Who are these three? He says: Śilaka by name, Śālāvatya (the descendant of Śalāvat); Caikitāyana (the descendant of Cikitāyana), Dālbhya (of the Dalbha lineage) or one belonging to two lineages; and Pravāhaṇa by name, Jaivali (the descendant of Jīvala)—these are the three. They said to one another: "We are indeed renowned as being skilled and proficient in the Udgītha."

Therefore, "come now, if you have permission, let us engage in a discussion—a formal debate—concerning the Udgītha, by means of presenting arguments and counter-arguments based on knowledge of the Udgītha. This is the meaning. And thus, in a dialogue with those who possess that knowledge, there occurs the destruction of erroneous graspings, the arising of new understanding, and the removal of doubt; for this reason, association with those possessing such knowledge must be undertaken—this is the purpose of the narrative (itihāsa), as is seen in the case of Śilaka and others.
"So be it," they replied, and sat down together. Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said, "Let the two venerable ones speak first; I shall listen to the words of two Brāhmaṇas as they speak.

Saying "So be it," they sat down together. There, because of his boldness, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to the other two: "May you two venerable ones speak first. From the context, it is clear that this one is the king; [he says], "I shall listen to the speech of you two Brāhmaṇas. Others say "speech devoid of meaning," because of the specific qualification "speech. Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "Come now, let me ask you a question. "Ask," he replied. 3. (3)
When these two had spoken, Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "Come now, if you will permit me, I shall ask you a question. Being thus addressed, the other said, "Ask.

"What is the goal of the Sāman? he asked. "Voice," he replied. "What is the goal of voice? "Breath," he replied. "What is the goal of breath? "Food," he replied. "What is the goal of food? "Water," he replied. (4)

Having obtained permission, he said: "What is the goal (*gati*) of the *sāman*?"—since the *udgītha* is the subject under discussion; for it is the *udgītha* that is introduced here as the object of meditation, and the text will later state, "the higher-and-higher *udgītha*. "Goal" means the support (*āśraya*), which is to say, the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*). Thus questioned, Dālbhya replied: "The tone (*svara*)," because the *sāman* consists of tone. It is logical that whatever constitutes the nature of something is its goal and its support, just as a jar and the like have clay as their support.

"What is the goal of sound? "Breath," he said; for sound is produced by breath, therefore breath is the goal of sound. "What is the goal of breath? "Food," he said; for breath is supported by food, according to the Vedic text, "Indeed, breath withers without food," and also, "Food is the bond. "What is the goal of food? "Water," he said, because food originates from water.

"What is the goal of the waters? "That world," he said. "What is the goal of that world? "One should not lead it beyond the heavenly world," he said. "We establish the *sāman* upon the heavenly world, for the *sāman* is a hymn of praise to heaven.

"What is the goal of the waters? "That world," he said, "for from that world rain originates. When asked, "What is the goal of that world? Dālbhya said: "No one should lead the *sāman* beyond that heavenly world to any other support," so he said. Therefore, we too establish the *sāman* in the heavenly world; the meaning is that we know the *sāman* to have its foundation in the heavenly world.
The *svargasaṃstāva* is that Sāman whose praise consists in praising [it] as heaven; for there is a Vedic text stating, "Heaven indeed is the world, and the Sāman is the Veda.

Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "O Dālbhya, your Sāman is indeed without a foundation. If someone were to say of you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would surely fall off. 6. (6)

The other, Śilaka Śālāvatya, said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "O Dālbhya, that Sāman of yours is indeed unestablished and unstable"—the meaning is that its course is not completed because it lacks the quality of being progressively higher (parovarīyas); the word *vai* serves to remind one of the traditional scripture (*āgama*), and *kila* indicates what is commonly reported. That is your Sāman.

But if someone who is unable to endure this and is ignorant of the *sāman* were now at this time to say, with a perverted understanding, "The *sāman* is unestablished, yet it is established"—then the head of that offender for speaking thus shall fall off, it will clearly fall away. When one has been told this, the head of that offender will indeed fall off in that very manner; there is no doubt. However, the intention is not that I myself am saying this.

[Objection: "If he has committed an offense deserving of decapitation, then his head must fall even if no one else speaks [the curse]; and if he is not guilty, it does not fall even if someone does speak it. Otherwise, there would be the arrival of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*). [Reply: This is not a fault, because the attainment of the fruit of a performed action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—depends upon place, time, and causal conditions (*nimitta*). That being so, even ignorance, which is the cause for the falling of the head, depends upon the condition of another person's speech.

"Come, let me know this from the Blessed One," [Nārada said]. "Know it," he replied. "What is the goal of that world? "This world," he replied. "And what is the goal of this world? "One should not lead it beyond its foundation," he replied. "We establish the Sāman upon this world as its foundation, for the Sāman is a praise of the foundation. 7. (7)

Thus addressed, Dālbhya said: "Indeed, I would like to know this from the venerable sir—the foundation of the Sāman. Being thus addressed, Śālāvatya replied: "Know it," he said. When asked by Dālbhya, "What is the goal of that world? Śālāvatya said: "This world. For this world nourishes that world through sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth; for the scriptures state, "From this [world], the gods subsist upon what is offered."

For it is directly perceived by all beings that the earth is the foundation; therefore, it is logical that this world is also the foundation of the *sāman*. When asked, "What is the goal of this world? Śālāvatya replied: "No one can lead the *sāman* beyond this world, which is its foundation. Therefore, we establish the *sāman* upon this world as its foundation; for it is praised as a foundation, meaning that the *sāman* is extolled as being the foundation itself.
And there is the Vedic scripture: "This [earth] is indeed the *Rathantara*."

To him, having spoken thus, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said: "O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite. If someone were to say this to you now, your head would surely fall off. "Your head would fall off," [he added]. "Well then, let me learn this from your reverence. "Learn it," the other replied. Thus ends the eighth section. [The text continues: To him who had spoken thus, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said: "O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite," and so on, as before. Thereupon Śālāvatya said: "Well then, let me learn this from your reverence. "Learn it," the other replied.

Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section. "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said. "Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone; they return into space at the end. Space is indeed greater than these; space is their ultimate resort. "This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high, which is infinite. For one who, knowing it thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as the higher than the high, there comes what is higher than the high, and he conquers worlds that are higher than the high."

Atidhanvan Śaunaka, having taught this to Udaraśāṇḍilya, said: "As many as their offspring shall know this Udgītha, for so long will there be a superior life for them in this world, and likewise in the other world. He who, knowing it thus, meditates upon it—for him there will indeed be a superior life in this world, and likewise in the other world; "in the world, in the world," they say.
Thus ends the ninth section. 9.
When the Kurus had been devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrayaṇa lived as a beggar with his wife Āṭikī in Ibhyagrāma.

In connection with the meditation on the *udgītha*, the meditations concerning the *prastāva* and the *pratīhāra* must also be explained; therefore, this [section] is commenced. The narrative, however, is for the sake of easy understanding. When the Kurus—the crops of the Kuru country—had been struck down, that is, destroyed by *maṭacīs*, which are thunderbolts (*aśani*), a famine arose. Then, together with his wife Āṭikī—who was so called because she had not yet developed the secondary sexual characteristics of a woman such as breasts—there was one named Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa, the son of Cakra.

An *ibhya* is one who is worthy of an elephant (*ibha*, i.e., a *hastin*), meaning a wealthy man or an elephant-driver. His village was an *ibhyagrāma*. There, having become a wanderer due to the lack of food—[the root] *drā* meaning "to go with contempt"—having gone a contemptible way, that is, having reached the final stage [of starvation], he lived, having taken shelter in someone's house.
He begged from an *ibhya* who was eating *kulmāṣa* beans. That man said to him: "There are no others than these which are placed here before me. 2. (2)

While wandering for the sake of food, he happened to find a wealthy man eating—that is, consuming—some *kulmāṣas*, which are inferior beans, and he begged from him. The wealthy man said to Uṣasti: "There are no other *kulmāṣas* besides these that are being eaten by me from this heap of leavings; as for these which have been placed—that is, thrown—into my vessel here, what can I do? Being thus addressed, Uṣasti replied:

"Give these to me," he said. The merchant gave them to him, Uṣasti. Taking some water nearby for a drink, he said, "Come, take this after-drink. Being thus addressed, he replied, "If I were to drink this, it would indeed be the leavings of my food that I have drunk. To him who had spoken thus, the other replied: (Note: *Eteṣām* means "of these"; *me* means "to me"; *dehi* means "give"—thus he spoke. *Tān* refers to those [fruits]; *asmai* refers to that Uṣasti; *pradadau* means "he gave. Having taken water standing near for drinking, he said: "Come, take this after-drink (*anupānam*). Being thus addressed, he replied: "If I were to drink it, this water would indeed (*vai*) become the leavings (*ucchiṣṭam*) of my [food] that has been drunk (*pītam*). To him who had spoken thus, the other replied.)
"Are these not also leftovers? "I would not have lived without eating them," he said, "for desire is my well. 4.

When asked, "Are these even these *kulmāṣa* beans not [already] leavings?", Uṣasti replied: "Indeed, I would not have lived, nor shall I live, without eating—without consuming—these *kulmāṣa* beans. The meaning is that he obtains the drinking of water according to his desire (*kāma*). Therefore, the intention is this: even for one who has reached such a state, who possesses knowledge, virtue, and fame, and who is capable of helping himself and others, there is no touch of sin (*aghasparśa*) even while performing such an act.

Even for him, if there were other means for his livelihood that were not loathsome, this loathsome act would lead to fault; the intention is that for one who performs it out of pride in his knowledge, a fall into hell is certain, as is understood from the mention of the word "starving.
He, having eaten, brought the remainder to his wife; even before she had finished, she became well-fed. Having accepted them, she set them aside.

Having eaten them, he gave out of compassion what remained—the leftovers—to his wife. She, Āṭikī, had already been well-fed (*subhikṣā*), meaning she had obtained a fine alms-meal even before these *kulmāṣas* were received. Nevertheless, out of the natural disposition of women, she did not disregard those *kulmāṣas*; taking them from her husband's hand, she set them aside. Then, as he was rising in the morning, he said: "If we could only obtain some food! We might obtain a measure of wealth. This king is going to perform a sacrifice; he might choose me for all the priestly offices (*ārtvijya*). (6)

Knowing her deed, as he was rising at dawn at the time of daybreak, leaving his bed or sleep, he spoke while his wife listened: "Alas! If we could obtain even a small portion of food, having eaten that food, we would be able to go and obtain a measure of wealth—a small amount of money—and from that our livelihood would be secured. And he stated the reason for obtaining that wealth: "That king is going to perform a sacrifice not far from here."

Because he was the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used; and that king, having found me worthy as a recipient, chose me for all the priestly functions—that is, for the performance of the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
His wife said to him, "Come, husband, here are these very *kulmāṣa* beans. Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice which had been spread out.

When he had spoken thus, Jāyā said: "Come now, my lord, take these very *kulmāṣa* beans which were placed in my hand by you. Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice which was being spread out and performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
There, he sat down near the Udgātṛ priests as they were about to chant the hymns. He then spoke to the Prastotṛ priest:

Having gone there, he approached the Udgātṛ priests and their assistants. An *āstāva* is that place where they sing praises; in that *āstāva*, he sat down near those who were about to chant—the meaning is that he sat close to them. Having sat down, he said to the Prastotṛ:
"O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Prastāva, your head will fall off.

Having addressed him as "O Prastotṛ" in order to draw his attention, [the Lord says]: "If you, being ignorant of that deity who has followed and is inherent in the *prastāva*—that portion of the chant—should chant the *prastāva*, then your head shall shatter even in my presence—that is, even though I am not visible to you. Otherwise, there would be no qualification for ritual action at all for those who know only the mechanics of the rite; and that is undesirable, because we observe that even the ignorant perform rituals, and because of the scriptural teaching regarding the path of the ancestors (*dakṣiṇa-mārga*).

Furthermore, for those who are ignorant and lack qualification [for knowledge], only the northern path would be heard of as the way; nor is the southern path caused solely by Smārta rituals, because of such scriptural texts as, "By sacrifice, by charity," and so forth. Moreover, due to the specific qualification, "Thus spoken by me," the lack of qualification for ritual action applies only in the presence of the Knower (the Guru), not universally to the Agnihotra, Smārta rituals, study, and the like.

Since permission is seen granted in various places, it is established that even those who know only the ritual action have qualification for that action—[as in the case of the threat], "Your head shall fall off."

In the same way, he said to the Udgātṛ: "O Udgātṛ, if you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will shatter. (10) In the same way, he said to the Pratihartṛ: "O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will shatter. They, being thus humbled, remained silent. (11) Thus ends the tenth section. 10.

(11) — In the same way, he spoke to the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ; the rest is the same as before. Having desisted—that is, having ceased—from their ritual duties, those beginning with the Prastotṛ remained silent out of fear of the falling of their heads, doing nothing else because of their [shared] desire for life.
Thus ends the commentary on the tenth section.
Then the sacrificer said to him:
"I indeed desire to know the venerable one. Uṣasti replied, "I am Cākrāyaṇa"—that is, he spoke thus, provided that my name has reached the path of your ears.
He said: "Indeed, I sought you, O Blessed One, for all these priestly duties; yet, through lack of success in finding you, O Blessed One, I have chosen these others.

The sacrificer replied: "It is true that I heard of you, O Blessed One, as one possessed of many virtues. I indeed sought you out and made every effort to find you for all the priestly functions; but having failed to find you, O Blessed One, I have chosen these others."

"Let the Blessed One indeed accept all my offerings free from blemish," [the sacrificer said]. "So be it," [the Blessed One replied]. "In that case, let these very [offerings] be fully granted for him who praises; however, you should give me as much wealth as you would give to them. "So be it," the sacrificer said. (3) — 3 —

"Let the Blessed One himself be mine for all the priestly offices (*ārtvijya*) for the sake of the ritual duties," he said. Uṣasti replied, "So be it. However, he added: "In that case, let these very priests whom you previously chose, now being fully authorized and permitted by me, perform the praises. But this must be done by you: whatever wealth you give to all of them—the Prastotṛ and the others—you should give that much to me as well.
Having been told this, the sacrificer said, "So be it."

Then the Prastotṛ approached him and said, "O venerable sir, you previously told me, 'If you, O Prastotṛ, chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Prastāva, your head will fall off. Which is that deity?

Now, having heard these words from Auṣastya, the Prastotṛ approached him; he came before Uṣasti with humility. [He asked: "O venerable sir, which is that deity who, as you previously told me, is inherent in the Prastāva division?"

"It is *prāṇa*," he said. "Indeed, all these beings enter into *prāṇa* alone and emerge from *prāṇa* alone. This deity is connected with the *prastāva*. If you had chanted the *prastāva* without knowing it, your head would have fallen off, as I told you.

When asked, he said, "It is *prāṇa*. "Is *prāṇa* the deity of the *prastāva*? "How so? At the time of dissolution, all beings, both stationary and moving, enter into *prāṇa* alone; at the time of origination, they emerge from *prāṇa* alone—that is, they rise up having *prāṇa* as their very self. Therefore, this deity is connected with the *prastāva*.

If you, being ignorant, had chanted that—had performed the chanting, the *prastāva* division—then your head would have fallen off, it would have fallen away, as I had said to you at that time: "Your head shall fall. Therefore, you have done well; the intention is that you have properly desisted from the action when forbidden by me.

Then he approached the Udgātṛ and said: "O Udgātṛ, if you chant the Udgītha without knowing that deity which is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will fall off—this is what the venerable one told me. Which is that deity?
(6) Thus the Udgātṛ asked: "Which is that deity who follows and is inherent in the Udgītha division?"

"Āditya," he said. "Indeed, all these beings sing to Āditya as he is high above. This deity is connected with the Udgītha. If you had sung the Udgītha without knowing it, your head would have fallen off, just as was said by me. Being thus questioned, he replied, "Āditya. Indeed, all these beings sing to—meaning they call out to or praise—Āditya as he is high above, that is, upward; this is because of the commonality of the word *uccha* (high/above), just as Prāṇa was [connected to the Udgītha] because of the commonality of the word *pra*. Therefore, "this deity" and so forth is to be understood as before.

Then the Pratihartṛ approached him and said, "O Venerable One, you said to me, 'If you perform the Pratihāra without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will shatter. Which is that deity? "It is exactly so," [the teacher replied]. Then the Pratihartṛ approached him again, saying, "Which is that deity inherent in the Pratihāra?"

When asked, he said, "Food. Indeed, all these beings live by bringing food toward themselves from every side as their very self. This deity, because of the commonality of the word *prati* (back/again), follows the *pratihāra* (response) division of the Sāman. The rest is the same; thus it has been explained that one should meditate upon the divisions of *prastāva*, *udgītha*, and *pratihāra* with the vision of Prāṇa, Āditya, and Food respectively. This is the collective meaning: the attainment of Prāṇa and the others, or the success of the ritual act, is the fruit. Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh section.
Now, therefore, follows the Udgītha of the dogs. Once, Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—went out to recite his private Vedic study.

In the preceding section, a state of hardship caused by the lack of food was described, characterized by eating leftovers, leavings, and stale food. Lest that state should occur, this next section concerning the attainment of food is now introduced. Therefore, the *udgītha*—the chanting of the *sāman* perceived by dogs (*śauva*)—is here set forth. In that regard, there was one named Baka Dālbhya (the son of Dalbha), or Glāva Maitreya (the son of Mitrā); the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and," for he was a *dvaimātura* (born of two lineages).

Because conceptual constructions (vikalpa) regarding the actual object are untenable, just as they are in the case of ritual actions; for [statements such as] "having two names" or "belonging to two lineages" are merely traditional recollections (smṛti). Furthermore, the sharing of the physical body by both is observed. Or, because his mind was fixed on the *udgītha*, he may have shown disregard for the seer (*ṛṣi*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of "for the purpose of Vedic study" (*svādhyāyārtha*). He went out from the village—that is, he departed—to a secluded place near water in order to perform his Vedic study. From the singular number in the words "he went out" (*udvavrāja*) and "he waited" (*pratipālayāṃcakāra*), it is indicated that this seer was alone.
Because the sage was waiting for the time of the *udgītha*, it is understood that he was performing his private recitation (*svādhyāya*) out of a desire for food; this is the intended meaning.
To him, a white dog appeared. Other dogs approached it and said, "Venerable sir, please bring us food, for we are hungry.

A deity or a seer, gratified by his private recitation (*svādhyāya*), assumed the form of a dog—a white dog—and appeared before that seer for the sake of bestowing grace upon him. Other small dogs approached that white dog and said: "May the Blessed One sing forth food for us; that is to say, may he produce it through singing."

Or rather, it is entirely reasonable to understand that the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), speech, and the others—the eaters of food who are satisfied by his own study—favor him by taking on his very form. "We are indeed hungry; we are indeed famished," they said. He replied to them, "Come to me right here in the morning. Then Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, as some say—waited there for the morning. 3. When this had been said, the white dog spoke to those young dogs: "Come to me right here, in this very place, every morning at daybreak. The lengthening of the vowel [in *samīyāta*] is a Vedic archaism, or it may be a scribal error for *samīyāta*. There, indeed, the seer Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—waited, meaning he remained there in expectation.
Just as those who are about to chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* [laud] here move forward while holding onto one another, so did they move forward; having sat down together, they uttered the sound "hiṃ. 4.

Those dogs, having come right there into the presence of the sage, just as the Udgātṛ priests here, when about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna hymn, move about closely joined and clinging to one another, so did they crawl along, seizing each other's tails with their mouths; that is to say, they moved about in circles. Having thus crawled together and sat down, once seated, they made the sound "hiṃ"; that is, they uttered the syllable *hiṃ*.
"Oṃ āma oṃ, let us eat oṃ; let us drink oṃ. May the god Varuṇa, Prajāpati, and Savitṛ bring food here, oṃ. O Lord of Food, bring food here, bring it here, oṃ. Thus ends the twelfth section.

"Oṃ! Let us eat, oṃ! Let us drink, oṃ! He is the *deva* because of his shining; *Varuṇa* because of his enveloping the world; *Prajāpati* because of his protecting creatures; and he is called *Savitṛ*, the Āditya, because of his impelling everything. By these synonyms, may that very Āditya, being such as he is, bring food to us here—may he bring it! Having thus uttered "hiṃ," they spoke again: "O Lord of Food (*annapati*)! For he is the lord because of his being the impeller of all food."

For not even a minute particle of food arises for living beings without its being cooked; therefore, he is the Lord of Food (*annapati*). "O Lord of Food, bring food to us here, bring it!"—the repetition is for the sake of emphasis. *Om*. Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section. This world indeed is the syllable *hāu*; the wind is the syllable *hāi*; the moon is the syllable *atha*; the Self is the syllable *iha*; and fire is the syllable *ī*. 1.

(1) This very world is indeed the *hāu*-syllable, the *stobha* well-known in the *rathaṃtara* Sāman. Because of this common connection based on the statement "This [earth] is indeed the *rathaṃtara*," one should meditate upon this *hāu*-syllable as the world. Vāyu is the *hāi*-syllable; the *hāi*-syllable is well-known in the *vāmadevya* Sāman. And because the origin of the *vāmadevya* Sāman is the connection between Vāyu and the waters, one should meditate upon the *hāi*-syllable through the vision of Vāyu due to this commonality. The Moon is the *atha*-syllable.

One should meditate upon the syllable *tha* through the vision of the Moon; for this world is established in food, and the Moon has food as its essence, and because of the commonality of the form of the letter *tha*. The syllable *iha* is the Self (*ātman*); *iha* is a ritual exclamation (*stobha*), for the Self is perceived directly and is designated by the word "here" (*iha*), and since *iha* is an exclamation, there is a similarity between them. The syllable *ī* is Agni; and all Sāmans have their finale (*nidhana*) in *ī*, thus there is a similarity between them.

Āditya is the syllable *ū*; the invocation (*nihava*) is the syllable *e*; the Viśvedevas are the syllable *auhoi*; Prajāpati is the syllable *hiṃ*; breath is the tone (*svara*); food is the syllable *yā*; and Speech is the Virāj. 2. (2) ————-

The Sun is the syllable *ū*; for they sing of the Sun as being high and above, and this stobha is the syllable *ū*; since it is a stobha within a Sāman dedicated to the deity Aditya, the Sun is the syllable *ū*. "Nihava" means calling out; the syllable *e* is the stobha, because they call out with the words "Come here" (*ehi*), and there is a similarity between them. The Viśvedevas are the syllable *auho-ī*; for a stobha is seen in the Sāman dedicated to the Viśvedevas. Prajāpati is the *hiṃkāra*, because of its indefinability and because the *hiṃkāra* is indistinct. Breath is the *svara*; "svara" refers to the stobha.

And because of the commonality of being the cause of the tone (*svara*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The *stobha* "yā yā" is food (*anna*), for it is said, "by means of food this [body] moves"; therefore, due to that commonality. The *stobha* "vāk" is either the *virāj*—which is a specific form of food—or a particular deity, since the *stobha* is seen in the *vairāja* Sāman.
The thirteenth *stobha*, which is undefined (*anirukta*), is the moving (*sañcara*) syllable *huṃ*.

It is "undefined" (*anirukta*) because, due to its unmanifest nature, it cannot be defined as "this" or "that"; therefore, it is "the transition" (*saṃcara*), meaning its essential form is being conceptualized. If one asks what this is, he says: it is the thirteenth *stobha*, the syllable *huṃ*. For this is indeed unmanifest; thus, the intention is that it should be meditated upon precisely in its undefined particularity. He states the fruit of meditating on the syllables of the *stobha*:

Speech milks its yield for him who knows this secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Sāmans—its yield being speech—as he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. "He who knows this secret doctrine, he who knows the secret doctrine. Thus ends the thirteenth section. Thus ends the first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

"Speech yields for him its milk," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained. He who knows this Upaniṣad—the vision concerning the *stobha*-syllables that are parts of the Sāmans, characterized as previously described—attains this aforementioned fruit; such is the meaning. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of marking the end of the chapter and the conclusion of the specific meditations concerning the components of the Sāman. The word "iti" [marks the end]. Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth section.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, Śrī Govinda Bhagavat...
The first chapter of the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the worshipful teacher,
is completed.
Aṃ. Now, the meditation upon the entire Sāman is indeed good. For what is good, they call "Sāma," and what is not good, they call "Asāman. 1.

Introduction: By the passage beginning with "Om is this syllable," meditation (*upāsana*) concerning the constituent parts of the Sāman has been taught as having manifold fruits. Immediately thereafter, meditation concerning the *stobha* syllables was mentioned—in every respect, that too was connected only to a single part of the Sāman. Now, the Scripture begins by intending to teach meditations concerning the Sāman as a whole, i.e., meditations whose object is the entire Sāman. For it is logical that after the meditations on the parts, the meditation concerning the whole should be stated. (1)

The meaning is: "of the whole," that is, of that which is distinguished by all its parts, consisting of five divisions (*pañcabhaktika*) and seven divisions (*sāptabhaktika*). The particle *khalu* serves as an ornament for the sentence. "The meditation on the Sāman is good" (*sādhu*). Because this passage is intent upon enjoining the perception of "goodness" (*sādhu-dṛṣṭi*) in the Sāman as a whole, the word "good" (*sādhu*) does not have the purpose of censuring the previous meditations. [Objection: But is it not the case that "goodness," which was not previously mentioned, is now being predicated of the Sāman as a whole? [Reply: No, because of the concluding summary: "He meditates on the Sāman as good" (*sādhu sāmety upāste*). The word "good" (*sādhu*) signifies "beautiful" or "excellent."

"How is this understood? He says: "That which is indeed well-known in the world as good, beautiful, and blameless, the experts call *sāman*. That which is not good, being the opposite, they call *asāman*. Regarding this, they also say: "He approached him with *sāman*" means "He approached him with what is good"; and "He approached him with *asāman*" means "He approached him with what is not good. (2) (2)

Regarding that very matter of distinguishing between the wholesome and the unwholesome, they also say: "He approached this king or vassal with *sāman* (conciliation). Who is he? The intention is: he is the one who might be suspected of falling into unwholesomeness. When people do not observe any unwholesome action such as imprisonment, they say in that case, according to their own worldly understanding, "He approached him with a good intention" (*sādhunā*). But where, on the contrary, they do observe an unwholesome action such as imprisonment, there they say, "He approached him without conciliation" (*asāmnā*), meaning "He approached him with what is unwholesome" (*asādhunā*).

Then they also say, "It is *sāman* for us, indeed! when something is good; they mean to say, "It is truly good. And they say, "It is not *sāman* for us, indeed! when something is not good; they mean to say, "It is truly not good. 3. (3)

Then others also say, "Sāman is our own self-awareness (svasaṃvedya)," expressing compassion by saying, "Alas! It has become so for us. This is what they mean: when something is good, they say, "Alas, it is good! When the opposite occurs, they say, "Alas, it is not sāman for us! That is to say, when something is bad, they say, "Alas, it is not good! Therefore, it is established that the words *sāman* and *sādhu* have the same meaning.
He who, knowing it thus, venerates the Sāman as "the good" (*sādhu*), will surely have good qualities come to him and incline toward him. Thus ends the first section.

Therefore, whoever meditates thus—"Sāman is good"—meaning he meditates on the Sāman as possessing the qualities of the good, knowing the entire Sāman to be endowed with the qualities of the good, for him this is the fruit: "abhyāśo ha" means quickly indeed; the word "yat" is used for the purpose of qualifying the action. It means that "good" (sādhu) things—virtues not opposed to the Śruti and Smṛti—will "ā ca gaccheyuḥ," i.e., they will come toward him; and not only will they come, but they will also "upa ca nameyuḥ," i.e., they will bow down to him; the meaning is that they will present themselves to him as objects of enjoyment. Thus ends the commentary on the first section.

One should meditate upon the *sāman* as fivefold in the worlds: the earth is the *hiṅkāra*, fire is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, the sun is the *pratihāra*, and the sky is the *nidhana*; thus it is with respect to the upward [directions]. 1.

What, then, are those things which, distinguished by the vision of the Good (*sādhudṛṣṭi*), are to be collectively worshipped as a whole? These are stated to be "the fivefold in the worlds" and so forth. Now, an objection might be raised: is it not contradictory that these are to be worshipped both through the vision of the worlds (*lokadṛṣṭi*) and through the vision of the Good? No, for the referent denoted by the word "Good"—whether it be *dharma* or *brahman*—is inherent in the effects such as the worlds, just as clay is inherent in its modifications such as jars. The referent expressed by the word "Good," whether it be merit (*dharma*) or Brahman, is in every way pervasive throughout the effects beginning with the worlds.

Therefore, just as the perception of a jar or similar object is invariably accompanied by the perception of clay or its like, so too the perception of the worlds and so forth is invariably accompanied by the perception of the *sādhu* (the virtuous/meritorious)—because the worlds and so forth are effects of *dharma*. Although the causality of Brahman and *dharma* is indistinguishable, it is nevertheless logical that *dharma* alone is denoted by the word *sādhu*, because the term *sādhu* is employed in reference to *dharma* in the statement: "One who performs good deeds becomes *sādhu*."

[Objection: But surely, since the cause is present within effects such as the worlds, that perception [of the cause] is already established by implication; therefore, it should not be said, "He venerates it as 'Sādhū sāma'. [Reply: No, because that perception is to be understood through scripture; for in all cases, only those attributes (dharmas) which are obtained from scripture are to be meditated upon, and not even existing attributes that are not scripturally sanctioned.

One should properly meditate upon the Sāman in its fivefold form—divided into five parts according to fivefold devotion—within the worlds, beginning with the earth. How so? "The earth is the *hiṅkāra*. Regarding the locative case used for "in the worlds," one should transpose it to the nominative and meditate by identifying the *hiṅkāra* with the earth, thinking, "The earth is the *hiṅkāra*. Alternatively, having transposed the locative sense from the worlds to the *hiṅkāra* and other parts, one should meditate by applying the perception of the earth and so forth to the *hiṅkāra* and so forth. In that regard, the earth is the *hiṅkāra*, because of their commonality as being first.

Fire is the *prastāva*. For in fire sacrificial rites are commenced (*prastūyante*); and the *prastāva* is a division of the Sāman. The intermediate space is the *udgītha*. For the intermediate space is the sky; and the *udgītha* is characterized by the syllable *ga*.
