The sun is the *pratihāra*, because it faces every living being [with the thought], "May he come toward me, may he come toward me. The heaven is the *nidhana*. For those who have gone from here are deposited (*nidhīyante*) in heaven. Thus, from the perspective of the worlds, there is the meditation on the Sāman regarding those things that are upward and moving upward. Now, regarding those that are downward: the heaven is the *hiṅkāra*, the sun is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, fire is the *pratihāra*, and the earth is the *nidhana*. 2. (2) ————

Now, when [the breaths] have returned and are facing downward, the fivefold meditation on the *Sāman* is taught. For the worlds are characterized by coming and going; since the meditation on the *Sāman* is prescribed according to their nature, it is therefore taught with respect to the returning worlds. The *Hikāra* is heaven, because of its priority. The *Prastāva* is the sun, for when the sun has risen, the activities of living beings are set forth (*prastūyante*). The *Udgītha* is the intermediate space, as before. The *Pratihāra* is fire, because fire is brought back (*pratiharaṇa*) by living beings. The *Nidhana* is the earth, because those who have come from there find their resting place (*nidhana*) here.

The worlds, both ascending and descending, become available to him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds. This is the second section. [The fruit of the meditation: The worlds, both ascending and descending—meaning those characterized by going and returning—become available (*kalpante*), that is, they become capable and established as objects of enjoyment for him. The construction "who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as the whole, the Good, in the worlds" applies everywhere, both in the fivefold and the sevenfold [meditations].
Thus ends the commentary on the second section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain: the preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*; the cloud arises, that is the *prastāva*; it rains, that is the *udgītha*; it flashes, that is the *pratīhāra*. 1. (1) —

One should meditate upon the fivefold *sāman* in rain. Its immediate succession [to the meditation on space] follows because rain is the cause for the stability of the worlds. The preceding wind is the *hiṃkāra*, because rain begins with the preceding wind, just as the *sāman* begins with the *hiṃkāra* and ends with the *nidhana*; therefore, the preceding wind is the *hiṃkāra* due to its being first. The cloud is born, that is the *prastāva*; it is well known that when clouds arise in the rainy season, it is the prelude (*prastāva*) to the rain; it rains, that is the *udgītha*, because of its excellence; it lightens and thunders, that is the *pratihāra*, because of its being taken back (*pratihṛta*); it stops raining, that is the *nidhana*, because of the commonality of completion.

He grasps its conclusion; it rains for him, and he causes it to rain—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain. 2. Thus ends the third section. (2) —The fruit of the meditation: it rains for him at his will; likewise, he causes it to rain even when there is no rain. "He who knows this," and so forth, is as explained previously.
Thus ends the commentary on the third section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters: that which is the gathering of clouds is the *hiṅkāra*; that which rains is the *prastāva*; those [rivers] which flow eastward are the *udgītha*; those which flow westward are the *pratihāra*; and the ocean is the *nidhana*. 1. (1)

One should meditate upon the fivefold *sāman* in all waters. Because all waters are preceded by rain, there is a sequence of proximity. When the cloud gathers—that is, when it becomes condensed through mutual union—and when it rises up, it is said that it "gathers" (*saṃplavate*); at that time, the commencement of the waters is the *hiṃkāra*. When it rains, that is the *prastāva*; the waters have begun to spread out in every direction. Those waters which flow eastward are the *udgītha*, because of their preeminence. Those which flow westward are the *pratihāra*, due to the commonality of the prefix *prati*. The ocean is the *nidhana*, because the waters find their final resting place (*nidhana*) therein.
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters, does not perish in water; indeed, he becomes possessed of water. Thus ends the fourth section.
(2) — He does not perish in water, provided he does not desire [to die there]; he becomes possessed of water as his reward.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons: spring is the *hiṅkāra*, summer is the *prastāva*, the rainy season is the *udgītha*, autumn is the *pratihāra*, and winter is the *nidhana*. 1.

(1) One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. Its immediate succession [to the meditation on the waters] follows because the establishment of the seasons has the aforementioned water as its cause. Spring is the *hiṃkāra*, because it comes first; summer is the *prastāva*, for the gathering of barley and other crops is introduced for the sake of the rainy season; the rainy season is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence; autumn is the *pratihāra*, because of the recovery (*pratiharaṇa*) of the sick and the dead; winter is the *nidhana*, because living beings find their resting place (*nidhana*) in the windless state.
The seasons become favorable for him; he becomes possessed of the seasons—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. (2) Thus ends the fifth section.

(2) — Regarding the fruit: the seasons become favorable for this meditator in accordance with the seasonal order as objects of enjoyment. The meaning is that he becomes "possessed of the seasons," endowed with the enjoyments pertaining to the seasons.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals: the goat is the *hiṅkāra*, the sheep is the *prastāva*, the cows are the *udgītha*, the horses are the *pratihāra*, and the human being is the *nidhana*.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals. Since the seasons proceed correctly, time is favorable for animals; thus there is an immediate connection [between the seasons and the Sāman]. The goat is the *hiṃkāra*, because of its preeminence or its primacy—according to the Vedic text: "The goat is the first of animals"; the sheep are the *prastāva*, because of the observed association between goats and sheep; cows are the *udgītha*, because of their excellence; horses are the *pratihāra*, because they carry back men; and man is the *nidhana*, because animals depend upon man.
"Animals indeed belong to him; he becomes possessed of animals—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in animals. [End of] the sixth section.
(2)—The fruit: "Animals indeed belong to him; he becomes possessed of animals"—the meaning is that he is endowed with the fruits of cattle, such as enjoyment, renunciation, and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman that is progressively higher within the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). For the vital breath is the *hiṅkāra*, speech is the *prastāva*, the eye is the *udgītha*, the ear is the *pratihāra*, and the mind is the *nidhana*. These are indeed progressively higher.

One should meditate upon the fivefold *sāman* as being progressively more excellent (*parovarīyaḥ*) with respect to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The meaning is that one should meditate on the *sāman* as characterized by the view of the vital breaths, each subsequent one possessing the quality of being more excellent than the preceding. For the *hiṃkāra* is the vital breath, because it is the first among those that are progressively more excellent. Speech is the *prastāva*, for everything is introduced (*prastūyate*) by speech; speech is more excellent than the vital breath—for speech can express even what has not been reached [by the senses], whereas the vital breath is the perceiver only of a fragrance already reached.

The eye is the *udgītha*; since the eye reveals a much wider range of objects than speech, the *udgītha* is superior to speech because of its excellence. The ear is the *pratihāra*, because it receives [sounds]; it is superior to the eye because one hears from all directions. The mind (*manas*) is the *nidhana*, for all objects brought in by the various senses are deposited within the mind as the objects of a person's experience. Furthermore, the mind is superior to the ear because it pervades the objects of all the senses; even objects beyond the reach of the senses remain within the domain of the mind.

For the reasons stated above, these—the vital breaths and so forth—are indeed "higher and higher" (*parovarīyāṃsi*). For one who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as the "higher and higher" within the vital breaths, there becomes something higher and higher; he conquers worlds that are higher and higher. Thus ends the fifth [section] of the pentad. This is the seventh section.

He who meditates upon the *sāman* as distinguished by this view—that it is "higher than the high" (*parovarīyaḥ*)—for him his life becomes higher than the high; thus the meaning has been stated. This concludes the meditation on the fivefold *sāman*, intended to fix the mind upon the subject about to be described regarding the sevenfold *sāman*. For one who is indifferent to the fivefold form seeks to fix the mind upon what is about to be taught. Thus ends the commentary on the seventh section. Now, one should meditate upon the sevenfold *sāman* in speech: whatever in speech is "hum," that is the *hiṅkāra*; whatever is "pra," that is the *prastāva*; whatever is "ā," that is the *ādi*. (1)

(1) — Immediately following this, the meditation upon the sevenfold Sāman in its entirety is now properly commenced. The locative case in "in speech" (*vāci*) is as before; the meaning is that one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman as characterized by the vision of speech. Whatever specific sound of speech there is, namely the syllable *hum*, that is the *hiṅkāra*, because of the commonality of the letter *h*. That form of sound which is *pra* is the *prastāva*, because of the commonality of the prefix *pra*. That which is *ā* is the *ādi* (beginning), because of the commonality of the letter *ā*. The *ādi* is the syllable *oṃ*, because it is the beginning of all.
That which is "ut" is the *udgītha*; that which is "prati" is the *pratihāra*; that which is "upa" is the *upadrava*; and that which is "ni" is the *nidhana*.

(2) That which is "ut" is the *udgītha*, because the *udgītha* is preceded by the prefix "ut"; that which is "prati" is the *pratihāra*, because of the commonality of the prefix "prati"; that which is "upa" is the *upadrava*, because the *upadrava* begins with the prefix "upa"; and that which is "ni" is the *nidhana*, because of the commonality of the prefix "ni."

To him who knows this thus and meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech, speech milks its yield—the yield of speech—and he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. This is the eighth section.
(3) —The meaning of "To him [speech] milks... and so forth has already been explained.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section.

Now, indeed, one should meditate upon this Sun as the sevenfold Sāman: "He is always the same (sama) with respect to me"—therefore he is the Sāman; "he is the same with respect to everyone"—therefore he is the Sāman.

In the first chapter, the meditation on the Sun as the *sāman* was taught with respect to the *sāman* as a whole. Now, however, one should meditate upon that very Sun as the sevenfold *sāman*, having superimposed it upon the *sāman* in its entirety by means of the division of its parts. But how can the Sun possess the nature of a *sāman*? It is said: just as there is a reason for its being the *udgītha*, there is a reason for its being the *sāman*. What is that? It is that it is always equal (*sama*), because it is devoid of increase or decrease; for that reason, the Sun is the *sāman*.

It produces the thought "toward me, toward me," which is equal [in all cases]; therefore, it is equal to all (*sarveṇa samaḥ*). Thus, it is *sāman*, meaning because of its equality (*samatvāt*). Since the status of being the *hiṃkāra* and so forth is understood from the very mention of the commonality with the *udgītha* division, as well as the commonalities mentioned regarding the worlds and so on, the reason for its being the *hiṃkāra* and so forth was not stated. However, since the reason for the Sun's being *sāman* has not been stated, and that reason is not easily understood, "equality" (*samatvam*) has been mentioned.

One should know that all these beings are dependent upon it. That which is before sunrise is its *hiṅkāra*; upon this the domestic animals are dependent; therefore they utter the sound *hiṃ*, for they partake in the *hiṅkāra* of this Sāman. 2. (2) ————-The provided text contains no Sanskrit. It is already in English. Therefore, there is nothing to translate. Here is the original text returned as is: "One should know that all these beings are dependent upon it. That which is before sunrise is its *hiṅkāra*; upon this the domestic animals are dependent; therefore they utter the sound *hiṃ*, for they partake in the *hiṅkāra* of this Sāman. 2. (2) ————-I hope it is correct.I hope it is correct.

One should know that all these beings about to be mentioned are dependent upon—that is, follow along with—that Āditya as his means of subsistence, part by part. How so? That form of Āditya which exists before sunrise is the *hiṃkāra* chant-portion (*bhakti*); in this regard, there is a correspondence: whatever constitutes his *hiṃkāra* portion, cattle—such as cows and the like—are dependent upon that Sāman of Āditya; the meaning is that they follow it and subsist upon its form as a chant-portion.

Since this is so, therefore those beasts perform the *hiṃ* before sunrise. Therefore, they are indeed partakers of the *hiṃ* of this Sāman called Āditya; for it is because their nature is to partake in its divisions that they behave in this way.

Now, that which occurs when [the sun] has just risen is the *prastāva*; human beings are dependent upon that part of it. Therefore, they are lovers of performance and lovers of praise, for they are partakers of the *prastāva* of this Sāman.

Now, that form of the Sun which appears at its first rising is the *Prastāva* of this Sāman called Āditya; human beings are dependent upon it, as before. Therefore, they desire praise (*prastuti*), for they partake in the *Prastāva* of this Sāman.

Now, that [form] which exists at the time of the cows' gathering is the *Ādi*; birds are dependent upon it. Therefore, they fly about in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) without any support, holding themselves aloft, for they partake in the *Ādi* of this Sāman.

Now, as for the time of *saṃgava*: that period at which the rays of light come together (*saṃgama*) is called *saṃgava*, or the time when the cows are together with their calves. That form of Sāvitra which exists at that time is the *ādi*—the specific division known as the syllable *Oṃ*. To this [division], birds (*vayāṃsi*) are attached. Because it is so, therefore those birds, being without support (*anārambaṇa*)—that is, without any external hold—fly about in the intermediate space, having taken themselves alone as their support, holding themselves as the very basis of their movement. Thus, due to the similarity of the letter *ā*, they indeed partake in this first division of the *Sāman*.

Now, that which occurs precisely at midday is the *udgītha*; the gods are dependent upon that part of it. Therefore, they are the best among the offspring of Prajāpati, for they are the sharers in the *udgītha* of this *sāman*. (5) Now, "precisely at midday" means at the exact middle of the day; that is the *udgītha* division. The gods are dependent upon that, because of their superior radiance at that time. Therefore, they are the most excellent (*sattama*) among the *prājāpatyas*, the descendants of Prajāpati, for they are the sharers in the *udgītha* of this *sāman*.

Now, that which is after midday and before afternoon is the *pratihāra* (response); to it the embryos are attached. Therefore, they are brought forth (*pratihṛta*) and do not fall away, for they partake in the *pratihāra* of this *sāman*.

Now, that form of the Sun which is after midday and before afternoon is the *pratihāra*; to it the embryos are attached. Therefore, being held up by means of the *pratihāra*—which is a portion of the Sun—they do not fall away, nor do they fall downward, even though there is an opening [for them to do so]. For the embryos of this *sāman* partake in the *pratihāra*.

Now, that which follows after the afternoon and precedes sunset is the *upadrava* [section]; the wild animals are dependent upon it. Therefore, when they see a man, they flee into the thickets or into holes, for they partake in the *upadrava* of this *sāman*.
Now, that which follows after the afternoon and precedes sunset is the *upadrava*; the wild animals are dependent upon it. Therefore, when they see a man...
Being afraid, they run toward a thicket, a forest, or a pit, thinking it is free from danger; for by seeing [them] running away, they become sharers in the calamity of this *sāman*.

Now, that which occurs at the first setting of the sun is its *nidhana*; the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are dependent upon that, therefore they lay [the deceased] down, for they are sharers in the *nidhana* of this *sāman*. Thus indeed one meditates upon yonder sun as the sevenfold *sāman*. Thus ends the ninth section. (8) — Section 9 — (8) —

Now, that which occurs when the sun, desiring to go to invisibility, has just set—that is the *nidhana* (concluding note). His ancestors are connected to that; therefore, they place them down—they deposit them upon the *darbha* grass in the form of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; for that purpose, they establish the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*). Because of their connection with the *nidhana*, the ancestors are indeed the sharers of the *nidhana* of this *sāman*.

Thus, for one who meditates upon yonder sun as the sevenfold *sāman* divided into seven parts according to its members, the attainment of that [sun] is the fruit—this is the completion of the sentence.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth section.

Now, one should indeed meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman as commensurate with the Self and transcending death. "Hiṅkāra" consists of three syllables; "Prastāva" consists of three syllables; thus they are equal. Introduction: Death is the Sun, because it causes the destruction of the world through time such as day and night. This meditation on the Sāman is taught for the purpose of crossing over that death.
"Ādi" consists of two syllables, and "pratihāra" consists of four syllables; therefore, by adding one syllable here, they become equal.

Now, immediately following this is the meditation on the *sāman* as the sphere of the sun that transcends death (*atimṛtyu*). It is "measured" (*saṃmita*) either by being equal to one's own limbs or by being equal to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and thus it is "beyond death" because it is the cause for conquering death. Just as in the first chapter the syllables of the names of the divisions of the *udgītha* were declared as objects of meditation under the name "udgītha," so here the syllables of the names of the sevenfold divisions of the *sāman* are collected together; by establishing their equality through groups of three, they are conceived as a *sāman* and are declared as objects of meditation.

The meditation on that [Sāman] involves reaching death through the commonality of the number of syllables within the range of death, and then effecting a transition by means of the syllable exceeding that, for the very purpose of transcending that death which is the Sun. One should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman as "beyond death" (*atimṛtyu*); it is called "beyond death" because it has transcended death through the number of its extra syllables. The syllables of the name of its first *bhakti* (division) are "hiṃkāra"; this name of the *bhakti* consists of three syllables. And the name of the *bhakti* "prastāva" likewise consists of exactly three syllables; thus, it is equal to the former.

"Udgītha" consists of three syllables; "Upadrava" consists of four syllables. By means of three [syllables] each, they become equal, and one syllable remains over; thus, those three syllables are equal. (3) "Ādi" consists of two syllables. In the enumeration of the sevenfold *sāman*, the syllable *oṃ* is called "Ādi. "Pratihāra" consists of four syllables. Therefore, by taking one syllable from here and adding it to the first two syllables, that [word] becomes equal as well.

The word *nidhana* consists of three syllables; thus it is equal. These, indeed, are twenty-two syllables. (4) The word *udgītha* consists of three syllables, and *upadrava* consists of four syllables; with three syllables each, they become equal. One syllable remains over—it is in excess. Since this results in inequality, he speaks in order to establish the equality of the *sāman*: "That [remaining syllable], though being one, becomes a three-syllabled word *akṣara*. Therefore, it is equal.

One reaches the sun as the twenty-first; for that sun over there is the twenty-first from here. With the twenty-second [syllable], one conquers what is beyond the sun—that which is the firmament (*nāka*), that which is free from sorrow.

(5) (4) "Nidhana" consists of three syllables; thus it becomes equal. Having thus established its quality as a *sāman* through the equality of these three syllables, the syllables are counted exactly as they occur: those syllables of the names of the seven *bhaktis* indeed amount to twenty-two.

He attains victory over the sun; indeed, his victory comes about through victory over the sun—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman as commensurate with the self and transcending death—meditates upon the Sāman. Thus ends the tenth section. (5) — 10 —

Therein, by means of the count of twenty-one syllables, one reaches the Sun, which is death. For this Sun is the twenty-first from this world by way of number, according to the Vedic revelation: "Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and that Sun is the twenty-first. By means of the remaining twenty-second syllable, one conquers—that is, transcends—what is beyond the Sun, which is death. And that which is beyond the Sun is...

What is that? It is *nāka*. *Ka* means happiness; its negation is *aka*. That which is not *aka* is *nāka*, meaning it is indeed happiness, because it is not within the domain of death. And it is *viśoka*, meaning free from sorrow, devoid of mental suffering—one attains that.

The meditation on the fivefold and sevenfold *sāman* has been explained without mentioning their specific names. Now, however, other meditations on the *sāman* that yield specific fruits are described, preceded by the mention of the names beginning with *gāyatra*. Just as the *gāyatra* and others are employed in ritual action in a specific order, so too is the mind the *hiṅkāra*, because the mind precedes all functions of the senses. Following that, speech is the *prastāva*; the eye is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence; and the ear is the *pratihāra*, because it receives [sounds].

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *nidhana*, because at the time of sleep, those [elements] previously mentioned find their dissolution (*nidhana*) in the vital breath. This *Gāyatra* Sāman is woven into the vital breaths, because the *Gāyatrī* has been praised as being identical with the vital breath.

He who thus knows this Gāyatra as woven upon the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) becomes possessed of vital breaths; that is to say, he becomes one whose organs are unimpaired. He reaches a full lifespan—a hundred years—since the scripture declares, "The full lifespan of a man is a hundred years. He lives long and radiantly. He becomes great through progeny and so forth, and great in fame. This is the vow for the worshiper of the Gāyatra: namely, that he should be high-minded, meaning his heart should not be mean-spirited.
Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh section.

When one rubs [the fire-drills] together, that is the *hiṅkāra*; when smoke arises, that is the *prastāva*; when it blazes, that is the *udgītha*; when it becomes embers, that is the *pratihāra*; when it subsides, that is the *nidhana*; when it is completely extinguished, that is the *nidhana*. This *rathantara* is thus interwoven in the fire. 1. (1)

The rubbing [of the fire-drills] is the *hiṃkāra*, because it comes first. From the fire smoke arises; that is the *prastāva*, because it follows immediately after. It blazes; that is the *udgītha*, for blazing possesses preeminence due to its connection with the oblation (*havis*). It becomes embers; that is the *pratihāra*, because the embers are drawn back (*pratihṛta*). The subsiding (*upaśama*) is so called because the fire still has a remainder; the complete subsiding (*saṃśama*) is when there is no remainder left. Because of the commonality of being a conclusion, this is the *nidhana*. This *Rathantara* Sāman is woven into the fire, for the fire is sung during the rubbing.

He who thus knows this Rathantara as interwoven in the fire becomes endowed with spiritual luster, becomes an eater of food, reaches a full lifespan, lives long, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not sip water facing the fire, nor should he spit toward it; that is his vow. Thus ends the twelfth section.

The phrase "He who... and so forth is as explained previously. *Brahmavarcas* is the splendor resulting from proper conduct (*vṛtta*) and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); whereas mere *tejas* is simply the state of radiance. An *annāda* is one whose digestive fire is kindled. He should not sip water nor eat anything while facing west, that is, with his face toward the fire; he should not spit—that is, he should not discharge phlegm. This is his vow. Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section.

The sound "hiṅ" is its invitation; the making known is its Prastāva; he lies with a woman, that is the Udgītha; he lies with each woman, that is the Pratihāra; he passes the time, that is the Nidhana; he reaches the further shore, that is the Nidhana. This Vāmadevya [Sāman] is thus woven into the couple. 1. (1) —-

He invites her and makes a signal; because it is the first step, that is the *hiṃkāra*. He makes himself known and pleases her; that is the *prastāva*. Lying together and going onto one bed; that is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence. Facing the woman toward the bed, turning toward the woman; that is the *pratihāra*. He passes the time through sexual union and reaches the end, the completion; that is the *nidhana*. This *Vāmadevya* chant is woven into the couple, due to the connection with the couple consisting of wind and water.

He who thus knows this Vāmadevya [Sāman] as woven upon the couple becomes possessed of a couple; he procreates from every couple; he reaches a full span of life; he lives long; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should not avoid anyone—that is his vow. Thus ends the thirteenth section. 13. (2)

The passage beginning with "sa ya" and so forth is as explained previously. "He becomes paired" means he becomes inseparable [from his wife]. "From pair after pair he procreates" expresses the fact that his seed is never in vain. "No woman whatsoever"—that is, not even a single woman who has come to his own bed seeking union—he should reject her, because this is enjoined as an ancillary part of the meditation on the Vāmadevya Sāman. Other Smṛti texts containing prohibitions apply elsewhere than this. Furthermore, since the knowledge of dharma is derived from the authority of scriptural statements, there is no contradiction between this [injunction] and the prohibitory scriptures.
Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth section.

When the sun has risen, that is the *hiṅkāra*; at midday, it is the *prastāva*; in the afternoon, it is the *udgītha*; in the late afternoon, it is the *pratihāra*; and as it sets, it is the *nidhana*. This *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is woven into the sun. (1) 1.

The rising sun is the *hiṃkāra*, because it is the first appearance [of the sun]. The risen sun is the *prastāva*, because it is the cause for the commencement (*prastavana*) of ritual actions. Midday is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*). The afternoon is the *pratihāra*, because cattle and other things are driven back (*pratiharaṇa*) toward their homes. When it sets, that is the *nidhana*, because living beings are deposited (*nidhāna*) in their homes at night. This *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is interwoven in the sun, because the *Bṛhat* has the sun as its deity.

He who thus knows this Bṛhat as woven into the sun becomes radiant, an eater of food, reaches a full lifespan, lives long, and becomes great in offspring, cattle, and fame. He should not revile the one who shines—that is his vow. Thus ends the fourteenth section.
(2) —The passage beginning with "He who" is as explained before. "He should not revile the one who shines"; that is his vow.

Thus ends the commentary on the fourteenth section. The gathering of clouds is the *hiṅkāra*; the cloud that arises is the *prastāva*; when it rains, that is the *udgītha*; when it flashes and thunders, that is the *pratihāra*; and when it ceases, that is the *nidhana*. This *vairūpa* [sāman] is woven into Parjanya. 1. (1)

Clouds (*abhra*) are so called because they cover (*abbharaṇāt*). A rain-cloud (*megha*) is so called because it sprinkles water (*udakasektṛtvāt*). The rest has already been explained. This *Sāman* named Vairūpa is woven upon Parjanya. Because Parjanya possesses many forms through clouds and other phenomena, it is "variegated" (*vairūpyam*). He who knows this Vairūpa as woven upon Parjanya acquires both deformed and well-formed cattle; he reaches a full lifespan, lives long, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not revile the raining cloud—that is his vow. Thus ends the fifteenth section. (2) — 15 — (2) —
He acquires and obtains animals that are both deformed and well-formed, such as goats, sheep, and so forth; this is the meaning. "One should not revile the raining cloud"—this is the vow.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth section.
Spring is the *hiṅkāra*, summer is the *prastāva*, the rainy season is the *udgītha*, autumn is the *pratihāra*, and winter is the *nidhana*; thus is the Vairāja Sāman woven into the seasons. (1)
(1) Spring is the *hiṅkāra*, because it comes first; summer is the *prastāva*, and so on as before.

He who thus knows this Vairāja [Sāman] woven into the seasons shines forth with offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he reaches a full lifespan, lives long, and becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. One should not revile the seasons—that is his vow. 2.

(2) He who knows this Vairāja [sāman] as woven into the seasons shines like the seasons—just as the seasons shine with their seasonal characteristics (*dharmas*), so does the knower shine with offspring and other blessings. The rest has been explained. "One should not revile the seasons; that is its vow.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixteenth section.

The earth is the *hiṅkāra*, the intermediate space is the *prastāva*, the sky is the *udgītha*, the quarters are the *pratihāra*, and the ocean is the *nidhana*; these are the *śakvarī* verses woven upon the worlds. 1.
"The earth is the *hiṅkāra*," and so on, as before. "The *Śakvarīs*" always takes the plural number, just like the *Revatīs*. They are interwoven in the worlds.

He who thus knows these *Śakvarīs* as interwoven in the worlds becomes a possessor of worlds; he reaches a full lifespan, he lives long, he becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. One should not revile the worlds—that is his vow. 2. Thus ends the seventeenth section. 17. (2)
"One becomes a world-possessor; that is to say, one is joined with the fruit of the worlds. One should not revile the worlds—that is his vow.
This concludes the commentary on the seventeenth section.

"The he-goat is the *hiṅkāra*, the sheep is the *prastāva*, the cows are the *udgītha*, the horses are the *pratihāra*, and the man is the *nidhana*. These are the *revatī* verses woven into the animals. (1)
(1)—"The *ajā* (goat) is the *hiṃkāra*, etc., as before. These [notes] are interwoven in animals.

He who thus knows these *revatī* verses as interwoven in animals becomes possessed of cattle, reaches a full lifespan, lives long, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not revile cattle; that is his vow. (2). Thus ends the eighteenth section. 18.
(2) — "One should not revile animals; that is his vow.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighteenth section.

Lobha is the *hiṅkāra*, the skin is the *prastāva*, the flesh is the *udgītha*, the bone is the *pratihāra*, and the marrow is the *nidhana*. This *yajñāyajñīya* Sāman is woven into the limbs [of the body].

(1) Hair is the *hiṅkāra*, because it is the first among the parts of the body. The skin is the *prastāva*, because of its immediate succession. The flesh is the *udgītha*, because of its excellence. The bone is the *pratihāra*, because it is held back [or counteracted]. The marrow is the *nidhana*, because it is the final part. Thus, this Sāman named *yajñāyajñīya* is interwoven within the limbs of the body.

He who thus knows this Yajñāyajñīya as woven into the limbs becomes possessed of limbs; he does not become crippled in his limbs; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives long; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. For a year he should not eat marrow; that is the vow—or rather, "he should not eat marrow" is the rule. Thus ends the nineteenth section. 19. (2)

"He becomes possessed of limbs" means he becomes complete in his limbs. He does not become deformed—that is, he does not become crooked—by means of a limb such as a hand or foot; that is to say, he does not become lame or withered. "For a year" means for the duration of one year, he should not eat—that is, he should not consume—the flesh of marrow. The use of the plural number is intended to include fish as well. Or, he should not eat marrow at all times; that is his vow. Thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth section.

Agni is the *hiṅkāra*, Vāyu is the *prastāva*, Āditya is the *udgītha*, the constellations are the *pratihāra*, and the Moon is the *nidhana*. This *rājana* chant is interwoven within the deities. (1) Agni is the *hiṅkāra* because he occupies the first position. Vāyu is the *prastāva* because of the common quality of being immediate [to the first]. Āditya is the *udgītha* because of his preeminence. The constellations are the *pratihāra* because they are drawn back [toward the sun]. The Moon is the *nidhana* because it is the final resting place for those engaged in ritual action. This *rājana* chant is interwoven within the deities because the deities possess radiance.

He who thus knows this Rājana woven into the deities attains the same world, the same power, and union with these very deities; he reaches a full lifespan, lives radiantly, becomes great through offspring and cattle, and great through fame. He should not revile Brahmins—that is his vow. Thus ends the twentieth section.

The fruit for the knower: he goes to—attains—the *salokatām* (residence in the same world), the *sārṣṭitām* (equal power), the *samānarddhitvam* (equality in prosperity), and the *sāyujyam* (union), which is the state of being joined together as one body and soul, with these very deities beginning with Agni. The word "or" (*vā*) is to be understood as elided here, as in "or residence in the same world," and so forth; for a specific result arises according to the particularity of one's contemplation (*bhāvanā*). He goes—that is, he attains [these]. Furthermore, because a combination [of all results] is not possible, [the text specifies them individually]. "He should not revile Brāhmaṇas"—this is his vow.
For there is a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "These Brāhmaṇas are indeed the gods manifest before our eyes"; thus, reviling Brāhmaṇas is equivalent to reviling the deities.
Thus ends the commentary on the twentieth section.

The triple Veda is indeed the *hiṅkāra*; these three worlds are the *prastāva*; fire, wind, and the sun are the *udgītha*; the stars, birds, and rays of light are the *pratihāra*; serpents, Gandharvas, and the ancestors are the *nidhana*. This Sāman is woven upon everything. 1. (1)

The triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) is the *hiṃkāra*. The immediate succession of the triple knowledge after the fire-altar and so forth is due to the scriptural statement that the triple knowledge is the effect of the fire-altar and the rest; it is the *hiṃkāra* because it is the first of all things to be performed. These three worlds are the *prastāva*, because they are the effects of those [fire-altars]. The fire-altars and so forth have the nature of the *udgītha* because of their preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*). The stars and so forth have the nature of the *pratihāra* because they are held back (*pratihṛta*). The serpents and so forth have the nature of the *nidhana* because of the commonality of the sound *dh*.

Because there is no specific distinction of name, the word "Sāman" refers to the entire collection of Sāmans; thus, the Sāman is woven upon everything. For everything begins with the threefold knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*). Indeed, the constituent parts of the Sāman, such as the *hiṃkāra*, are to be meditated upon through the vision of the threefold knowledge and so forth. This applies even to the previous meditations on the Sāman: whatever Sāman is woven upon whatever [object], that Sāman is to be meditated upon through the vision of that object. This is because, just as clarified butter is consecrated by a particular mental visualization, so too are the auxiliary elements of ritual action. "He who knows this Sāman as woven upon everything becomes everything. (2) 2 — (2) —

The fruit of the one who knows the totality of all objects is this: he becomes everything; that is to say, he becomes the Lord of all. For if his state as "all" were not literal, it would be impossible for him to receive offerings from those situated in all directions.
Regarding this, there is this verse: "That which is fivefold, three by three—there is nothing greater or higher than that. (3) (3)

Regarding this matter, there is also this verse as a mantra: "There is no other entity whatsoever that is greater than or beyond those fivefold triads—which are declared to be three each, such as the three Vedas and so forth, divided into five ways by the *hiṅkāra* and other parts. The meaning is that no other distinct thing exists; for within those very triads, everything is included.

He who knows that knows all. All the quarters bring tribute to him. One should meditate upon it with the thought, "I am everything. That is the vow; that is the vow. 4. Thus ends the twenty-first section. 21. (4)

He who knows this *sāman* as having all things as its essence—this means that he knows everything and becomes omniscient. All the quarters, meaning those situated in every direction, bring tribute—that is, they provide enjoyment—to such a knower. "I am everything"—in this manner one should meditate upon this *sāman*; this indeed is his vow. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the meditation on the *sāman*. Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-first section. "I choose the resonant *sāman*, which is beneficial for cattle"—this is the *udgītha* of Agni. It is unexpressed (unarticulated) in the case of Prajāpati, and expressed (articulated) in the case of Soma; it is soft [in the case of Soma].
The smooth [chant] belongs to Vāyu, the powerful to Indra, the krauñca to Bṛhaspati, and the apadhvānta to Varuṇa; one may employ all of these, but one should avoid that which belongs to Varuṇa. 1.

In connection with the meditation on the *sāman*, the excellence of specific modes of chanting and so forth is taught for the *udgātṛ* priest, because of their connection to specific fruits. "Resounding" (*vinardi*) means possessing a distinguished resonance, a particular tone similar to the lowing of a bull; this refers to the chanting (*gāna*), as is understood from the supplementary statement of the text. And that [chanting] belongs to the *sāman*, is beneficial to cattle (*paśavya*), and pertains to Agni (*agnidevatya*). "Udgītha" means the high-pitched singing. A certain sacrificer or the *udgātṛ* priest thinks: "I choose—that is, I pray for—such a [chanting] characterized by these qualities."

That specific mode of singing which is "unexpressed" (*anirukta*), meaning unspecified as being like such-and-such, belongs to Prajāpati; it has Prajāpati as its deity because of Prajāpati’s own unexpressed nature. That which is "expressed" (*nirukta*), i.e., clear and distinct, is the *udgītha* belonging to Soma; that is the meaning. The singing that is soft and smooth belongs to Vāyu; it has Vāyu as its deity. The singing that is smooth yet powerful, endowed with great effort, belongs to Indra; it is the *aindra* song. The *krauñca* song, resembling the cry of the *krauñca* bird, belongs to Bṛhaspati; it is the *bārhaspatya* song.
The song of Varuṇa is that which is discordant and resembles the sound of cracked bell-metal. One should attend to all of them or employ them, but one should avoid the song of Varuṇa alone.

One should sing, thinking in one's mind: "May I sing forth immortality for the gods; may I sing forth the *svadhā* offering for the ancestors; may I sing forth hope for men; may I sing forth grass and water for animals; may I sing forth the heavenly world for the sacrificer; may I sing forth food for myself. Thus, meditating on these with the mind, one should chant without negligence. 2. (2) —

"May I sing for the gods the attainment of immortality; may I secure it; may I sing for the ancestors the *svadhā* offering; for humans, hope—that is, prayer, what is prayed for; for animals, grass and water; for the sacrificer, the heavenly world; and for myself, food—may I sing this. Thinking and meditating thus in his mind, he should chant the praise with vigilance, [attending] to the vowels, sibilants, consonants, and so forth.

All vowels are the self of Indra; all sibilants (*ūṣman*) are the self of Prajāpati; all consonants (*sparśa*) are the self of Death. If someone should reproach him regarding the vowels, he should say to that person: "I have sought refuge in Indra; he will answer you.

(3) All vowels, beginning with *a*, are the selves of Indra—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose function is power—standing in the place of limbs of his body. All sibilants, such as *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, are the selves of Prajāpati, whether he be Virāj or Kaśyapa. All consonants, the mutes beginning with *ka*, are the selves of Death.

If someone should reproach such an Udgātṛ regarding the accents, saying, "An accent has been wrongly employed by you," being thus reproached, he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Indra, the vital breath, as my protector while employing the accents; that very god, Indra, will speak to you what must be said to you and will give the answer. Thus he should speak to him.

Now, if one should reproach him regarding warm things, he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Prajāpati; he will look upon you. And if one should reproach him regarding tangible objects, he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Death; he will burn you up. 4. (4) —-

Now, if they should reproach him for his hot things in the same manner, he should say to them: "I have sought refuge with Prajāpati; he will look upon you and crush you to pieces. And if they should reproach him for his touchables, he should say to them: "I have sought refuge with Death; he will burn you and reduce you to ashes."

All vowels should be pronounced with resonance and strength, thinking: "I am bestowing strength upon Indra. All sibilants (*ūṣman*) should be pronounced unswallowed, unhurried, and open, thinking: "I am surrendering my self to Prajāpati. All stops (*sparśa*) should be pronounced with slight contact and without being pressed together, thinking: "I am avoiding my self from Death. Thus ends the twenty-second section. (5) — 22 — 5 —

Since the vowels (svaras), beginning with *a*, are the self of Indra and the others, therefore all vowels should be pronounced resonant and powerful. Likewise, [one should think]: "I bestow power upon Indra; I confer power. Similarly, all sibilants (*ūṣmans*) should be unswallowed—meaning they are not forced inward—and unexpelled—not cast outward—but open, endowed with the effort of openness (*vivṛta-prayatna*). [One should think]: "I surrender my own self to Prajāpati; I offer it. All the stops (*sparśas*) should be pronounced gently and slowly, neither pressed down nor thrust forward.
"Gradually avoiding death as if it were a child, [one should think] 'I shall avoid death for myself.

Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-second section. There are three branches of duty (*dharma-skandha*): sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first; austerity alone is the second; and the student (*brahmacārī*) who dwells in the house of his teacher is the third, exhausting himself completely in the house of his teacher. All these attain worlds of merit (*puṇya-loka*); but he who is established in Brahman attains immortality. 1.

(1) — The passage beginning with "There are three branches of duty" (*trayo dharmaskandhāḥ*) is commenced for the purpose of prescribing the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the syllable *Oṃ*. One should not think that the fruit is obtained solely from meditating on the *Oṃ* that constitutes a part of the *Sāman*, such as the *Udgītha*; rather, the intention is that the fruit of immortality—which cannot be attained even by all the meditations on the *Sāman* or by ritual actions (*karman*)—is obtained through the meditation on the *Oṃ* alone. Its mention here within the context of the *Sāman* is for the sake of its praise.

The three groups of threefold dharmas are the "dharmaskandhas," meaning divisions of dharma. As to what they are, he says: sacrifice (yajña), such as the Agnihotra and others; study (adhyayana), which is the practice of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas according to the rules; and giving (dāna), which is the distribution of goods to those who beg, outside the sacrificial altar according to one's capacity—this is the first dharmaskandha, which is designated by the householder because it is inherent in the householder and is performed by him.

"First" means "one," though it does not mean "the first" because of the mention of a second and a third. "Austerity alone is the second"; by "austerity" is meant *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth. One who possesses that is an ascetic (*tāpasa*) or a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), but not one who is "established in Brahman"—for it is heard that immortality belongs to the one established in Brahman—meaning one who is merely established in the duties of his stage of life (*āśrama*). This is the second division of dharma. A "student of sacred knowledge" (*brahmacārī*) is one whose habit is to dwell in the teacher's family; thus he is a "resident in the teacher's family."

The third division of dharma is one who, for life—until the very end—exhausts himself by means of restraints in the teacher’s family, wearing away the body. From the qualification "for life" and so forth, it is understood that this refers to the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student). For the *upakurvāṇa* (temporary student), since his purpose is the acquisition of Vedic study, the attainment of a world of merit through his studentship does not follow. All these three types of persons belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) become possessors of worlds of merit through their respective duties as described; those whose worlds are meritorious are these "possessors of worlds of merit," namely the persons in the stages of life.

The remaining one not yet mentioned is the wandering mendicant (parivrāj), the fourth, who is "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃstha)—that is, perfectly situated in Brahman. He attains immortality, which is distinct from the worlds of merit and consists of the state of being deathless in an absolute sense, not merely relative like the immortality of the gods and others; for immortality is distinguished here as separate from the worlds of merit.

And if immortality were merely a superior state among the worlds of merit, then it would not have been taught as distinct from the "worlds of merit. From this distinct instruction, it is understood that immortality is absolute. Furthermore, the presentation here of the fruits of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) is for the purpose of praising the practice of the *praṇava*, not for the purpose of enjoining those fruits; for if it were both for the praise of the practice of the *praṇava* and for the injunction of the fruits of the duties of the stages of life, there would be a split in the sentence.

Therefore, by restating the fruits of the stages of life (āśrama) as established in the Smṛtis, the text praises the service of the Praṇava by declaring its fruit to be immortality (amṛtatva). This is just as the service of Pūrṇavarman yields the fruit of merely clothing one's devotees, whereas the service of Rājavarmā yields a fruit equal to sovereignty—so it is here. And the Praṇava is that Truth, the Supreme Brahman, because it is its symbol; for the Kaṭha Upaniṣad records: "For this syllable alone is Brahman; for this syllable alone is the Supreme. Thus, it is logical that immortality results from its service.

Regarding this, some say: "It is stated here that for all four stages of life (*āśrama*) without distinction, the attainment of meritorious worlds through the performance of their own duties occurs when they are devoid of knowledge, as expressed in the words, 'All these become possessors of meritorious worlds. The wandering mendicant (*parivrāja*) is not excluded here; for even for the wandering mendicant, there is knowledge, as well as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), and austerity (*tapas*) itself. In the passage 'Austerity is the second,' both the wandering mendicant and the ascetic (*tāpasa*) are included by the word 'austerity.'"

Therefore, among those four [orders], it is he who is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*)—that is, the practitioner of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om)—who attains immortality. This is because there is no distinction regarding the eligibility of all four orders, and because being established in Brahman is not prohibited for them; furthermore, it is possible for one to be established in Brahman even when there is a lapse in one's own specific duties. Moreover, the term *brahmasaṃstha* is not conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) to refer only to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), as it functions by taking its primary basis from the act of being "established in Brahman. For words that are based on conventional usage do not depend upon such a basis.

Moreover, it is logical that all [ascetics] abide in Brahman. Wherever there is a basis for abiding in Brahman, it is improper to restrict the term *brahmasaṃstha*—which denotes one who possesses such a basis—to the single subject of the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), as there is no reason for such a limitation. Furthermore, immortality does not result from the mere duties of the wandering mendicant stage of life alone, because that would entail the uselessness of knowledge (*jñāna*).

If it is argued that knowledge conjoined specifically with the duty of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is the means to immortality, we say no; for there is no distinction in their being duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, the claim that "duty qualified by knowledge" is the means to immortality applies equally to the duties of all stages of life. Nor is there any scriptural statement to the effect that liberation belongs only to the wandering mendicant who is established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*), and not to others. Moreover, the established doctrine of all the Upanishads is that liberation comes from knowledge.
Therefore, whoever is established in Brahman while remaining within the duties prescribed for his own stage of life, he attains immortality.

No, because there is a contradiction between the causal sign (nimitta) of karma and the condition (pratyaya) of ignorance. For, having taken as its cause the conceptualization of the distinctions between the agent and other factors of action, the fruit of action, and so forth, [ignorance prompts one to think]: "Do this," "Do that."

Injunctions regarding action are set forth with the intent that "one should not act. Furthermore, that cause [of such injunctions] is not created by the scripture, for it is observed among all living beings. The cognition produced by the scripture—consisting of the forms "Being is one only, without a second," "All this is indeed the Self," and "All this is indeed Brahman"—which takes the form of knowledge, does not arise without first subduing the innate cognition of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit, which is the cause of the injunctions to act; for there is a contradiction between the cognitions of difference and non-difference.

For indeed, the cognition of the oneness of the moon and so forth does not arise upon the removal of the cataract without first subverting the cognition of the various [appearances] such as the double moon produced by the cataract, because of the mutual contradiction between the cognitions of knowledge and ignorance.

This being the case, he for whom that cognition of difference—upon which the injunctions for ritual action are based—is subverted by the cognition of oneness produced by the authority of such scriptural statements as "Being... is one only, without a second," "That is the Truth," and "The differentiation of modifications is untruth," has desisted from all ritual actions, since the cause [for their performance] has ceased; and he, having desisted from action, is said to be "established in Brahman."

And he must be a wandering mendicant alone, because no other state is possible; for another person is one whose cognition of difference has not ceased, and perceiving, hearing, thinking, and knowing "the other," he thinks, "Having done this, may I attain that. For one who acts in this manner, there is no state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*), because he possesses the conviction of a false intention regarding modifications that are merely a matter of verbal designation.

Furthermore, when the cognition of difference has been sublated by the realization that it is unreal, the cognition of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*)—in the form "this must be done by this person" or "by me"—is no longer tenable; just as for a discerning person, the notion of surface or impurity in space is untenable once sublated. If one does not desist from ritual actions even after the cognition of difference has been sublated, then the scriptural statement enjoining the cognition of unity would be rendered invalid, just as it was previously before the sublation of the cognition of difference.

Since the prohibitive injunctions regarding the eating of forbidden food and so forth possess authority, it is logical that the statement concerning oneness also possesses authority, because all the Upaniṣads have that as their ultimate purpose. If it is argued that this would entail the lack of authority for the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karma*), we say no; for their authority is established with respect to persons who still possess the unannulled cognition of difference, just as dream-cognitions and the like are authoritative prior to awakening. If it is argued that the authority of the injunctions for ritual action is abolished because they are not practiced by those who possess discrimination (*vivekin*), we say no; for we observe that the injunctions for optional rites (*kāmya-vidhi*) are not abolished.

For it is not the case that because those possessing discernment do not perform rites for desired ends—on the grounds that being motivated by desire is not praiseworthy—the injunctions for such rites are abolished, since they are indeed performed by those who possess desire. Likewise, although those established in Brahman and knowing Brahman do not perform ritual acts, the injunctions for them are not abolished, as they are indeed performed by those who do not know Brahman.

If it is argued that, just as for wandering mendicants there is no cessation of activities such as begging for alms even when the cognition of oneness has arisen, so too for householders and others there is no cessation of rites such as the *agnihotra* once that cognition arises—this is not so; for in the investigation of the validity [of scripture], human behavior does not serve as an example. Indeed, one does not observe someone performing even a prohibited act such as sorcery (*abhicaraṇa*) simply because it is forbidden; for a discerning person, even if devoid of hatred toward an enemy, would not perform such sorcery.

Furthermore, when the notion of difference—which is the cause for engaging in the performance of ritual acts—is sublated, there remains no motivating cause for the *agnihotra* and other such rites, just as hunger and so forth are the motivators for a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) in the act of begging for alms. If it is argued that here too the fear of sin (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance serves as the motivator, we say no; for one who possesses the notion of difference is the one entitled (*adhikṛta*) to the rite. We have already stated that he who possesses the notion of difference—that is, one whose cognition of difference has not been destroyed by knowledge—is the one entitled to ritual action.

For indeed, only he who is authorized for a ritual action incurs sin by its non-performance, not one whose authorization has ceased, just as a student (brahmacārin) does not incur sin by failing to perform the specific duties of a householder. If it be argued that, in this case, everyone established in their own stage of life (āśrama) who has produced the realization of oneness is a wandering mendicant (parivrāj), we say no; because the cognition of distinction between "self" and "owner" has not ceased, and because the other stages of life exist for the sake of ritual action—as the scripture states: "Then I shall perform ritual action."

Therefore, because the relationship of owner and owned does not exist, the mendicant alone is a wandering ascetic (*parivrāj*), not the householder or others. If it is argued that for the wandering ascetic there is no possibility of the occurrence of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) because the cognition of difference caused by injunctions has been sublated by the cognition produced by the injunction regarding the realization of oneness, we say no; for such an occurrence is possible when one is displaced from the cognition of oneness by hunger and other such needs, since [the restraints] serve the purpose of cessation [from worldly activity]. Nor is there the possibility of engaging in what is prohibited, because the prohibitions have already been established prior to the arising of the cognition of oneness.

For one who has fallen into a well or upon a thorn at night does not fall into that very same place when the sun has risen. Therefore, it is established that the mendicant alone, whose ritual duties have ceased, is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*). As for what was said—that for all those devoid of knowledge there is the world of merit—this is true. And as for what was said—that the wandering mendicant is also mentioned by the word "austerity"—that is incorrect. Why? Because the state of being "established in Brahman" is possible only for the wandering mendicant who has ceased the perception of duality.

For we have already stated that he alone is what remains. Furthermore, for one who possesses the knowledge of oneness, there is a cessation of asceticism (tapas), just as there is with the Agnihotra and other rites. Indeed, the obligation to perform asceticism would apply only to one who possesses the notion of duality. By this, the capacity for being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) during the intervals between ritual acts, as well as the lack of prohibition [regarding such intervals], has been answered. Likewise, the charge that knowledge is useless—on the grounds that only one who possesses knowledge and has ceased from action becomes a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*)—has also been answered.

As for what was further stated—that the term *brahmasaṃstha* is not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), just as words like *yava* or *varāha* are not—this has been refuted; for it is only for him [the mendicant] that being "established in Brahman" is possible, and not for anyone else. Furthermore, as for the claim that words established by convention do not take on a causal basis (*nimitta*), that is not so, because we observe words such as *gṛhastha*, *pakṣa*, and *parivrājaka*.

Even though words are derived from such causes as living as a householder, wandering as a mendicant, or being a carpenter, they are seen to be conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for specific referents—namely, the householder and the mendicant as particular stages of life (*āśrama*), and the carpenter as one possessing a specific caste—not wherever those causes may occur, because of the absence of such conventional usage.

Likewise, here too, the term *brahmasaṃstha* must apply specifically to the Paramahaṃsa, known as the "one who has transcended the stages of life" (*atyāśramin*), who is a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) from whom all ritual actions and their means have ceased, because the fruit of supreme immortality is heard [in this context]. Therefore, this alone is the renunciation (*pārivrājya*) declared in the Veda, and not that which involves the possession of the sacrificial thread, the triple staff, the water-pot, and so forth; for the Śruti says, "Shaven-headed, without possessions, unattached," and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad says, "[The knowledge] superior to the stages of life, the supreme purifier," and so on.

And from such Smṛti texts as, "Without praise and without salutation," and from such Smṛti texts as, "Therefore, the ascetics who have seen the further shore do not perform ritual action; therefore, the knower of dharma has no external marks, being one whose marks are unmanifest."

As for the renunciation of action accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, that is false, because they accept the reality of the cognition of distinctions between action, agent, and fruit. And as for the non-agency accepted by the Buddhists due to their acceptance of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), that too is unreal, because they accept the existence of one who accepts it. Furthermore, the acceptance of non-agency by the ignorant out of laziness is also unreal, because the cognition of agency has not been sublated by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, it is established that only for one who possesses the cognition of oneness produced by the means of knowledge of the Vedānta is there the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatva*), characterized by renunciation (*pārivrājya*) which consists in the cessation of ritual action. By this, it follows as a matter of course that when a householder possesses the realization of oneness, renunciation is necessarily attained.

[Objection: But surely one who renounces would incur the fault of extinguishing the sacred fire, according to the Vedic text: "He who extinguishes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods. [Reply: No, because it has been extinguished by the divine; for that very fire is extinguished when the vision of oneness arises, according to the Vedic text: "The fire-nature of the fire has departed. Therefore, the householder who renounces incurs no fault. To define that state established in which one attains immortality, he says:

Prajāpati brooded over the worlds; from them, thus brooded upon, the threefold knowledge issued forth. He brooded over that [knowledge]; from it, thus brooded upon, these syllables issued forth: *bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *svar*. 2. (2)

Prajāpati—either Virāj or Kaśyapa—having directed his attention toward the worlds, performed austerity (tapas) with the desire to extract their essence; that is to say, he applied intense heat, meaning he engaged in meditative concentration. From those worlds thus heated, the triple knowledge (trayī vidyā), which constitutes their essence, flowed forth; that is to say, it became manifest within the mind of Prajāpati. He performed austerity upon that [knowledge] as before. From that knowledge thus heated, these syllables flowed forth: the vyāhṛtis "Bhūr," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svar."

He brooded over them; from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable *Oṃ* flowed forth. Just as all leaves are pierced by a thorn, so is all speech pierced by the syllable *Oṃ*. The syllable *Oṃ* is indeed all this; the syllable *Oṃ* is indeed all this. Thus ends the twenty-third section. (23) (3)

He brooded upon those syllables; from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable *oṃ* issued forth. As to what that Brahman is like, he says: "Just as all leaves—meaning all the various parts of leaves—are pierced, perforated, and pervaded by a stalk, such as the midrib of a leaf; even so, by the syllable *oṃ*, which is Brahman and serves as the symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self, the whole of speech—the entire collection of sounds—is pierced. For there is a Vedic scripture stating: 'The letter *a* is indeed all speech.'"

And because the modification of the Supreme Self is a mere name, it is said: "The syllable Om is indeed all this. The repetition [of the word "indeed"] is for the sake of emphasis. The description of the creation of the worlds and so forth is for the purpose of praising the syllable Om. Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-third section. The exponents of Brahman say: "That which is the morning libation belongs to the Vasus; the midday libation belongs to the Rudras; and the third libation belongs to the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas. (1)

Introduction: Having set aside the syllable *oṃ*—which, in the context of the meditation on the *sāman*, was subordinate to ritual action—and having exalted it as a means to immortality because it is a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the author speaks as follows (1), desiring to teach the *sāman*, the oblation (*homa*), the mantra, and the rising (*utthāna*), which are constituent parts of the very sacrifice under discussion.

The exponents of Brahman say: "That which is known as the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) belongs to the Vasus. By them—being the lords of the morning libation—this world has been brought under control. Likewise, by the Rudras, who are the lords of the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*) has been brought under control. And by the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas, who are the lords of the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*), the third world has been brought under control. Thus, no other world remains for the sacrificer. Where, then, is the world of the sacrificer? How could one who does not know this perform [the sacrifice]? Only one who knows it should perform it. (2)

(2) — Therefore, where indeed is the world of the sacrificer for whose sake he sacrifices? The intention is that there is no world at all—according to the Vedic scripture: "He who sacrifices sacrifices indeed for the sake of a world. And in the absence of a world, that sacrificer who does not know—that is, does not understand—the means of acquiring that world, characterized by the *sāman*, the *homa*, and the rising of the mantra, being ignorant, how could he perform the sacrifice? In no way whatsoever can his status as an agent be logically established; this is the meaning.

Because the passage is intended as a praise of the knowledge of the *sāman* and so forth, it does not prohibit the agency of one who is ignorant but knows only the ritual action (*karman*). For if it were both for the sake of praising the knowledge of the *sāman* and for the sake of prohibiting the agency of the ignorant, the sentence would be split. Furthermore, we have already stated the reason why ritual action exists even for the ignorant in the first section concerning Upastha. Now, one who knows this means of attaining the *sāman* and so forth should perform it: before the commencement of the *prātaranuvāka*, sitting behind the *gārhapatya* fire facing north, he sings the *sāman* dedicated to the Vasus.

"What is that which is to be known? He says: Previously, before the commencement of the *prātaranuvāka* litany, sitting behind the *gārhapatya* fire facing north, he sings the *sāman* dedicated to the Vasus (*vāsava*), [beginning]:

Then he offers the oblation: "Homage to Agni, the dweller on earth, the dweller in the world! Find a world for me, the sacrificer! This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; I am entering it. 5. (5)

Immediately after that, he offers an oblation with this mantra: "Homage to Agni! We bow down before you, O dweller of the earth, who resides upon the earth; O dweller of the world, who resides in the world—meaning, the dweller of both earth and the world. Find—that is, obtain—for me, for myself, the sacrificer, a world. This indeed is my world, the sacrificer’s; I shall go there. Having said, "O Sacrificer, after your life has passed, [this is] your world," and saying, "Svāhā! Remove the crossbar," he stands up. To him, the Vasus present the morning libation. 6. (6)

In this world, the sacrificer—meaning "I," having died after the end of my life—offers with the exclamation *svāhā*. Having uttered this mantra, "Drive away, remove the bolt—the bar of the door to the worlds"—he stands up. In this way, through these [offerings], the world connected to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is ransomed from the Vasus. Then those Vasus bestow the morning pressing upon the sacrificer.

(13) Likewise, having sat down facing north before the Āhavanīya fire, he sings the Sāman dedicated to Āditya and the Sāman dedicated to the Viśvedevas, respectively for the sake of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) and universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*).

This sacrificer, indeed, who knows thus—that is, who knows the measure and the true nature of the sacrifice as described, such as the Sāman and so forth—knows it exactly as stated. The repetition of the phrase "he who knows thus" is for the purpose of concluding the chapter.
