Aṃ. That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods. Of it, the sky is the cross-beam, the atmosphere is the cake, and the rays are the sons. 1.

Introduction: The connection [of this chapter] with the beginning of the book is established by the passage "That sun indeed... and so forth. At the end of the immediately preceding chapter, it was stated: "He knows the measure of the sacrifice. Furthermore, specific Sāmans, oblations, mantras, and ritual procedures pertaining to the sacrifice were taught as constituent parts of the sacrifice for the attainment of particular fruits. And Savitṛ, who consists of the fulfillment of all sacrifices, shines with great splendor. He, being the fruit of the actions of all living beings, is visibly sustained by everyone.

Therefore, immediately after the description of the sacrifice, the Śruti begins as follows: "I shall now prescribe the meditation concerning Savitṛ, which is the effect of that [sacrifice] and yields the most excellent fruit among all human goals.

"That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," and so forth. It is called "honey" (*madhu*) because it gladdens (*modana*) the gods, just like [the honey of] bees. And he will explain how the sun is the cause of gladdening for the Vasus and others, since the sun consists of the fruit of all sacrifices. How is it honey? He says: of that honey, heaven itself is the cross-beam (*tiraścīnavaṃśa*), just as there is a cross-beam for the honey of bees; for heaven is perceived as if it were extending horizontally.

The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is like a honeycomb; because it hangs as if suspended from the branch of heaven, it is called a "honeycomb" due to its similarity to one. Furthermore, it is a honeycomb because it is the support of the honey, which is Savitṛ. The rays (*marīcayaḥ*) are the beams of light, and the waters situated within those rays are terrestrial, drawn forth by Savitṛ. For it is known from scripture: "These waters indeed belong to Svarāj, namely the rays. Since they are contained within the rays situated in the honeycomb of the intermediate space, they appear like the seeds of bees; thus they are called "sons" (*putrāḥ*), just as the sons of bees are contained within the cells of the honeycomb.

Those rays of his which extend eastward are its eastern honey-cells. The *Ṛg* verses are the honey-makers; the *Ṛgveda* is the flower; those are the immortal waters. These very *Ṛg* verses... (2)... 2. —-

Of that Savitṛ, who is the substratum of honey, those rays which extend eastward—that is, toward the eastern direction—are his eastern honey-veins (*madhunāḍyaḥ*), meaning they are like the channels of honey, the apertures that serve as the receptacles for honey, because they flow forward (*prāñcanāt*). Therein, the *ṛc*s themselves are the honey-makers (*madhukṛtaḥ*); they are called honey-makers because, like bees, they produce the honey that is the red-colored essence residing in Savitṛ. Since they take up essences and produce honey, the *Ṛgveda* itself is their flower, just as a flower is the source from which bees gather nectar.

In this context, since the collection of *ṛc*s and *brāhmaṇa*s is called the *Ṛgveda*, and because it is impossible for a flow of nectar in the form of an object of enjoyment to arise from mere sound alone, the term "*Ṛgveda*" here refers to the ritual action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda*. For from that [action], there is the possibility of a flow of honey consisting of the fruit of the ritual. Just as bees collect water from flowers, so too, having taken up water from the ritual action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda*—which stands in the place of the flower—the honey is produced by means of the *ṛc*s.

"What are those waters? he asked. He replied: "Those waters, when employed in ritual action in the form of soma, clarified butter, and milk, are cast into the fire; through their cooking, they become 'immortal' (*amṛta*)—that is, they become waters of extreme sweetness because they serve the purpose of immortality. Taking up their essence, these very *ṛc*s are like bees taking nectar from flowers. These *ṛc*s brooded over this *Ṛgveda*. From it, thus brooded upon, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. (3)

These *ṛks*, when employed in ritual action, were as if they "heated" (*abhyatapyan*)—that is, performed an intense brooding upon—the *Ṛgveda* and the action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda*, which stands in the place of a flower. For it is logical that an action being performed through *ṛk* mantras that have attained the status of constituent parts (such as the *śastra* recitations) releases the essence that produces honey, just as flowers do when they are sucked by bees. This is what [the text] says: "of that *Ṛgveda* which was heated."

What is this essence (*rasa*) which is said to have emerged from the heat applied to the *Ṛk* and the honey? It is fame—renown; splendor—the radiance residing in the body; the senses—the non-deficiency of the organs endowed with capacity; vigor—meaning power or capability; and food—both food itself and that which is edible, by the consumption of which the sustenance of the gods occurs day after day. This essence was produced from the ritual action characterized by sacrifice and the like.
That flowed forth; it took refuge all around the sun. That, indeed, is this red form of the sun. Thus ends the first section.

That [essence], beginning with fame (*yaśas*) and ending with food (*annādya*), flowed forth—that is, it flowed out specifically, it departed. Having gone there, it took refuge on all sides, on the flank, in the eastern part of the sun; the meaning is that it resorted to the sun. For people perform actions in order to obtain results characterized by fame and so forth, thinking, "We shall enjoy the honey called the fruit of action accumulated in this sun"—just as farmers cultivate fields for the sake of harvests. That is now being shown directly for the sake of inspiring faith.
This, indeed, is that. What is it? It is this red form of the sun which is seen when it rises.
Thus ends the commentary on the first section of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those which are its southern rays are its southern honey-cells; the Yajus-formulas themselves are the honey-makers, the Yajurveda itself is the flower, and those are the immortal waters.

(1) Now, "those which are its southern rays," and so forth, is the same as before. The Yajus-formulas themselves are the honey-makers, employed in the rituals prescribed by the Yajurveda, just like the honey-makers previously described. The ritual action prescribed by the Yajurveda occupies the place of the flower and is therefore called the "flower. Those very [substances], such as Soma and the rest, are the immortal waters.

These very Yajus formulas brooded over this Yajurveda. From it, thus brooded upon, there was born its essence: fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. That flowed forth; it took refuge around the sun. This, indeed, is that which is the white form of the sun. Thus ends the second section.
(3) — "These very sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) brooded upon this Yajurveda," and so forth; all [this] is the same [as before]. "This honey is seen as the white form of the Sun.
This concludes the commentary on the second section.
Now, those rays of his which extend westward are its western honey-cells; the Sāmans are the honey-makers, the Sāmaveda is the flower, and those are the immortal waters.
These very Sāmans heated that Sāmaveda. From it, thus heated, there arose as its essence (*rasa*) fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
(2) [The author] did not comment upon this verse. "That flowed forth; it took refuge all around the sun; that, indeed, is this black form of the sun. Thus ends the third section.
Now, "those which are its western rays," and so forth, is the same [as before]. Likewise, the honey of the Sāmans; this is the black form of the Sun...
thus ends the commentary on the third section.
Now, those which are its northern rays—these indeed are its northern honey-cells, and the Atharva-Aṅgirasas are the honey-makers.

The Itihāsas and Purāṇas are its flower; they are those waters of immortality. (1) Those very Atharva-Aṅgirasas performed austerities upon this Itihāsa-Purāṇa. From it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. (2)
(2) He did not comment upon this verse. "It flowed forth; it took refuge all around the sun. That indeed is this which is the supreme black form of the sun. ... Thus ends the fourth section.

Then, "those rays of his which point upward," and so forth, is the same [as before]. The *Atharvāṅgirasas* are the mantras seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras; when employed in ritual action, they are the "honey-makers. The *Itihāsa-purāṇa* is the "flower. It is established that these two—the *Itihāsa* and the *Purāṇa*—are to be applied as constituent parts of the ritual during the *pāriplava* nights of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. This honey is the supreme black form of the Sun; the meaning is that it is exceedingly black. Thus ends the commentary on the fourth section.
Now, those rays of his that go upward are indeed its upward honey-cells; the secret teachings are the honey-makers; Brahman is the flower; and those are the immortal waters. (1)

These indeed are the secret instructions. These [sages] performed austerity upon this Brahman. From it, thus heated, glory, splendor, the senses, vigor, food, and essence were born. That flowed forth; it took refuge around the sun. That is indeed this which appears as if shimmering in the center of the sun.

(3) Now, "those rays of his which are upward," and so forth, as before. The secret, hidden, and esoteric instructions (*ādeśāḥ*)—such as the rules regarding *lokadvārī* and other such meditations (*upāsanāni*) concerning the components of ritual action—are the honey-makers; Brahman itself, under the heading of "Sound" (*śabda*), known as the *praṇava*, is the flower. The rest is the same. This honey of the Sun appears to be agitated within, as if moving, to one whose vision is concentrated.

These, indeed, are the essences of essences; for the Vedas are the essences, and these are their essences. These, indeed, are the nectars of nectars; for the Vedas are the nectars, and these are their nectars. Thus ends the fifth section. 5. (4)

These aforementioned specific forms, such as the red and so forth, are the "essences of essences. Of which essences? He says: because the Vedas are the "essences" (*rasa*) since they are the quintessence (*sāra*) flowing from the world, these specific forms like the red are the "essences of those essences"—meaning they are the ultimate essence even among those [Vedas] that have entered into the state of ritual action (*karman*). Likewise, they are the "nectars of nectars"; for the Vedas are indeed nectars because of their eternity, and these forms like the red are the nectars of those [Vedas]. This statement beginning with "the essences of essences" is a praise of the ritual action—namely, that its fruit consists of such distinguished nectars.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth section.
Now, that which is the first nectar, the Vasus subsist upon it with Agni as their mouth. Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. 1.

In that regard, the first nectar, characterized by the color red, the Vasus—who are masters of the morning libation—subsist upon it through Agni as their mouth; that is to say, being presided over by Agni, they subsist [upon it]. Since it is stated, "From food, the essence was produced," one might assume they consume it in mouthfuls; this is denied: "The gods indeed neither eat nor drink."

How, then, do they subsist? It is said: having seen—that is, perceived and experienced through all the sense organs—this very aforementioned immortal red form, they are satisfied. This is because seeing has as its purpose the perception [of objects] through the door of all the sense organs. Now, it was stated that "having seen the red form"; how can the red form be an object of other senses? No, for fame and the rest are accessible to the ear and other senses respectively. Fame is grasped by the ear, and the form of light (tejas) is visual.

The *indriya* (organ) is the capacity of the instrument, inferable from the effect of grasping objects. *Vīrya* (vital energy) is strength, the enthusiasm residing in the body, the state of being possessed of *prāṇa*. *Anna* (food) is that which, being consumed daily, serves to maintain the body. For every essence (*rasa*) is of this nature; seeing it, all are satisfied. When it is said, "the gods are satisfied upon seeing it," the meaning is that they are satisfied by experiencing all this through their own instruments [of perception]. Abiding in the sun and free from the defects of the body and its instruments, such as foul odors, they enter into this very form and emerge from this very form. 2.

(2)—Do they live upon the nectar without making any effort? No. How then? Having observed this very form and realizing, "Now is not our time for enjoyment," they enter into it and remain indifferent. When indeed the time for enjoying that nectar arrives, then they rise up from this nectar—meaning, for the sake of enjoying the nectar—from this form; that is, they become full of enthusiasm. For in this world, the attainment of enjoyment is never seen for those who lack enthusiasm, who do not act, and who are indolent.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Vasus alone, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar with Agni as his mouth; he enters into this very form and emerges from this form. 3.

Whoever knows this very process as it has been described— the flowing of the honey-essence from the flowers of the rites enjoined by the Ṛgveda, its resting upon the sun and its red form, its location within the channels of the rays extending toward the eastern direction, its being enjoyed by Vasu, and how one who knows it attains unity with him, subsists through Agni as his mouth, finds satisfaction by mere sight, rises at the time of his own enjoyment and descends when that time passes— he too, like Vasu, experiences everything exactly in that same way.
"As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, for so long shall he attain the lordship and sovereignty of the Vasus. Thus ends the sixth section. 6.

For how long a time does the knower subsist upon that nectar? It is said: As long as the sun rises in the east, the eastern direction, and sets in the west, the western direction—for that long is the period of enjoyment for the Vasus; for that very same length of time, he becomes one who attains, that is, goes all around, the sovereignty and self-rule of the Vasus. He is not like one who dwells in the lunar sphere, a mere performer of ritual acts, dependent and serving as food for the gods; rather, he attains sovereignty, self-rule, and the state of being a self-ruler (*svarāḍ*).
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth section.

Now, as for that second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it through Indra as their mouth; indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink, but they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. 1. (1) [No commentary provided for this verse.]

They enter into this very form and emerge from this very form. He who knows this immortal [state] thus—becoming one of the Rudras himself, and with Indra as his mouth—having seen this very immortal [state], he is satisfied; he enters into this very form and emerges from this very form.

(3) Now, as for that second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it, and so on, [the rest] is the same. As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice as long does it rise in the south and set in the north; for that long he attains the sovereignty and self-rule of the Rudras. 4. Thus ends the seventh section. 7.
(4) — As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that duration—double the time—it shall rise in the south and set in the north; such is the period of enjoyment for the Rudras.
Thus ends the commentary on the seven sections.
Now, as for that third nectar, the Ādityas subsist upon it with Varuṇa as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar.
They enter into this very form and emerge from this very form.
(2) [The commentator] did not comment on this verse.
He who thus knows this nectar becomes one of the Ādityas; having Varuṇa as his mouth, he beholds this very nectar and is satisfied. He enters into this very form and emerges from this form. .. 3 ..
(3) [The commentator] did not comment on this verse.

As long as the sun rises in the south and sets in the north, twice that long he shall rise in the west and set in the east; for so long he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Ādityas. Thus ends the eighth section. 8.

Likewise, it rises in the west, the north, and above, and sets in the reverse order; that it does so with each subsequent direction taking twice as long as the preceding one is the non-Purāṇic view. For the Purāṇikas have stated that the time of the Sun’s rising and setting is equal in the cities of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma in the four directions, because its circumambulation of Meru on the summit of Mānasottara is uniform. Regarding this, the following solution has been stated by the Teachers (Ācāryas).

The depopulation of cities such as Amarāvatī and the others would occur at intervals doubling successively. Furthermore, what is called the "rising" of the sun is simply its coming within the range of vision for the living beings dwelling there, and its "setting" is the passing out of that range; in the ultimate sense, neither rising nor setting exists. Moreover, in the absence of those living beings dwelling there, even though the sun continues to travel along that very same path, it neither rises nor sets for them, because there is no longer any coming into or passing out of the range of their vision.

Likewise, the city of Saṃyamanī remains for twice as long as Amarāvatī; therefore, with respect to the living beings residing there, it is said that [the sun] rises as if from the south and sets in the north—this being said in consideration of our own [human] perception. The same logic applies to the cities in the north as well. And for all of them, Mount Meru is situated to the north. When the sun has reached midday in Amarāvatī, it is seen rising in Saṃyamanī; when it has reached midday there, it is seen rising in Vāruṇī.

Likewise, [the sun appears] in the north, because the process of circumambulation is the same. For the inhabitants of Ilāvṛta, whose solar rays are blocked on all sides by the mountain ramparts, the sun appears to rise directly overhead and set in front of them, due to the entry of the sun's light through the openings above the mountains. Similarly, it is inferred from the sign of the doubling of the time of enjoyment that those who subsist on the nectar of the Ṛgveda and so forth, as well as the immortals, possess twice the vigor of each successive region. The rising, setting, and other activities of the gods such as Rudra and the wise one are common to all.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section.
Now, as for that fourth nectar, the Maruts subsist upon it through Soma as their mouth. Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar.
They enter into this very form and emerge from this very form.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Maruts alone, becomes satisfied by beholding this very nectar with Soma as his mouth. He enters into this very form and emerges from this form.
As long as the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, twice as long does it rise in the north.
"Setting in the south, he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Maruts.
Thus ends the ninth section.
Now, as for the fifth nectar, the Sādhyas subsist upon it with Brahmā as their mouth; indeed, the gods [do not eat].

They eat and they drink; having seen this very nectar, they are satisfied. They enter into this very form and emerge from this form. He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Sādhyas, [attains] through Brahman itself... 1 ...they enter into this very form and emerge from this form. 2 ...he who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Sādhyas, through Brahman itself...

Beholding this very nectar with his mouth, he is satisfied; he enters into this very form and emerges from this very form. As long as the sun rises in the north and sets in the south, for twice that duration it rises above.

"Rising hitherward and setting thitherward, he shall indeed attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Sādhyas. Thus ends the tenth section. Thus ends the seventeenth section. 17. This is the fire-altar as it is in the self. Thus ends the twentieth section. 20. "Now, concerning the fire-altar: its bricks are the days and nights; its clods are the half-months; its earth-pans are the seasons; its enclosing stones are the months; its two kindling-sticks are the year. This is the fire-altar as it is in the world of the gods. Thus ends the twenty-sixth section. 26. "Now, concerning the fire-altar as it is in the world of man: its bricks are the bones; its clods are the marrow; its earth-pans are the flesh; its enclosing stones are the skin; its two kindling-sticks are the life-breath. This is the fire-altar as it is in the world of man. Thus ends the twenty-seventh section. 27. "Now, concerning the fire-altar as it is in the self: its bricks are the syllables; its clods are the vowels; its earth-pans are the consonants; its enclosing stones are the breaths; its two kindling-sticks are the mind. This is the fire-altar as it is in the self. Thus ends the twenty-eighth section. 28. Thus ends the twenty-ninth section. 29. This is the fire-altar as it is in the world of the gods. Thus ends the thirtieth section. 30. This is the fire-altar as it is in the world of man. Thus ends the thirty-first section. 31. This is the fire-altar as it is in the self. Thus ends the thirty-second section. 32. He attains the sovereignty and self-rule of the Sādhyas. Thus ends the thirty-third section. 33. "Now, having risen above that, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the middle. This is the fire-altar as it is in the world of the gods. Thus ends the thirty-eighth section. 38. "Now, concerning the fire-altar as

(1)—Having thus performed, through rising and setting, the favor toward living beings for the purpose of their experiencing the fruits of their own karma, and having withdrawn those multitudes of living beings into himself upon the exhaustion of that experience of karmic fruits—then, after that, following the period of favoring living beings, having risen and emerged within himself, because of the non-existence of those living beings toward whom he had risen, he remains established in his own self; he shall neither rise nor set, being alone, without a second, partless, and staying in the very midst of his own self.

In that regard, a certain wise man, whose conduct was equal to that of the Vasus and others, who partook of the nectar of immortality such as Rohita and the rest, having approached the Sun—who is his own Self—according to the aforementioned sequence and being composed, beheld this mantra. Having arisen, he spoke to another who questioned him: "From the world of Brahmā have you come? Does the Sun, revolving there with day and night, exhaust the lifespan of living beings just as he does for us here?"

Being thus questioned, he replied: "In that regard, concerning the matter as asked and as stated, this verse occurs; it was spoken by the Yogin—this is the statement of the Śruti: 'Truly, there it never sets nor does it ever rise. By that truth, O God, may I not be at variance with Brahman. (2)

(2) "Indeed, that from which I have come—the world of Brahmā—therein, indeed, is not that which you ask about. For there the sun has never set, nor has it ever risen; at no time, in any place whatsoever, has it ever gone down or emerged."

When it was said, "The world of Brahman (brahmaloka) is devoid of rising and setting," [the teacher] responded as if taking an oath: "O gods, you who are witnesses, listen! By this truth—that the word spoken by me is true—may I not be at variance with Brahman, that is, with the nature of Brahman; let there be no non-attainment of Brahman for me.
The Śruti says that he spoke the truth: "Verily, for him the sun neither rises nor sets; for him it is always day, who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman in this way. 3.

(3) Indeed, for one who knows Brahman as described, the sun neither rises nor sets, nor does it go down; rather, for this knower of Brahman, it is always day, forever, because he is self-luminous. "He who knows this secret Upanishad of Brahman as described"—the meaning is that he understands, in this manner, the triad beginning with the lineage (*vaṃśa*) through its distributive application (*tantreṇa*), the connection with immortality, and whatever else we have stated. The meaning is that the knower becomes the eternal, unborn Brahman, which cannot be delimited by the times of sunrise and sunset.
Brahmā told this to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; Manu told it to his offspring. And this very same Brahman, a father told to his eldest son Uddālaka Āruṇi.

Now, this very knowledge of the Honey—Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha spoke it to Virāj Prajāpati; he, in turn, to Manu; and Manu proclaimed it to the subjects beginning with Ikṣvāku. Thus [the text] praises the knowledge, saying that it has come down through a distinguished succession starting from Brahmā. Furthermore, this very knowledge of the Honey—the realization of Brahman—his father spoke to Uddālaka Āruṇi, his eldest son.
"One should indeed declare this Brahman-knowledge to one's eldest son, or to a worthy disciple.

This indeed is that which has been stated: one may also proclaim this Brahman to another—specifically to an eldest son who is worthy of all affection, or to a beloved disciple who is fit and capable; but not to anyone else whatsoever. Even if one were to give him this entire earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, this [teaching] alone is more than that, this alone is more than that. Thus ends the eleventh section. (6) — 11 — (6) —-

One should not proclaim this to anyone else whatsoever. Two types of "sacred fords" (tīrtha)—namely, teachers and the like—are permitted among the many such "fords" that might be encountered. Why, then, is the scope of the "ford" restricted for this knowledge? He says: even if someone were to give this entire earth, encompassed by waters and surrounded by the ocean, to this teacher as the price for this knowledge—a full and abundant wealth consisting of all the means of enjoyment—[one should still not teach it to anyone other than the teacher].
This is not its ransom; for even compared to that gift, this very gift of the Madhu-vidyā has greater fruit—that is, it yields more abundant results. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh section.
"The Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here. The Gāyatrī is speech; speech indeed sings forth all this being."

And it protects... 1 ...Introduction: Since this knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) possesses such extraordinary fruits, it must be explained by means of another method as well; thus the passage beginning with "The Gāyatrī indeed... is commenced. And Brahman is taught by way of the Gāyatrī because it is difficult to comprehend—being devoid of all specific attributes and only accessible through the negation of attributes such as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Although there are many meters (*chandas*), the Gāyatrī alone is selected as the gateway to the knowledge of Brahman on account of its preeminence.

Because of the bringing of Soma, because of the bringing of the syllables of other meters, and because of the pervasion of other meters—and thus due to its pervading all the *savanas*—the *gāyatrī* holds primacy in the sacrifice. Furthermore, since the Brāhmaṇa has the *gāyatrī* as his essence, he does not find anything more weighty than the *gāyatrī*, just as one would not find anyone more venerable than one's mother; for it is well known that even Brahman itself is said to be so. Therefore, Brahman is expressed by means of the *gāyatrī* alone:
(1) ———— [The verse follows].

The word "vai" has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*): "Gāyatrī indeed. Whatever exists here as this entire world of beings—the whole multitude of living things, whether stationary or moving—all that is Gāyatrī alone. Since it is impossible for that which is merely a metrical form (*chandomātrā*) to be all beings, [the text] brings about speech (*vāk*), whose nature is sound, as the cause of Gāyatrī, stating: "Gāyatrī is indeed speech. For speech is this entire world of beings.

Because speech, being of the nature of sound, sings of—that is, names—all beings, saying, "This is a cow," "This is a horse," and so forth; and because it protects—that is, guards—one who is being turned away from fear on all sides by means of speech, such as, "Do not be afraid of that! What fear has arisen for you? and so on, he is protected by speech. That which sings of beings and protects them is indeed Gāyatrī, for there is no difference between speech and Gāyatrī. It is called Gāyatrī because of its singing (*gāna*) and its protecting (*trāṇa*).
That which is indeed Gāyatrī is this very earth; for upon her everything that exists is established, and it does not exceed beyond her. 2.

That Gāyatrī which has such characteristics and consists of all beings is indeed this very earth. But how is it that this earth is Gāyatrī? It is said: because of its connection with all beings. How is there a connection with all beings? For on this earth everything—both the stationary and the moving—is established; it does not exceed nor go beyond this very earth.

Just as the Gāyatrī is connected to the elements through its functions of singing (*gāna*) and protecting (*trāṇa*), so too the earth is connected to the elements because it is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhāna*) of the elements; therefore, the Gāyatrī is the earth.
That which is the earth is indeed this very body within this person, for upon it these vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are established, and they do not transcend this. 3.

That which is indeed that earth is this very Gāyatrī; it is this very thing. What is that? It is this body within this person—the aggregate of causes and effects—which exists while living, because the body is of the nature of earth (*pārthiva*). How is it that the body is the Gāyatrī? It is said: for in this [body] these vital breaths (*prāṇas*), denoted by the word "beings" (*bhūta*), are established. Therefore, like the earth, the body is the Gāyatrī because it is the locus where the vital breaths denoted by the word "beings" are established; for the vital breaths do not exceed this body.
That which is the body in the person is indeed this very thing, namely this heart within the person; for upon it these vital breaths are established, and they do not go beyond it. 4.

That which is the body in the person is indeed this Gāyatrī. That which is this heart, called the lotus, within this person—that is the Gāyatrī. How so? He says: for in this [heart] these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established; therefore, like the body, the heart is the Gāyatrī. And the vital breaths do not exceed this [heart]. According to the Śruti, "The vital breath is the father; the vital breath is the mother," and "not harming any beings," the vital breaths are what is denoted by the word "beings" (*bhūta*). This is that four-footed and sixfold Gāyatrī; concerning this, it is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: (5) — "The Gāyatrī has taken hold of the earth, and with three feet she has entered into heaven. She, who is all this, shines forth beyond the mortal. (RV 1.90.6) The Gāyatrī has taken hold of the earth with one foot; with three feet she has entered into heaven. She, who is all this—whatever there is here—shines forth beyond the mortal. What is this "all"? It is the three worlds. The Gāyatrī has taken hold of the three worlds with one foot; with three feet she has entered into heaven. She, who is all this—whatever there is here—shines forth beyond the mortal. What is this "all"? It is the three Vedas. The Gāyatrī has taken hold of the three Vedas with one foot; with three feet she has entered into heaven. She, who is all this—whatever there is here—shines forth beyond the mortal. What is this "all"? It is the vital breaths. The Gāyatrī has taken hold of the vital breaths with one foot; with three feet she has entered into heaven. She, who is all this—whatever there is here—shines forth beyond the mortal. What is this "all"? It is this very self. The Gāyatrī has taken hold of this self with one foot; with three feet she has entered into heaven. She, who is all this—whatever there is here—shines forth beyond the mortal. What is this "all"? It is this [self] itself. This self is the Gāyatrī. This [self] is all this; for whatever is here, whether moving or stationary, all that is contained within this self. Now, the Gāyatrī is speech, and speech is the Gāyatrī. Whatever is here, whether moving or stationary, all that is supported by speech. Therefore, they say of a man who knows much, "He speaks much"; for from speech he arises, and in speech he is established. This is the Gāyatrī with its feet and its forms. This very Gāyatrī, being of the nature of *chandas*, consists of four feet and six syllables per foot; it is sixfold—being composed of speech (*vāk*), the elements (*bhūta*), the earth (*pṛthivī*), the body (*śarīra*), the heart (*hṛdaya*), and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it becomes sixfold. Although speech and vital breath are mentioned for other purposes, they are nonetheless modes of the Gāyatrī, because otherwise the completion of the number six would be impossible. With reference to this meaning, this Brahman called Gāyatrī—which follows the Gāyatrī and is expressed through the medium of the Gāyatrī—is further illuminated by the following *ṛc* verse: "Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that."
"One foot of His is all beings; three feet of His are the immortal in heaven.

(6) — So great is the majesty (*mahiman*), that is, the expansion of the power (*vibhūti*) of this entire Brahman known as Gāyatrī, which consists of its four-footed and sixfold modification (*vikāra*) explained as "Gāyatrī is one foot of Brahman. Therefore, greater than and more vast than that [modification] characterized as Gāyatrī—which is a mere beginning in speech (*vācārambhaṇamātra*)—is the Puruṣa, the Person, who is the form of ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*), the unmodified, the Filler of all (*puruṣa*) because He fills everything and because He dwells within the city (*puri*).

Of this [Gāyatrī], one foot consists of all beings—fire, water, food, and so forth, including all things moving and stationary. Its three feet are the three remaining parts; thus it is "three-footed" (*tripāt*). The meaning is that the immortal three-footed entity called Puruṣa is established in the "heaven"—that is, within its own self which is luminous.

"That which is indeed Brahman is this very thing: the space that is outside the person. That which is the space outside the person—" (7) (Note: The provided text ends with the opening of section 7. The translation reflects the portion given.)

That which was indeed described as the three-quarter immortal Brahman by means of the mouth of the Gāyatrī—this, verily, is that; this very thing is it. That which is well-known as the elemental space outside the person—that indeed is what was called the space outside the person. This, verily, is that which is the space within the person; that indeed is what is the space within the person. 8. (8)

This indeed is that which is the space within the person, within the body. Verily, that which is the space within the person is this very space which is within the heart; it is full and unchanging. He who knows this obtains full and unchanging prosperity. 9. Thus ends the twelfth section. 12. (9) — 3.12.9

This indeed is that very space which is within the heart, in the lotus of the heart. How can there be a threefold division of that which is one single space? It is said in reply: in the external space, which is the object of the senses and the locus of the waking state, an abundance of suffering is observed. Within the body, in the space that constitutes the locus of dreaming, suffering becomes much less intense. Furthermore, for one who perceives dreams, in the space situated within the heart, one desires no object of desire whatsoever and sees no dream at all.

Therefore, space (*ākāśa*), which consists of the cessation of all suffering, is the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Consequently, it is appropriate to describe even this single element as having a threefold division. Starting from the external world and proceeding inward toward the person, the contraction of space within the heart is intended to praise the heart as the locus for the concentration of the mind—just as it is said: "Of all the three worlds, Kurukṣetra is distinguished; half of Kurukṣetra is [sacred], and half of that is Pṛthūdaka. It is just like that.

This very Brahman, known as the space within the heart (*hārda-ākāśa*), is full and all-pervading; it should not be thought of as being limited merely to the heart, even though the mind is concentrated within the space of the heart. It is "non-active" (*apravarti*), meaning its nature is not to be set in motion from anywhere or toward anything; it is of an indestructible nature (*anucchitti-dharmaka*). Unlike other elements which are limited and subject to destruction, the space within the heart is not so.

One obtains full, non-ceasing, and imperishable prosperity, glory, and the fruit of one’s virtues as a visible result. The meaning is that he who knows—that is, understands—the Brahman characterized by the aforementioned qualities of being full and non-ceasing, attains its very nature even while living here in this world.

Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section. Of this very heart, there are five openings for the gods. That which is its eastern opening is the breath (prāṇa), that is the eye, that is the sun; one should meditate upon it as splendor and the eating of food. He who knows this becomes resplendent and an eater of food. 1.

(1) With the words "Of that, indeed," etc., the text begins for the purpose of prescribing the qualities of the door-keepers and others as ancillaries to the meditation on Brahman known as Gāyatrī. Just as in the world, door-keepers who have been brought under control through service to a king lead to the attainment of the king, so it is here as well. "Of that" refers to the previously mentioned heart.

Of this [body], which has just been described, there are five "divine apertures" (*devasuṣayaḥ*)—that is, five openings that serve as gateways for attaining the heavenly world. They are called "divine apertures" because they are protected by the gods, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the sun (*āditya*), and others. Of this heart, which is the abode of the heavenly world, that eastern aperture—the opening or door facing east—is the *prāṇa*. That specific wind which moves through that door, situated therein, is called *prāṇa* because it breathes forward (*prāganiti*).

The eye is indeed connected with and non-different from that [vital breath]; likewise, that Āditya—according to the Śruti, "Āditya is indeed the external vital breath"—abides in the heart by way of being established in the eye and form. For it is said in the Vājasaneyaka: "In what is that Āditya established? In the eye," and so forth. Indeed, the deity of the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu) alone is both the eye and Āditya together with their substratum. And the text will later state: "The oblation offered with the words 'Svāhā to Prāṇa' pervades all this."

This very [breath] called *prāṇa* is Brahman, because it acts as the gatekeeper of the heavenly world. One who desires to attain the heavenly world should meditate upon this [Brahman] as radiant, since it has the form of the sun in the eye, and as food-eating, since it is the essence of Savitṛ. By these two qualities, one becomes radiant and an eater of food, and is freed from disease; for one who knows thus, this is the fruit of those qualities. Furthermore, the primary fruit is that the gatekeeper, being brought under control through meditation, becomes the cause for attaining the heavenly world.

Now, that which is its southern aperture is the Vyāna breath, that is the sense of hearing, and that is the moon. One should meditate upon this as both prosperity and fame; he who knows this becomes prosperous and famous.

Now, that which is its southern cavity, the specific vital air situated therein, is called *vyāna* because it performs vigorous action, or because it breathes variously by separating the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. The sense organ of hearing is indeed connected to that. Likewise, that is the moon—according to the Vedic revelation, "The quarters and the moon were created by the ear. Their common substratum is as before. This constitutes the fact that both the ear and the moon are causes of knowledge and food; therefore, they possess the nature of *śrī* (prosperity).

And because fame and renown arise from knowledge, it is called "fame" (*yaśas*) since it is the cause of fame. Therefore, one should meditate upon it through these two qualities; the rest is the same as before.

Now, that which is its western aperture is *apāna*, that is speech, that is fire—this one should meditate upon as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and food-eating (*annādya*). He who knows this becomes possessed of spiritual luster and an eater of food.

Now, that which is its western aperture, the specific vital air situated therein, is called *apāna* because it carries away urine, feces, and so forth by exhaling downwards. Speech is likewise [so named] due to its connection with that [air]; similarly, fire [is so named]. This "brahman-splendor" (*brahmavarcasa*) is the luster resulting from conduct and Vedic study; it is called "brahman-splendor" because conduct and Vedic study are connected with fire. Because it is the cause of swallowing food, *apāna* is the "eater of food" (*annādya*). The rest is the same [as before].

Now, that which is its northern aperture is the Samāna breath; it is the mind, it is Parjanya. One should meditate upon it as fame and splendor. He who knows this becomes possessed of fame and possessed of splendor.

Now, that which is its northern cavity—the cavity situated in the north—is the specific vital air (vāyu-viśeṣa) located therein; it is called *samāna* because it carries equally what has been eaten and drunk. The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) connected to that is the mind (*manas*). That is the deity Parjanya, whose nature is rain, as well as the waters caused by Parjanya, according to the Vedic revelation: "The waters and Varuṇa were created by the mind. This very thing is also *kīrti* (fame), because knowledge of the mind is the cause of fame. Fame is renown that extends beyond one's immediate presence; it is glory (*yaśas*).

Fame is that which is perceived by one’s own senses; it is renown, prosperity, splendor, and the loveliness inherent in the body. Furthermore, because it arises from glory, it is called "glory. The rest is the same as before. Now, that which is its upward channel is the *udāna* breath, it is air, it is space. One should meditate upon this as vigor (*ojas*) and greatness (*maha*). He who knows this becomes vigorous and great. 5. (5) ————-

Now, that which is its upper cavity is the *udāna* [vital breath]. Starting from the soles of the feet and moving upward, it is called *udāna* because it "breathes out" (*aniti*) while performing actions for the purpose of ascending and for excellence. That is the wind (*vāyu*), and its substratum is space (*ākāśa*). Because these two—wind and space—are the cause of vigor (*ojas*), they are called *ojas*; and because of their greatness, they are called *maha*. The rest is the same as before.

These five persons of Brahman are indeed the gatekeepers of the heavenly world. He who knows these five persons of Brahman as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world, in his family a hero is born; he attains the heavenly world—he who knows these five persons of Brahman as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world. 6.

These aforementioned five persons of the Brahman within the heart (*hārdasya brahmaṇaḥ puruṣāḥ*), by virtue of their connection to the five gates, are like royal servants stationed at the doors; they are the gatekeepers of the heavenly world within the heart. For by these—the eye, ear, speech, mind, and breath—which are directed outward, the gates for attaining the Brahman within the heart are blocked. Indeed, this is evident: because the senses are unsubdued and because one is rooted in the falsehood of attachment to external objects, the mind does not abide in the Brahman within the heart.

Therefore, it has been truly said that these five persons of Brahman are the gatekeepers of the heavenly world. Hence, he who knows and meditates upon them—endowed with the aforementioned qualities—as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world, brings them under his control through meditation. Just as one brings the gatekeepers of a king under control by means of service, he reaches the heavenly world unhindered by them, even as a king [reaches] the heart-Brahman. Furthermore, in the family of this knower, a heroic son is born, because of his service to heroic persons.

And by the discharge of that debt, it serves as the cause for engaging in the meditation on Brahman; consequently, since this leads indirectly to the attainment of the heavenly world, the attainment of the heavenly world alone is the single fruit.

Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the highest worlds above all others—that is indeed this light which is here within the person. This is the perception of it: when one perceives warmth through touch in this body. This is the hearing of it: when, having closed one's ears, one hears as if a sound, as if a roar, as if from a blazing fire. One should meditate upon this as "the seen and the heard," for such a person becomes beautiful of aspect and renowned.
He who knows this becomes so; he who knows this becomes so. (7) Thus ends the thirteenth section.

Now, that which is said—"this wise one attains the heavenly world by serving heroic men"—and "three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven," this very thing must be brought within the range of the senses of sight and hearing by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*), just as fire and other things are inferred by smoke and other signs. For in this way, there will be a firm conviction regarding the matter as it has been stated—namely, a certainty [of its reality] through its non-difference [from the perceived].

Therefore, he says: "Beyond that"—that is, beyond this heaven, the world of *dyu*; the word "paraḥ" (beyond) is used with a change of gender. "The light shines"—because it is self-luminous and eternally manifest, it is said to "shine" as if it were shining, for a flaming characteristic such as that of fire and the like is impossible [in its case]. The phrase "on the backs of all" (*viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*) is explained as "on the backs of everything" (*sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*), meaning "above the cycle of transmigratory existence" (*saṃsāra*). For the entire cycle of existence is indeed [the realm of] *saṃsāra*, since that which is not within *saṃsāra* is one and without differentiation.

To eliminate the suspicion that *anuttameṣu* might be a *tatpuruṣa* compound, he says: "in the highest worlds. Because the Supreme Lord, in his manifested form as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, is in close proximity to Satyaloka and the other higher realms, it is said: "in the highest worlds. "This indeed is that"—namely, this very light which is within this person, in the middle [of the heart], which is perceived through the signs graspable by the eye and the ear, namely heat and sound.

That which is grasped by the skin in the form of touch is grasped by the eye alone, because the skin provides a firm conviction [regarding the object] and because color and touch are invariably concomitant.

But how does that light come to be within the range of touch and sight? To this he says: "When"—at which time—"this," which is an adverbial modifier, [means] when one perceives by means of the hand, through contact, the state of heat—the quality of warm touch—which coexists with form, within this body; for that heat is the mark (*liṅga*) of the light of the conscious Self (*caitanyātmajyotiṣaḥ*) which has entered the body for the purpose of differentiating name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), because of its non-deviation. Indeed, heat never deviates from the living Self.

For it is known that one will live while it is warm and die when it is cold; and because at the time of death the heat merges into the supreme deity, it attains non-distinction with that which is beyond. Therefore, warmth is an uncommon mark (liṅga), just as smoke is for fire. Thus, this "vision" (dṛṣṭi) of that supreme [Self] is a means of seeing, like a direct perception—this is the meaning. Likewise, this "hearing" (śruti) of that light is also said to be a means of hearing.

Whenever a person desires to hear the sign of light—that is, wishes to listen to it—then, having closed this organ (the ear)—the word "this" being an adverbial modifier meaning "having covered it," i.e., having shut it with both fingers—he hears a sound like a roar, a "ninada" which is like the rattling of a chariot; or a sound like a bellowing, like the lowing of a bull; and just as one hears the sound of a fire burning outside, so too he hears that sound within the body. This is that light.

Because it possesses the qualities of being seen and heard, one should meditate upon it as "the seen and the heard. From such meditation, one becomes *cakṣuṣya* (lovely to look at) and *darśanīya* (handsome), and *śruta* (learned) and *viśruta* (widely renowned). The fruit that results from meditating on the quality of touch is here attributed to form, expressed by the term *cakṣuṣya*; this is because form and touch are co-existent, and because being handsome is a desirable quality. In this way, the fruit of the knowledge becomes logically consistent, whereas it would not be so if the fruit were merely the possession of softness and other tactile qualities. He who knows these two aforementioned qualities in this manner attains the world of heaven; however, the previously mentioned unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭa-phala*) remains. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth section:
"All this, indeed, is Brahman, for it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; therefore, one should meditate with a tranquil mind. Now, a person consists of volition (*kratu*);
as is his volition in this world, so does he become after departing from here. He should therefore form a firm resolve. (1)

Introduction: Desiring to prescribe the worship of that very same Brahman—who is immortal, possesses infinite qualities and infinite powers, and is to be meditated upon through various distinctions—as being endowed with specific attributes and powers, he says:

"Everything" (*sarvam*) means the whole. The particle "indeed" (*khalu*) is a grammatical expletive used for the purpose of ornamenting the sentence. This world—transformed by name and form and being the object of perception and other means of knowledge—has Brahman as its cause; it is called *brahma* because it is the greatest (*vṛddhatama*). To the question, "In what way is everything Brahman?", he says: "Because it is born from that, dissolves into that, and breathes in that" (*tajjalān*). Everything is born from that Brahman through the sequence of fire, water, and food; therefore, it is "born from that" (*tajjam*).

Likewise, by that very same process of birth in reverse order, it is dissolved into that very Brahman; it merges with it as its own self, and thus it is "tallam" (that-dissolved). Likewise, during that very time of maintenance, it breathes and moves—that is, it acts. Thus, through its identity with Brahman, it is undifferentiated across the three periods of time, because it cannot be perceived apart from it. Therefore, this world is indeed that [Brahman]. And how this is one and non-dual, we shall explain in detail in the sixth chapter.

And because all this is Brahman, therefore, being tranquil—meaning free from defects such as attachment and aversion—and self-controlled, one should meditate upon that which is all-Brahman through the qualities about to be described. How should one meditate? One should form a *kratu*—*kratu* meaning resolve, determination, or an unwavering conviction that "it is exactly thus and not otherwise"—one should form that *kratu*; this connects with the word "meditate" (*upāsīta*), which occurs later in the sentence.

But what is the purpose to be accomplished by the instrument of sacrifice (*kratukaraṇa*), or how is the sacrifice to be performed? And how is the instrument of sacrifice the means for achieving the intended goal? To explain this matter, there is the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*). The phrase "Now indeed" (*atha khalu*) has the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*): because the person—the individual soul (*jīva*)—consists of sacrifice, is predominantly sacrifice, and is of the nature of resolve (*adhyavasāya*).

"According to his resolve" (*yathākratuḥ*): whatever his resolve (*kratu*) is, that he is "according to his resolve"—whatever his determination or whatever his conviction was while living in this world, in that very way he becomes after departing from and dying to this body; the meaning is that he becomes one whose nature consists of the fruit corresponding to his resolve. For this is indeed seen from the scriptures: "Whatever state of being he remembers when he leaves the body at the end," and so forth.

Since this arrangement is thus established by the authority of the scriptures, therefore, knowing this, one should perform the sacrifice—namely, that sacrifice which we shall describe. Since it is thus logically established through the authority of the scriptures that the fruit corresponds to the sacrifice, therefore that sacrifice must be performed.

[He is] consisting of mind, having the vital breath for a body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, the performer of all actions, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, without speech, and without concern.

How so? "Consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) means having the mind as its primary constituent. That which is called "mind" (*manas*) is so named because one thinks (*manute*) by means of it; it becomes engaged with objects through its own function. He is "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) by means of that mind; thus he appears as if engaged [with objects] and as if withdrawn from them. For this very reason, he has "the vital breath as his body" (*prāṇaśarīra*). The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), in which the two powers of cognition and action are conjoined, according to the Vedic scripture: "That which is the vital breath is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that which is wisdom is the vital breath."

He whose body is *prāṇa* (vital breath) is "one whose body is *prāṇa*" (*prāṇa-śarīra*), according to another scriptural passage: "Consisting of mind, the leader of the body that is *prāṇa*. He is "effulgent in form" (*bhārūpa*); he whose form is light—that is, whose form is characterized by consciousness—is effulgent in form. He is "of true resolve" (*satya-saṃkalpa*); he whose resolves are true, that is, unfailing, is one of true resolve. The meaning is that the resolve of the Lord does not have uncertain results, as is the case with the resolves of worldly beings. [The phrase] "the resolve of the Lord has uncertain results like that of worldly beings" is repeated for emphasis.

Because the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of transmigrating beings is obstructed by "untruth" (*anṛta*), which is the cause of false results, the text will later state that their resolve has false results: "For they are obstructed by untruth. "Ākāśātman" means one whose self (*ātman*)—that is, whose essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is like space (*ākāśa*). Such likeness to space on the part of the Lord (*īśvara*) consists in his omnipresence, subtlety, and being devoid of form and other such qualities.

"Performing all actions": because the entire universe is created by that Lord, He is "one whose action is everything. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "For He is the creator of all. "Possessing all desires": He is "one whose desires are all," meaning His desires are entirely free from defect. This is according to the Smṛti: "Among beings, I am desire not opposed to dharma. Now, one might object: since the statement "I am desire" (kāmo'smi) uses a singular noun, the use of the *bahuvrīhi* compound "possessing all desires" (*sarvakāma*) is not possible here.

No, because desire would then be something to be accomplished, and it would follow that the Lord, like sound and other objects, exists for the sake of another. Therefore, just as "one who has all desires" (*sarvakāma*) here is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, so too in the phrase "I am desire" (*kāmo'smi*), the meaning must be understood as a *smṛti* (recollection). He is "possessed of all odors" (*sarvagandha*) because all odors are conducive to his happiness; this is according to the *smṛti*: "The holy odor is in the earth. Likewise, the tastes (*rasa*) are also to be understood in the same way.

This is because scripture declares that the perception of demerit, odor, and taste is caused by connection with evil, as the Śruti states: "Therefore, by means of it [the nose], one smells both the fragrant and the foul-smelling; for this [organ] is pierced by evil. Furthermore, there can be no contact with evil for the Lord, since defects such as ignorance (avidyā) are impossible in His case.

This entire world is *abhyāttaḥ*—that is, pervaded by Him. The suffix *-niṣṭhā* is used here in the agentive sense for the root *at*, which means "to pervade. Likewise, He is *avākī*: that by which one speaks is *vāk*; or rather, *vākaḥ* is derived from the root *vac* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an instrument (the organ of speech). One who possesses such a thing is *vākī*; one who does not possess it is *avākī*. Furthermore, the negation of speech here is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the scriptures mention smell, taste, and so forth; thus, the organs of smell and the rest would otherwise be attributed to the Lord for the purpose of perceiving odors and other objects.

Therefore, by the negation of speech, those [organs] are also negated, based on such Vedic mantras as: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears. "Anādara" means the absence of agitation; for agitation would occur upon attaining what has not yet been attained by one whose desires are unfulfilled. But for the Lord, who has all desires fulfilled and is eternally content, there is no agitation whatsoever.

This Self of mine within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet; this Self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, and greater than these worlds. 3.

This Self of mine, possessing the qualities described, is within my heart—inside the lotus of the heart—and is subtler than the subtle (*aṇīyān*), as shown by the examples "than a grain of rice" or "than a grain of barley," and so forth, for the purpose of demonstrating extreme minuteness. Fearing that by saying it is "subtler than *śyāmāka* grain or *śyāmāka* rice," it might be understood as having a limited atomic dimension, he begins the refutation of that with the words: "This Self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth," and so on.

By showing its greatness through a comparison with that which is greater in measure, [the text] demonstrates its infinite magnitude, beginning with "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and ending with "greater than these worlds.

"He who possesses all works, all desires, all odors, all tastes—he who has pervaded all this, who is without speech and without concern—this is my Self within the heart; this is Brahman. After departing from here, I shall attain Him. Thus spoke Śāṇḍilya, indeed, there is no doubt for one who has this [conviction]. Thus spoke Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya. Thus ends the fourteenth section. (14) (4)

The Lord, characterized by the qualities as previously described, is to be meditated upon, but not as qualified by those qualities alone—just as when it is said, "Bring the king's man" or "Bring the one with brindled cows," the bringing does not extend to the qualifier itself; this same logic would apply here as well. Therefore, to preclude that [misconception], the words beginning with "the performer of all actions" are stated again. Consequently, the Lord is to be meditated upon precisely as qualified by the attributes such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and so forth.

For this very reason, unlike in the sixth and seventh [chapters], he does not here consecrate [the seeker] to sovereignty with the words "That thou art" or "The Self alone is all this"; rather, he does so based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the passage: "This is my Self, this is Brahman; having departed from hence, I shall attain that. For the word "Self" (ātman) here does not denote the inner self (pratyagātman), because the genitive case in "my" (mama) indicates a relationship [of possession], and because the phrase "I shall attain that" indicates a distinction between object and agent.

[Objection: But does not the sixth [chapter] also show that the merging into Being (*sat-sampatti*) is separated by another time, in the passage "Then I shall be merged"? [Reply: No, because that passage is intended to mean the persistence of the remaining impressions of the commenced [karma]; it does not have the sense of being separated by another time, for otherwise there would be the consequence of subverting the meaning of "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).

Although the word "self" (ātman) has the sense of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and although the context of "all this is indeed Brahman" states, "This is my self within the heart; this is Brahman," nevertheless, without entirely abandoning even a slight sense of concealment, it is said: "Having departed from here, from this body, I shall attain that Self."

For one who knows thus, for whom there may be the realization, "I am attaining the Self according to the form of my resolve," thinking, "Truly, indeed, I shall become thus after death; I shall not become otherwise"—and in this matter regarding the connection between the resolve and its fruit, there is no doubt—that wise man attains the state of the Lord exactly as he intended. This is what the sage named Śāṇḍilya said; indeed, he spoke thus. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourteenth section:
"The chest whose belly is the intermediate space, whose base is the earth, does not decay."

The directions are its corners, and the sky is its upper opening. This is that treasure-chest containing all wealth; in it, this entire universe is supported. Introduction: It was stated that "in his family a hero is born. However, the mere birth of a hero is not sufficient for the protection of the father; as another Vedic text says, "Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is worthy of the world. Consequently, the present inquiry into the treasure-chest (kośa) is commenced for the purpose of ensuring such longevity for him. Although it was not mentioned immediately following the discussion on the most venerable knowledge due to being interrupted by other topics, it is now begun.

(1) He whose belly is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and whose interior is hollow is this "Antarikṣodara"; he is a "treasury" (*kośa*), for, due to similarity in many respects, he is like a treasury. And he has the earth as his base (*bhūmibudhna*); that which has the earth as its foundation or root is "bhūmibudhna. He does not decay nor perish, because he consists of the three worlds. For he persists for the duration of a thousand ages (*sahasrayuga*). Indeed, all the directions are his corners (*srakti*). The sky is the upper opening of this treasury.

This very sheath, possessing the qualities described above, is the "receptacle of wealth" (*vasudhāna*); for in it is deposited the "wealth" known as the fruits of the actions of living beings, and thus it is the receptacle of wealth. Within it rests—meaning it is supported and situated—all this universe, comprising the entirety of the fruits of the actions of living beings along with their means, which is perceived through direct perception and other valid means of knowledge.

Of these, the eastern quarter is named Juhū, the southern is named Sahamānā, the western is named Rājñī, and the northern is named Subhūtā; their calf is Vāyu. He who knows this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters does not weep over the death of a son. I know this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters; may I not weep over the death of a son. 2. (2)

Of this [body], the eastern direction is its front part; it is named *juhū* because ritualists, facing east, offer oblations (*juhvati*) in this direction—thus it is named *juhū*. The southern direction is named *sahamānā* because living beings in the city of Yama endure (*sahante*) the fruits of their evil deeds in this direction—thus it is named *sahamānā*. Likewise, the western direction is named *rājñī*; it is presided over by King Varuṇa, or it is so called due to its connection with the color of twilight.

The northern quarter is called *Subhūtā* because it is presided over by prosperous lords such as Īśvara, Kubera, and others; thus it is named Subhūtā. The wind is the calf of those quarters, because the wind is born from the directions, as seen in expressions such as "the east wind" (*purovāta*). Whoever desires long life for a son knows this wind—the calf of the quarters endowed with the aforementioned qualities—as the Immortal (*amṛta*); he does not weep the "son's weeping," that is, he does not weep on account of a son, meaning his son does not die.

Since the consciousness regarding the treasury, the quarters, and the calf is thus distinguished, therefore, desiring the life of my son, I know and recognize this wind as the calf of the quarters. Therefore, do not weep for my son; let there be no "son-weeping" on my account caused by the death of my son. I take refuge in the unharmed treasury with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such; I take refuge in the vital breath with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such; I take refuge in *bhūḥ* with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such; I take refuge in *bhuvaḥ* with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such; I take refuge in *svaḥ* with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such. 3. (3) ————-

"I take refuge in the inviolable, imperishable treasure-store as described; I have taken refuge for the sake of my son’s life. He pronounces his son’s name three times, saying, "By this one, by that one, by that one. Likewise: "I take refuge in Prāṇa—by this one, by that one, by that one"; "I take refuge in Bhūḥ—by this one, by that one, by that one"; "I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ—by this one, by that one, by that one"; "I take refuge in Svaḥ—by this one, by that one, by that one. In every case, he pronounces the name again and again, saying, "I take refuge. When I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa," Prāṇa indeed is all this being, whatever exists; it was to that very thing that I took refuge. 4. (4) —-

When I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa," that was stated for the purpose of explanation. Prāṇa indeed is all this being, which is this world. As he will say later, "As the spokes in the hub. Therefore, by that exposition of Prāṇa, I have reached—that is, I have become one who has taken refuge in—all that. Now, when I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I meant "I take refuge in the earth, I take refuge in the intermediate space, I take refuge in heaven.
Likewise, when I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I meant that I take refuge in the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
And when I said, "I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ," I meant this: I take refuge in Agni, I take refuge in Vāyu, and I take refuge in Āditya. 6.
Now, when I said, "I take refuge in *bhuvaḥ*," I meant that I take refuge in Agni and the other [deities].

And when I said, "I take refuge in *svaḥ*," I meant that I take refuge in the Ṛgveda, I take refuge in the Yajurveda, and I take refuge in the Sāmaveda; I meant that very thing, I meant that very thing. Thus ends the fifteenth section.

Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in *svaḥ*," I meant that I take refuge in the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas. Thereafter, one should mutter the mantras mentioned above; then, having meditated properly upon the previously described undecaying treasure-chest together with its calves in the form of the directions. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth section.

Man, indeed, is the sacrifice. His twenty-four years constitute the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). The Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī; therefore, the Vasus are connected to it. The Vasus are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for they cause all this to dwell (*vāsayanti*). 1.

Introduction: The meditation (*upāsana*) and recitation (*japa*) for the sake of a son’s longevity have been explained. Now, prescribing this meditation and recitation for one's own long life, the author says: for only by living does one personally partake in the fruits such as sons, and not otherwise. Therefore, a person accomplishes the self as the sacrifice—(1)—

The "person" (puruṣa) is the aggregate of the body and its organs, characterized by life, exactly as commonly known; the word *vāva* is for the purpose of emphasis, meaning that the person alone is the sacrifice. For he establishes the nature of the sacrifice through commonalities. How so? Those twenty-four years of the life-span of that person constitute the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) of the sacrifice called "person."

By what commonality? He says: The *gāyatrī* metre consists of twenty-four syllables, and the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*) of the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*) belongs to the *gāyatrī*. Therefore, a person endowed with a twenty-four-year lifespan is identical to the morning extraction; thus, by virtue of this similarity to the ritual sacrifice, he is a "sacrifice. Likewise, for the two subsequent stages of life, the identification with the other two extractions should be stated based on the commonality of the number of syllables in the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* metres.

Furthermore, the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) of this human sacrifice belongs to the Vasus, just as it does in the ritual sacrifice; that is to say, the Vasus, the gods, are "attached to" or follow it as its presiding deities. Since the Vasus—Agni and the others—are likewise present in the human sacrifice as they are in the ritual sacrifice, the text specifies them further: "The Vasus are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)," meaning the senses such as speech and the vital airs (*vāyu*). For it is because these [breaths] cause this entire collection of living beings, beginning with man, to "dwell" (*vas*) that they are called Vasus.

Indeed, when the vital breaths dwell within the body, all this world dwells there; otherwise, it does not. Thus, they are called Vasus both because of their dwelling (*vasana*) and because they cause things to dwell (*vāsana*).

If, at this stage of life, something should afflict him, he should say: "O Prāṇas, O Vasus, extend for me this morning libation and the midday libation, so that the sacrifice may not be lost in the midst of the Prāṇas and the Vasus. Thereupon he rises up from it and becomes free from disease. 2.

If, while he is a performer of the sacrifice at this age completed by the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), some cause for fear of death such as disease or the like should afflict him—that is, should produce suffering—then that person who is a performer of the sacrifice, regarding himself as the sacrifice, should speak—that is, should recite—this mantra: "O vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*), O Vasus, this morning libation of mine, which belongs to my sacrifice, exists; may you extend it toward the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) by means of the midday libation of life."

"Make it joined, unified, and continuous"—this is the meaning. "May I, the sacrifice, not be lost among you, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the riches (*vasus*), who are the masters of the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*); may I not perish, may I not be cut off"—this is the meaning. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the mantra. By means of that recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), he rises up from, emerges from, that affliction. Having emerged and being liberated, he indeed becomes free from disease (*agada*) and free from affliction (*anupatāpa*).

Now, those forty-four years constitute the midday pressing (*mādhyandinaṃ savanam*). The *triṣṭubh* meter consists of forty-four syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. The Rudras are dependent upon it. The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the Rudras, for they make all this weep.

... 3 ... Now, regarding "those forty-four years" and so forth, the rest is the same. They are called Rudras because they weep (*rudanti*) and cause [others] to weep; for these vital breaths are cruel in their middle age, and therefore they are the Rudras.

If, at this stage of life, something should afflict him, he should say: "O Prāṇas, O Rudras, extend for me this midday pressing and the third pressing; may the sacrifice not be lost among you, the Prāṇas, the Rudras. Thereupon he rises up from that [affliction] and becomes free from disease. 4. (4) No commentary provided for this verse.

Now, those forty-eight years constitute the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*). The Jagatī meter has forty-eight syllables, and the third libation belongs to the Jagatī; therefore, the Ādityas are connected to it. The Ādityas are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for they take up all this. If, during this stage of life, anything should afflict him, he should say: "O vital breaths, O Ādityas, extend this third libation, my life-force! May the sacrifice not be lost upon me in the midst of the vital breaths, the Ādityas! Thereupon he rises up from that [affliction] and becomes free from disease.

(6) Likewise, the Ādityas are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). For they take up (*ādadate*) this collection of sound and other objects; therefore, they are called Ādityas. "The third pressing is life" means that it completes—the sense being that it continues and brings to completion—the sacrifice, which consists of one hundred and sixteen years. The rest is the same. Showing that knowledge, when firmly established, leads to its fruit, he cites an example:

Knowing this, Mahidāsa Aitareya indeed said: "Why do you afflict me with this [fasting], since I shall not depart because of it? He lived for one hundred and sixteen years. Whoever knows this lives for one hundred and sixteen years. Thus ends the sixteenth section. 16. (7)

This is indeed the vision of sacrifice that Mahidāsa by name—the son of Itarā (Aitareya)—who was learned in it, spoke. "O disease, why do you afflict me with this torment? Since I am the Sacrifice, I shall not depart, I shall not die, because of this torment caused by you; therefore, your labor is in vain. This is what he said—this is the connection with the preceding. Having reached such a firm resolve, he lived for one hundred and sixteen years.

Anyone else who possesses such a certainty also lives for one hundred and sixteen years; that is to say, he who knows—that is, understands—the aforementioned accomplishment of the sacrifice. Thus ends the commentary on the sixteenth section of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

When he is hungry, when he is thirsty, and when he does not find pleasure—these are his initiations (dīkṣā). (1) The statement beginning with "when he is hungry" is a general reference to sacrifice, which connects back to the preceding [section] concerning the person (puruṣa). "When he is hungry" means he desires to eat; likewise, "when he is thirsty" means he desires to drink; and "when he does not find pleasure" refers to the cause of not obtaining what is desired and so forth. Whatever suffering of this kind he experiences, these are his initiations, because of the commonality of suffering, just as in the case of a ritual sacrifice.

Now, when he eats, when he drinks, and when he enjoys himself—that is, when he experiences pleasure through contact with desired objects and the like—he attains similarity to the *upasad* rites. For the *upasad* rites possess a certain ease due to the observance of the milk-vow (*payovrata*), and there is a sense of relief because the days of restricted eating are drawing near; thus, there is a commonality between eating and the other acts and the *upasad* rites.
Now, when one laughs, when one eats, and when one engages in sexual intercourse, he overcomes that [evil] by means of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns alone.

(3) Now, when one laughs, when one eats— that is, consumes— and when one engages in sexual intercourse, he attains equality with those [hymns] through the commonality of possessing sound (*śabdatva*).
Now, as for austerity,
charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness— these are its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), because they share the common quality of nourishing righteousness (dharma).

Therefore they say, "He will press [the Soma]" (*soṣyati*) or "He has pressed [the Soma]" (*asoṣṭa*); for that [birth] is his very re-birth, and death itself is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). And because the sacrifice is the person (*puruṣa*), therefore when his mother gives birth to him, others say of his mother, "She will press [the Soma]" (*soṣyati*); and when she has given birth, they say, "Pūrṇikā has pressed [it]" (*asoṣṭa*). Just as in the ritual sacrifice one says, "Devadatta will press the Soma" or "Yajñadatta has pressed the Soma," it follows from this commonality of terminology that the person is the sacrifice.

Furthermore, the very re-birth of this sacrifice called "man"—that which consists in his connection with the words "he will beget" (*soṣyati*) and "he begot" (*asoṣṭa*)—is like the ritual of a formal sacrifice. Moreover, death itself is the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) of this human sacrifice, because of the commonality of being the final completion.
