At the time of his end, he should reflect upon these three [formulas]: 'Thou art the imperishable; thou art the unshakable; thou art sharpened by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This Brahman has four quarters: speech is one quarter, breath is one quarter, the eye is one quarter, and the ear is one quarter—this is with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). This very Brahman called "mind" (*manas*) has four quarters—that is, it has four parts. How does the mind-Brahman have four quarters? In this context, speech alone is the fourth foot of the mind as Brahman, with reference to the other three feet—for by means of speech, like a foot, one stands toward the objects to be expressed, such as cows and so forth; therefore, speech is like a foot of the mind. To him who had spoken thus, the other—the leader—replied: "Are! This king is base and wretched; why do you disparage him by saying, 'Who is he that possesses such greatness? You speak of him with such great respect as if he were Raikva Sayugvān. 'Sayugvān' means one who possesses a *yugvan*—that is, a cart (*gantrī*). You speak of this man as if he were Raikva; the intention is that it is improper and unsuitable to speak of him in such a way, as if he were Raikva."
The other said, "Who indeed is this Raikva with the cart that you speak of? To him who had spoken thus, Bhallākṣa said: "Listen as to who that Raikva is.

Just as all the lower throws of dice go to one who has won the *kṛtāya* throw, even so everything that people do that is good goes to him; he knows what he knows—he who knows that is the one of whom I speak.

Just as in the world, *kṛta*—known by the name *kṛta* and well-known in the context of gambling as a four-sided die—is victorious for those engaged in the game, then for that victorious one, the others—the three, two, and one-sided dice named *tretā*, *dvāpara*, and *kali*—converge, come together, and are subsumed within it; the meaning is that since the three, two, and one-sided dice exist within the four-sided *kṛta* die, they are included therein.

Just as in this illustration, so too everything that all creatures in the world perform as good—that is, the entire collection of auspicious and righteous acts—converges upon and is contained within this Raikva, who stands in the place of the *kṛtāya* (the highest die), while those standing in the place of the *tretā* and other dice are included within him. What is that? Whatever righteous deeds all beings in the world perform, all of that is included within the merit of Raikva; and the meaning is that the fruit of all the religious merits of all living beings is included within his own fruit. Likewise, it applies to anyone else who knows that which is to be known.

What is that? That which is to be known—Raikva knows it; and whoever else knows that object of knowledge, him too [the sage] approaches as being like Raikva, including the entire collection of duties pertaining to all living beings and their fruits—this is understood from the context. Such a person, even though he be a mere *araikva* (one who is not Raikva), is addressed by me as a "knower" (*vidvān*) when spoken of in this way; the intention is that he alone becomes one who occupies the position of the *kṛtāya* throw, just like Raikva.

Now Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa overheard this. As he was rising, he said to his charioteer, "O Āṅgāri, do you speak of Raikva as if he were Sayugvā? "But who is this Sayugvā Raikva? [The charioteer replied. Then King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, staying upon the roof of his palace, heard these words of the swan—words which were of the nature of a censure directed at himself and of the nature of praise for another wise man such as Raikva. Remembering those words of the swan, he passed the remainder of the night reflecting upon them again and again.

Then the king, being awakened by the bards with words of praise while still rising from his bed or even while abandoning sleep, spoke to the steward (Kṣattṛ): "O dear boy, why do you speak of me as if I were Raikva with the cart? (2)—"O Raikva, these six hundred cows have been brought for you by me; here is this gold necklace and this chariot drawn by mules. Accept this wealth. Regarding the address "O Śūdra": [An objection is raised: "But surely this man is a king because of his connection with the *kṣattṛ* (charioteer), for it was said, 'He spoke to the *kṣattṛ*'; moreover, since one approaches a Brāhmaṇa to acquire knowledge and a Śūdra lacks the qualification [for such knowledge], how can Raikva speak this inappropriate word, 'O Śūdra'? To this, the teachers say: Upon hearing the words of the swan, grief entered him; having heard of the greatness of Raikva, he rushed toward him out of that grief. Thus, the Ṛṣi, demonstrating his own indirect knowledge [of the truth], addressed him as "O Śūdra."

"Or rather, he approached him for the sake of acquiring knowledge with wealth alone, like a *śūdra*, and not through service; it was not that he was a *śūdra* by birth. Others, however, say: "He spoke to him as 'a *śūdra*' out of anger because only a small amount of wealth had been brought. And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the fact that the bringing of much wealth is mentioned.
Then, having understood the sage's intention, Janaśruti Pautrāyaṇa again set out, taking an additional thousand cows as well as his own daughter, who was pleasing to the sage.

He said to him: "Raikva, here are a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this wife, and this village in which you dwell; O venerable sir, instruct me further. [4] (4–5) — Raikva replied: "Here are a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, and this wife—my daughter brought for the sake of a wife—and this village in which you reside; all of that has been prepared by me for your sake."

"Taking all this, please instruct me, O Venerable One. Thus addressed, [the teacher] spoke while "upholding"—that is, knowing—the face of the king's daughter who had been brought there as a wife for him, which was the very gateway, the sacred point (*tīrtha*) for the imparting of knowledge. For the statement of Knowledge is well known: "The celibate student, the giver of wealth, the wise man, the learned scholar, and the beloved—through these, or through Knowledge itself, one imparts Knowledge; these six are my sacred points (*tīrthāni*). Knowing this and upholding it, he spoke.

"You brought these cows"—that is, you have brought them—and whatever other wealth there was, [the ellipsis of the sentence is] "that is well done. The address "O Śūdra" is merely a repetition of what was said before, and not due to any other cause as previously [explained]. By this very opening—the gateway for receiving knowledge—you are making me converse; the meaning is that you are causing me to speak.

These very villages, known as Raikvaparṇas, are famous among the Mahāvṛṣa regions; in those villages where Raikva had lived, the king gave them to that Raikva. Air, indeed, is the absorber (*saṃvarga*). "Air" refers to the external air; the particle "indeed" (*vāva*) serves for emphasis. It is called the "absorber" because of its absorbing, gathering, or swallowing [of other elements]. Since it brings the deities to be mentioned later—fire and the others—into its own nature, it is the absorber; thus, the quality known as absorption is to be meditated upon in air, following the analogy of the inclusion of the *kṛta* throw within the dice-game.

How is it that the air is the "absorber"? He says: When, at which time, fire goes out—that is, reaches extinction and becomes still—then that fire goes unto the air alone; it attains the very nature of the air. Likewise, when the sun sets, it goes unto the air alone. When the moon sets, it goes unto the air alone.

Now, one might ask: how can the sun and the moon, while remaining in their own essential forms, merge into the wind? This is not a fault, because at the time of setting, their disappearance is caused by the wind; for the sun is led to its setting by the wind, since movement is the effect of the wind. Alternatively, at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), when the sun and moon lose their specific forms, they would indeed merge into the wind in the form of light (*tejas*).

Likewise, when the waters dry up—that is, reach a state of desiccation—they merge into the air alone. Since the air indeed withdraws these [elements], beginning with fire, which possess great power, therefore the air is to be meditated upon as having the quality of being the "absorber" (*saṃvarga*). Thus has been stated the vision of the absorber among the deities with respect to the divine realm.

Immediately following this, the vision of the absorber (*saṃvarga*) within the self is stated. The vital breath (*prāṇa*), indeed, is the primary absorber. When that person sleeps—at whatever time—he absorbs speech into himself, just as fire absorbs into the wind; the eye into the breath, the ear into the breath, and the mind into the breath. For it is the breath that absorbs all these, beginning with speech. These two, indeed, are the two absorbers characterized by the quality of absorbing: Vāyu alone among the gods is the absorber, and the primary breath among the vital functions such as speech.

(5) Now, this narrative is commenced for the purpose of praising these two. *Ha* indicates a traditional report (*aitihya*). Śaunaka—the offspring of Śunaka—and Kāpeya, who belongs to the lineage of Kapi, as well as Abhipratārin by name, the offspring of Kakṣasena (a Kākṣaseni), were seated for a meal and were being served by cooks. At that time, a religious student (*brahmacārī*), one who was proud of his knowledge of Brahman, begged (*bibhikṣe*)—that is, he asked for alms—from them. Having perceived the religious student’s pride in his knowledge of Brahman, and desiring to test him, they both did not give him alms; they did not give it to him, thinking, "What will he say?"

He said: "The student [asked about] the four of the Great-Souled One"—this is the accusative plural. "One god" refers to Vāyu, who has swallowed the fires and so forth, or Prāṇa, who has swallowed speech and so forth. Who is he? He is Prajāpati; he has swallowed (*jagāra*), that is, he has consumed them. Some take this as the question: "Who is he who wakes? [The answer is: "The guardian of the world. That which is called "world" (*bhuvana*) is so named because beings (*bhūtāni*) exist within it; it refers to the entire realm beginning with the earth (*bhūḥ*). Its "guardian" (*gopāḥ*) means its protector, its preserver, its keeper.

"O Kāpeya, mortals—those subject to death or lacking discrimination—do not perceive, do not know, that Prajāpati who dwells manifoldly, O Abhipratārin, in the forms of the internal self (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaivata*), and the elemental (*adhibhūta*). Indeed, for that Prajāpati, this food is not given, though it is brought day after day and prepared for his consumption.

Then Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting upon those words of the students and considering them in his mind, approached the student. Having arrived, he said: "As for that which you said—'mortals do not perceive it'—we do perceive it. How so? It is the Self of all that is stationary and moving. Furthermore, having withdrawn and swallowed the deities, such as Agni and the rest, within itself, it is their progenitor and producer again in the form of Vāyu from the perspective of the divine."

Internally, he is the progenitor of speech and the other [senses] in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as well as of all creatures. Alternatively, he is the *ātman*, the progenitor of the gods—Agni, speech, and so forth—as well as of all creatures, both stationary and moving. He has golden fangs; that is to say, his fangs are immortal and unbroken. He is *babhasa*, one whose nature is to devour. He is *anasūri*: a *sūri* is a wise man; one who is not a *sūri* is an *asūri*; the negation of that is *anasūri*, meaning he is indeed a *sūri*.

The knowers of Brahman declare that the greatness—the majesty and manifestation—of this Prajāpati is great, exceeding all measure, and immeasurable. For, while not being eaten or consumed by others himself, he eats—that is, consumes—the "non-food" which consists of fire, speech, and the other elements. The particle *vā* is used here as an expletive. O student, we indeed worship this very Brahman characterized as described above; the word "we" connects with the distant verb "we worship."
Others explain: "We do not worship this; rather, we worship the Supreme Brahman itself. He said to his servants, "Give alms to him.

Therefore, they indeed gave [the food] to him, for they were the objects of begging. Those who are swallowed—Agni and the others—and he who is their swallower, Vāyu, together with the other five beginning with speech; likewise, there are five others internal to them, namely speech and the rest, along with the vital breath (prāṇa). All these become ten by number. Being ten, they constitute that [totality]: four are one-angled (ekāṅka), thus making four; three are three-angled (tryaṅka), thus making three others; two are two-angled (dvyadyaṅka), thus making two more; and one is one-angled (ekāṅka), thus making one last. In this manner...

Ten virtuous men constitute that which is made (*kṛtam*). Since this is so, therefore, in all ten directions, both the ten beginning with Fire and the ten beginning with Speech are food itself, due to the commonality of the number ten; for the Śruti says, "The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food. Thus they are food because they possess the number ten. For that very reason, the ten are contained within the "made" (*kṛta*), as we have stated by way of their fourfold nature. This very Virāj, being the number ten, is both food and the eater of food, by virtue of its being the "made."

For in the *kṛta* [number] the number ten is included; therefore, it is both food (*anna*) and the eater of food (*annādin*). Likewise, the knower, having become the self of the ten deities, is the Virāj by virtue of the number ten—being food through the *kṛta* number and the eater of food through that same number. By means of this food and eater of food, this entire world situated in the ten directions is seen—that is, perceived—as being constituted by the *kṛta* number. For one who knows thus, everything connected with the ten directions becomes seen and perceived as being of the nature of the *kṛta* number.

Furthermore, he becomes an eater of food, he who knows thus—that is, one who perceives as described. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the meditation.
Thus ends the commentary on the third section.
Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jabālā: "Mother, I wish to live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). Under what lineage shall I live? What indeed is my lineage? 1.

(1) Having unified the entire world—consisting of speech and so forth, fire and so forth, and praised as the relationship between food and the eater of food—and having divided it into sixteen parts, the instruction is now begun that the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) should be applied to it. The narrative is intended to demonstrate that faith (*śraddhā*) and austerity (*tapas*) are auxiliary members of the meditation on Brahman. One named Satyakāma—*ha* being a particle indicating tradition—Jābāla, the offspring of Jabālā, addressed his own mother, Jabālā. He called out to her.

"Brahmacarya is for the purpose of learning the Veda; O Sir, I wish to dwell in the teacher's family. What is my lineage? What is my lineage?"—"What indeed am I, of what lineage? She said to him, "I do not know this, dear one, what your lineage is. In my youth, while wandering about as a servant, I obtained you. Therefore, I do not know what your lineage is. But I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. You should speak of yourself as Satyakāma Jābāla. 2. (2) ————-

Being thus questioned, Jabālā said to her son: "I do not know this lineage of yours, my dear, as to what *gotra* you belong to. When asked, "Why do you not know? she replied: "In my husband's house, I was a servant whose nature was solely that of one performing service—moving about much, attending to guests, visitors, and the like. Because my mind was entirely occupied with service, it did not occur to me to remember such things as my lineage. And in my youth, at that time, I obtained you."

At that very time your father passed away; therefore I am without a protector. Being such, I do not know what your *gotra* is. My name is Jabālā, and your name is Satyakāma. Therefore, you should say to your teacher, "I am Satyakāma Jābāla"—this is the implication if you are questioned by your teacher. He then went to Gautama Hāridrumata and said, "I shall live as a religious student (*brahmacarya*) under your lordship; I would approach you, O Blessed One. (3–4)

Satyakāma went to Gautama Hāridrumata—the son of Haridruma, a descendant of the Gautama lineage—and said: "I shall live the life of a religious student under you, O Venerable One; therefore, I would approach you as a pupil. To him who had spoken thus, Gautama said: "Of what lineage are you, my dear? For a pupil whose family and lineage are known should be initiated. Thus questioned, Satyakāma replied.

He said: "I do not know this, sir, to what lineage I belong; however, I once questioned my mother, and when I asked her, my mother replied to me as before: 'I was constantly wandering about,' and so forth. I remember her words. Thus, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla."

He said to him, "Of what lineage are you, my dear? He replied, "I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am. I asked my mother, and she answered me: 'In my youth, while I was wandering much as a servant, I conceived you; therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. Thus, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla. 4. (3–4)

Satyakāma went to Gautama Hāridrumata—the son of Haridruma, a descendant of the Gautama lineage—and said: "I shall live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) under you, O Venerable One; therefore, I would approach you as a disciple. To him who had spoken thus, Gautama said: "Of what lineage (kiṃgotra) are you, my dear? For a disciple whose family and lineage are known is to be initiated. Thus questioned, Satyakāma replied.

He said: "I do not know this, sir, to what lineage I belong. However, I asked my mother; being thus questioned by me, my mother replied to me as before, saying, 'I was much occupied with wandering,' and so forth. I remember her words. Thus, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla."

He said to him: "A non-Brahmin is not fit to speak thus. Bring fuel, my dear; I will initiate you. You have not departed from the truth. Having initiated him, he set aside four hundred lean and weak cows and said: "Follow these, my dear. As he was driving them away, he said: "I shall not return until they have become a thousand. He lived away for many years, and when they had become a thousand— Thus ends the fourth section. 4. (5) —-

Gautama said to him: "This speech, which is endowed with sincerity and truth, is not fit to be uttered by one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, especially so. For Brāhmaṇas alone are naturally straightforward, and no others. Since you have not departed from the truth—which is the duty of the Brāhmaṇa caste—I shall therefore initiate you as a Brāhmaṇa."

"O gentle one, bring fuel for the fire-offering intended for internal purification," he said; having spoken thus, he initiated him and, having driven out from the herd of emaciated and weak cattle, he set aside four hundred and forty cows and said: "O gentle one, follow after these cows. Being thus addressed, as he was driving them toward the forest, he said: "I shall not return, nor shall I come back, until [the herd] has reached a full thousand."

Having spoken thus, he led the cows into the forest abounding in grass and water and free from the pairs of opposites; there he dwelt for a long period of years. When those cows, having been properly tended, had reached the number of one thousand—at that time—the bull addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "The cows have arrived, my dear. This concludes the commentary on the fourth section.
(1) "We have reached the number of one thousand; lead us to the teacher's family.

When the deity Vāyu, who presides over the northern direction, was satisfied by his faith and austerity, he entered into a bull and assumed the form of a bull in order to show him grace. Then that bull addressed him, calling out, "Satyakāma! Satyakāma replied to him, saying, "Yes, venerable sir. "My dear boy, we have now reached the number of one thousand; your promise is fulfilled. Therefore, lead us to the teacher's family."

"And I shall tell you a quarter of Brahman. "Let the Blessed One tell it to me," [he said]. To him he spoke: "The eastern direction is one part, the western direction is one part, the southern direction is one part, and the northern direction is one part. This, my dear, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named 'The Radiant'."

Furthermore, "I shall tell you, the supreme Brahman, one quarter (pāda). Being thus addressed, he replied: "May the Blessed One tell it to me. Being thus addressed, Ṛṣabha said to him, Satyakāma: "The eastern direction is a single part (kalā), a fourth portion of a quarter of Brahman."

Likewise, the western quarter is a part, the southern quarter is a part, and the northern quarter is a part. My dear, this is indeed one four-part foot of Brahman—one whose parts (kalās) are four, thus it is "four-part"—named "The Radiant" (Prakāśavān), meaning that which has "The Radiant" as its designation. Similarly, the other three feet of Brahman are also four-part.

"Agni will tell you one quarter," [the teacher said]. On the following day, Satyakāma drove the cows toward his teacher's home. When they reached the place where they were to stay for the evening, he built a fire, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down behind the fire facing the east. "Agni will tell you one quarter," [the teacher had said], and then [the teacher] ceased speaking. Then, on the next day, Satyakāma, having performed his daily obligatory duties, drove the cows toward his teacher's home.

Moving slowly, they set out toward the teacher’s house. At whatever time and place they arrived together at evening, having come together in one spot, he built up the fire, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down behind the fire facing east, meditating on the words of the bull.
The fire addressed him: "Satyakāma! "Revered sir," he replied.

"Dear boy, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. "Let the Blessed One tell it to me. He said to him: "The earth is one part, the intermediate space is one part, the sky is one part, and the ocean is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman called 'the Endless' (Anantavān).
Agni addressed him, calling out, "Satyakāma! Satyakāma replied to him, "Yes, Blessed One," giving his response.

He who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "the infinite," becomes infinite in this world; he wins worlds that are infinite—he who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "the infinite. Thus ends the sixth [section].

"Dear boy, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. "Let the venerable sir tell it to me. He said to him: "The earth is one part, the intermediate space is one part, the sky is one part, and the ocean is one part"—thus Agni spoke of a vision that has the Self as its object. "This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named 'the Endless' (Anantavān).

"Hamsa will tell you a quarter," [Agni said]. On the following day, he drove the cows out. Where they settled for the evening, there he built up a fire, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down behind the fire, facing east. 1.
(1) [The commentator] did not comment on this verse. A swan, having approached him, said, "Satyakāma! "Revered sir," he replied. (2) ...

That Fire said, "The Haṃsa shall tell you a quarter," and having said this, he ceased. The Haṃsa is the Sun, because of its whiteness and because of the commonality of flying. "On the morrow," and so forth, is the same as before. [Uddālaka said: "O gentle one, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. [Śvetaketu said: "May the venerable sir tell me. He said to him: "Fire is a sixteenth part, the Sun is a sixteenth part, the Moon is a sixteenth part, and lightning is a sixteenth part. This, O gentle one, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named 'The Luminous. 3. (3) [Note: No commentary was provided for this verse.]

He who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Luminous," becomes luminous in this world; he wins luminous worlds—he who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Luminous. Thus ends the seventh section. (4) — 7 — (4) —

"Agni is a portion, the sun is a portion, the moon is a portion, lightning is a portion—this indeed, O Somya, is the light. Thus he taught that perception has as its object only light. From this, the identity of the *haṃsa* with the sun is understood. The fruit for the knower: he becomes luminous and endowed with brilliance in this world; and having died, he conquers the worlds of those who possess light, such as the moon, the sun, and others. The subsequent portion is the same. This concludes the commentary on the seven sections.

"The water-bird (*madgu*) will tell you the foot," he said. On the following day, he drove the cows forward. When they reached the place where they were to stay for the evening, he kindled the fire there, penned the cows, added fuel to the fire, and sat down behind the fire facing the east.

(1) "The swan (*haṃsa*) will tell you the foot," [the other] said, and then he ceased speaking. The *madgu* is a water-dwelling bird; and because of its connection with the waters, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "On the following day," and so forth, is as before.
The water-bird swooped down toward him and addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Yes, venerable sir.

That water-bird was Prāṇa, and he spoke of his own domain and his own vision: "Prāṇa is the quarter," and so forth, ending with "the one possessing a support. By "support" is meant the mind (*manas*), for it is that in which the enjoyments brought by all the sense organs reside; thus, the quarter is called "possessing a support" because it exists within that [mind].

"Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman. "Tell me, Venerable Sir," [he replied]. To him he said: "Breath is one part, the eye is one part, the ear is one part, the mind is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named 'Possessing a Dwelling' (*āyatanavān*).

That swan, Breath, spoke only concerning its own domain, beginning with "Breath is one part" and ending with "named Possessing a Dwelling. "Dwelling" (*āyatana*) refers to the mind, because it is that in which the enjoyments brought forth by all the sense organs reside; thus, the quarter is named "Possessing a Dwelling."

He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "possessing a support," becomes one who possesses a support in this world; he wins worlds that possess a support—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "possessing a support. [Thus ends the eighth section. He who meditates upon that foot in that very manner becomes one who possesses a support—that is, one who has a foundation—in this world. He wins from here worlds that possess a support, meaning worlds that have space. "He who, knowing this thus," and so forth, is as explained previously.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section.
He reached the teacher’s family, and the teacher addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! "Revered Sir," he replied in assent.
Having thus become a knower of Brahman, he reached the teacher’s household. The teacher addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Revered sir.

"My dear boy, you shine like one who knows Brahman. One who knows Brahman has serene senses, a smiling face, and is free from anxiety, having accomplished his purpose. Therefore, the teacher said, 'You shine like one who knows Brahman. Reflecting on this, he asked, 'Who indeed has instructed you? And Satyakāma replied, 'Not humans; it was the deities who have instructed me. His intention was: 'What other human being would dare to instruct me, a disciple of the venerable one?'"

"Therefore, he declared, 'Others than men [have taught me]. But the venerable one said, 'Tell me what you know according to my desire; what is the use of what others have said? I do not value that,' such was his intention.
'O dear one, you shine like a knower of Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you? 'Others than men,' he declared, 'but the venerable one himself should tell me according to my desire.

Furthermore, for it has been heard by me from seers who are like the Blessed One, equal to the Blessed One, that regarding this matter, knowledge indeed reaches its highest state of excellence—its most perfect realization—only when learned from a teacher. Therefore, having been told, "The Blessed One himself should speak," the teacher spoke to him that very same knowledge which had been declared by the deities. In this regard, not even a single part—not even a mere fragment—of the sixteen-fold knowledge was left out (*na vīyāya*), meaning nothing was omitted.
The repetition [of the final phrase] is intended to mark the completion of the knowledge.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth section.

Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla. He tended his sacred fires for twelve years; while he was letting other students depart after their studies were complete, he did not let him depart. Introduction: [The author] begins by stating, "I shall again speak of the knowledge of Brahman in another manner," as well as the destination of those who know it and the science of the fires. The narrative is similar to the previous one, intended to demonstrate that faith and austerity are the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman.

Upakosala by name, the son of Kamala (Kāmalāyana), lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla. For twelve years, for the sake of traditional instruction, he served the sacrificial fires for that teacher; he performed the service of the fires. That teacher, having caused the other students to learn the Veda, had them perform the ceremonial return home (*samāvartana*), but he alone did not cause Upakosala to perform it.
His wife said to him, "The student has performed his penance; he served the fires well. Let not the fires speak against you; tell this to us. But even without telling him, he went away on a journey.

His wife said to that teacher: "The religious student has performed his penance and has properly and completely tended the fires. Yet the venerable one does not allow him to return, even though he is devoted to the fires. Knowing this, let the fires not speak ill of you—let them not reproach you. Therefore, teach him the desired knowledge for Upakosala. Although he was thus addressed by his wife, he did not say anything at all and simply went away on a journey.

He, Upakosala, resolved to fast due to a mental affliction. His teacher’s wife said to him as he sat silently in the fire-sanctuary: "O student, eat! Why indeed do you not eat? He replied: "There are many desires in this person, and various misfortunes; I am filled with diseases. Therefore, I shall not eat. 3.

(3) He, Upakosala, resolved—that is, he fixed his mind—to fast, that is, to undertake a fast, because of a mental affliction, that is, suffering. To him, who was staying silently in the fire-sanctuary, the teacher’s wife said: "O student, eat—consume food! For what reason indeed, for what cause, do you not eat?"

He said: "In this person—who is unfulfilled and subject to nature—there are many various desires regarding what must be done; there are various calamities, meaning diseases and anxieties concerning duties which involve passing beyond [one's limits]; I am filled with these, and therefore I shall not eat. Then the fires deliberated: "The student has been tormented; he served us well. Come, let us speak to him. They said to him: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman. (4)

(4) When the religious student had finished speaking and remained silent, then the three fires, won over by his service and filled with compassion, spoke together, saying: "Come now, let us all instruct this religious student—who is devoted to us, suffering, ascetic, and full of faith—in the knowledge of Brahman. Having thus deliberated, they said to him: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman."

He said, "I understand that breath is Brahman; but I do not understand *ka* and *kha*. They said, "That which is indeed *ka* is the same as *kha*; that which is *kha* is the same as *ka*. Thus they explained to him both breath and space. Thus ends the tenth section. (5) — 10 —

The religious student replied: "I understand what you have said—that 'Brahman is prāṇa'—because the meaning of the word is well-known. That specific vital air (vāyu-viśeṣa) in which life exists and which ceases upon its departure is commonly established in the world as 'prāṇa'; therefore, it is appropriate that Brahman-hood belongs to it. Thus, because the meaning of the word is well-known, I understand that 'Brahman is prāṇa. But I do not understand 'Ka' and 'Kha'."

But surely, since the words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* are well-known to have as their objects pleasure (*sukha*) and space (*ākāśa*), how can there be ignorance on the part of the religious student? Indeed, he thinks: "How can that which is called *kaṃ*, namely pleasure, which perishes in a moment, and that which is called *khaṃ*, namely insentient space, be Brahman? And how could the word of the Blessed One be anything other than authoritative? Therefore, he says, "I do not know."

When the religious student had spoken thus, those fires said to him: "That which we have called *kaṃ* is indeed *kha*, the ether (*ākāśa*). Thus, being qualified by *kha*, *kaṃ* is distinguished from the pleasure born of the contact between the sense objects and the senses—just as a blue lotus, when qualified by the word "blue," is distinguished from red and other colors. Know that whatever we have called *kha*, the ether, that very thing is *kaṃ*, pleasure.

And thus, when space (*kha*) is qualified by bliss (*sukha*), it is distinguished from elemental, insentient space—just like a blue lotus. The meaning is that the bliss resides in [transcendental] space and not in other worldly space, and space is the substratum of bliss and not the other kind of elemental space. Now, if space is [qualified] by bliss...

It is intended to be qualified; let there be only one qualifier—either "that which is *kaṃ* (bliss) is indeed *kha* (space)," in which case the other is redundant; or "that which is *kha* is *kaṃ*," in which case the former is the qualifier. But have we not already stated that the exclusion of both bliss and space from worldly bliss and space is intended? If it is argued that once space is qualified by bliss, the exclusion of both follows as a matter of course, that is true; however, it is specifically the space qualified by bliss that is enjoined as the object of meditation.

However, it would not be prescribed that pleasure (*sukha*), as a qualifying attribute of space (*ākāśa*), is itself the object of meditation; for the inclusion of a qualifier is exhausted by its function of restricting the qualified object. Therefore, space (*kha*) qualifies pleasure (*ka*) as well, so that both may be the objects of meditation. And how is this determined? From the connection of the word *ka* with the word *brahman*, as in "What is Brahman? (*kaṃ brahma*). For if the intention were to teach that space qualified by the attribute of pleasure is the object of meditation, the Agnis would have said first, "What and space are Brahman" (*kaṃ khaṃ brahma*).

But they did not speak in this manner; rather, they said, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman. Therefore, for the sake of removing the student's delusion, the designation of the words *ka* and *kha* as being in a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified—beginning with "That which is indeed *ka*" and so forth—is entirely appropriate.

The Śruti declares this very statement spoken by the fires for our understanding: "To me, to that Brahmacārin, they said: 'Prāṇa'—and his 'Ākāśa', meaning the Ākāśa within the heart (*hārda*) which is related to Prāṇa as its substratum, because it is designated as possessing the quality of bliss. And both that Ākāśa, distinguished by the quality of bliss, and the Prāṇa residing therein—which is called 'Brahman' precisely due to its contact with Brahman—the fires spoke of both Prāṇa and Ākāśa collectively as 'Brahman'. Thus ends the commentary on the tenth section.
Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: "The earth, fire, and food—this person who is seen in the sun, that am I; he alone am I. 1.

The fires, having come together, spoke the Veda to the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Immediately thereafter, they each began to teach the knowledge pertaining to their own respective domains. In that regard, first the Gārhapatya fire instructed him, the student: "Earth, fire, food, and the sun—these are my four bodies."

In this regard, the statement "I am that person who is seen in the sun; and that which is the Gārhapatya fire, I am that very person in the sun"—this is a declaration of identity through a process of reversal. There is no relationship between the Gārhapatya fire and the sun similar to the relationship between earth and food, characterized by being the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*). Rather, because their attributes of being the eater (*attṛtva*), the cooker (*paktṛtva*), and the illuminator (*prakāśana*) are indistinguishable, the absolute oneness of these two is emphasized.
However, earth and food are related to these two by virtue of being objects of enjoyment.

He who, knowing it thus, worships it, shakes off evil-doing, becomes a possessor of the world, reaches a full lifespan, and lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish; we serve him both in this world and in that world—he who, knowing it thus, worships it. 2. Thus ends the eleventh section.

Whoever thus meditates upon the Gārhapatya fire—as described above—divided fourfold as food and the eater of food, he destroys and annihilates evil-doing, that is, sinful action. He becomes possessed of a world, a world-possessor through our Agni-world, just as we are. And in this world, he attains and reaches a full lifespan of a hundred years. He lives brightly and radiantly; that is to say, not obscurely.

And his inferiors and those men who are his—meaning those born of his lineage—do not perish; that is to say, there is no interruption of his lineage. Furthermore, we enjoy and protect him while he lives in this world and in the next world. This is the fruit for one who, knowing it thus, meditates upon it as described.
Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh section.
Then Anvāhāryagārgya instructed him further: "The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon—this person who is seen in the moon, that am I; he indeed am I.

He who, knowing it thus, worships it, shakes off evil-doing, becomes a possessor of the world, reaches a full lifespan, and lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish; we enjoy him both in this world and in yonder world—he who, knowing it thus, worships it. Thus ends the twelfth section. 12.

(2) Then, indeed, the Anvāhāryapacana fire—the Dakṣiṇāgni—instructed him: "Water, the quarters, the stars, and the moon—these are my four bodies. Having divided myself fourfold, I abide in the Anvāhāryapacana fire. Therein, that person who is seen in the moon, I am he; I am indeed he," as before. Because of the connection with food and because of the commonality of being light (*jyotis*), there is oneness between the Anvāhāryapacana fire and the moon, as well as because of the connection with the southern quarter.

The connection of the waters and the stars with food is as before; for it is well known that the stars are objects of enjoyment for the moon. Because the waters produce food, they constitute the "food" aspect of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire—just as the earth constitutes that of the Gārhapatya fire. The rest is the same. Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section.
Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, and lightning. That person who is seen in the lightning—that am I; that indeed am I. (1)

(1) [The commentary] did not comment upon this verse: "He who, knowing it thus, worships it, shakes off evil deeds; he becomes a possessor of the world, he reaches his full lifespan, he lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish. We indeed serve him—both in this world and in the yonder world—who, knowing it thus, worships it. (2) Thus ends the thirteenth section. 13. (2) ————

Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, and lightning—these are my four bodies as well. That person who is seen in the lightning, I am he," and so forth, as before, due to the commonality [of attributes]. Because heaven and space have their own substrata, the connection between lightning and the Āhavanīya fire is solely by way of being objects of enjoyment. The rest is the same. Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth section.

They said, "Upakosala, this is our knowledge of the Self; but the teacher, O Somya, will tell you the way. The teacher arrived, and the teacher addressed him: "Upakosala! He replied, "Venerable sir. "Your face, my dear, shines like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, pray, has instructed you? "Who indeed would instruct me, sir? he said, while as it were concealing [the others]. "These fires here are surely different from what they used to be," he said, pointing toward the fires. "What, then, my dear, did they say to you? 1–2. They said, "Upakosala, this is our knowledge of the Self; but the teacher, O Somya, will tell you the way. The teacher arrived, and the teacher addressed him: "Upakosala! He replied, "Venerable sir. "Your face, my dear, shines like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, pray, has instructed you? "Who indeed would instruct me, sir? he said, while as it were concealing [the others]. "These fires here are surely different from what they used to be," he said, pointing toward the fires. "What, then, my dear, did they say to you?"

They, having come together, said: "O Upakosala, my dear, this is your knowledge of us—the meaning is, the knowledge of the fires—and the previously mentioned knowledge of the Self, namely, 'Breath is Brahman,' 'Ka (pleasure) is Brahman,' and 'Kha (ether) is Brahman. But the teacher will tell you the way for the attainment of the fruit of this knowledge. Having said this, the fires ceased. In due time, his teacher arrived. And the teacher addressed that disciple, saying, "Upakosala!"

"This," he replied, "is what they have indeed told you, my dear, concerning the worlds. But I shall tell you that [which is different]: just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this. 'Let the venerable sir tell it to me,' [said Naciketas]. He said to him: 3. Thus ends the fourteenth section. (2) ————- (Note: The phrase "He said to him" refers to the commencement of the next section.)

"Venerable sir," he replied. "My dear boy, your face shines clear like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you? Being thus addressed, he replied: "Who, indeed, would instruct me—that is, who would provide instruction—O Venerable Sir, while you were away? Here, the word *apahnute* (he conceals) is connected with the distant verb *apanihnuta* (he conceals); the intention is that he does not conceal [the fact], nor does he state exactly what was said by the fires.

How so? He addressed the fires with an intonation (*kāku*) that revealed them, saying: "Surely these fires have been served by me, for they appear as if trembling upon seeing you, whereas previously they were otherwise. Thus he spoke to the fires, pointing them out.

"Son, what indeed did those fires tell you? Thus questioned, he replied, "They said this"—that is, he acknowledged only a mere portion, not everything exactly as it was spoken by the fires. Therefore the Teacher says: "O son, they indeed told you about the worlds, such as the earth and so forth, but not Brahman in its entirety."

"I shall tell you that Brahman which you desire to hear; listen to the greatness of the knowledge of that Brahman as it is being spoken by me—just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so too sin does not cling to, nor attach itself to, one who knows the Brahman as I shall describe it. When the teacher had spoken thus, Upakosala said, "May the Blessed One tell it to me. To him the teacher spoke.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourteenth section.

This person who is seen in the eye by those whose vision has turned inward, who are endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and who are peaceful and discerning—he is the seer of seeing, according to other scriptural passages such as "the eye of the eye. Now, an objection may be raised: what was said by the fires is false, because they stated, "But the teacher will tell you the way," implying he would speak only of the path, and because the fires lacked knowledge of future events. This is not a fault, because the statement that "he is seen in the eye" is a restatement of the seer, who is indeed the space of bliss.

"This is the Self of living beings," he said, having spoken thus; that very reality of the Self which we have described is immortal—possessing the nature of not dying and being indestructible—and for that very reason it is fearless, for fear arises only where there is the apprehension of destruction, and in its absence there is no fear; and for that very reason this is Brahman, the Great and Infinite.

Furthermore, this is the majesty of this Puruṣa in the eye, who is Brahman: even if one pours clarified butter or water upon that place, the eye, it goes only to the eyelashes and only to the eyelids; it does not adhere to the eye, just as water does not adhere to a lotus leaf. This is the majesty of the location itself; what need is there to mention the stainlessness of the Puruṣa in the eye who occupies that location?
Such is the intended meaning. (2)

They call this person, as described above, "Saṃyadvāma. Why? Because all *vāmāni*—that is, desirable, praiseworthy, and beautiful things—converge upon him and come together toward him; therefore, he is Saṃyadvāma. Likewise, all desirable things converge upon one who knows this, provided that he knows thus.

He is indeed the *vāmanī* (the bringer of all that is desirable). For he leads, brings, and carries all *vāmāni*—that is, the fruits of meritorious deeds—to living beings in accordance with their merit, making them his own attributes. The fruit for the knower is this: "He who knows thus leads all that is desirable. (4) He is indeed the *bhāmanī* (the bringer of light). For he shines and blazes in all worlds through forms such as the sun, the moon, and fire, according to the Vedic scripture: "By His light all this is illumined. Thus, because he leads lights (*bhāmāni*), he is the *bhāmanī*. He who knows thus also shines in all worlds.

(5) Now, the destiny of the knower of Brahman as described above is being stated. Whether the officiating priests perform the funeral rites (*śavya*) for one who knows thus when he has died, or whether they do not perform them—in either case, that knower is not hindered by those funeral rites even if they are left undone, nor does he fail to attain Brahman; nor does he gain any superior world through the performance of the funeral rites, according to another scriptural passage: "He increases neither by action nor does he become less."

By showing disregard for the funeral rites (*śavakarman*), he praises knowledge (*vidyā*); it does not mean, however, that the funeral rites should not be performed by one who possesses such knowledge. For elsewhere, when funeral rites are not performed, some obstruction to the commencement of the fruits of actions is inferred; whereas here, at the time of the commencement of the fruit of knowledge, he shows the commencement of the fruit for the possessor of knowledge without obstruction, regardless of whether the funeral rites take place or not.

Those who meditate upon the one characterized by such qualities as "consisting of bliss," "abiding in the eye," "the gatherer of good," "the leader," and "the illuminator," as well as the knowledge of Agni together with Prāṇa—for them, whether they perform other ritual acts or not, in every case they attain the Light; that is to say, they reach and enter the deity who presides over the Light.

From the light-rays [he goes] to the deity of light; from the day to the deity presiding over the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight, the deity of the bright fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward toward the northern direction—the deities of the northern course; from those months to the year, the deity of the year; from that year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; and from the moon to lightning.

Then, a certain person who is not human (amānava)—one who is not born in the human creation (mānavī sṛṣṭi), thus being "non-human"—coming from the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), leads those [souls] situated there to Brahman residing in Satyaloka. This is because of the designations of "the goer," "the goal to be reached," and "the leader"; for if the attainment were merely of Brahman as pure Being (sanmātra), such designations would be untenable. Indeed, it is more appropriate to say in that context, "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. For [the author] will later describe the realization of pure Being through the elimination of all distinctions.

Furthermore, a path that has not been seen does not present itself for the purpose of traveling, according to another scriptural text: "That which is unknown does not benefit one. This is called the *devapatha* (the path of the gods), because it is characterized by the gods—namely, the deities presiding over the light and so forth—who act as its guides. It is called the *brahmapatha* (the path of Brahman) because it leads to Brahman as the goal and is thus characterized by Brahman.

Proceeding by this path, those who go do not return to this human whirlpool—belonging to Manu, characterized by the creation of Manu—which is called a "whirlpool" (*āvarta*) because, like a water-wheel, they revolve again and again upon the wheel of the continuous succession of birth and death; they do not enter that. The repetition of the phrase "they do not return" (*nāvartante*) is for the purpose of indicating the completion of this knowledge along with its fruit.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth section.

This indeed is the sacrifice that blows here; for as it blows, it purifies all this. Since it purifies all this as it blows, therefore it is the sacrifice. Its two paths are mind and speech. Introduction: In this section on secret doctrines (*rahasyaprakaraṇa*), because of the context and the commonality of being *āraṇyaka* (forest-texts), the *vyāhṛtis* must be prescribed as expiations when a flaw occurs in the sacrifice, and silence must be observed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who is the Brahman-priest; therefore, this [section] begins.

Of these two, one he prepares with his mind, while the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ prepare the other with their speech. When, after the Prātaranuvāka has been commenced but before the Paridhānīyā verse, the Brahman speaks out [interjects], this is indeed that very Vāyu who blows here; for this sacrifice is established upon Vāyu—this is well known from the Śrutis. The particles *ha* and *vai* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) used to indicate a matter that is already established as a fact. Indeed, it is well known in the sacred texts that the sacrifice is supported by Vāyu.

This is known from such Vedic texts as, "Svāhā to Vāte-dhāḥ," and "This indeed is the sacrifice which blows here. For wind alone, by virtue of its nature as motion, is the substratum of action; as it is heard in scripture: "Wind alone is the initiator of the sacrifice; wind is its foundation. As this [wind] moves and vibrates, it purifies—that is, it cleanses and refines—this entire world. Indeed, there is no purification for that which is unmoving; for the removal of defects is observed in what moves, not in what is stationary.

And because he purifies all this, therefore he alone is the sacrifice, since he purifies (*yatpunāti*). Of this very sacrifice thus characterized, speech is occupied with the utterance of mantras, and the mind is occupied with the knowledge of things as they truly are; these two, speech and mind, are the two tracks (*vartanī*), the paths, by which the sacrifice, being extended, proceeds—those are the two tracks.

"For the sacrifice is the successive progression of speech and mind, which possesses the movement of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*)," so says another Vedic text. Therefore, since the sacrifice proceeds by means of both speech and mind, speech and mind are called the two "tracks" (*vartanī*) of the sacrifice. If he prepares only one track, the other is left neglected; his sacrifice perishes. Just as a one-legged person walking or a chariot moving on a single wheel comes to ruin, even so does his sacrifice perish. When the sacrifice perishes, the sacrificer perishes along with it. Having sacrificed, he becomes worse off. (3) (2) [No commentary provided for this verse.]

Now, when at the morning recitation (*prātaranuvāka*) performed for the dawn (*uṣas*), the Brahman priest does not speak out before the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*), they prepare both paths; neither one is neglected. (4) Of those two paths, the Brahman priest—one who possesses the knowledge of discernment—prepares one path by means of the mind; the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ—these three priests—prepare the other path, characterized by speech, by means of speech alone. This being so, in the sacrifice, the two paths consisting of speech and mind are to be prepared.

Now, when the *prātaranuvāka* litany has been commenced—that is, at whatever time it has begun—if the Brahman priest breaks his silence by speaking before the final concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) of that recitation, then he prepares only one of the two paths of speech. While the path of the mind is being prepared by the Brahman, the other [path of speech] fails, perishes, and becomes defective. That sacrifice, being unable to proceed by means of either of the two paths of speech, comes to ruin.

"How so? he says: Just as a one-legged man, walking and traveling along a path, comes to grief, or as a chariot, moving and traveling with only one wheel, comes to grief, even so does the sacrifice of this sacrificer come to grief—that is, it perishes—when performed by a bad Brahmin. As the sacrifice comes to grief, the sacrificer follows after it in its ruin; for the sacrificer has the sacrifice as his life-breath. Therefore, when the sacrifice is ruined, his own ruin is likewise certain. Having performed such a sacrifice, he becomes more wretched—that is, more sinful.

Just as a chariot moving on both wheels remains steady when traveling on two tracks, even so does his sacrifice remain steady; as the sacrifice remains steady, the sacrificer follows it in remaining steady, and having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous. Thus ends the sixteenth section. Prajāpati brooded over the worlds. From them, as they were being brooded upon, he extracted their essences: Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Āditya from the sky.

Introduction: Here, silence is prescribed for the Brahman priest; when there is a failure in that role or in the duties of the Brahman, as well as in other duties such as those of the Hotṛ, the Vyāhṛti-homa is the expiation. Therefore, he states that the Vyāhṛtis must be prescribed for that purpose—(1)—

Prajāpati performed austerity directed toward the worlds; that is, with the desire to extract their essence, he practiced meditation characterized as austerity. From those worlds being thus heated, he extracted—that is, he took up—their essences in the form of their vital juices. Which ones? The essence of fire from the earth, the essence of wind from the intermediate space, and the essence of the sun from heaven.

He performed austerity upon these three deities; from them being thus heated, he extracted their essences: the Ṛg-verses from fire, the Yajus-formulas from wind, and the Sāman-chants from the sun. 2. (2)

Again, in the same manner, he brooded upon these three deities, beginning with Fire. From them, too, he extracted the essence, the sap, which is the triple knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*). He brooded upon this triple knowledge; from it, as it was being brooded upon, he drew forth the essences: "Bhūḥ" from the *Ṛg* verses, "Bhuvaḥ" from the *Yajus* formulas, and "Svaḥ" from the *Sāman* chants. 3. (3) [No commentary provided for this verse.]

If, however, it should be damaged by the Ṛgveda, he should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with the words "Bhūḥ Svāhā. By means of the essence of the Ṛcs, by the vigor of the Ṛcs, he thereby mends the breach in the Ṛcs of the sacrifice.

He again brooded over this triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). From it, as it was being brooded upon, he extracted its essence: from the *ṛc* verses he took the *vyāhṛti* "bhūḥ"; from the *yajus* formulas, the *vyāhṛti* "bhuvaḥ"; and from the *sāman* chants, the *vyāhṛti* "svaḥ". Therefore, these Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) are the essences of the worlds, the gods, and the Vedas. Consequently, if in that sacrifice something should be damaged on account of an *ṛc*, due to a connection with an *ṛc*—that is, if the sacrifice should incur a flaw—one should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with the words "bhūḥ svāhā". That is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case.

How so? It is by means of the *ṛcs* themselves; "that" (*tat*) is an adverbial modifier. By the essence (*rasa*), the vigor (*vīrya*), and the power (*ojas*) of the *ṛcs*, he joins together—that is, he repairs—the damage, the breakage, or the wound that has arisen in the sacrifice associated with the *ṛcs*.

Now, if it should be damaged through the *yajus*, one should offer an oblation into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the words "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! By means of the essence, the vigor, and the power of the *yajus* themselves, he joins together the damage in the sacrifice associated with the *yajus*.
5. (5) [No commentary provided for this verse.]

Now, if it should be damaged during the Sāman, he should offer an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Svarga! Svāhā! By means of the essence of the Sāmans, by means of the vigor of the Sāmans, he thereby mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured in the Sāmans.

Now, if there should be a failure on account of the *yajus* (the sacrificial formula), one should offer an oblation into the *dakṣiṇāgni* with the words, "Bhuvaḥ svāhā. Likewise, in the event of a failure on account of the *sāman*, one should offer an oblation into the *āhavanīya* fire with the words, "Svaḥ svāhā. In this way, as before, he repairs the sacrifice. However, in the case of a failure on account of the *brahman* (the officiating priest), one should offer oblations into all three fires with the three *vyāhṛtis*. For that failure pertains to the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), according to the Vedic scripture: "By what [means] is the office of the *brahman* performed? By this very triple knowledge. Or else, another rule must be sought for a failure occurring on account of the *brahman*.

Just as one might join gold with salt, silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and wood with leather... [7] ...so, by the power of these worlds, of these deities, and of this triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā), he joins together what was torn in the sacrifice. Indeed, that sacrifice is truly "made medicinal" where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus. [8]

(8) It is as follows: one might join gold with salt; for that [salt], such as alkali or sal ammoniac (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), makes what is hard soft. One might join silver, which cannot otherwise be joined, with gold; likewise tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and leather with leather-binding. In this same way, by means of the vigor—known as the essence (*rasa*) and called vital power (*ojas*)—of these worlds, of these deities, and of this triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), one joins together whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.

This sacrifice is indeed like one performed by a physician—a man afflicted by disease [is healed] by a well-trained doctor; such is this sacrifice. What is it? It means that sacrifice in which the *brahmán* priest is one who knows thus—that is, one who knows the expiatory offerings (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of the aforementioned *vyāhṛti* oblations. This sacrifice indeed flows toward the north where such a knowing *brahmán* is present. Regarding such a knowing *brahmán*, there is this traditional verse: "Whithersoever it turns back, thither it goes. 9. (9)
Furthermore, this sacrifice indeed becomes inclined toward the north, sloping northward and rising toward the south; the meaning is that it is the cause for attaining the highest path.

This occurs when there is a Brahman priest who knows thus. Regarding such a knowing Brahman priest, this following verse is intended as a praise of the Brahman: "From whichever part of the sacrificial ground the sacrifice of the officiating priests turns back, becoming impaired, he goes forth—meaning he repairs and protects—that very impairment of the sacrifice by means of expiation."

Just as a single man, a charioteer, protects the Kurus and their horses, even so does the Brahman priest who knows this protect the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests. Therefore, one should appoint only such a person as the Brahman priest, and not one who does not know this—not one who does not know this. Thus ends the seventeenth section. Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

The *brahmā* priest is so called because he practices silence (*mauna*), or because he possesses knowledge through reflection (*manana*). Therefore, the *brahmā* alone protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), just as a mare protects horses that have mounted them. One who knows this indeed protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the priests by removing the defects committed by them. Since the learned *brahmā* is thus distinguished, one should therefore appoint only such a person—who knows the aforementioned *vyāhṛtis* and so forth—as the *brahmā*, and never one who does not know this.
The repetition [of the concluding phrase] marks the end of the chapter.
Thus ends the commentary on the seventeenth section,
composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order.
The fourth chapter of the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is completed. Om.
He who knows the eldest and the best indeed becomes the eldest and the best. Verily, the vital breath (prāṇa) is the eldest and the best. 1.

Introduction: The higher path (uttarā gati) pertaining to the knowledge of Brahman with attributes (saguṇabrahmavidyā) has been described. Now, in this fifth chapter, having first restated that same path for the householder who knows the five fires as well as for those of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas) who possess faith and are devoted to other forms of knowledge, the text begins with the intent of generating dispassion by describing another path connected with the southern direction—characterized by smoke and so forth—which belongs to those who perform mere ritual acts (kevalakarmin), and a third path which is even more miserable than that, consisting of repeated return (punarāvṛtti). This cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) must now be explained.

In the preceding text, the mention of "prāṇa" has been made many times—for instance, in such passages as "Prāṇa is superior to speech and the others," and "Prāṇa indeed is the absorber. How is it that prāṇa is superior among speech and the rest, given that there is no difference in their being agents that act in combination? And how is it to be meditated upon? With the desire to teach its qualities of superiority and so forth, the following section is commenced: (1) ————- [The text continues with the Upanishadic passage.]

Whoever indeed knows the eldest—that which is first by age—and the most excellent—that which is superior by qualities—he himself becomes both the eldest and the most excellent. Having enticed the person with this result and directed his attention toward it, [the text] says: "Breath (prāṇa) alone is the eldest by age, compared to speech and the other [senses]; for while the person is still in the womb, the activity of breath attains its own nature prior to that of speech and the others, by means of which the embryo grows."

Since the formation of the constituent parts and locations such as the eyes occurs first, and only afterwards do speech and the other organs acquire their functions, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the eldest in terms of age. Its preeminence, however, will be demonstrated by the illustration beginning with "the well-bred horse" (*suhaya*). Therefore, in this aggregate of body and organs, the vital breath alone is both the eldest and the most excellent. "He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) becomes the most excellent among his own people; speech, indeed, is the most excellent.

Whoever knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*)—the best at clothing, the best at covering, or the most wealthy—he indeed becomes the most excellent among his own kinsmen. But who, then, is the most excellent? It is said: Speech (*vāk*) is indeed the most excellent; for eloquent men dwell [in prosperity], they overcome others, and they become the wealthiest; therefore, speech is the most excellent.
Whoever knows the firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), he stands firm both in this world and in the yonder world. Sight (*cakṣus*) is indeed the firm foundation. 3. (3) —-

He who knows the foundation indeed becomes firmly established in this world and in that other world beyond. What, then, is the foundation? It is said: the eye, verily, is the foundation. For by means of the eye, seeing both the level and the uneven ground, one becomes firmly established; therefore, the eye is the foundation. He who knows prosperity—verily, all desires, both divine and human, fall to his lot. The ear, verily, is prosperity. 4. (4)

Verily, for one who knows prosperity (*saṃpad*), both divine and human desires indeed prosper for him. What then is prosperity? He says: the ear (*śrotra*) is indeed prosperity. Because by means of the ear the Vedas are grasped and their meaning is understood, from that rituals are performed, and from those [rituals] comes the prosperity of desires; thus, because it is the cause of the prosperity of desires, the ear is indeed prosperity. Verily, he who knows the abode (*āyatana*) becomes an abode for his own people; the mind (*manas*) is indeed the abode. 5. (5) ————-

"Whoever knows the abode (*āyatana*) truly becomes the abode of his own people"—this is the meaning. "What is that abode? he says: "The mind (*manas*) is indeed the abode. The mind is the abode, the support, for the objects presented by the senses, which are intended for the enjoyer and exist in the form of mental impressions (*pratyaya*). Therefore it is said: "The mind is indeed the abode. Then, indeed, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) disputed among themselves regarding who was superior, each saying, "I am more excellent than you; I am more excellent! (6)

Then indeed those vital breaths (*prāṇas*), possessing the qualities as previously described, disputed among themselves for the sake of superiority, each saying, "I am superior, I am superior. Those vital breaths went to their father Prajāpati and said, "Venerable sir, who among us is the best? He said to them, "He among you, upon whose departure this body appears most wretched, he is the best of you. 7. (7) ————-The final answer is: Then indeed those vital breaths (*prāṇas*), possessing the qualities as previously described, disputed among themselves for the sake of superiority, each saying, "I am superior, I am superior. Those vital breaths went to their father Prajāpati and said, "Venerable sir, who among us is the best? He said to them, "He among you, upon whose departure this body appears most wretched, he is the best of you. 7. (7) ————-

Thus disputing among themselves, they approached their father Prajāpati, the progenitor, in order to ascertain who among them was the best, and said: "O Blessed One, which one of us is the most excellent, superior in qualities?"—in this manner they questioned him.

The father said to them: "Among you, when whichever one has departed, this body shall appear as if most wretched—even more wretched than when life was present—as a corpse, untouchable and impure; he, among you, is the best. He spoke thus with a tone of irony, desiring to avoid causing them distress.

Speech departed from that body. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the dumb live—breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—so [did we]. Then Speech entered back into the body.

The eye departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the blind, though not seeing, live by means of the breath, speak by means of speech, hear by means of the ear, and think by means of the mind—so it was. Then the eye entered back in. The ear departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as..."

Deaf, they did not hear; yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and thinking with the mind, they said, "It is thus. Then the ear entered [the body]. Then the mind departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and asked, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as children without minds breathe with the breath, speak with speech, see with the eye, and hear with the ear—it was thus. Then the mind entered [the body].

(11) When the vital breaths had been thus addressed by the father, that speech indeed departed (*uccakrāma*). Having departed and stayed away for a full year, having ceased from its own function, it returned and said to the other vital breaths: "In what way, by what means, were you able to live—that is, to maintain yourselves—without me? They replied: "Just as [the dumb]... and so forth; "just as in the world the *kalās*—that is, the mute—live without speaking with speech."

How so? "Breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind"—the meaning is that they were performing all the functions of the senses. "In this way we lived" is the sense. Having realized its own inferiority relative to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), speech indeed entered back in; the meaning is that it became engaged once more in its own function. The rest is the same: "The eye indeed departed, the ear indeed departed, the mind indeed departed," and so forth. "Like children who are mindless" means those whose minds are not yet fully developed.

Then, as the vital breath (prāṇa) was about to depart, it pulled out the other vital breaths just as a fine horse might tear out its foot-tethers; and they, having gathered around it, said: "O Venerable One, remain! You are the best among us;
do not depart. 12. (12)

When speech and the others had been thus examined, immediately thereafter, what did that principal breath do as it was about to depart—that is, desiring to go out? It is said: just as in the world a fine horse—a beautiful steed—when struck with a whip by its rider for the sake of testing, might tear up, dig out, and root up the pegs used for binding its feet, even so did it tear up and root out the other vital breaths, such as speech and the rest.

Those vital breaths, being agitated and unable to remain in their own places, gathered together and said to the chief vital breath: "O Blessed One, become our lord, for you are the best among us; do not depart from this body. Then Speech said to him: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent one. Then the Eye said to him: "Insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation. 13. (13) [No commentary provided for this verse.]
Then the ear said to him: "As I am the abundance, so are you that abundance. Then the mind said to him: "As I am the abode, so are you that abode. 14. (14)

Then Speech and the others, establishing the preeminence of the Breath through their own functions, spoke—just as subjects bring tribute to a king. How so? First, Speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), [the word] 'yat' (insofar as) is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is, 'insofar as I possess the quality of being the most excellent. 'Thou art that most excellent' means that by virtue of that quality of being the most excellent, thou art that most excellent; the meaning is that thou possessest that quality. Alternatively, the word *tat* (that) may also be an adverbial modifier."

"This quality of being Vasiṣṭha is yours, created by you; it is yours, yet out of ignorance it was conceived by me as 'mine'. The same should be applied to the subsequent cases regarding the eye, the ear, and the mind.

"Indeed, they do not call these 'speeches,' nor 'eyes,' nor 'ears,' nor 'minds'; they call them simply 'breaths' (prāṇas), for the breath indeed becomes all of these. Thus ends the first section. (15) 1.15.1–5.

This is the statement of the Śruti: "What has been said by speech and the other organs to the chief vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) is appropriate; for in the world, neither common people nor those learned in the scriptures refer to the instruments such as speech and so forth as 'speech,' 'eyes,' 'ears,' or 'minds. Rather, they refer to them and speak of them simply as 'breaths' (prāṇāḥ). Since the chief vital breath indeed becomes all these various groups of instruments beginning with speech, therefore what was said by speech and the others to the chief vital breath is entirely fitting. Thus [the text] seeks to conclude the meaning of the section.

Now, how is this reasonable? For it is as if conscious persons were disputing for their own superiority that they would compete with one another; indeed, it is not possible for the eye and the other organs to speak individually after having set aside speech. Likewise, their departure from the body, their re-entry, their journey to Brahman, or the praise of the vital breath (prāṇa) would not be tenable [if they were unconscious]. In this regard, since the speech and other organs are presided over by conscious deities such as Agni, their possession of consciousness is established as a matter of course.

If it is argued that this contradicts the tenets of the logicians (*tārkika*), [we reply: no, because we accept that the Lord is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) when there is more than one conscious being in a single body. Those logicians who do accept a Lord maintain that the internal instruments and organs, such as the mind, as well as external things like the earth, proceed according to fixed rules only when presided over by the Lord—just like a chariot and so forth. Furthermore, we do not admit that even conscious deities such as Fire (*agni*) and others are the enjoyers within the body.

What then? It is accepted that the Lord is the ruler by mere superintendence over those various powers—which possess instruments and effects, which are distinct forms of the single deity Prāṇa, and which comprise millions of variations such as the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva). For He is without instruments, according to the description in the Vedic mantra: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears."

The followers of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad recite such passages as, "Behold Hiraṇyagarbha being born," and "He generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning. We shall explain later that the "enjoyer" (bhoktṛ) is the individual soul (jīva), which is distinct from the body and connected with the fruits of action.

Furthermore, the dialogue among speech and the other organs described here is a figurative construction intended to determine the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa) through the method of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka)—just as in the world, when men dispute among themselves regarding who is superior, they ask someone who is an expert in their specific qualities, "Who among us is the best by virtue of our qualities?"

He said to them, "Strive one by one to accomplish this task; he among you by whom this task is accomplished shall be your best. Thus addressed, they strove accordingly and determined their own or another's superiority. In the same way, the Śruti imagined this conventional narrative regarding speech and the other organs—how indeed might the wise man realize the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa), seeing that life is observed to continue even in the absence of each individual organ like speech, but not in the absence of the vital breath?

And thus says the Śruti of the Kauṣītakins: "One lives deprived of speech, for we see the mute; one lives deprived of sight, for we see the blind; one lives deprived of hearing, for we see the deaf; one lives deprived of mind, for we see infants; one lives with arms cut off; one lives with thighs cut off," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the first section.

He said, "What will be my food? They replied, "Whatever there is here, even down to dogs and birds. Now, this is indeed the food of the breath; for "an" is the manifest name of the breath. Indeed, for one who knows this, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food. 1. (1)

The principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) said: "What shall be my food?"—the Śruti, having imagined the principal breath as the questioner and the speech and other organs as the responders, says: "Whatever kind of food is well-known in this world, from dogs along with dogs to birds along with birds—that which is the food of all living beings, that is your food," so said the speech and the others.

In order to establish that everything is food for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and that the vital breath is the eater of all food, the Śruti, withdrawing from the form of the invented narrative, speaks in its own direct form: "That which is here in this world, whatever food is eaten by living beings—that is food for *ana*; it is eaten by *prāṇa* alone. The meaning is that all that is eaten is the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and it is consumed by *prāṇa* itself.
