The word *ana* is the perceptible name of *prāṇa*, intended to demonstrate its quality of pervading all types of activity. For if it were preceded by the prefix *pra-*, there would only be a specific, limited understanding.

And thus, the mention of the name of the eater of all food is this direct perception: "ana" is the explicit designation of the eater of all foods. Indeed, for one who knows thus—for one who knows Prāṇa as described, thinking, "I am Prāṇa, abiding in all beings, the eater of all foods"—for such a knower, there is indeed nothing whatsoever that is to be eaten by living beings which becomes "ananna," that is, inedible; the meaning is that everything becomes food for one who knows thus, because the knower has become Prāṇa itself. From Prāṇa, indeed...
"Regarding this, another scriptural passage begins, 'He rises in the breath and sets in the breath,' and continues, 'For one who knows thus, the sun indeed rises; for one who knows thus, he sets.

He said, 'What shall be my garment? They replied, 'Water. Therefore, when about to eat, one wraps oneself with water both before and after; thus one becomes a possessor of clothing and remains unclothed [by the cold]. (2)

(2) Then the Prāṇa spoke again—the conceptualization is just as before: "What shall be my clothing? "Water," said Vāk and the others. Since water is the clothing of this Prāṇa, therefore learned Brāhmaṇas, when they are about to eat—that is, while they are eating—and after they have eaten, do this: what is it? With water, which serves as his clothing, they wrap him—that is, they perform the act of clothing—for the principal Prāṇa, both before the meal and after the meal.

He becomes one who obtains clothing, or one whose nature is to obtain clothing; the meaning is that he actually acquires clothing. He is not naked. Since being not naked is already established by virtue of his obtaining clothing, the phrase "he is not naked" means that he possesses an upper garment.

The sipping of water for the sake of purification, which is known to occur both before one is about to eat and after one has eaten, is here enjoined merely as a meditation that "in that [water] is the dwelling of the vital breath"—expressed by the words "they clothe him with waters. It is not a separate act of sipping; just as food being eaten by ordinary living beings is regarded merely as the food of the vital breath, so it is here. This is because the questions and answers—"What is my food? and "What is my clothing?"—are identical in nature.

If the sipping of water (*ācamana*) were performed as something previously unestablished for the sake of that [instruction], then even food such as worms would have to be prescribed as edible for the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Since both the question and the answer are equal in being intended for the purpose of knowledge, and since the context pertains to knowledge, it is not appropriate to assume the "half-old-woman" logic (*ardhajaratīya-nyāya*). As for the claim that the well-known sipping of water—which serves the purpose of purification (*prāyatya*) and the purpose of providing non-nakedness for the *prāṇa*—does not apply here, we do not say that the sipping of water serves both purposes in that manner.

What then? We say that the instruction is intended to produce the realization that water, which serves as the means for sipping (ācamana) for the sake of purification, is the "garment" of the vital breath (prāṇa). In that case, the objection regarding the defect of the sipping serving two purposes is untenable. If it is argued that this realization would apply only to the sipping performed for the purpose of a garment, we say no; for there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) in a sentence intended to convey the knowledge of the garment, if it were to enjoin a previously unenjoined sipping for the sake of a garment and simultaneously enjoin the realization of it as being for the sake of non-nakedness.
This is because there is no evidence for the sipping having both those purposes.

Having taught this very [doctrine] to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, Satyakāma Jābāla said: "Even if one were to teach this to a withered stump, branches would surely spring up from it and leaves would grow.

(3) This vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is now being praised. How so? Having taught this vision of the vital breath to Gośruti by name—the son of Vyāghrapada is called Vaiyāghrapadya—to that person named Gośruti, Satyakāma Jābāla spoke these further words which are about to be related.

"What did he say? he asks, and replies: "Even if one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) were to declare this vision to a withered stump, branches would indeed spring up and leaves would grow upon that stump; how much more so if one were to declare it to a living person! Following this, the rite known as *mantha* is commenced for the knower of the aforementioned vision of the vital breath.

Now, if he should desire to go to a great [world], having been initiated on the new moon day, he should, on the night of the full moon, prepare a mash of all herbs mixed with curds and honey; then, having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To the eldest, to the best, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash. 4.

Now, immediately thereafter, if one should wish to attain greatness—that is, if one should desire to go to, or long for the attainment of, greatness—this rite is prescribed for him. For when greatness exists, prosperity (*śrī*) approaches; for one who possesses prosperity, wealth is naturally acquired; from that, the performance of ritual acts follows; and from that, one will set out upon either the path of the gods (*devayāna*) or the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*). Having accepted this purpose, this rite is intended for one who seeks greatness, not for one who desires the enjoyment of sense-objects.

The following rule regarding time and so forth for him is stated: having been initiated on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), he should observe the discipline of sleeping on the ground and so forth like one who has been initiated; the meaning is that he becomes possessed of such duties as austerity, truthful speech, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and so on. However, he does not undertake the entire collection of ritual acts belonging to initiation itself, because the rite called *mantha* is not a modification (*vikāra*) of those. Furthermore, from another scriptural text stating "one who observes the *upasad* vows," he undertakes austerity in the form of consuming only milk, which is a cause of purification.

On the night of the full moon, he begins the ritual: taking as much as possible—however small—of all herbs, both cultivated and wild, and having husked them, he grinds them raw into a paste. According to another Vedic text (*śruti*), he places this into a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, shaped like a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa*, pours curd and honey into it, and churns it. Having placed it before him, he offers an oblation of clarified butter into the domestic fire (*āvasathya*) at the place for pouring, saying, "To the Eldest, to the Best, Svāhā!
He should then pour the residue clinging to the ladle into the churned mixture, letting the remainder fall down.

Having offered clarified butter into the fire with the formula, "To Vasiṣṭha, svāhā," he should pour the remnants into the mash. Having offered clarified butter into the fire with the formula, "To Pratiṣṭhā, svāhā," he should pour the remnants into the mash. Having offered clarified butter into the fire with the formula, "To Sampad, svāhā," he should pour the remnants into the mash. Having offered clarified butter into the fire with the formula, "To Āyatana, svāhā," he should pour the remnants into the mash. (5) — The rest is the same; [he offers] "To Vasiṣṭha, Pratiṣṭhā, Sampad, Āyatana, svāhā," and having offered each in that same manner, he should pour the remnants into the mash.

Then, having stepped back and placed the stirred offering in his joined palms, he mutters: "Amo by name art thou; for 'Amo' is all this. He is indeed the eldest, the best, the king, the sovereign lord. May he lead me to seniority, excellence, kingship, and sovereignty, so that I alone may be all this.

Then, having stepped back and moved slightly away from the fire, he places the churned mixture in his joined palms and mutters this mantra: "Ama by name you are, for all this is indeed yours. *Ama* is the name of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For by means of food, the vital breath breathes within the body; therefore, because the substance of the churned mixture is food, it is praised as being the vital breath itself with the words, "Ama by name you are. Why? Because *ama*—meaning "together with" (*saha*)—all this entire world belongs to you who have become the vital breath. Therefore [it is so called].

For that *mantha*—the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—is indeed the eldest and the best; for this very reason, it is the king, the radiant one, and the sovereign lord who, presiding over all, protects everything. May that *mantha*, the vital breath, lead me too to its own state, endowed with the multitude of qualities such as being the eldest and so forth; may I become this entire world, like the vital breath itself. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra.

Then, indeed, with this ṛc he sips water foot by foot: with "We choose that of Savitṛ," he sips; with "the food of the god," he sips; with "the best, the all-sustaining," he sips; and with "we meditate upon the swift bounty of Bhaga," he drinks it all. Having rinsed the bronze vessel or the cup, he lies down behind the fire, either on a skin or on the bare ground, restraining his speech and remaining unyielding. If he should see a woman, he should know: "The rite has been successful. 7. (7)

Immediately thereafter, one sips and consumes with this verse about to be recited, taking it foot by foot—that is, one consumes each morsel with each individual quarter-verse of the mantra. That food belongs to Savitṛ, the impeller of all; and having unified the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with the Sun, it is said: "We choose the form of the churned drink of the Sun. The intention is: "By consuming this food belonging to Savitṛ, may we become attuned to the very nature of Savitṛ."

The phrase "of the god Savitṛ" is to be connected with the preceding word. *Śreṣṭham* means most praiseworthy, the best among all foods, the most nourishing (*sarvadhātama*)—that is, the most excellent sustainer (*dhārayitṛtama*) or the supreme ordainer (*vidhātṛtama*) of the entire world; in every respect, it is an epithet of the food. *Turam* means quick, swift, or rapid; the remainder of the sense is that this is the very nature of the divine god Savitṛ. *Dhīmahi* means "we should meditate upon. The intention is that those whose selves have been purified by this distinguished food should contemplate [Him].

Or else, [the meaning is]: "We have performed the ritual action that is the cause of attaining greatness, the glory of Bhaga; let us meditate upon—that is, contemplate—that. And he drinks all the residue of the churning. Having rinsed—that is, having washed—the *kaṃsa*, which is a vessel shaped like a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa* shaped like a *camasa*, made of udumbara wood.

Having drunk [the water] and sipped it, he lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east, either on a skin, or on an antelope hide, or on a bare mound of earth, or simply on the ground; "vācaṃyamaḥ" means being restrained in speech, that is, silent; "aprasāhaḥ" means not being overcome or assailed by undesirable dreams such as those involving women and the like, which implies being one whose mind is fully controlled. If, being in such a state, he should see a woman in his dreams, then he should know: "This rite of mine has been successful."

Regarding this, there is this verse: "When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desired objects, one should know that success will attend therein; in that vision of the dream, in that vision of the dream. (8) Thus ends the second section.

Regarding this matter, there is also this verse as a mantra: "When, in dreams—meaning in dream-vision or at the time of dreaming—one sees a woman during rites performed for specific desires (kāmya-karma) aimed at fulfilling those desires, one should know that there will be success therein; that is to say, one should know that the accomplishment of the fruits of those actions will come to pass. The intention is that this occurs when such auspicious dreams as seeing a woman and so forth have taken place. The repetition [of the word 'karma'] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the ritual. Thus ends the commentary on the second section.

Introduction: The courses of transmigratory existence, beginning from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, must be described for the sake of generating detachment in those seeking liberation; therefore, this narrative is commenced—(1)—

Śvetaketu by name—*ha* being used in the sense of tradition—was the son of Āruṇi (the descendant of Aruṇa), specifically the grandson of Āruṇi; he went to the assembly, that is, the council, of the Pañcālas. To him who had arrived, Pravāhaṇa by name—the son of Jīvala, known as Jaibali—said: "O boy, did your father instruct you? The meaning is: "Have you been instructed by your father? Being thus addressed, he said: "Indeed, I have been instructed, O Venerable Sir," indicating this with the word *anu*. (2)

He said to him: "If you have been instructed, do you know what happens to creatures after they depart from this world—that is, where they go? Do you know that? The other replied, "No, Venerable Sir; I do not know that which you ask. [The teacher continued: "In that case, do you know how they return? He replied, "No, Venerable Sir."

"Do you know the point of divergence (*vyāvartana*)—the place of mutual separation—for the two paths, the way of the gods (*devayāna*) and the way of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*), for those who travel together?

(3) Do you know how that world belonging to the fathers—which they reach and from which they return—is not filled, even though many are departing [to it]? He replied, "I do not know, O Venerable Sir."

"Do you know how—by what sequence—when the fifth libation, numbering five, has been offered, the waters produced by those libations and the waters serving as the means for those libations come to have 'human speech' (*puruṣavacasaḥ*)? That is to say, when they are offered in sequence and become the sixth libation, they come to have human speech, meaning they are designated by the word 'person' (*puruṣa*) and receive the name 'person'. Being thus addressed, he said, "No indeed, venerable sir"; the meaning is: "I do not know anything at all regarding this. (4)

Then, being thus ignorant, why did you say, "I have been instructed"? For how could one who does not know these groups of matters asked by me claim among the learned, "I have been instructed"? Thus, Śvetaketu, having been pressed and exhausted by the king, went to his father’s presence and said to him: "Without having actually instructed me—that is, without providing the instruction—your honor indeed told me at the time of my return home, 'I have instructed you.'"

(5) — Since a *rājanyabandhu*—one whose kinsmen are *rājanyas*, meaning one who is himself of bad conduct—asked five questions, numbering five, I was not able to explain even one of them; that is, I was not able to determine their meaning specifically according to their sense.

The father said to him: "My dear son, just as you spoke these questions to me immediately upon my arrival, saying, 'I was not able to explain even one of them,' know me to be in that same state; the meaning is that by the sign of your own ignorance, you should know that I too am ignorant regarding those matters."

How so? Just as I do not know—not even one single one—of these questions, meaning that just as you yourself, my dear, do not know these questions, so too I do not know them. Therefore, you should not harbor a misconception regarding me. Why is this so? Because I do not know them; for if I had known these questions, why would I not have told them to you, my dear son, on a previous occasion at the time of your return home?

"I have not spoken [of this]," he said; having said this, Gautama by lineage went to the presence of King Jaivali. To him, Gautama, who had arrived, he offered the appropriate hospitality. And Gautama, having been received as a guest and having stayed there, rose early the next morning when the king had gone to the assembly hall.

"Bhajana" means a portion, worship, or service; or "sabhāgaḥ" means one who exists together with a portion, that is, one being honored by others. Gautama himself went forth to meet the king. The king said to him, Gautama: "O venerable Gautama, choose—pray for—a boon, a desirable object, from among human wealth, such as villages and the like, pertaining to men. Gautama replied: "O King, let human wealth remain with you alone."

"Speak to me—that very speech characterized by the five questions which you uttered in the presence and near my son, the prince. When addressed thus by Gautama, the king became distressed and sorrowful, wondering, "How indeed shall this be? (6) [No commentary provided for this verse] (7).

Having fallen into distress and considering that the Brahmin was not to be refused, and thinking that knowledge must be imparted according to the proper rule, he commanded Gautama, saying, "Dwell [here] for a long time"—that is, he gave this order. By stating the reason for his action, he asks the Brahmin's forgiveness for what he had previously announced as the king’s gift of knowledge and what he subsequently ordered when saying, "Dwell for a long time."

The king said to him: "O Gautama, although you are a Brahmin possessed of all knowledge, since you have spoken to me in such a manner—that is, with words characterized by that very [limited] knowledge—you should know this because of your ignorance; therefore, speak that same speech concerning knowledge to me."

In this regard, it must be said: since it is well known in the world that in this manner—by which means this Vidyā did not previously go from you to the Brāhmaṇas, nor were the Brāhmaṇas ever instructed by this Vidyā—therefore, in former times, in all the worlds, the governance and authority over disciples belonged exclusively to the Kṣatriya, that is, to the Kṣatriya caste alone.

"This knowledge has come down through the lineage of Kṣatriyas alone for all this time; nevertheless, I shall impart it to you. After its transmission to you, it will go to the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, you should forgive what I have said. Having spoken thus, the king imparted that knowledge to him.

*Commentary on the Third Section:* "Truly, O Gautama, that world over there is a fire. The sun is its fuel, the rays are its smoke, the day is its flame, the moon is its embers, and the stars are its sparks. (1)

Introduction: This question—"In the fifth oblation, the waters"—is resolved first, because the resolution of this one will be conducive to the resolution of the others. That commencement of the effects of the two *agnihotra* oblations has been described in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "The departure, the path of the two oblations, their support, their satisfaction, their return, and their rising toward the world. Regarding that, these are the questions.

And their removal has been explained in that very same place: "When those two oblations have been offered, they rise up; they enter the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). They make the intermediate space itself the *āhavanīya* fire, the wind the fuel, and the rays the bright oblation. They satisfy the intermediate space, and from there they rise up," and so forth; in this very manner, as before, they satisfy heaven and then return. Having entered this earth and satisfied it, they enter the person (*puruṣa*).

"Then, having entered a woman, he becomes one who rises up toward the world. In that context, it was stated that the mere commencement of the effects of the two *agnihotra* oblations occurs in this manner; however, here, desiring to enjoin the meditation upon those effects—characterized by the transformation of the *apūrva* of the *agnihotra*—as fivefold fires as a means for attaining the Northern Path (*uttaramārga*), he says:

"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," and so forth. Here, when the two Agnihotra oblations are offered in the evening and morning—oblations consisting of milk and other substances, preceded by faith, and characterized by the fuel, smoke, flame, coals, and sparks of the Āhavanīya fire, as well as by the causal agents such as the sacrificer—they ascend through the intermediate space and enter the heavenly world. These two become subtle elements; because they consist essentially of water, they are designated by the word "water" (*ap*), and because they have faith as their cause, they are designated by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*).

The locus of those two is fire, and whatever else is related to it, such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth, is mentioned. Furthermore, that very meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the two oblations as being fire and so forth is likewise indicated: "That world indeed is the fire, O Gautama"—just as the *āhavanīya* fire is here the locus for the *agnihotra*. Of that fire called the heavenly world, the sun itself is the fuel-stick (*samidh*), for by it that world is kindled and shines; thus, because of its kindling (*samindhana*), the sun is the fuel-stick. The rays are the smoke, because they rise from it.

For from the fuel, smoke rises. The day is the flame, because of the commonality of light and because it is an effect of the sun. The moon is the embers, because it becomes manifest upon the subsiding of the day; for indeed, embers become manifest upon the subsiding of the flame. The stars are the sparks, because of the commonality of being scattered like the particles of the moon. Into this very fire, the gods offer faith (*śraddhā*); from that oblation, King Soma arises. 2. Thus ends the fourth section. 4. (2)

In this very fire as previously described, the deities—the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer appearing in the form of Agni and the other gods from the perspective of the deities (*adhidaivata*)—offer *śraddhā*. By *śraddhā* are meant the subtle waters, permeated by faith, which take the form of the state resulting from the transformation of the *agnihotra* oblation. This is because, in the inquiry concerning the oblations, it is heard that "in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called man" (*pañcamyām āhutāv āpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavanti*), establishing water as the substance to be offered; furthermore, it is known from scripture: "Faith, indeed, is water; beginning with faith itself, they lead it forth and proceed with the sacrifice."

They offer that faith, which is formless, as an oblation. From that oblation, King Soma arises as the transformation of those waters denoted by the word "faith" when offered into the fire of the heavenly world. Just as it was stated that the essences of the flowers of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures—carried by the bees of the *Ṛk* and so forth—initiate an effect in the sun characterized by glory and the like, such as the red color and so on; in the same way, these subtle waters denoted by the word "faith," which are inherent in the oblations of the *agnihotra*, enter the heavenly world and [attain] the lunar state.

The sacrificers, who are the performers of the *agnihotra* oblations, begin the rite which results in its fruit. Consisting of the oblations and permeated by the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the oblations, they are drawn by the ritual act in the form of the oblation; entering the heavenly world along with the waters of faith (*śraddhā*), they become the moon. For it was for this purpose that the *agnihotra* was offered by them. However, in this context, it is primarily the transformation of the oblation itself—through the sequence of connection with the five fires—that is intended for the sake of meditation, not the destiny of the sacrificers.
He will describe that [path] for the ignorant later on by way of smoke and so forth, and for the wise, the northern path produced by knowledge.

Thus ends the commentary on the fourth section. "Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; its fuel is the wind, its smoke is the cloud, its flame is lightning, its embers are thunderbolts, and its sparks are hailstones. (1)

(1) — He states the meaning for the second stage of the oblation: "Parjanya, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Parjanya is a specific deity presiding over the instruments of rain. Of that [fire], the wind (*vāyu*) is the fuel (*samit*), for by the wind the fire of Parjanya is kindled, as rain is observed when the east wind and others blow strongly. The cloud (*abhra*) is the smoke, because it is a product of smoke and is perceived like smoke. The lightning (*vidyut*) is the flame (*arcis*), due to the commonality of luminosity. The thunderbolt (*aśani*) is the embers (*aṅgāra*), because of its hardness or its connection with lightning.
The sparks are the flashes of lightning; the crackling sounds are the rumbling of the clouds, due to their common quality of being scattered.
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma as an oblation; from that offering, rain comes into being. 2. Thus ends the fifth section. 5. (2)

In this very fire, the gods offer King Soma as before. From that oblation, rain comes into being; the waters called *śraddhā*, having transformed into the form of Soma, reach the fire of Parjanya in the second stage and transform into rain—thus according to the commentary on the fifth section.

"Earth, O Gautama, is indeed fire," and so forth, as before. Of that fire called earth, the year alone is the fuel (*samit*), for it is by the time of the year that the earth is kindled for the production of rice and other crops. Space is its smoke, for space is seen rising from the earth just as smoke rises from fire. Night is its flame, for night is appropriate to the earth which is non-luminous by nature because it consists of darkness—just as a flame is appropriate to fire.
The quarters are the embers, due to the commonality of being pacified. The intermediate directions are the sparks, due to the commonality of being minute.
(2) — "In that [fire]" and so forth is the same as before. From that oblation, food consisting of rice, barley, and so forth, comes into being.

Thus ends the commentary on the sixth section. "O Gautama, man indeed is the fire. His speech is the fuel, his breath is the smoke, his tongue is the flame, his eye is the embers, and his ear is the sparks. 1.

Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. His speech is the fuel, for by speech, through the mouth, man is kindled; he is not mute. His breath is the smoke, because it issues from the mouth like smoke. His tongue is the flame, because of its redness. His eye is the embers, because it is the seat of light. His ear is the sparks, because of their similarity in being scattered about. Into this very fire, the gods offer food; from that oblation, semen comes into being. 2. Thus ends the seventh section. 7. (2)

The rest is the same. They offer food prepared from rice and other grains. From that oblation, semen comes into being. Thus ends the commentary on the seven sections. "O Gautama, woman indeed is the fire. Her lap is the fuel; when one addresses her, that is the smoke; the vulva is the flame; what one performs within is the embers; and the pleasures are the sparks. (1)

(1) A woman, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Her lap is the fuel, for by that she is kindled for the production of sons and so forth. When he addresses her, that is the smoke, because addressing arises from the woman. The womb is the flame, because of its redness. What he does within is the embers, because of its connection with fire. The pleasures of delight are the sparks, because of their minuteness. Into this very fire the gods offer semen; from that offering, the embryo comes into being. 2. Thus ends the eighth section. 8.

(2) "Into this very fire, the gods offer semen; from that oblation, the embryo comes into being. Thus, by way of the sequence of offerings consisting of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen, it is the waters themselves that have become the embryo. In this context, because the waters are inherent in the oblation, there is an intention to emphasize their predominance—namely, that "the waters, at the fifth oblation, come to be called 'man'. However, it is not the case that the waters alone initiate the effects such as soma and the rest, nor is it the case that the waters exist without having been made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*).

Even though [the elements] are made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*), the acquisition of specific designations is observed—such as "this is earth," "these are waters," or "this is fire"—based on the predominance of one or another [element]. Therefore, it is the combined elements themselves that, due to the predominance of water and being associated with action, are called "waters" when they initiate effects such as Soma and so forth. And an abundance of fluidity is observed in Soma, rain, food, semen, and bodies. Although the body consists primarily of earth (*pārthiva*), it contains much fluidity. In that regard, when the fifth oblation has been offered, the waters take the form of semen and become the embryo. Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section.
Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called "man. That embryo, enveloped by the amnion, having lain within for ten or nine months, or for as long as it takes, is then born.

Once born, he lives for the duration of his lifespan. When he has passed away and reached his destiny, they carry him from here back to the very fires from which he came and from which he was produced. Thus ends the ninth section.

Thus, it has been explained that "in this way, indeed, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"; this constitutes one question. As for what was stated in the Vājasaneyaka—that the two oblations, having returned from the heavenly world and so forth, enter the earth, a man, and a woman respectively, and then rise up toward the world—that is mentioned here as a relevant digression. And here, in the first question, it was asked: "Do you know where people go from here?"

And this is its commencement: that embryo, which is the fifth specific transformation of the waters—consisting of those [substances] denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā) that are inherent in the act of offering—is enveloped by the *ulba*, that is, covered and encased by the *jarāyu* (the chorion); having lain within the mother's womb for ten or nine months, or for as long as the time may be, whether less or more, it is then born immediately thereafter.

The passage beginning with "enveloped by the *ulba*" is stated for the purpose of inducing dispassion (*vairāgya*). For indeed, the dwelling in the mother’s womb is miserable; it is a place filled with urine, feces, wind, bile, phlegm, and the like, where the embryo—smeared by those substances, covered by the impure cloth of the *ulba*, and possessing as its seed the impurity of blood and semen—grows through the entry of the essence of what the mother has eaten and drunk, while its power, strength, vigor, energy, wisdom, and movement are all suppressed.

Then, for one being oppressed at the gateway of the womb, the emergence—that is, birth—is even more painful; this instills detachment by noting that after having lain within [the womb] for an exceedingly long time—nine or ten months, which are unbearable even for a single moment—[one is born].

(2) Thus born, for as long as his lifespan lasts, he performs karma for the sake of going and coming again and again like a water-wheel, or for the sake of revolving horizontally like a potter's wheel, and he lives for as long as the lifespan acquired through karma endures.

When this person has reached the end of his lifespan and is dead—departed according to destiny and directed by his own karma toward the next world—if he was entitled to perform Vedic rituals or to possess knowledge, then they carry him, once dead, from this village to the fire for the sake of the fire, that is, the officiating priests or the sons carry him for the funeral rites.

To that very fire from which he came—having come from the presence of the fire through the sequence of oblations beginning with faith—and from whom he was produced and born from the five fires, they carry him back; the meaning is that they cause him to reach his own source, the fire itself.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth section.

Now, those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity—they attain the light; from the light, they go to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to the six months during which the sun moves northward. 1. (1) [No commentary provided for this verse.]

From the months [he goes] to the year, from the year to the sun, from the sun to the moon, from the moon to the lightning. There is a person who is non-human; he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods.
Thus [it is said]. 2. (2) —-

The question, "Do you know where creatures go from here? has now presented itself and must be answered. In that regard, those householders who are qualified and have risen toward the world, and who know—meaning they understand—in this very way the aforementioned vision of the five fires, thinking, "We have been born in succession from the fires beginning with the heavenly world; we are of the nature of fire, having the five fires as our self"—they are the ones [who know].

How is it understood that those who "know thus" are said to be householders alone and no others? For the author will later state that those householders who do not know thus, but are solely devoted to sacrifices (*iṣṭa*), public works (*pūrta*), and charity (*datta*), go to the moon by way of smoke and so forth.

And those forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*) characterized by the term "forest" (*araṇya*), as well as wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), who worship with faith and austerity—their journey by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) will be described along with those who know thus. By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and because of their connection to the oblations of the *agnihotra*, only householders are understood here by the phrase "they know thus. Now, one might object: there are also celibate students (*brahmacārin*) who are not included, since they are neither indicated by the mention of "village" nor by the mention of "forest"; how, then, is the conclusion by elimination established? This is not a fault.

On the basis of the authority of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, the northern path of Aryaman is well known for those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), namely the lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*); therefore, they too shall go along with the forest-dwellers. As for the students (*upakurvāṇaka*), however, since they exist for the purpose of mastering the Veda, they do not require a specific mention here. [Objection: If the state of having sublimated vital energy is accepted as the cause for attaining the northern path on the authority of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, then the knowledge of "being thus" (*itthaṃvit*) would become useless. [Reply: No, for it is meaningful with respect to householders.

For those householders who do not know this [way], the path beginning with smoke from the south is well known by their very nature. But for those among them who know thus—that is, who know the Brahman with qualities (saguṇa) or some other [form]—they proceed by the northern path, according to the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him or not, [the fire] leads them only to light.

[Objection: Is it not improper that only the *ūrdhvaretas* (those of perpetual chastity) and not the householders should go by the northern path, given that both are equal in terms of being *āśramins* (stages of life), especially since the householders possess a greater abundance of Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra*?

This is not a fault, for they are indeed impure. For them, attachment and aversion arise from the association with enemies and friends; likewise, merit and demerit arise from the motives of injury and favor. Furthermore, many causes of impurity—such as violence, falsehood, deceit, and lack of celibacy—are unavoidable for them; therefore, they are impure. Because of this impurity, there is no journey by the northern path. On the other hand, others are pure because they avoid violence, falsehood, deceit, lack of celibacy, and so forth, and they are free from passion (*virajas*) because they avoid enmity, friendship, disease, hatred, and the like.

For them, the subsequent path is the appropriate one. And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "Those unwise ones who desired offspring went to the cremation grounds; those wise ones who did not desire offspring indeed attained immortality. Since there is an identical path for such householders and forest-dwellers, and since the fruit is the same—immortality—it follows that knowledge would be useless for the forest-dwellers.

And thus there would be a contradiction with the Śruti: "Neither do the sacrificial fees go there, nor those who are ignorant though ascetic," and "He does not benefit him [who knows] this without knowing it"—these would be contradictory. This is not so, because what is intended by "immortality" (amṛtatva) is the state of abiding until the dissolution of all beings. Regarding that very point, it has been stated by the authors of the Purāṇas: "The state until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called immortality."

And with reference to that which is absolute immortality, there are scriptural texts such as, "The sacrificial gifts do not go there," and "He does not benefit him who knows [Brahman] without knowing this. Therefore, there is no contradiction. If it is argued that there is a contradiction with such scriptural texts as, "They do not return again," and "They do not return to this human whirlpool," we say no; for there is the qualification "to this human [whirlpool]," and also the statement, "For them, there is no return here."

For if they were not to return at all, the specific qualifications "this" and "here" would be meaningless. If it is argued that "this" and "here" refer merely to the general form (*ākṛti*), we say no; since the meaning of eternal non-return is already understood from the word "non-return" itself, the postulation of a "form" is useless. Therefore, because the specific meanings of "this" and "here" must have purpose, one must assume a return elsewhere.

Furthermore, for those who possess the realization that "Being alone, one, without a second," there is no departure by way of the artery at the crown of the head along the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi), as stated in the passages: "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" and "Therefore, it became all this."

"His vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here," according to hundreds of such scriptural passages. If it is argued that the meaning should be construed as "the vital breaths of that soul desiring to depart do not depart [from the body], but go along with it," we say no; for this would render the qualification "they are merged right here" purposeless, and because the departure together with the vital breaths is already established by the statement, "All the vital breaths follow after it departs. Therefore, this doubt—that the breaths do not depart—is entirely unfounded.

Even when it is argued that because liberation is distinct from the course of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) along with the living self (*jīva*) is suspected, and thus it is said "they do not depart," even then the qualification "they are merged right here" would be purposeless. Furthermore, neither movement nor the state of being a living self (*jīvatva*) is possible for one who is separated from the vital breaths; for the Self (*ātman*), which is omnipresent and partless, the distinction of the living self is caused solely by its connection with the vital breaths, like sparks from a fire. Therefore, upon separation from them—

If the scriptures (*śruti*) are authoritative, it is impossible to conceive of the soul as having a "living-ness" (*jīvatva*) or a "motion" (*gati*), nor can it be imagined that a minute particle of the Existent (*sat*) called the soul departs, rending the Existent and creating a hole within it. Therefore, from the passage, "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality," it is understood that for the worshiper of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahma*), there is a departure through the artery along with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); and this immortality is merely relative, not liberation (*mokṣa*) itself. This is evident from the specific qualification following the description of "that unconquered city" and "the lake Airammadīya": "This is the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) belonging to them alone."

Therefore, there are householders who know the five fires, and those who are forest-dwellers and wandering mendicants in the wilderness, together with celibate students, who worship [the path] characterized by faith and austerity—meaning they are full of faith and are ascetics; the word "worship" (upāsate) here signifies "intentness upon" (tātparya), as in the expression "they worship [the path of] sacrifice, public works, and charity."

Furthermore, according to another Vedic text, those who meditate upon Brahman as the True (Satya), known as Hiraṇyagarbha, they all attain—that is, reach—the Radiance (*arciḥ*), the deity presiding over the radiance. The rest is the same as explained in the commentary on the fourth path. This path of the gods has been described as terminating at Satyaloka, and not beyond the cosmic egg, based on the wording of the mantra: "That which is between the Father and the Mother."

Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, "Sacrifice and meritorious works are charity," they pass into smoke; from smoke, into night; from night, into the waning half of the month; from the waning half of the month, they go along the six months during which the sun moves southward—these [people] do not reach the year.

The word "atha" (now/then) serves the purpose of introducing a new subject. These householders who are in the village—"village" being a specific qualification of householders intended to distinguish them from forest-dwellers—just as "forest" is a specific qualification for forest-hermits (*vānaprastha*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) intended to distinguish them from householders; [the text mentions] "sacrificial rites and works of public utility": *iṣṭa* refers to Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra*, while *pūrta* refers to the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, gardens, and so forth.

"Gift" (*datta*) refers to the distribution of goods to worthy recipients outside the sacrificial altar according to one's ability; "worship" (*upāsate*) means they practice such acts as service and protection, because the word "iti" here indicates a manner or type. Because they are devoid of true insight (*darśana*), they reach—that is, they attain—the smoke, meaning the deity presiding over smoke.

Having passed the night presided over by Dhūmra, they reach the deities of the night; likewise, they reach the deities presiding over the dark fortnight, who have the dark fortnight as their presiding deity. From the dark fortnight, they reach those six months during which the sun moves toward the southern direction; the meaning is that they reach the deities presiding over the six months of the sun's southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). The plural form "months" is used because the deities of the six months travel in groups. Among them—

These performers of ritual acts under discussion do not reach the year—that is, the deity presiding over the year. Why, then, is there even the occasion for reaching the year, such that it must be denied? For there is indeed such an occasion: the southern and northern solstices are constituent parts of the single year; and in that context, for those who have set out on the path beginning with light, it was stated that they reach the year as a whole from the months of the northern solstice.

Therefore, since here too, having heard of the attainment of the southern solstitial months—which are constituent parts of that [year]—the attainment of the year as a whole, being their composite, follows by the same logic as before, its attainment is prohibited: "They do not reach the year. From the months they go to the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers to space; from space to the moon. That is King Soma, the food of the gods; that the gods consume. 4. (4)

From the months they go to the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers to space; and from space to the moon. Who is this moon that is reached by them? It is this King Soma who is seen in the atmosphere, the food of the Brahmins, and the food of the gods. The gods, Indra and the others, consume that moon as their food. Therefore, having gone by way of smoke and so forth and having become the moon, the performers of ritual acts are consumed by the gods. But surely, the performance of sacrifices and other rites would lead to misfortune if, having become food, they were to be consumed by the gods.

This is not a fault, because by the word "food" (*anna*), merely their being instruments [of enjoyment] is intended; for they are certainly not consumed by the gods by means of swallowing mouthfuls. What then? They become mere instruments for the gods, like women, cattle, servants, and so forth. Furthermore, the word "food" is seen to be used for such instruments—as in "women are the food of men, cattle are the food [of men], the subjects are the food of kings," and so on—and yet, even though those women and others are objects of human enjoyment, it does not follow that they lack enjoyment [themselves].

Therefore, although these performers of ritual action (*karmiṇaḥ*) are objects of enjoyment for the gods, they are happy and sport with the gods. And their body, fit for the enjoyment of pleasure, is produced from water (*āpya*) upon the lunar orb. This was stated previously: "The waters, denoted by the word *śraddhā*, when offered as an oblation into the fire of the heavenly world, become King Soma. Those waters, conjoined with karma and accompanied by the other elements, reach the heavenly world and, having attained the state of the moon, become the originators of the bodies and so forth for those who worship the sacrifices and other rites.

And when the final oblation of the arrow has been offered into the fire and the body is being consumed by that fire, the waters arising from it, together with the smoke, envelop the sacrificer from above, reach the lunar orb, and become the external constituent of the body, serving as the place for the *kuśa* grass and the clay. With the body thus begun, they remain enjoying the fruits of their sacrifices and other meritorious deeds. Having dwelt there until the exhaustion of those merits, they then return again by this very same path—the way they came—back to space; from space they go to air, having become air they become smoke, having become smoke they become mist...

Until the exhaustion of that karma which is the cause for its enjoyment—*saṃpāta* means that by which they fall together, namely the exhaustion of karma; *yāvat-saṃpātam* means until the exhaustion of karma—they, having dwelt in that lunar orb, then immediately thereafter return again by this very path (*adhvan*) which is about to be described. From the use of the term "return again," it is understood that they had previously gone to and returned from the lunar orb more than once.

Therefore, having accumulated karma such as sacrifices and other rites in this world, they go to the moon; and upon the exhaustion of that [karma], they return. It is not possible for them to remain there even for a single moment, because the karma that is the cause of their stay has been exhausted—just as a lamp goes out when its oil is exhausted.

In this regard, does one descend from that [moon] upon the exhaustion of all the karma by which one ascended to the lunar orb, or rather with some remainder? What follows from this? If there were the exhaustion of every single action, then liberation would occur for one while still remaining in the lunar orb; let alone whether one would remain right there or not, liberation would be attained, and for one who has returned from there, the experience of a body and so forth in this world would be impossible. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such Smṛti texts as, "Then, by the remainder... and so on.

Now, it may be argued that even apart from *iṣṭāpūrta* and *datta*, there exist many other actions in the world of men that serve as the cause for bodily experience, and since these are not experienced in the lunar sphere, they remain undestroyed; thus, there is no contradiction in saying that only those actions by which one ascended to the lunar sphere are exhausted. Furthermore, the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is not contradictory because all actions share the common nature of being *karman*. For this very reason, there is no fault in the conclusion that liberation occurs right there [in the lunar sphere].

Furthermore, since it is possible for each individual being to initiate actions that have as their fruit the experience of many diverse births, and since the exhaustion of all karma within a single birth is not logically tenable—given the traditional teaching that certain acts such as the killing of a Brahmin initiate multiple births—and given that those who have reached the state of stationary beings (plants, etc. and are utterly deluded cannot possibly initiate the karma that serves as the cause for upward advancement; and finally, because for those who are embryos and are being aborted, karma is impossible, the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) would be untenable.
Therefore, there is no experience of all karmas in a single birth.

As for what some say—that because the substratum of all karmas is destroyed, karmas generally initiate a new birth—it is not tenable that some karmas remain without initiating anything while others initiate a birth, since death is the manifestor of all karmas, just as a lamp is the manifestor of its own objects.

That is incorrect, because it is accepted that everything has everything as its essence (*sarvātmakatva*). For if everything has everything as its essence, then—due to being restricted by place, time, and causal conditions—it is not possible for anything anywhere to undergo suppression in its entirety, nor is it possible for manifestation in its entirety; this would likewise apply to actions (*karman*) together with their substrata. And just as [in the case of the soul], various contradictory latent impressions (*vāsanā*) formed by previous births as humans, peacocks, monkeys, and so forth, are present when a karma leading to monkeyhood begins to produce a monkey birth.

They are not destroyed; likewise, it is logical that even the karmas which serve as the causes for attaining another birth are not destroyed. For if all the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) from the experiences of previous births were destroyed, then when a monkey-birth had been commenced by karma having a monkey as its cause, a newborn monkey would not possess the skill of clinging to its mother’s belly while she moves from one branch to another; this is because such an action has not been practiced in this present life.

Nor can it be said that he was a monkey in the very birth immediately preceding the present one, because of the Vedic scripture: "Knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior experience. Therefore, since there is no complete destruction of all karma along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the possibility of residual karma remains. Since this is so, transmigration is established by means of that residual karma which has not yet been exhausted; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

What is that path toward which they return? It is said: they return "by the same way as they came" (*yathetam*), meaning according to the manner in which they arrived. But was it not stated that the sequence of their journey was from the months to the world of the fathers (*pitṛloka*), from the world of the fathers to space (*ākāśa*), and from space to the moon? The return is not in that same order; rather, it is from space to air, and so forth. How then can it be said that they return "by the same way as they came"? This is not a fault, because their arrival at space and their arrival at earth are common to both journeys. Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule here that they must return *exactly* as they came; they may also return in a different manner.

But the rule is that they return again. Therefore, this phrase "as they came" is intended as an illustration. Consequently, they first reach the elemental ether (*ākāśa*). Those waters which were the constituent elements of their bodies in the lunar sphere dissolve upon the exhaustion of those karmas that were the cause of their enjoyment there—just as a solid form dissolves through contact with fire. Having dissolved, while remaining in the intermediate space, they become subtle, as if having become the element of ether itself.

From the intermediate space they become the wind; established in the wind and having become the wind, they are carried hither and thither. Together with them, one whose karma is exhausted becomes the wind. Having become the wind, together with them he becomes smoke. Having become smoke, he becomes mist, which consists merely of the form of carrying water.

Having become a cloud, it rains; having rained, those [waters] are born here as rice and barley, herbs and trees, sesame and beans. Indeed, from this state it is most difficult to escape. For whoever eats food and whoever sheds semen, he becomes that very thing again. 6. (6) —-

Having become a cloud, it then becomes a rain-cloud capable of pouring forth; having become a cloud, it then rains down upon elevated regions. The meaning is that, in the form of rain-showers, one whose residual karma remains falls. These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, beans, and so forth. Because those whose karma has been exhausted are manifold, they are indicated by a plural number. Because those in the preceding stages, such as the clouds, possess a single uniform nature, they are indicated by a singular number.

Because there are thousands of locations such as mountain slopes, fortresses, rivers, oceans, forests, and desert regions where those who have fallen [into the pit] are caught by the torrents of rain, for that reason indeed it is *durniṣprapataram*—difficult to escape from, difficult to get out of, difficult to emerge from—since, being carried away from the mountain slope by the flow of water, they reach the rivers, from there the ocean, and then they are devoured by crocodiles and other creatures; and even these are devoured by others.

And right there in the ocean, they dissolve along with the crocodile; drawn up again by the clouds from the waters of the sea, they fall through the showers of rain into an inaccessible region such as a desert or a rocky slope, where they remain, perhaps eventually swallowed or devoured by wild beasts and other creatures.

They too would be subject to such cycles of transformation by others; sometimes, having been born among non-edible stationary beings, they would wither away right there. Even for those born among edible stationary beings, contact with the body of a seed-discharging being is indeed difficult to obtain because of the vast number of stationary beings—this is why their escape is difficult. Alternatively, "durniṣprapataram" means more difficult to emerge from, more difficult to get out of, than this state of being rice, barley, and so forth. One should understand that one *t* sound has been elided in the word "durniṣprapataram."

The state of being rice, barley, and so forth is difficult to escape from; even more difficult to escape than that is the connection with the body of one who emits semen (the *retaḥsij*). This is because those who have been eaten by children whose semen is withheld, or by the elderly, perish in the interval due to the multiplicity of food-eaters. Only occasionally, by a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," are they eaten by those who emit semen; when this happens, for those who have attained the state of being semen-emitters, there is the attainment of the functioning of their karma.

How so? For whosoever eats food—whether it be one who emits semen joined with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), or one who emits semen into a woman during her fertile period—he becomes predominantly that very thing, that is, he takes on that very form. This "predominance" refers to the abundance of the limbs and form [of the eater]. Thus, the latent disposition (*anuśayin*), having entered within the womb of the woman in the form of semen, assumes the form of the semen-emitter, because the semen is permeated by the form of the semen-emitter; for another scriptural text states: "From all his limbs, light was produced."

Therefore, the meaning is that he indeed takes on the form of the one who emits the semen. For instance, from a man a man is born, possessing the very form of a cow when born from a cow, and not the form of another species; therefore, it is logical that "he becomes that very thing again.

However, as for those others—distinct from those with residual karma (*anuśayin*)—who, without ascending to the lunar orb, attain the state of rice, barley, and so forth right here through terrible evil deeds, and subsequently the state of humans and so forth, for them it is not as difficult to emerge [from their state] as it is for those with residual karma.

Why is this so? Because by means of their karma, they have taken on bodies such as rice and barley; thus, when the cause for that enjoyment is exhausted and the bodies of rice and other plants perish, they—possessing consciousness—migrate to ever-new other bodies acquired according to their karma, like leeches, because of another scriptural passage: "He becomes conscious; he passes over into consciousness itself."

Even though they depart for another body with their sensory organs withdrawn, nevertheless, like in a dream, they go to the other body endowed with consciousness (*savijñāna*), by means of the knowledge and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) manifested through karma that causes the attainment of another body, according to the authority of scripture. Likewise, the journey via the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) and the path of smoke (*dhūma-ādi*) occurs with manifest consciousness, as if in a dream, because the journey is caused by karma that has attained its functional state.

In that same way, for those possessed of latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) who have been born as rice and so forth, a connection with the body of a woman and a seed-discharger while still possessing consciousness is not possible; for there is no persistence of conscious beings during the cutting, threshing, and grinding of rice and other grains.

Now, since the transition to another body is the same for those descending even from the lunar orb, it would be logical that they possess consciousness throughout, like a leech. If that were the case, then the terrible experience of hell—which begins from the lunar orb for those who perform sacrifices (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and so forth and lasts until their birth as Brāhmaṇas and others—would follow. And this being so, the practice of sacrifices and the like, which is enjoined, would lead only to misfortune. Furthermore, the authority of the Śruti would be undermined, because Vedic actions would be connected with harmful results.

No, for there is a distinction [between the two cases], like that between climbing a tree and falling from it. Since the karma of one desiring to attain another body has already begun its operation, it is logical that he possesses consciousness through the cognition manifested by that karma—just as one climbing to the top of a tree does when desiring to grasp its fruit. Likewise, those traveling by way of the light (*arcis*) and so forth would possess consciousness, as would those seeking to ascend to the lunar orb by way of smoke (*dhūma*) and so forth.

The state of being endowed with consciousness is not [absent] for those desiring to descend from the lunar orb as it is for those falling from the top of a tree; rather, just as it is observed that those struck by a mallet or similar instrument—whose faculties are obstructed by a swoon caused by the sensation of that blow—are devoid of cognition while being carried from one place to another by their own bodies, so too is it for those desiring to descend from the lunar orb toward another body such as a human one, whose watery bodies have been dissolved due to the exhaustion of the karma that was the cause of their enjoyment in heaven.

For those whose organs are obstructed, they—having not yet abandoned the waters that constitute the seed of the body—descend through this world in the sequence beginning with space, as if in a state of swoon. Due to their organs being obstructed, they become conjoined with the stationary bodies of various births caused by past karma, while their consciousness remains unmanifest. Likewise, during the stages of reaping, threshing, grinding, processing, eating, digestion into juices, and the emission of semen, they remain as if in a swoon, because the karma that initiates another body has not yet attained its fruition.

Since they persist in all states without abandoning their connection with the water that serves as the seed of the body, their possession of consciousness is not contradicted, just as in the case of a leech. However, the absence of consciousness during the interval is like that of one who has fainted; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it is not possible to infer that Vedic rituals possess a dual nature (i.e., being both causes of merit and demerit) on the grounds that they involve violence, because such violence is enjoined by the scriptures.

Based on the Vedic scripture, "One should not harm any living beings except at the sacred sites [of sacrifice]," it is not accepted that violence enjoined by the Śāstra is a cause of demerit (*adharma*). Even if its status as a cause of demerit were accepted, just as poison and the like are neutralized by mantras, its removal is possible; thus, there is no possibility of the commencement of the effect of suffering from Vedic rituals, just as the consumption of poison is neutralized by a mantra.

Therefore, those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, it is certain, attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya. But those here whose conduct has been foul will, it is certain, attain a foul womb—either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla.

Among those who possess latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) therein, those whose conduct (*caraṇa*)—meaning their character (*śīla*)—is pleasant and beautiful in this world are designated as "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇa*). For those who are free from cruelty, falsehood, and deceit, the existence of auspicious latent dispositions can indeed be discerned. These are called "those of pleasant conduct," meaning those for whom there is auspicious karma characterized by such pleasant conduct.

By that residual merit from their past actions, remaining after their enjoyment in the lunar sphere, they—*abhyāśo ha* being an adverb meaning "very quickly"—would attain (*āpadyeran*), that is, reach, a pleasant womb (*yonim*) free from cruelty and other such traits, namely the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya, in accordance with their own past deeds. On the other hand, those who are the opposite of that, whose actions are characterized by base conduct (*kapūyacaraṇa*) and who possess impure latent tendencies (*aśubhānuśaya*), would very quickly attain a base womb according to their karma.

They would enter a foul womb, devoid of connection with dharma and loathsome—either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla, precisely according to their own karma. But those who belong to neither of these two paths become these small creatures that return repeatedly; they are born and die—this is the third place. Therefore, that world is not filled up. One should therefore feel aversion toward it. On this point there is this verse: 8. (8) ————-

As for those twice-born ones whose conduct has been pleasant, if they remain established in their own duties as performers of sacrifices and the like, they go by way of smoke and so forth, returning again and again like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*). If, however, they should attain knowledge, then they go by way of light and so forth. But when they neither cultivate knowledge nor perform sacrifices and the like, then they go by neither of these two paths—the aforementioned paths characterized by light and smoke respectively.

These small beings—gnats, mosquitoes, insects, and the like—are those who return repeatedly. Therefore, the meaning is that having fallen away from both paths, they are indeed born and die again and again. This is said as a description of the continuous succession of their births and deaths: "Be born, die, be born, die. It refers to activity impelled by the Lord (or by destiny). The implication is that time is spent solely in the form of birth and death; there is no time for auspicious actions or for worldly enjoyments.

This third station, characterized by small creatures, is in relation to the two previously mentioned paths for those wandering in *saṃsāra*. It is because of this that even those who go by the southern path return again; for those who are not qualified for knowledge and ritual action, there is simply no going by the southern path, and thus that world is not filled up. The fifth question has been explained by the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*). The first [question] has been resolved by the two paths, the southern and the northern.

There is also a divergence between the southern and northern paths—the casting of the dead into the fire is common to both; from there, they diverge: some proceed by way of light (*arcis*) and so forth, while others proceed by way of smoke (*dhūma*) and so forth. Furthermore, reaching the six months of the northern and southern solstices, they unite and then diverge again: some reach the year, and others, after the months, reach the world of the fathers (*pitṛloka*). Thus it has been explained. Moreover, the return of those whose residual karma (*anuśaya*) is exhausted is stated to be from the lunar orb through the sequence of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

The non-filling of that world has been stated by its own word: "Therefore, that world is not filled. Since the course of transmigratory existence is thus miserable, one should feel revulsion toward it.

And because small creatures, their moments of existence defined by the experience of sensations born of birth and death, are cast into a terrible and insurmountable darkness—as if into a bottomless ocean without a boat, hopeless of crossing over—one should therefore feel disgust for such a course of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), one should feel loathing, one should be filled with revulsion—thinking, "May I not fall into such a terrible great ocean of *saṃsāra*. To this effect, there is this verse in praise of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*).

The thief of gold, the drinker of *surā*, the violator of the guru’s bed, and the slayer of a Brahmin—these four fall; and the fifth is he who associates with them. (9) The "thief of gold" is one who steals the gold of a Brahmin; the "drinker of *surā*" is one who, being a Brahmin, drinks the intoxicating liquor; the "violator of the guru’s bed" is one who dwells with the wife of his teacher; and the "slayer of a Brahmin" is one who kills a member of the priestly caste. These four fall [into hell]. And the fifth is he who associates with them.

Now, he who knows these five fires in this way—even if he associates with those [who do not know them], he is not tainted by evil; he becomes pure, cleansed, and possesses a world of merit, provided he knows thus, provided he knows thus. 10. Thus ends the tenth section.

Now, furthermore, he who knows the five fires as they have been described—even if he associates with those who commit great sins—he is not tainted by evil; he remains pure. Purified by that vision of the five fires, he becomes one whose world is meritorious—that is, one for whom there is a "meritorious world" such as that of Prajāpati and others—provided he knows thus, knowing the entire collection of matters asked in the five questions as they were stated. The repetition is intended to demonstrate the conclusion of the determination of all the questions. Thus ends the commentary on the tenth section.

Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi—these great householders and great Vedic scholars, having come together, engaged in this inquiry: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? Introduction: By those traveling by the southern path, the state of being mere food has been described.

"It is the food of the gods," and "the gods eat it"; furthermore, the miserable course of transmigratory existence characterized by small creatures has been described. Desiring to avoid both these defects, the subsequent portion of the text is commenced for the purpose of establishing the state of being the eater of Vaiśvānara, as indicated by such signs as, "You shall eat food and see what is dear. The narrative, however, is for the sake of easy comprehension and for demonstrating the proper method of imparting this knowledge.
They agreed, saying, "Venerable sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self; let us go to him. And so they went to him.

Prācīnaśīla by name; Aupamanyava, the descendant of Upamanyu. Satyayajña by name; Pauluṣi, the descendant of Pulūṣa. Likewise, Indradyumna by name; Bhāllavi, the descendant of Bhallava, and his own descendant is Bhāllaveya. Jana by name; Śārkarākṣya, the descendant of Śarkarākṣa. Buḍila by name; Āśvatarāśvi, the descendant of Aśvatarāśva.

All these five were great householders (*mahāśāla*), meaning they were endowed with spacious halls; they were great Vedic scholars (*mahāśrotriya*), meaning they were perfected in sacred learning, study, and conduct. Being such as they were, they gathered together and held a deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*)—that is, they engaged in inquiry—asking: "Who is our Self (*ātman*)? What is Brahman? Here, the words *ātman* and *brahman* function as mutual qualifiers and qualified.

The term "Brahman" excludes the Self as limited by the body, while the term "Self" excludes the worshipability of a Brahman such as Āditya who is distinct from the Self. Through non-difference—understanding that "the Self alone is Brahman" and "Brahman alone is the Self"—it is established that Vaiśvānara, the Self of all, is Brahman and that He is the Self, as indicated by such signs as "your head would have fallen off" and "you would have become blind."
He reflected: "These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me; I shall not be able to answer them all. Come now, I shall instruct another.

Even though they deliberated, they did not reach a certainty; thus, they sought out an instructor for themselves. Uddālaka was indeed well-known by name; "Bhagavantaḥ" means venerable ones. This Āruṇi, the offspring of Aruṇa, currently studies—that is, remembers—this very Vaiśvānara Self which we intend. "Come, let us now go to him"; having thus resolved, they went to him—to that Āruṇi.
Aśvapati said to them, "Venerable sirs, this Kaikeya Aśvapati is currently studying this very Vaiśvānara Self. Come, let us go to him. So they went to him.

(4) Upon seeing them, he understood the purpose of their arrival and made arrangements for it. How so? He thought, "These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me about Vaiśvānara. I may not be able to provide a complete answer to everything they ask; therefore, let me now appoint another teacher for them whom I shall instruct."

When they had arrived, he had separate dwellings prepared for them. Rising in the morning, he said: "In my realm there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard, no one who has not established the sacred fires, no one who is ignorant, and no one who acts wantonly—much less a wanton woman. Venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice; as much wealth as I shall give to each individual officiating priest, so much shall I give to you, venerable sirs. Please stay. 5. (4)
Having thus prepared them, he said to them: "Sirs, this man is Aśvapati by name; he is the son of Kekaya, a Kaikeya, and he is currently studying this very Vaiśvānara Self," and so on, as before.
They said: "For whatever purpose a person acts, that indeed one should speak of; you are now studying this very Vaiśvānara Self—teach us that. 6. (5)

When they had arrived, the king, through his domestic priests and servants, caused separate honors and offerings to be made for each of them. On another day, as the king was rising in the morning, he approached them with humility and said, "Accept this wealth from me."

Thinking, "Having been rejected by them, they surely perceive some fault in me, since they do not accept wealth from me," and desiring to demonstrate his own virtuous conduct, he says: "In my kingdom, there is no thief who steals the property of others; no miser who fails to give despite possessing wealth; no drinker of intoxicants, being a foremost among the twice-born; no one who has not established the sacred fires while possessing a hundred cows; no one who is unlearned in accordance with his qualification; no libertine who goes to the wives of others; and for that very reason, how could there be a wanton woman?"

The meaning is that she does not become one who acts wickedly. When they replied, "We have no need for wealth," he said: "Thinking it to be small, these [brahmins] do not accept the wealth; however, O venerable sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice in a few days. For that purpose, I have prepared wealth such that I shall give to each officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) as prescribed; likewise, I shall give to each of you venerable ones. May the venerable sirs stay and witness my sacrifice."

He said to them, "I shall answer you in the morning. With fuel in their hands, they returned to him in the forenoon. Without initiating them [with the sacred thread], he spoke this to them. Thus ends the eleventh section.

Thus addressed, they said: "Whatever purpose or motive a man may have for which he approaches someone, he should state that very purpose. This is the rule of conduct for the virtuous: 'This indeed is the reason for my coming. We, moreover, are seekers of the knowledge of Vaiśvānara. You know this very Self as Vaiśvānara correctly; therefore, tell that very thing to us."

"Aupamanyava, upon which Self do you meditate? "On the sky itself, O Venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self called 'the Well-Radiant' (sutejas), which you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, in your lineage, pressed Soma, further-pressed Soma, and continuously pressed Soma are seen.

"How did he speak? [The author] says: He asked, "O Aupamanyava, which Self as Vaiśvānara do you meditate upon? Now, one might object: "Is this not improper—that a teacher should question his disciple? This is not a fault, because of the principle seen in the *Nyāya* tradition: "Approach me with what you already know; thereafter I shall tell you more. Furthermore, elsewhere too, a question from a teacher to a disciple who lacks presence of mind is seen for the purpose of generating insight, as in the case of Ajātaśatru: "Where was it then? From where..."

"This has come," [he said]. "I meditate upon Vaiśvānara as heaven itself, O venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is Vaiśvānara, known as 'Sutejas'—the one whose splendor (*tejas*) is beautiful; for he is the Self (*ātman*), since [heaven] constitutes a limb of that Self."

Because you worship that Self as a single part of Vaiśvānara, therefore in your family, well-pressed Soma in the form of the ritual substance is seen—both that which has been pressed (*suta*) in the ritual and that which has been excellently pressed (*prasuta*) and poured out (*āsuta*) in the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) and so forth; the meaning is that those born in your lineage are exceedingly devoted to ritual action.

"You see food that is dear; he who eats food sees what is dear. This becomes true for one in whose family this word of Brahman is preserved—he who thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self. "But this is merely the head of the Self," he said. "Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me. Thus ends the twelfth section. (12) (2)

Being one whose digestive fire is kindled, you eat food and behold your dear and desired sons, grandsons, and so forth. Another person also eats food here and beholds what is dear; he possesses a son, a grandson, and a great-grandson, and so on—this is the fruit of ritual action (*karmitva*) and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in the family for anyone who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara exactly as described. However, this [Vaiśvānara] is only the head of the self that is Vaiśvānara; it is not the entire Vaiśvānara.

Therefore, because you meditated upon Vaiśvānara as the whole [without distinguishing his parts], your head—meaning your skull—would have fallen off, that is, it would have dropped, had you not come to me. The intention is: "You have done well, since you have come to me.
Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section.

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi, "O Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate? He replied, "Sir, O King, I meditate upon Āditya alone. [The other] said, "This indeed is the all-formed Self, Vaiśvānara, whom you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, many all-formed things are seen in your family...

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi: "O Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate? He replied, "The Sun alone, O Venerable King. The Sun is "all-formed" (*viśvarūpa*) because it possesses white, blue, and other colors, or because it consists of all forms, since all forms indeed belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; therefore, the Sun is all-formed. From meditating upon that, much wealth of various forms is seen as an instrument for your purposes here and in the hereafter within your lineage.

"A chariot yoked with mules has followed you; a female servant and a gold necklace have come to you; you shall eat food and see what is dear; he eats food and sees what is dear, and there arises spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family—he who thus meditates upon this Self as Vaiśvānara.
