'But this is only the eye of the Self,' he said. 'You would have become blind had you not come to me. Thus ends the thirteenth section. Furthermore: "A chariot yoked with two mares is a *aśvatarī-ratha*; a female servant and a gold necklace (*dāsī-niṣka*)."

A *niṣka* joined with female slaves is a "slave-*niṣka*" (*dāsīniṣka*). "You would eat food," and so forth, is the same as before. However, Savitṛ is the eye of Vaiśvānara; because you did not worship him by means of the comprehensive conception [of Vaiśvānara], you would have become blind—you would have been deprived of sight—had you not come to me, as stated previously.

Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya Vaiyāghrapadya: "Upon what Self do you meditate? He replied, "Venerable King, upon Vāyu alone. [The teacher said: "This Vaiśvānara Self that you meditate upon is indeed the 'one whose paths are manifold. Therefore, offerings come to you from various directions, and rows of chariots follow you in various directions.

Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, whom do you meditate upon as the Self? and so on, as before. He whose paths are separate—that is, whose paths are manifold due to the various divisions of the wind such as the *āvaha*, *udvaha*, and others—is this wind called "Pṛthagvartman" (the one with separate paths). From meditating upon that Vaiśvānara Self as Pṛthagvartman, diverse offerings—offerings characterized by garments, food, and the like—come to you from various directions; even rows of chariots (*rathaśreṇayaḥ*) follow after you.

"You shall eat food; you shall see what is dear. He who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way, there will be spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family. But this is only the breath of the Self," he said. "Your breath would have departed had you not come to me. [The rest] beginning with "You shall eat food" is the same [as before]. "But this is only the breath of the Self," he said. "Your breath would have departed—that is, it would have gone out—had you not come to me. Thus ends the fourteenth section. (14) (2) — "You shall eat food," etc., is the same [as before]. "But this is only the breath of the Self," he said. "Your breath would have departed, i.e., it would have gone out, had you not come to me."

Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya: "Upon what Self do you meditate? He replied: "On space alone, O Venerable King. [The Teacher said: "This Vaiśvānara Self that you meditate upon is indeed the 'Abundant' (*bahula*). Therefore, you are abundant in offspring—consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth—and in wealth, such as gold and the like.

[Note: The passage beginning with *atha ha uvāca janam* is the same as before. This Vaiśvānara Self is "abundant" because space is all-pervading and because one meditates on its quality of abundance. Thus, you are abundant in offspring characterized by sons, grandsons, etc., and in wealth such as gold.]

"You will eat food and see what is dear; he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family. However, this is only the trunk of the Self," he said. "Your trunk would have perished had you not come to me. Thus ends the fifteenth section. (15) (2)

"But this doubt remains: the trunk is indeed the body of Vaiśvānara. Because the root *dih* means 'to increase,' and since the body is composed largely of flesh, blood, bones, and so forth, that is its 'trunk' (*saṃdeha*). [He said: 'Your body would have perished—that is, it would have been shattered—if you had not come to me.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth section. Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi Vaiyāghrapadya: "Upon which Self do you meditate? "On water alone, O Venerable Sir."

"O King," he said, "this indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is wealth; it is this Self that you meditate upon. Therefore, you are wealthy and prosperous. (1) Then he spoke to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, and so forth, as before. This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is wealth, whose form is riches. Food is water, and from food comes wealth. Therefore, you are wealthy—possessing riches—and prosperous, because the body's nourishment is caused by food.

"You will eat food and see what is dear; he who venerates this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family. But this is only the bladder of the Self," he said. "Your bladder would have burst had you not come to me. This is the sixteenth section. (This is the bladder of Vaiśvānara the Self; the bladder is the place for the collection of urine. "Your bladder would have burst"—it would have become split—"had you not come to me.")

Thus ends the commentary on the sixteenth section. Then [the King] said to Uddālaka Āruṇi Gautama: "Gautama, upon what Self do you meditate? He replied, "Sir, Your Majesty, I meditate upon the Earth itself. [The King said: "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is the Foundation; it is the Self that you meditate upon. Therefore, you are firmly established with offspring and cattle. 1. (1) [No commentary provided for this verse.]

"You will eat food and see what is dear; he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food and sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). "But these are only the feet of the Self," he said. "Your feet would have withered away had you not come to me. (Thus ends the seventeenth section. 17. (2)

Then he said to Uddālaka, and so on, as before. [Uddālaka] replied, "The earth alone, O venerable King. "This indeed is the foundation; it is the feet of Vaiśvānara. Your feet would have withered away—they would have become shriveled and slackened—if you had not come to me.
Thus ends the commentary on the seventeenth section. (1)

He said to those who possessed the aforementioned vision of Vaiśvānara: "You indeed—[the particles] *vai* and *khalu* being merely expletives—you, though knowing this one Vaiśvānara Self as non-different, eat food as if it were separate; that is to say, with the notion of a limited self, like those born blind [who perceive] an elephant."

But he who [meditates upon] this one [Self] as distinguished by the aforementioned members—beginning with the sky as the head and ending with the earth as the feet—as being "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*): it is called "measured by a span" because it is measured (*mīyate*) or known through the internal [members] beginning with the sky as the head and ending with the earth as the feet; or because it is measured as the eater within the instruments such as the mouth; or because its magnitude is equal to the spatial extent from the heavenly world down to the earth.

They are called *prādeśas* because they are indicated (*ādiśyante*) by means of the scripture (*śāstreṇa*) in an extensive manner (*prakarseṇa*); thus, the heavenly world and so forth are themselves *prādeśamātra*, having that specific measure. In another recension (*śākhāntare*), however, they conceive of [the Self] as being *prādeśamātra* because it extends from the head down to the chin. But here, that is not intended, because of the concluding statement beginning with "Of this very Self" (*tasya ha vā etasyātmanaḥ*).

Because it is measured as the inner self through the realization "I am," it is called *abhivimāna*. This very Self is Vaiśvānara—the Lord who is the Self of all; He is Vaiśvānara because He leads (*nayati*) all men (*viśvān narān*) to their respective destinations according to their merit and demerit. Alternatively, He is Vaiśvānara because He is the man (*nara*) of all (*viśva*) due to being the Self of all, or because He is led (*nīyate*) by all men (*viśvaiḥ naraiḥ*) as the inner self (*pratyagātmatayā*) through His manifold manifestations. He who meditates upon Him in this way becomes an eater of food in all worlds, such as the heavenly world and others, and in all beings.

Among all moving and non-moving things, within the selves consisting of body, senses, mind, and intellect—it is indeed in these that the designation "self" is imagined—he who knows Vaiśvānara eats food as one whose self is everything (*sarvātmā*). This means he does not eat like an ignorant person who, identifying solely with the physical body, eats food.

Why is this so? Because of this: of that very same Vaiśvānara Self under discussion, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brilliantly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartmātmā* (the self of diverse paths), the trunk is *bahula* (vast), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), and the feet are the earth itself. Alternatively, this statement is for the purpose of injunction—meaning, "one should meditate thus."

Now, desiring to identify the Agnihotra sacrifice with the eating of one who knows Vaiśvānara, the text says: "The chest of this eater, Vaiśvānara, is indeed the sacrificial altar (vedi), because of the similarity in shape. The body hairs are the sacrificial grass (barhis), for the hairs are seen spread out upon the chest as if on an altar. The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, for from the heart the mind is led forth as it were, being immediately adjacent to it; therefore, the Anvāhāryapacana fire is the mind. The mouth is the Āhavanīya fire, for food is offered into it here as the Āhavanīya. Thus ends the commentary on the eighteenth section.

Now, that which he should offer as the second [oblation], let him offer it with the words: "Svāhā to Vyāna! Thereby Vyāna is satisfied. When Vyāna is satisfied, the ear is satisfied; when the ear is satisfied, the moon is satisfied; when the moon is satisfied, the quarters are satisfied. When the quarters are being satisfied, whatever is presided over by the quarters and the moon—that is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, he himself is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). Thus ends the twentieth section. 20.
(2) He did not comment on this verse.

(1) — This being so, that food which first comes at the time of eating for the purpose of a meal, that is "to be offered" (*homīya*); it is to be offered because what is intended here is merely the fulfillment of the *agnihotra*, and thus the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to the *agnihotra* does not apply here. As for how that eater should offer the first oblation (*āhuti*), he says: with the mantra "Svāhā to Prāṇa. From the word "oblation," the meaning is that one should cast into [the mouth] a portion of food according to the measure of a sacrificial cutting (*avadāna*). By that, Prāṇa is satisfied.

(2) When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is satisfied, the eye is satisfied; when the eye is satisfied, the sun and the heaven, and so forth, are satisfied; and whatever else the heaven and the sun preside over as their domain, that too is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, he himself, while eating, becomes satisfied—this is directly perceived. Furthermore, [he is satisfied] through progeny and other such things. "Radiance" (*tejas*) is the brilliance or luster residing in the body, or perhaps boldness; "brahmic splendor" (*brahmavarcasa*) is the radiance resulting from virtuous conduct and the study of the Vedas.
Thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth section.

Then, that third oblation which one should offer, one should offer it with the words, "Svāhā to Apāna! Thereby Apāna is satisfied. When Apāna is satisfied, speech is satisfied; when speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied; when Agni is satisfied, the Earth is satisfied;
when the Earth is satisfied, whatever exists that rests upon both the Earth and Agni—that is satisfied. Following that [satisfaction]...
"He becomes satisfied; he is satisfied with offspring, with cattle, with food, with splendor, and with the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-first section.
Now, that which he should offer as the fifth oblation, he should offer with the words: "To the out-breath, svāhā! Thereby the out-breath is satisfied.

[The commentary] did not comment upon this verse. In the *Udāna*: "When one is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; when the skin is satisfied, the wind is satisfied; when the wind is satisfied, space is satisfied; when space is satisfied, whatever is presided over by both wind and space—that too is satisfied."
Following that, he becomes satisfied; he becomes satisfied with offspring, with cattle, with food, with splendor, and with the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
This is the same for the second, third, fourth, and fifth [offerings].
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-third section.
He who, not knowing this, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice—just as if he were to remove the live coals and pour the oblation into ashes, so would that [sacrifice] be.

Whoever, being ignorant of this aforementioned vision of Vaiśvānara, performs the well-known Agnihotra sacrifice—that act of his offering in the Agnihotra would be equivalent to removing embers that are unfit for an oblation and pouring it instead into ashes; such is his Agnihotra when compared with the Agnihotra of one who knows Vaiśvānara. Thus, by means of censuring the conventional Agnihotra, the Agnihotra of the knower of Vaiśvānara is praised.

Now, for one who, knowing this thus, performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. (2) And for this reason, this *agnihotra* is distinguished. How so? Now, for one who, knowing this thus, performs the *agnihotra*—that is, for one possessing the aforementioned knowledge of Vaiśvānara—the phrase "in all worlds" and so forth has the meaning already explained; for [the terms] "his offering is made" and "he eats food" have the same meaning.
Just as a tuft of reed-grass thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so all the evils of one who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, are consumed. 3.

Furthermore, just as the tuft of a reed-stalk, when thrown into or cast upon a fire, would be consumed and burnt away quickly, even so all the evils—known as merit and demerit—accumulated over many births, as well as those existing prior to the arising of knowledge and those coexisting with knowledge, are consumed and would be burnt away for this wise one who has become the Self of all and is the eater of all food, with the exception of those evils that have begun this present body.
Because its fruit has already begun to manifest—like an arrow shot toward a target—it does not burn him. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra and eats...
therefore, indeed, if one who knows this should give even the remnants of his food to a Caṇḍāla, it would be offered by him into his own Vaiśvānara; concerning this, there is this verse: 4.

Even if he were to give leavings to a Caṇḍāla—one to whom giving leavings is forbidden—even if he were to do that which is prohibited, it would indeed be offered into the Vaiśvānara fire residing within his own self; it would not be a cause for demerit. Thus, [the text] praises knowledge alone. Regarding this purpose of praise, there is this verse, which is also a mantra:
"Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother, so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra"—"they wait upon the Agnihotra.

Just as in this world hungry children wait upon their mother, thinking, "When will our mother give us food?", so do all beings who subsist on food wait upon the Agnihotra meal of one who knows thus, thinking, "When indeed will he eat? The meaning is that the entire world becomes satisfied by the eating of the knower. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-fourth section. Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govinda Bhagavat...

The fifth chapter of the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the worshipful teacher, is completed. There was once Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi. His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). My dear, in our family there has never been one who, without having studied the Vedas, has become like a mere Brahmin by birth. 1.

(1) — The story of the father and son is intended to demonstrate the supreme excellence of knowledge. His father, Āruṇi, considering his son to be a worthy vessel for knowledge and observing that the time for his initiation had passed, said to him: "O Śvetaketu, go to a teacher who is a fitting match for our family and dwell there in studenthood (*brahmacarya*)."

And this is not proper—that one born of our family, O dear one, should become like a mere Brahmin by name (*brahmabandhu*) without having studied the Vedas, claiming "the Brāhmaṇas are my kinsmen" while not himself following the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa.
