That Śvetaketu, having been addressed by his father, approached a teacher at the age of twelve and remained with him until he was twenty-four years old; during that time, having studied all four Vedas and understood their meaning, he became "mahāmanāḥ"—one whose mind is great and profound, or one whose mind considers itself peerless compared to others—and being "anūcānamānī," one who fancies himself a learned scholar (anūcāna), he returned home arrogant and of an unbending nature.

[He brought him] home. Seeing his son in such a state—one whose character was not in harmony with his own, who was arrogant and conceited—the father spoke to him out of a desire to lead him into the True Dharma: "Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are now so high-minded, considering yourself learned in the Vedas, and are so arrogant, have you asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? How indeed, venerable sir, does that instruction come about? (3) — 3 —.

"Śvetaketu, since you are so high-minded, considering yourself learned in the Vedas, and yet are so arrogant—what excellence have you attained from your teacher? Or [have you learned] that *ādeśa*—by which is meant that which is to be pointed out, namely that which is accessible solely through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher—or rather, that *ādeśa* by which the Supreme Brahman is pointed out? Have you asked your teacher about that *ādeśa*? He describes that *ādeśa*: "By hearing which *ādeśa*, even what has not been heard becomes heard; what has not been thought becomes thought; and what has not been reasoned becomes reasoned."

"What is unknown becomes known, and what is uncertain becomes certain. Even after studying all the Vedas and mastering everything else that is to be known, one remains as if his purpose were unfulfilled so long as he does not know the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); this is understood from the narrative. Having heard this wonderful thing, he said: "How indeed can it be that by the knowledge of one thing another thing becomes known?
Thinking thus, he asks: "In what way, O Blessed One, does that instruction come about?"

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'" (4). "Listen, my dear, to how that instruction is: just as in the world, when one clod of clay—which serves as the cause of things such as bracelets and jars—is known, all other things made of clay, the entire collection of clay-modifications, become known. How can it be that when the cause, the clod of clay, is known, the effect, which is different, becomes known? This is not a fault, because the effect is not something other than the cause."

If you think that when one thing is known, another is not known—this would indeed be true if the effect were something other than the cause; but it is not so, for the effect is not other than the cause. How then is it in the world that "this is the cause" and "this is its modification"? Listen: it is a mere beginning in speech, a verbal handle, a support of words.

What is that? The modification is a mere name; "name" (*nāmadheya*) means nothing but a name—the suffix *-dheya* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). It is merely a support for speech, a name alone; there is no such thing as a modification as a real entity. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is only clay; clay alone is the real entity. Just as, my dear, by means of a single ingot of copper, everything made of copper would be known—the modification being a mere support for speech, a name, while "copper" alone is the truth—so it is.

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single piece of gold—a lump of gold—one would know everything else belonging to its modifications, such as bracelets, crowns, armlets, and so forth; [the phrase] 'a mere matter of speech' and so on is the same. Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter one would know all iron, [the phrase] 'a mere matter of speech, a modification, a name—iron only is real'—even so, my dear, is that instruction. (6) — 6 —

"Just as, my dear, by knowing a single piece of black iron—meaning a lump of black iron characterized by a nail-cutter—one would know all black iron, that is, the entire range of objects made from black iron; the rest is the same. The employment of multiple illustrations is for the purpose of following the various distinctions of the subject matter and for the sake of firm conviction. "In this way, my dear, is that instruction which has been spoken by me. When the father had said this, the other replied:
"Surely those venerable ones did not know this; for had they known it, why would they not have told it to me? Let the venerable one himself tell it to me. "So be it, Soma," he said.

"Surely those venerable, worshipful gurus of mine did not know—indeed, they were not aware of—this matter which you have spoken. For if they had known this matter, how could they not have told it to me, who am virtuous, devoted, and a follower? Therefore, I think they did not know it. Thus he spoke, even though it meant expressing his subordination to his guru, out of fear of being sent back to the teacher's house.

"Therefore, let the Blessed One himself tell me that reality by knowing which omniscience may be mine; let him speak. Thus addressed, his father said, "So be it, my dear Somya. This concludes the commentary on the first section. "In the beginning, my dear Somya, this was Being alone, one only without a second. Regarding this, some say: 'In the beginning this was non-being alone, one only without a second; from that non-being, being was born. (1)

(1) — "Being alone was Being" (*sadeva saditi*): [this refers to] the mere existence that is the subtle, undifferentiated, all-pervading, one, stainless, partless consciousness, which is understood from all the Vedāntas. The word *eva* (alone) is for the purpose of restriction. What is it that is restricted? He says: this world—that which is perceived as modified, possessing name, form, and action—was indeed Being alone; this is connected with the word *āsīt* (was). When was this Being alone? It is said: "in the beginning," i.e., prior to the origin of the world.

Is this not already existent now, such that it is qualified by the phrase "was in the beginning"? No. How then is there a qualification? Even now this is indeed existent; however, because it possesses the qualifications of name and form and is the object of the word and cognition "this," it becomes "this. Prior to its origination, on the other hand, it was accessible only through the word and cognition of "Existence" (sat) alone; thus it is determined that "in the beginning this was Existence alone. For prior to origination, no object can be grasped as "this" with a specific name or form, just as in the state of deep sleep.

Just as one who has arisen from deep sleep perceives pure existence, understanding that in deep sleep there was only the reality of pure being, so too [was it] prior to creation; such is the intended meaning.

Just as it is said in the world: a potter who, desiring to produce a jar or the like in the forenoon, has spread out a lump of clay and then gone to another village, and having returned in the afternoon, perceives there the effect divided into many varieties such as jars, bowls, and so forth, and says, "In the forenoon, this jar, bowl, and the rest were merely clay alone"—so too is it said here: "In the beginning, this was Being alone. "Only one" (*eka*) means that there is nothing else existing apart from its own effects; thus it is called "only one. "Without a second" (*advitīya*) means...

Just as, apart from clay, another instrumental cause such as a potter is observed to transform the clay into the form of a jar or the like, so too, a second distinct entity that might serve as a cooperative cause for Being (*sat*) apart from Being itself is precluded by the term "without a second" (*advitīya*). By "without a second," it is not merely that a second entity which might have been expected is denied; rather, it means that no second entity exists at all for this [Being], and thus it is "without a second."

[Objection: But surely, even in the Vaiśeṣika system, co-presence with "Being" (sat) is possible for everything, because the word and the cognition "existent" (sat) recur in the case of substances, qualities, and so forth—as seen in such expressions as "existent substance," "existent quality," and "existent action. [Reply: This would indeed be true now; however, prior to production, the Vaiśeṣikas do not admit that this effect was already existent, since they maintain the non-existence of the effect prior to its production. Furthermore, they do not accept that Being alone, without a second, existed prior to production.

Therefore, this "Being" (sat) which is the cause is said to be different from the "Being" imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, based on the examples of clay and so forth. Regarding that matter—the determination of the reality prior to its origination—some nihilists (vaināśika), while determining the reality, say: "Prior to its origination, this world was non-being (asat), merely the absence of Being; in the beginning, it was one only, without a second. For the Buddhists imagine that the reality prior to origination is merely the absence of Being; they do not accept another entity that is the opposite of Being.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that reality consists in that which is grasped as "existent" or "non-existent," being either as it truly is or the opposite thereof. Now, if the nihilists (Vaināśikas) intend that prior to creation there was merely the absence of existence, how can they speak of a connection with time, a connection with number, and non-duality—expressing it as, "Prior to creation, this was non-existent, one, and without a second"? Indeed, this is not tenable for those who accept mere existence and non-existence.

The admission of mere non-existence is also untenable, because it is impossible for there to be an admitter in the absence of an admission. If it is argued that the admitter is admitted only now and did not exist prior to origination, we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an entity prior to its origination. Thus, the conceptualization that "prior to origination it was simply non-existent" is untenable.

If it is objected: "But how, if the meaning of a word is the form (*ākṛti*) of an object, can the meanings of the words and the sentence in the statement 'Being alone, indeed, without a second' be established? And if they cannot be so established, does this not follow that the sentence would be invalid?"—this is not a fault, because the sentence has as its purpose the exclusion of the apprehension of "being" (*sat*). Now, the word "being" (*sat*) denotes the form of being (*sadākṛti*). Furthermore, the two words "one alone, without a second" are in grammatical apposition with the word "being"; and likewise is the phrase "this was."

In this context, the negative particle (*nañ*) employed in a sentence affirming existence (*sadvākya*) relies upon that very affirmative sentence and turns away the cognition whose object is the meaning of that affirmative sentence—namely, the cognition characterized by [the thought] "this was Being alone, one, without a second"—from the meaning of that affirmative sentence. It is just as a man mounted on a horse, while maintaining his hold on the horse, turns it away from an object facing it; it does not, however, denote the non-existence of Being itself. Therefore, this sentence beginning with "this is non-existent" (*asadeva*) and so forth is employed solely for the purpose of removing a person's erroneous apprehension.

For by demonstrating a misconception, one can then turn [the student] away from it; thus, because it serves a purpose, the statement regarding "non-existence" (*asat*) is established as being based on scripture (*śrauta*) and authoritative. Therefore, there is no fault. Consequently, from "non-existence"—which consists of the total absence of everything—the "existent" (*sat*), that which is real, is born, having come into being. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Then he said: "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? How could the existent be born from non-existence? "In the beginning, my dear, this was only the existent (*sat*), one alone without a second. (2)

Having thus shown the position of the great nihilists (*mahāvaināśika*), [the text] refutes this contrary apprehension: "But from what source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), my dear, could it be so—that 'from non-being, being is born'? How could this be? The meaning is that it is not possible from any source of valid knowledge. As for the claim that a sprout is seen to arise upon the destruction of a seed, and therefore it arises from non-existence itself—that too is contradicted by their own admission.

How so? First, those parts of the seed that are characterized by the seed's configuration certainly persist even in the sprout; they are not destroyed upon the production of the sprout. Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣikas do not admit that the seed’s form and configuration exist as real entities distinct from the seed’s parts, such that it would be destroyed when the sprout is produced. If, on the other hand, it did exist as a real entity distinct from the parts, then there would be a contradiction with their own tenets.

Now, if it is argued that the form of the seed’s configuration (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) accepted conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) is destroyed, then what is this so-called "conventional reality"? Is it a non-entity (*abhāva*), or is it an entity (*bhāva*)? If it is a non-entity, there is no example [to support the argument]. If, on the other hand, it is an entity, even so, the sprout does not arise from a non-entity; for the sprout arises from the parts of the seed. If it is argued that those parts are also destroyed, we say no, because the same logic applies to their parts as well.

Just as for the Nihilists (vaināśika) there is no whole (avayavin) consisting of the form and configuration of a seed, so too there are no parts; thus, for them as well, the destruction [of the cause] is untenable. Since the parts of the seed have their own subtle parts, and those parts have yet other subtler parts, this regress does not cease, and consequently, destruction is impossible in all cases. Furthermore, because the cognition of existence persists, existence itself does not cease; thus, for the proponents of existence (sadvādins), the production of the existent from the existent will be established.

However, for those who maintain that what is non-existent [arises], there is no illustrative example for the arising of the existent from the non-existent. For proponents of existence, the arising of a jar from a lump of clay is observed, because the effect exists when the cause exists and does not exist when the cause is absent. If the jar were to arise from non-existence alone, one seeking a jar would not take up a lump of clay; furthermore, the application of the word and the notion of "non-existence" would follow after the jar and so forth, which is not the case. Therefore, the arising of the existent from the non-existent does not occur.

As for what they say—that the cognition of clay is the cause of the cognition of a jar, and thus the cognition of clay is called the cause of the cognition of a jar, but that in ultimate reality neither the clay nor the jar exists—this too means that an existing cognition of clay is the cause of an existing cognition of a jar; therefore, there is no arising of existence from non-existence.

If it is argued that the sequence between the cognition of the clay and the cognition of the jar is merely one of immediate succession (*ānantaryamātra*) by way of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittikatayā*), and not a relationship of material cause and product (*kāryakāraṇatva*), we say no. For when the uninterrupted succession of cognitions is being considered, the nihilists (*vaināśika*) lack any external example [to support their position]. Therefore, he said: "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so?"—that is, in what manner or by what means could the existent (*sat*) be born from the non-existent (*asat*); the intention is that there is no possible mode of illustration whatsoever for the production of the existent from the non-existent.

Having thus demolished the position of the proponents of non-existence (*asadvādin*), he concludes with the establishment of his own position: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*). Now, one might object: even for the proponent of Being (*sadvādin*), it is not observed that Being arises from Being, since we do not see one jar arising from another jar. True, it is so; it is not the case that one distinct Being arises from Being. What then? Being itself persists in a different configuration—just as a snake becomes coiled, or as clay exists through various distinctions such as powder, a lump, a jar, or potsherds.

If this is so—that everything exists in every state—how can it be said that "this was non-existent prior to its production"? Have you not heard the restriction "only Being" (*sadeva*) applied to the effect denoted by the word "this"? [Objection: In that case, it follows that prior to production, only the non-existent existed, and not that which is denoted by the word "this," such that now "this" has been produced. [Reply: No, because it is precisely Being itself that persists as the object of the word and cognition "this," just as clay itself persists as the object of the words and cognitions "clod," "jar," and so forth—it is just like that.

[Objection: But surely, just as the clay substance is [real], so too are the lump and the jar; therefore, because they are objects of a cognition different from the cognition of "Being" (*sat*), the collection of effects must be a distinct entity from "Being," just as a cow is distinct from a horse. [Reply: No, because although the lump and the jar mutually exclude one another, they do not exclude the nature of clay. Even though the jar excludes the lump and the lump excludes the jar, nevertheless, the lump and the jar do not exclude the nature of clay. Therefore, the lump and the jar are merely clay.

A cow deviates from being a horse, or a horse from being a cow; therefore, jars and the like are merely the configurations of clay and other materials. In the same way, it is logical that all this is merely the configuration of Being (*sat*), and that "before its production, it was Being alone," because modification is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*). But is not Being partless? For the Śruti says: "It is without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, stainless; for the divine Person is formless, both within and without, and unborn. Etc.

How can a modification or a structural form be possible for that which is partless? This is not a fault, because a modification or structural form is possible from the parts of "Being" (sat) as they are conceptually constructed by the intellect—just as the form of a snake arises from the parts of a rope and so forth. For the Śruti declares: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real"; thus, Being alone is real—even at the time when this [world] is perceived, it is in reality one without a second.

Then It thought: "May I be many; may I procreate. It emitted heat. That heat thought: "May I be many; may I procreate. It emitted water. Therefore, wherever a person feels heat or perspires, from that very heat water is produced.

"That Being" (tat sat) "thought" (aikṣata), meaning it performed the act of seeing. For this reason, the Pradhāna imagined by the Sāṃkhyas is not the cause of the world, because the Pradhāna is admitted to be insentient. This Being, however, is sentient, because it is a seer. As to how it thought, he says: "May I become many, may I be abundant, may I be born forth, may I be produced in abundance," just as clay [becomes many] through the forms of jars and so on, or as a rope and the like [appear as many] through the forms of snakes and so on imagined by the intellect.

"In that case, everything that is perceived is indeed non-existent, like a rope being perceived in the form of a snake and so forth. We say: no, because it is precisely the existent that is perceived otherwise through the distinction of duality; we do not maintain that anything is non-existent anywhere. Just as the logicians, having imagined another entity distinct from the existent, then declare that very same thing to be non-existent prior to its production and after its destruction, we never at any time or place imagine any name, object of naming, or entity other than the existent.

Indeed, everything that is designated and everything that is designated as something else is so only through a cognition of it as being other than what it is; just as a rope alone is designated as a "snake" through the cognition of it as a snake, or as in common worldly usage, a lump, a jar, and so forth, are designated by the words "lump," "jar," and so on through a cognition of them as being other than the clay.

But for those who perceive the rope as distinct [from the snake], the designation "snake" and the cognition thereof cease; and just as for those who perceive clay as distinct [from its products], the words and cognitions such as "jar" cease, so too for those who perceive Being (*sat*) as distinct, the words and cognitions of other modifications cease—according to such scriptural passages as, "From which speech turns back, along with the mind, not having reached it," and "In the unutterable, the supportless. Having thus perceived, that [Being] emitted heat; it brought forth heat.

Now, an objection may be raised: "From this very Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)—in another scriptural passage it is heard that from space came air, and from that, as the third, fire. How then is it not contradictory for fire to be created here as the first [element] from that very [Self], and for space to be created from that same [Self]? This is not a fault, because the interpretation that "after the creation of space and air, that Being created fire" is logically consistent. Alternatively, the sequence of creation is not intended to be emphasized here.

All this is an effect pre-existing [in its cause]; therefore, it is intended that [the cause] is existent, one, and without a second, as evidenced by the examples of clay and so forth. Alternatively, because the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) is intended to be explained, [the text] describes the creation of fire, water, and food alone. "Fire" is well-known in the world as that which burns, cooks, and illuminates, and which is red. That fire, created by the Existent, "thought"—meaning that the Existent, abiding in the form of fire, thought—as before: "May I become many; may I procreate."

It emitted water; "water" refers to that which is well-known in the world as being liquid, viscous, flowing, and white. Since water is the effect of fire, therefore, wherever and at whatever time a person grieves, suffers heat, perspires, or breaks into a sweat, from fire alone do waters then arise.

Those waters thought, "May we become many; may we procreate. They created food. Therefore, wherever it rains, there indeed food becomes most abundant; from the waters alone that edible food is born. Thus ends the second section. 2. (4)

Those waters, as before, brooded—meaning they contemplated while remaining in that state of non-distinctness. [They thought: "May we become many, may we become abundant, may we be reproduced, may we come into being. They created food characterized by the earth; for food is of the nature of earth. Since food is the product of water, therefore in whatever place it rains, there food becomes most abundant and plentiful. Thus, that edible food is produced from water alone.

It was previously stated that "they created food" refers to the earth; however, here, because of the qualification "food and what is edible," rice, barley, and so forth are meant. And food is well known by its form to be heavy, stable, sustaining, and dark.

But surely, the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) is not perceived in fire and the other elements, because there is an absence of prohibitions against violence and the like, and because effects such as fear are not observed therein; how then can it be said that "that fire saw," and so forth? This is not a fault. Since fire and the others are transformations of the cause that is the Seer, and since they produce their specific effects in a fixed sequence, the element is said to "see" precisely because it is the Seer itself. But is not the status of being a Seer attributed to the Existent (*sat*) only figuratively? No.

Since the "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) of the Existent (sat) is understood solely through the word [of scripture], it is not possible to assume it is used figuratively. In the case of fire and the rest, however, the absence of primary seeing is inferred; therefore, it is appropriate to assume that their seeing is figurative. But could it not be inferred that even the Existent is insentient, since it is a cause like clay?

Therefore, since the Pradhāna itself is insentient yet exists for the sake of a sentient being, and because it produces effects characterized by a fixed temporal sequence, it can be inferred that "it thought, as it were"; thus, this "thinking" is merely figurative. Moreover, the metaphorical attribution of sentience to the insentient is observed in the world, such as when one says, "the bank wishes to fall"—this could likewise apply to the *sat*. [Objection: No, because in the passage "That is the True, That is the Self," there is an instruction regarding the Self with respect to that [Pradhāna].

If it is argued that the teaching of a self has also been uttered—just as in the expression "Bhadrasena is my self," where the term "self" is used metaphorically for what is not the self because it performs all functions for it—we say no; for there is the teaching of liberation for one who intends the truth with the thought "I am Being," in the words, "For him, the delay is only so long."

If it is argued that this too is merely a statement—[we reply: for one whose intention is directed toward the Self, which is the primary reality, the proximity to liberation exists; thus, even the instruction regarding liberation is indeed stated, just as in common worldly usage one who has set out to go to a village might say, "I have reached the village," out of consideration for haste—it is similar to that. [But this is not the case here], because of the opening statement: "By the knowledge of which, the unknown becomes known. When that One is known, everything becomes known, because everything is non-different from It, and because of the declaration of non-duality.

Furthermore, there remains nothing else to be known that has been taught by the Śruti or is to be inferred from a logical mark (liṅga), on account of which the instruction regarding liberation would have to be regarded as figurative. Moreover, if one were to assume that the entire meaning of this chapter is figurative, the effort of the one who makes such an assumption would be in vain; for the knowledge of the means to achieve the goal of human existence has already been attained through reasoning alone. Therefore, since the Veda is authoritative, it is not proper to abandon the literal meaning of what is heard [in scripture]. Thus, it is established that the cause of the world is a conscious being. This concludes the commentary on the second section.

Indeed, for these beings, there are only three kinds of origins: born from an egg, born from a living being, and born from a sprout. (1) — Regarding these beings, such as birds and so forth, which are entered by a living soul (*jīva*); the word "these" (*eṣām*) refers to them because they are indicated perceptibly, and not to fire and the other elements, since their tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) will be explained later; for if tripartition did not exist, a perceptible indication would be untenable. Furthermore, the term "deity" (*devatā*) is applied to fire and the others, as in: "These are the three deities."

Therefore, for these beings—namely birds, animals, plants, and so forth—there are indeed only three seeds (causes) and no more. What are they? They are stated as follows: "the egg-born" (*āṇḍaja*). That which is born from an egg is "egg-born"; the egg-born itself is the "egg-born," such as birds and the like. For it is observed that from birds, snakes, and so forth, other birds, snakes, and the like are born. Thus, a bird is the seed of birds, a snake is the seed of snakes, and likewise, anything else born from an egg is the seed of its own kind; this is the meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that what is born from an egg is called "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*), and therefore it is logical that the egg itself is the seed? How then can the egg-born be called the seed? [Reply: This would indeed be so, if the scripture were dependent upon your will; however, the scripture is independent, since it states that the egg-born and so forth are the seeds, and not the eggs and so forth. Furthermore, it is observed that in the absence of the egg-born and so forth, there is an absence of their respective lineages, but not in the absence of the eggs and so forth. Therefore, the egg-born and so forth alone are the seeds of the egg-born and so forth.

Likewise, "born from a living being" (*jīvaja*) means that which is produced from a living being, namely humans, cattle, and so forth, specifically those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*). "Born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*): a "sprout" (*udbhid*) is that which breaks through [the earth], namely a stationary being (*sthāvara*); that which is born from that is *udbhijja*. Alternatively, a "sprout" is a seed; that which is born from that is *udbhijja*, meaning the seed of stationary beings, i.e., the seed of stationary things. The categories of "born from sweat" (*svedaja*) and "born from decay" (*saṃśokaja*) are included within "born from an egg" (*aṇḍaja*) and "born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*) respectively, as far as possible. In this way, the restriction that there are "only three seeds" becomes logically consistent.
This deity reflected: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form.

This deity—the one under discussion, called "Being" (*sat*), the source of fire, water, and food—was previously described as having reflected, "May I become many," just as before. That very purpose of becoming many was not yet accomplished; therefore, she again performed reflection, having once more resolved upon that same purpose of becoming many.

How so? Ah! Now, remembering her own self—the very soul that existed in her own intellect and which, as experienced in a previous creation, sustains the vital breaths—she says, "by this living self," referring to these three aforementioned deities, fire and the rest. By the expression "by the self who is the agent of sustaining the vital breaths," she shows that it is not distinct from her own self, being indistinguishable from it in its nature as pure consciousness.

Having entered [the egg] through contact with the subtle elements of fire, water, and food, and having thereby acquired specific consciousness, [she thought]: "I shall differentiate name and form; I shall make them manifest. The meaning is: "I shall distinguish them such that one can say, 'This is so-and-so by name' and 'This is such-and-such by form.'"

Now, one might object: this is not logical—that a deity who is beyond transmigratory existence (*asaṃsārin*) and omniscient should, with full awareness, form the intention, "I shall enter a body that is the locus of many hundreds of thousands of evils and experience suffering," and then actually enter it while possessing absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*). It is true that this would not be logical *if* she had intended, "I shall enter [the world] in my own unmodified form" and "I shall experience suffering"; but it is not so.

How, then, is it so? Because of the statement, "having entered by means of this living self (jīva) as the inner controller. For that which is called the *jīva* is merely a reflection of the Deity, produced by the contact of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors with the subtle elements (*bhūtamātra*)—like the reflection of a person entered into a mirror, or like that of the sun and other luminaries in water and the like.

This manifestation of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*) resulting from the connection of the Deity, who possesses inconceivable and infinite power, with the intellect and other faculties, arises from the failure to discern the true nature of the Deity; it is the cause of various conceptual cognitions such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded."

Because it has entered [the body] merely as a reflection in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), the deity is not connected by itself with the pleasures, pains, and so forth belonging to the body—just as a person, the sun, and others, having entered into a mirror, water, and so on, merely as reflections, are not affected by the defects of the mirror, the water, and so on; so too is the deity. "Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not tainted by external ocular defects."

"Just as one [space], being external, is not tainted by the suffering of the world, so the single inner Self of all beings is not tainted by the suffering of the world," and "He is eternal and omnipresent like space," so it is said in the *Kaṭhaka*; and "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," in the *Vājasaneyaka*. But if the individual soul (*jīva*) is merely a shadow, would it not follow that it is purely illusory, and likewise its existence in this world and the next? This is not a fault, because we accept its reality insofar as it has the Existent (*sat*) as its Self. The entire collection of modifications, such as name and form, is real only through the Self that is the Existent; by itself, however, it is truly unreal, as in the text: "Modification is a mere handle of speech, a name."

Because it has been stated thus: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is likewise. For there is a well-known maxim: "The offering corresponds to the recipient" (*yakṣānurūpo hi baliḥ*). Therefore, since all worldly transactions and all modifications are real in their nature as Being (*sat*), and are unreal if they were other than Being, no fault can be raised here by the logicians (*tārkika*s). Just as it can be said that mutually contradictory dualistic doctrines are merely the fabrications of one's own intellect and do not rest upon reality.
"Let me make each of these threefold. This deity, having entered into these three deities by means of this very living self, differentiated names and forms. 3.

Having thus entered into these three deities, He reflected: "Let me manifest name and form, which exist as seeds within my own self in an undifferentiated state. Then He thought: "I shall make each one of these three deities threefold"—that is, in the process of making each one threefold, there shall be predominance for each one individually, while the other two shall be subordinate. Otherwise, there would be only a single threefold manifestation, like that of a rope, rather than a distinct threefold manifestation for each of the three.

For in this way, fire, water, and food would each obtain their own distinct names and designations—such as "this is fire," "these are waters," and "this is food. And when they have obtained their own distinct names and designations, the purpose would be the establishment of the correct conventional usage regarding these deities.

Having perceived this, that very deity, having entered these three deities by means of this very life-breath (*jīva*)—just as described above—like the orb of the sun, first entered the cosmic body (*vairāja-piṇḍa*) and then the bodies of the gods and others, and according to its own volition, unfolded names and forms, saying: "This one has such a name; this one has such a form.
It made each of those three deities threefold. "Now, my dear, learn from me how each of these three deities becomes threefold. Thus ends the third section. (3) (4)

And of those deities, she made each one threefold, threefold, by way of their qualities being primary or secondary. Let it be for now that the aggregates of the deities and so forth, having been differentiated by name and form, consist of the three elements of fire, water, and food; however, as to how each of these three external deities becomes threefold, threefold—one after another—outside of these aggregates, listen to me as I speak and understand it clearly from my illustration.
Thus ends the commentary on the third section.

That which is the red form of Agni is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "Agni-ness" of Agni has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. 1. (1)

Regarding that tripartition of the deities which has been explained, an illustration of it is now stated—an illustration being that which is cited for the purpose of establishing the whole by means of the establishment of a single part. This is what he says: "Know that which is the well-known red form of fire (agni) once it has been tripartite is the form of light (tejas) before it was tripartite. Likewise, that which is the white form of fire itself is the form of water (āpas) before they were tripartite."

Know that whatever is black is the very form of this fire, and it belongs to food—that is, to the earth which has not yet been made tripartite. This being so, that "fire-ness" which you conceive of as belonging to fire, apart from these three forms, has now departed; it has gone away.

The meaning is that the cognition of fire which you previously possessed has ceased, along with the word "fire," prior to the discriminative knowledge of the three forms [of the fire]. Just as a crystal, when perceived in conjunction with a visible red accessory, becomes the cause for both the word and the cognition "this is a ruby" until there is discriminative knowledge of the accessory and the crystal; but upon that discriminative knowledge, the word and cognition of "ruby" would cease for the one who possesses that discriminative knowledge—in the same way.

Now, one might object: "What is achieved here by the conceptualization of 'intellect' (*buddhi*) and 'word' (*śabda*)? Before the discrimination of the three forms was made, there was only fire; it is logical that the 'fire-ness' of that fire departed upon the discrimination of its red and other forms, just as the absence of a cloth occurs when the threads are pulled away. This is not so. For fire is merely intellect and word; as it is said: "The modification called 'fire' is a beginning in speech, a mere name"—the meaning is that it is name-only. Therefore, even the cognition of fire is indeed false.

What, then, is true in that regard? "The three forms alone are true"—this is for the purpose of determination, meaning that not even an atom's worth of truth exists apart from the three forms. That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The solar nature has departed from the sun; it is a mere modification, a name arising from speech; the three forms alone are true. 2–4.

Likewise, the passage beginning with "Whatever [quality] belongs to the sun, whatever to the moon, whatever to lightning," and so forth, is the same [as before]. Now, an objection may be raised: "But surely, my dear, having said, 'Learn from me how each of these three deities becomes threefold,' the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) was shown through four examples—fire and the others—pertaining only to *tejas* (heat/light), and no example for the triplication of water and food was shown. This is not a fault.

The Śruti considers that examples concerning other objects should likewise be understood in this same manner. The example of fire (*tejas*) is given for illustrative purposes, as it possesses color and its meaning is easily established. There is no example given for smell (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*), because these three [qualities] cannot coexist [in fire]. Indeed, smell and taste do not exist in fire. There is no example given for touch (*sparśa*) and sound (*śabda*), because it is impossible to demonstrate them separately [from their respective substrates].

If the entire world is composed of the threefold [elements], then—just as with fire and the others—it is true that there are only three forms; just as the "fire-ness" of fire has departed, so too the "world-ness" of the world has departed. Likewise, since food is a shoot from water, it is true that only water exists, and food is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇa*). Similarly, since water is a shoot from fire, it is merely a matter of verbal designation, and fire alone is true. Furthermore, since fire is a shoot from Being (*sat*), it is merely a matter of verbal designation, and Being alone is true. This is the meaning intended to be expressed.

But surely, since air and space have not yet been included among fire and the other elements, they remain unaccounted for; likewise, smell, taste, sound, and touch also remain. How, then, could everything else that is unknown become known through the knowledge of "Being" (sat)? Or, if it were so known, some other method must be stated for knowing those remaining things. This is not a fault, because everything is seen to be present within a substance that possesses form.

How so? First, since sound and touch are perceived in fire, which possesses color, the existence of air and ether—which possess the qualities of touch and sound respectively—is inferred therein. Likewise, taste and smell are included within water and earth, which possess color. By demonstrating the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of these three—fire, water, and earth, all of which possess color—the Śruti considers that everything is known through the three forms alone, because everything else is a modification (*vikāra*) contained within them.

For there is no perception of air or ether, nor of their qualities—smell and taste—without first setting aside material substances that possess form. Alternatively, the Śruti intends the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) even of those things possessing form merely for the sake of illustration.

Just as it is true that when the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) has been performed, there are only three forms, so too is the same principle applicable to the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*); for since everything is a modification of Being (*sat*), by knowing Being, all this becomes known. Thus it is established that Being alone is the one, non-dual reality. Therefore, it is well said: "When that One is known, all this becomes known."

That which is the red form of the moon is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "moon-ness" has departed from the moon; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. 3. (2–4)

Likewise, the passage beginning with "Whatever [belongs] to the sun, whatever to the moon, whatever to lightning," and so forth, is the same. Now, an objection may be raised: "But, my dear, how indeed these three divinities each become threefold—that do you learn from me"; having said this, the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) was shown by means of four examples, such as fire and the rest, which pertain only to *tejas* (heat/light), and no example for the tripartition of water and food was shown. This is not a fault.

The Śruti considers that examples belonging to other domains should likewise be understood in this same manner. The example given for fire (*tejas*) is intended as an illustration; for it possesses color and its meaning is easily established. There is no example given for smell (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*), because these three [qualities] cannot coexist [in fire]. Indeed, smell and taste do not exist in fire. There is no example given for touch (*sparśa*) and sound (*śabda*), because it is impossible to demonstrate them separately [from their respective substrates].

If the entire world has been made tripartite, then just as with fire and the other elements, the three forms alone are real; the "world-ness" of the world has departed, just as the "fire-ness" of fire [has departed]. Likewise, since food is a shoot from water, water alone is real, and food is merely a verbal handle (*vācārambhaṇa*). Similarly, since water is a shoot from fire, its status as a mere verbal handle follows, and fire alone is real. And since fire is a shoot from Being (*sat*), its status as a mere verbal handle follows, and Being alone is real—this is the meaning intended to be expressed.

But surely, air and space remain uncomprehended, as they are not included among fire and the other elements; likewise, smell, taste, sound, and touch remain uncomprehended. Thus, how could everything else that is unknown become known by knowing the "Being" (sat)? Or else, some other method for knowing them must be stated. This is not a fault, because everything is seen to be present within a substance that possesses form.

How so? First, since sound and touch are perceived in fire, which possesses color, the existence of air and ether—which possess the qualities of touch and sound respectively—is inferred therein. Likewise, taste and smell are included within water and earth, which possess color. By demonstrating the threefold compounding (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of these three—fire, water, and earth, all of which possess color—the Śruti considers everything that is included within them to be known through the three colors alone, because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of those [three].

For there is no perception of air or ether, nor of their qualities—smell or taste—after having set aside a material substance possessing form. Alternatively, the Śruti intends the tripartition even of those things possessing form merely for the sake of illustration.

Just as in the case of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), it is true that there are only three forms, so too the same principle applies to the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*); because everything is a modification of Being (*sat*), by knowing Being, all this becomes known. Thus, it is established that Being alone is one and without a second, the Reality. Therefore, it is well said: "When that One is known, all this becomes known."

That which is the red color of lightning is the color of fire; that which is white is the color of water; that which is black is the color of food. The "lightning-ness" of lightning has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three colors are real. 4. (2–4)

Likewise, the passage beginning with "Whatever [belongs] to the sun, whatever to the moon, whatever to lightning," and so forth, is the same. Now, an objection may be raised: "But surely, O dear one, having said, 'Learn from me how each of these three deities becomes threefold,' the tripartition was shown by means of four examples—fire and the others—all of which concern light (*tejas*) alone; no example for the tripartition of water and food was shown. This is not a fault.

The Śruti considers that examples concerning water and other elements should likewise be understood in this very same way. The example given for fire is intended as an illustration; for it possesses color and its meaning is thus clearly established. There is no mention of smell and taste because these three qualities cannot coexist [in fire]; indeed, neither smell nor taste exists in fire. There is no mention of touch and sound because they cannot be demonstrated separately [from their respective substrates].

If the entire world has been made tripartite, then—just as in the case of fire and the other elements—it is only the three forms that are real; the "world-ness" of the world has departed, just as the "fire-ness" of fire [has departed]. Likewise, since food is a shoot from water, it is only water that is real, while food is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇa*). Similarly, since water is a shoot from fire, it is merely a matter of verbal designation, while fire alone is real. And since fire is a shoot from Being (*sat*), it is merely a matter of verbal designation, while Being alone is real—this is the meaning intended to be expressed.

[Objection: But surely, since air (*vāyu*) and space (*antarikṣa*) have not been included among fire and the other elements because they are not yet tripartite (*atrivṛtkṛta*), they remain [unaccounted for]; likewise, smell, taste, sound, and touch also remain. How, then, could everything else that is unknown become known through the knowledge of "Being" (*sat*)? Or else, some other method for knowing them must be stated. [Reply: This is not a fault, because everything is seen to be present within a substance that possesses form (*rūpavat*).

How so? First, since sound and touch are perceived in fire, which possesses color, the existence of wind and space—which possess the qualities of touch and sound respectively—is inferred therein. Likewise, taste and smell are included within water and earth, which possess color. By demonstrating the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of these three—fire, water, and earth, all of which possess color—the Śruti considers that everything is known through those three forms alone, because everything else is a modification (*vikāra*) contained within them.

For there is no perception of air or ether, nor of their qualities—smell or taste—after having set aside a material substance possessing form. Alternatively, the Śruti intends the tripartition even of those things possessing form merely for the sake of illustration.

Just as it is true that when the triadic process (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) has been performed, there are only three forms, so too the same principle applies to the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*); for since everything is a modification of Being (*sat*), by knowing Being, all this becomes known. Thus it is established that Being alone is one and without a second, the Reality. Therefore, it is well said: "When that one thing is known, all this becomes known. Indeed, those who knew this in the past—the great householders and great Vedic scholars—said: "Nowadays, no one will be able to cite anything to us that has not been heard, not thought, or not understood," for they had realized this very truth. 5.

(5) Those who knew this—the ancient, long-past men of great households and great Vedic learning—said, indeed, as is well known: "What did they say? He replies: "In our family, today even now, no one at all shall mention anything unheard, unthought, or unknown among those possessing the aforementioned knowledge; none shall so mention it. The intention is that for those born in our lineage, everything is already known, because they possess true knowledge.

Furthermore, as to how they came to know everything, he says: because from these three—the forms of the red, etc.—which had been made tripartite and were thus known, they understood that all other remaining things are exactly like this, they became all-knowing through that knowledge; such is the meaning. Alternatively, "from these they understood" means that from these known examples, namely fire and so forth, they understood everything else.

"That which appeared as if red—that was the form of fire; thus they understood it. That which appeared as if white—that was the form of water; thus they understood it. That which appeared as if black—that was the form of food; thus they understood it. (6–7)

How so? When that which was being perceived as something else—such as the form of a dove and so forth—appeared as if it were red to those former knowers of Brahman, they understood: "That is the form of fire. Likewise, that which was perceived as if it were white, they understood: "That is the form of water"; and that which was perceived as if it were black, they understood: "That is the form of food.

In this very way, even that which was extremely difficult to discern, and which remained as if unknown and not specifically grasped, they understood: "That too is a combination, a collection, of these three deities."

Thus, first, the external object has been understood as being like fire and so forth; now, however, my dear, understand from me as I speak how these three aforementioned deities, having reached the person—the aggregate of causes and effects characterized by the head, hands, and so on—and being utilized by the person, each become threefold within the person. Having said this, he spoke:

"That which was, as it were, unknown—namely, that these very deities, when combined, [become one]—they understood that. Now, my dear, understand from me how each of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold. Thus ends the fourth section. (6–7) — IV, 4 —

How so? When that which was being perceived as something else—such as the form of a dove and so forth—appeared as if it were red to those ancient knowers of Brahman, they understood: "That is the form of fire. Likewise, that which was perceived as if it were white, they understood: "That is the form of water"; and that which was perceived as if it were black, they understood: "That is the form of food.

In this very way, even that which was extremely difficult to discern, which remained as if unknown and was not specifically grasped, they understood: "That too is merely a combination, a collection, of these three deities."

Thus, first, the external object has been understood, like fire and so forth. Now, however, my dear, understand from me as I speak how these three aforementioned deities, having reached the person—the aggregate of causes and effects characterized by the head, hands, and so on—and being utilized by the person, each become threefold within the person. Having said this, he spoke [the following].
This concludes the commentary on the fourth section.
Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts: its grossest constituent becomes feces, its middle constituent becomes flesh, and its subtlest constituent becomes the mind. 1.

Food that is eaten and consumed is divided into three parts by the digestive fire as it is being cooked. How so? Of that food which is thus divided into three, the grossest element—the coarsest substance, the coarsest portion of what has been divided—becomes feces. That middle portion of the food-element, having been transformed through the sequence of chyle and so forth, becomes flesh.

That element which is the smallest and most subtle, having reached the heart and entered the subtle channels called *hitā*, becomes the mind (*manas*) by producing the stability of the aggregate of the organs of speech and so forth. Transforming into the form of the mind, it effects the accumulation of the mind. Consequently, because the mind is accumulated from food, it is understood to be merely material (*bhautika*), and not eternal or partless as defined in the Vaiśeṣika system.

Furthermore, when it will be stated that "the mind is its divine eye," that too is not with reference to eternity; rather, it is with reference to its capacity for operating upon all objects of the senses—subtle, concealed, and distant. And as for the eternity [of the mind] relative to the objects of the other senses, that too is merely relative, as we shall explain based on the Vedic revelation: "Being... one only, without a second. Water, when drunk, is divided into three parts: its grossest constituent becomes urine, its middle constituent becomes blood, and its subtlest constituent becomes breath.

In the same way, water that is drunk is divided into three parts. Of these, that which is the grossest constituent becomes urine; that which is the middle constituent becomes blood; and that which is the subtlest becomes the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For it will be said later: "The vital breath consists of water; it would fail in one who does not drink. Food that is eaten is divided into three parts. Of that, the grossest constituent becomes bone; the middle constituent becomes marrow; and the subtlest constituent becomes speech. 3. (3)

In the same way, the fire [of digestion]—the oil, ghee, and so forth that are eaten and consumed—is divided into three parts. Of that, the coarsest constituent becomes bone; the middle one becomes marrow, which is the oily substance within the bones; and the subtlest becomes speech. For it is well known in the world that through the consumption of oil, ghee, and such, speech becomes clear and capable of speaking.

"Verily, my dear, the mind consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. "Please, venerable sir, explain this to me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. (5) Thus ends the fifth section.

(4) Since this is so, my dear, the mind consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. But surely, those that eat only food, such as mice and the like, possess speech and vital breath; likewise, those that subsist on water alone, such as the fish and crocodiles of the sea, possess mind and speech; and similarly, it can be inferred that even those who drink only oil possess vital breath and mind.

If these [elements] exist [in their unmixed state], how can it be said there that "the mind, my dear, consists of food" and so forth? This is not a fault, because everything has been made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*), and thus everything is present everywhere. For no one eats food that has not been made tripartite, nor is water drunk that has not been made tripartite, nor does anyone consume fire that has not been made tripartite. Thus, it is not contradictory that even those who eat food—such as mice and others—possess speech and vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so on.

Thus instructed, Śvetaketu said: "Venerable sir, please instruct me further once more—that is, explain again by means of an illustration how the mind, my dear, consists of food (annamaya), for even now a firm conviction regarding this matter has not arisen within me."

The intention is that it is difficult to discern how the food, water, and oil products consumed within a single body—which is indistinguishable in its composition of fire (*tejas*), water (*ap*), and earth (*anna*)—accumulate as the subtle constituent elements (*dhātu*) of mind, breath, and speech without overstepping their own respective natures; therefore, he said, "Tell me more. To him who had spoken thus, the father replied, "So be it, Soma; listen here to an illustration of how this which you ask is possible.
This concludes the commentary on the fifth section.

In that mind, the supreme deity has entered by means of the individual soul (jīva)—just as a person enters a mirror by means of a reflection, or as the sun and other luminaries enter water and similar surfaces by means of their reflections—that mind consists of food (annamaya) and is joined with speech and breath, which consist of light (tejomaya). Composed of that [mind] and situated within it, the individual soul is enabled to perform its worldly activities of thinking, seeing, hearing, and so forth; and upon the cessation of those [activities], it attains its own true nature as the deity.

This has been stated in another Śruti passage: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7); "Having become a dream, the conscious one transcends this world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9); "This very Self is Brahman, consisting of knowledge, consisting of mind," and so forth; "By means of the dream, [it withdraws] the body," and so forth; and "Breathing, it becomes what is called breath," and so forth.

Desiring to explain to his son that state of abiding in that supreme deity who has become one's own self—the state of this very person who, having reached what is called "mind" while residing in the mind, has turned away from the objects of the senses by means of the tranquility of the mind—Uddālaka Āruṇi, it is said, spoke to his son Śvetaketu: "The end of sleep," meaning the middle of sleep; for "sleep" is the name for the activity of seeing, and its "end" is deep sleep (*suṣupta*).

Alternatively, "the end of dream" means the true nature of dream. In that context as well, it effectively refers to deep sleep, because of the scriptural statement, "He becomes merged in his own self"; for those who know Brahman do not accept that the merging of the individual soul (jīva) into its own self occurs anywhere other than in deep sleep.

For in that case, just as when a mirror is removed, the reflection of a person residing in the mirror merges back into that very person himself, so too, upon the cessation of the mind and other organs, the supreme deity—who had entered the mind in the form of the individual soul (jīva) as a reflection of consciousness for the purpose of differentiating names and forms—returns to her own self, abandoning the state of being an individual soul known as the "mind. Therefore, it is understood that the state of deep sleep alone is what is expressed by the term "the end of dream" (svapnānta).

But where one who is asleep sees dreams, that dream-vision is conjoined with pleasure and pain; thus it is the effect of merit and demerit. For it is well known that merit and demerit are the originators of pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, it is only through the support of ignorance (*avidyā*) and desire (*kāma*) that merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*apuṇya*) can initiate their effects, namely the experience of pleasure and pain, and not otherwise. Thus, since one is joined with ignorance, desire, and action—the causes of transmigratory existence—one does not "merge into oneself" during the dream state. This is established by such scriptural passages as: "He is untouched by merit, untouched by evil; for at that time he has crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart," and "This, indeed, is his state free from desire; this is the supreme bliss. Etc.

He says, "I shall show you your own form as the deity, entirely free from the state of being a living soul (jīvatva)," while in deep sleep itself: "O dear one (somya), understand clearly—meaning, grasp with firm attention—as I describe to you the end of dream (svapnānta). When does this end of dream occur? It is said: at that time when this name "he sleeps" (svapiti) belongs to a person about to sleep. For it is well known in the world that one "sleeps."

He states that this name is figurative: when it is said that "the person sleeps," at that time he becomes *saṃpanna*—that is, joined with or become one with—the deity who is always denoted by the word *Sat*. Having abandoned his individual form as a living soul (*jīva*), which was produced by contact with the mind and other faculties and had entered into the mind, he has *apītaḥ*—that is, gone back into—his own true nature, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, for this reason, worldly people say of him, "he sleeps."

The intention is that the attainment of one's own self is understood even from the well-known usage of the term "guṇa" (merger); for [the word *apīta*] implies that one has indeed gone back into one's own self (*svam ātmānam apītaḥ*). But how is the attainment of one's own self known among common people? They say it is because sleep arises as a result of the fatigue caused by waking. For in the waking state, one becomes exhausted due to experiencing various labors such as pleasure and pain caused by merit and demerit.

Consequently, there occurs a cessation from their respective functions of the organs, which have become exhausted due to the fatigue caused by their single-pointed activity. This is supported by scriptural texts such as, "Speech indeed becomes weary; the eye becomes weary," and so forth. Likewise, in passages such as, "Speech is withdrawn, the eye is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, the mind is withdrawn," these organs are shown to be swallowed up by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). While the vital breath alone remains unwearied and stays awake within the nest of the body, the individual soul (*jīva*), in order to dispel its exhaustion, attains its own self in the form of the deity.

The cessation of fatigue cannot occur except through abiding in one's own true nature; thus, the common worldly understanding—that "he has gone to his own"—is logical. For it is observed in the world that those afflicted by diseases such as fever find rest only when they are freed from them and established in their own self; the same should be understood here as well. This is also supported by scriptural texts such as: "Just as a hawk or a falcon, having flown about, becomes weary... and so forth. (2)

In this regard, there is this illustration for the point already stated: just as a bird, bound and tethered by a string held in the hand of a bird-catcher, flies in every direction seeking release from its bonds, yet failing to find or reach any other place of refuge or rest elsewhere than the bond itself, it resorts only to that very bond.

In this very way, my dear, just as in this illustration, that mind—the mind under discussion, which consists of sixteen parts and is nourished by food—is determined; and the individual soul (jīva), having entered it, residing in it, and being characterized by it, is designated as "that mind"—just as one might refer to the occupants of a bed by the name of the bed itself.

That adjunct called *manas* is the individual soul (*jīva*). Having fallen into and traversed, in the waking and dreaming states, various directions characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth—these being taught by ignorance, desire, and karma—the meaning is that it has experienced them. Not having found elsewhere a "dwelling," a place of rest, from its own Self which is called *Sat*, it goes to *prāṇa* alone. By the term *prāṇa* is meant the supreme deity called *Sat*, who is indicated by *prāṇa* as the support of all effects and instruments; for the scriptures state, "The breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*) and "He whose body is *prāṇa*, whose form is light" (*prāṇaśarīro bhārūpaḥ*).

Therefore, one resorts to that deity, Prāṇa, who is indeed designated as Prāṇa. For, my dear, the mind has its binding in Prāṇa—that is, it has its support in the deity characterized by Prāṇa; "mind" here refers to the individual soul (jīva) as characterized by that mind.

Thus, having shown the son the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the root of the world, by means of the well-known term "sleeping" (*svapiti*), [the teacher] speaks next, desiring to show that the root of the world is Being (*sat*) even through the succession of causes and effects such as food and so forth: "Know the true essence (*satattva*) of hunger and thirst. Here, "hunger" (*aśanā*) is the desire to eat (*aśitum icchā*); the suffix *san* is elided; and "thirst" (*pipāsā*) is the desire to drink (*pātum icchā*). These two are "hunger and thirst. Know their true essence—that at which time a person receives this name.

What is that? It is "he wishes to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*), meaning he desires to eat. Then, for what reason does that person have the name [of hunger]? He says: when the food eaten by the person—which was solid—is carried away by the water he has drunk, which liquefies it and transforms it into the state of chyle and so forth, then the eaten food is digested. And at that time, his name "he wishes to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*) occurs figuratively; for every living being desires to eat once the food has been digested.

In this context, the name *aśanāyā* is well known in the sense of being the "leader of water" (*apām aśita-netr-tvāt*). Just as one who leads cattle is called *gonāyaḥ*, meaning a cowherd (*gopāla*), and likewise one who leads horses is called *aśvanāyaḥ*, meaning a horse-keeper; and one who leads men is called *puruṣanāyaḥ*, such as a king or a general—so too do common people at that time call water *aśanāyā*, with the elision of the visarga.

This being so, this body—which has been produced by food that was eaten and transformed into the state of sap and other constituents—is like a sprout or shoot that has emerged and grown from within a banyan seed. My dear son, understand this very sprout, which is the effect known as the body, to have arisen just like the sprouts of a banyan tree or similar plants. "What is there to be understood in this regard? It is said: "Listen; because it is an effect like a sprout, this thing called the body cannot be without a root. Having been told this, Śvetaketu said: (4) ————

"If this body is thus rooted like the sprout of a banyan tree or similar plant, then where might the root of this body be?"—being asked thus, the father said: "Where might its root be? It is other than food; food is the root"—this is the intended meaning. How so? For food that has been eaten, moistened by water, and being digested by the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), is transformed into the state of *rasa* (nutritive essence). From *rasa* comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; from fat, bones; from bones, marrow; and from marrow, semen.

Likewise, food consumed by a woman undergoes transformation through the sequence of rasa and so forth, becoming blood. By means of these two—the semen and the blood—which are products of food and joined together, and by the food being consumed daily and thus filling them, the sprout of the body, rooted in food, is fully produced, just as a wall is built up day by day with lumps of clay; this is the meaning.

As for that food which was pointed out as the root of the body-sprout—that too, because it possesses destruction and origination just like the body, has itself arisen from some root and is merely a sprout; therefore he says: "Just as the body-sprout has food as its root, even so, my dear, by means of this sprout of food, which is an effect, seek out and realize water, which is the root of the sprout of food."

Since water also possesses destruction and origination, it too is merely a sprout. Therefore, my dear, through water as a sprout—its effect—seek its cause, fire, as the root. Since fire also possesses destruction and origination, it too is a sprout. Therefore, my dear, through fire as a sprout, seek Being (*sat*) as the root—the one, non-dual, ultimate reality—in which all this world is superposed through ignorance, like the collection of illusory constructs such as a snake upon a rope; this world is a modification consisting of speech, a mere name, and unreal. That is the root of this universe.

Therefore, O gentle one, all these creatures—characterized by the stationary and the moving—have Being as their root (*sanmūlāḥ*) and Being as their cause (*satkāraṇāḥ*). Not only do they have Being as their root, but even now, during the time of their existence, they have Being as their abode (*sadāyatanāḥ*), meaning they have Being as their support. For indeed, there is no existence or stability for a jar or similar objects without depending upon clay. Thus, because the creatures have Being as their root like clay, those creatures have Being as their abode. And finally, they have Being as their foundation (*satpratiṣṭhāḥ*); that is, Being alone is their foundation—their dissolution, their completion, their end, and their final remainder. (5)
Now, he says that even now the search for the root of existence must be conducted by means of the "thirst" (aśuṅa): "at which time," meaning at whatever time, "this" [being] "thirsts."

"One who desires to drink becomes a *puruṣa*. Like the expression "one who desires to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*), this too is merely a figurative name. The waters that carry the food which has been softened and eaten would moisten and loosen the body—the "sprout of food"—if they were not dried up by heat due to the abundance of water. And when those waters are thoroughly dried up by heat and are being transformed into the state of the body, the desire to drink arises in the person; at that time, the person is said to "thirst."

This is what he says: "That very fire, at that time, having drunk the water and so forth, dries them up and leads them—meaning transforms them—into the state of blood and vital breath within the body. This is just as in the case of 'the cow-leader' (*gonāya*), and so on, which is the same [as explained previously]. Thus the world designates that fire as *udanya*—that which leads water (*udaka*) is *udanya*; *udanyam* is a Vedic form (*chāndasam*), and in that case also, it is as before. Of the waters too, this very thing called the body is the sprout (*śuṅga*), and nothing else; the rest is the same as before."

"O gentle one, a person consists of sixteen parts. Do not eat for fifteen days, but drink water as you wish; for breath (*prāṇa*) consists of water, and it will not be cut off from one who drinks. The subtlest constituent of the food that has been eaten deposited its power in the mind. That power of the mind, nourished by food, is intended to be designated as the "parts" (*kalā*) of a person by being divided into sixteen portions. Endowed with that power—nourished by food and divided into sixteen parts—the person, characterized as the aggregate of cause and effect and distinguished by the living self (*jīva*), is called "one of sixteen parts."

When this [food] exists, the person becomes a seer, a hearer, a thinker, a knower, an agent, and a cognizer, capable of all actions; and when it is diminished, there is a loss of capacity. And the text will say: "Then the seer is one who subsists on food," and so forth. The capacity of every effect and cause is produced by the mind alone. For in the world, people are seen to be strong when endowed with mental power, and some even subsist on meditation (*dhyāna*) because food is the essence of everything. Therefore, mental vigor is produced by food.

That person who possesses sixteen parts is this "sixteen-part person" (*ṣoḍaśakalaḥ puruṣaḥ*). If you wish to perceive this directly, do not eat for fifteen days—do not take food—but drink water as you desire. For if you do not drink water, your vital breath (*prāṇa*) will be severed; it will come to an end, because we have already stated that the vital breath consists of water and is a transformation of water. Indeed, an effect cannot endure without the support of its own cause.

He did not eat for fifteen days; then he approached his father and said, "What shall I recite, sir? [The father replied,] "The Ṛg-verses, my dear, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants. He said, "They do not occur to me, sir.

Having heard this, desiring to perceive directly that the mind consists of food (*annamaya*), he did not eat for fifteen days—that is, he took no food. Then, on the sixteenth day, he approached his father. Having approached him, he said, "What shall I recite, sir? The other said, "Study the Ṛg-verses, my dear, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants."
Thus addressed by his father, he said: "The Rigveda and the others do not indeed appear to me; they are not seen in my mind," the meaning being that they do not manifest themselves, O venerable sir.

He said to him: "Just as, my dear, of a great kindled fire only a single ember the size of a firefly might remain, and it would not burn much from that [fire], even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts only one part remains. With that, you do not now perceive the Vedas. Learn [the means], and then you will understand them from me. 3. (3)

When he had spoken thus, the father said: "Listen to the reason why those [Vedas], such as the Ṛgveda and others, do not manifest to you. He said to him: "Just as in the world, my dear, of a great fire—that is, one of large dimension that has been kindled and built up with fuel—if a single ember, the size of a firefly, were to remain or be left over after it has been extinguished, one would not burn much at all, even slightly more than that, by means of that ember; even so, indeed—"

"My dear, of those sixteen parts of yours accumulated by food, one part—a single limb—must remain as a residue. With that [part], which is now like a firebrand the size of a glowworm, you do not at this time experience or comprehend the Vedas. But after hearing my word, you will understand it all completely; meanwhile, eat. He ate, and then he approached him. Whatever he asked him, he understood it all. 4.
