He ate his meal exactly as instructed. Immediately thereafter, he approached his father with the desire to serve him. When the son had arrived, the father questioned him regarding whatever was contained in the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas, whether in the form of the texts themselves or the collection of their meanings. Śvetaketu understood all of that, both in meaning and in text. The father said to him: "Just as, my dear, if from a large blazing fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left, and one were to kindle it by adding grass to it, it would burn much more than before...

His father said to him again: "Just as, my dear, of a great fire that has been kindled," and so on, the rest being the same; if a single ember, no larger than a firefly, were left of the extinguished fire, one should kindle it by adding grass and powder, and thus increase it. With that ignited ember, one could burn much more than its previous size.

"In this way, my dear, of your sixteen parts, one part remained; it was restored by food and kindled. By means of that, you now experience the Vedas. For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. Then he understood it from him—yes, he understood it. Thus ends the seventh section. (6) — 7 — (6) —

"In this way, my dear, of those sixteen parts of food which were of the nature of power, one part remained—indeed, it remained—for you who had not eaten for fifteen days. One by one, with each day, each part was diminished like the moon during the dark fortnight. That remaining part, however, having been replenished, increased, and built up by the food you ate, blazed forth—"the lengthening [of the vowel] is a Vedic license—the meaning being that it flared up and grew."

*Prājvālīt* is an alternative reading; in that case, the meaning is that, being kindled by him, she herself burst into flames. "By her, having been increased, you now—*etarhi*, at this time—experience (*anubhavasi*) and perceive the Vedas. Thus, he concludes that the mind's nature of consisting of food (*annamayatva*) is established through both its departure and its persistence: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food," and so forth.

The intention is that just as this fact—that the mind consists of food—is established for you, so too is it established that "breath consists of water" and "speech consists of fire. Śvetaketu understood (*vijajñau*)—that is, he came to know—this which was stated by his father regarding the composition of the mind and the other organs from food and the rest. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is intended to mark the end of the section on the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).
Thus ends the commentary on the seventh section.

Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: "My dear, learn from me the state of deep sleep. When a person here is said to 'sleep,' then, my dear, he has become united with Being (*sat*); he has gone back into himself (*svam apītaḥ*). Therefore they say of him, 'he sleeps,' for he has gone back into himself.
"My dear, when curd is being churned, that subtle essence which rises upward, having gathered together, goes upward in the form of butter; that becomes clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*)."

"Just as a bird tied with a string, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon its very bond; even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For, my dear, the mind is fastened to the vital breath.

Just as in this illustration, my dear, so indeed when food—such as boiled rice and the like—is being eaten and consumed, and is churned by the digestive fire accompanied by air as if by a churning-stick, that subtle essence (*aṇimā*) which rises upward becomes the mind (*manas*); that is to say, it comes together with the constituents of the mind and accumulates the mind.

"O gentle one, learn from me about hunger and thirst. When a person is said to 'be hungry,' it is the waters that lead away the food that has been eaten. Just as one speaks of a 'leader of cattle,' a 'leader of horses,' or a 'leader of men,' so too they call water 'aśanāya' (the leader of food). Now, O gentle one, recognize this sprout that has emerged here; it cannot be without a root.
"In the same way, O gentle one, of the water being drunk, that which is the subtlest essence rises upward; that becomes the vital breath (prāṇa)."

"Where could its root be, if not in food? In this very way, my dear, seek water as the root by means of food as the sprout; seek fire as the root by means of water as the sprout; seek Being as the root by means of fire as the sprout. All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support.
"In this very way, my dear, when fire is being consumed, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward; it becomes speech."

Now, when a person is said to be "thirsty," it is the fire-element alone that leads away what has been drunk. Just as one says "cow-leader," "horse-leader," or "man-leader," so does one call that fire-element "water-leader" (*udanyeti*). In this regard, my dear, know that this very sprout has emerged; it cannot be without a root.

"The mind, my dear, consists of food; the vital breath consists of water; speech consists of fire"—the intention of this statement is that what I have said is indeed logical. Therefore, let all this be so in the case of water and fire. However, regarding the fact that the mind consists of food, I have not yet reached a firm conviction. Therefore, "May the venerable sir please explain to me further, by means of an illustration, how the mind consists of food. "So be it, my dear," the father replied. This concludes the commentary on the sixth section. "Where could its root be, other than in water? My dear, seek the root of fire through water as its sprout; [seek] the root of water through fire..."

"My dear, seek the root of existence by means of its shoot. My dear, all these creatures have their root in Being, have Being as their abode, and have Being as their support. Now, my dear, just as these three divinities, upon reaching a person, each become threefold, that has already been explained previously for you, my dear, concerning this person."
The restrained person’s speech merges into the mind; the mind into the breath; the breath into heat; and the heat into the supreme deity.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Real; that is the Self; "That thou art, Śvetaketu."
"Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. (Thus ends the eighth section.
"Just as, my dear, honey-makers prepare honey by collecting the juices from various trees of different species and reducing them to a single unity—"
They cause [the juices] to attain their essence...

(1) As for what you ask—namely, "Day after day, having attained the Being, those who have attained the Being do not know that 'we have attained the Being'—for what reason is that?"—listen here to an illustration: Just as in the world, my dear, honey-makers—those who make honey, namely the honey-bees—produce honey, that is, they bring it to completion, being devoted to that task.

How so? Having gathered together the juices of trees from various sources, from various origins, and from various directions, they bring those juices to a state of unity, a single condition, as honey; they cause the juices to attain the nature of honey.

Just as those juices there do not obtain distinction, thinking, "I am the juice of this tree; I am the juice of that tree," even so, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know: "We are merging into Being. 2. (2) —-

Just as those juices, having attained oneness through their state as honey, do not find distinction within that honey—how so? "I am the juice of this mango tree" or "I am the juice of this jackfruit tree"—for in the world, when many conscious beings have come together, there is an attainment of distinction such as, "I am the son of such-and-such," or "I am the grandson of such-and-such"; and having attained such distinction, they do not become intermingled.

The intention is that, in this case, although there are juices of many kinds of trees—such as sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, and so forth—once they have attained oneness as honey, no distinction between them as sweet and so forth is perceived. Just as with this illustration, my dear, in exactly the same way, all these creatures, day after day, having entered into *sat* at the time of deep sleep, as well as at death and cosmic dissolution, do not know—that is, they do not discern—"We are entering into *sat*" or "We have entered into *sat*."
In this world, they become whatever they are here—whether a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or an insect, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito; they become that very thing. 3.

And because they attain Being (sat) even while remaining ignorant of the true nature of the Self as Being, therefore—whatever species they had assumed in this world as a result of their past actions, such as those of tigers and so forth, thinking "I am a tiger," "I am a lion"—being marked by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of that karma and knowledge, even though they have entered into Being, they return again with that very same state; having come back from Being, they become again a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito.

Whatever they were in this world previously—that is, what they had become—that very same thing they become again upon returning. Even though separated by an interval of thousands of millions of ages, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that was formed in the past for a transmigrating creature does not perish; for another Vedic text says, "For rebirths occur according to one's knowledge. "That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. Thus ends the ninth section. (4) — 9 — (4) —

Those creatures which, having entered into that [Being], manifest themselves again; whereas those others who, being intent upon the True Being (sat-satyātman), enter into that subtle essence (aṇubhāva) which is the True Self and do not return—this "subtle essence" and so forth has already been explained. Just as in the world, a person who has slept in his own house, having risen and gone to another village, knows "I have come from my own house," why is it that living beings do not possess the knowledge "I have come from the True Being"? "Please let the venerable one explain this further to me"—being thus addressed, the father said, "So be it, my dear. Thus ends the commentary on the ninth section.

"My dear, these rivers flow eastward from the front and westward from the back; they enter the ocean and become the ocean itself. Just as they do not know there, 'I am this one,' or 'I am that one'—listen to the illustration for that: My dear, just as these rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, flow eastward—that is, they stream toward the eastern direction."

Afterwards, toward the western direction, the rivers such as the Sindhu and others flow westward; they are drawn from the ocean, the reservoir of waters, by the clouds and fall again in the form of rain, taking the form of rivers such as the Gaṅgā. These rivers enter once more into that very ocean, the reservoir of waters, and become that ocean itself. Just as those rivers, having attained oneness with the ocean in that state, do not know or perceive: "I am this Gaṅgā," or "I am this Yamunā."

In the very same way, my dear, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know that they have come from Being. Here they become—whether a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gnat, or a mosquito; whatever they are, that they become. 2–3.

In the very same way, my dear, all these creatures, because they do not know [their true nature] when they have merged into Being (*sat*), therefore, having come from Being, they do not know: "We are coming from Being," or "We have come. It is observed in the world that waves, ripples, foam, bubbles, and the like, having arisen in water, return again to that state and perish.

While he was thus crying out, some compassionate person, having untied and released him from his bindings exactly as they were fastened, would say to him: "The Gandhāras are in this direction; go in that northern direction. Released from his bonds by that compassionate person, that wise man—being instructed and intelligent, and capable of discerning the path for entering the village as directed by another—would eventually reach the Gandhāras themselves by inquiring from village to village.

Nor is it any other person of deluded intellect or one thirsty for the sight of foreign lands. As this illustration has been described: a man from his own country, Gandhāra, whose eyes were bound by thieves, who was undiscriminating, confused about the directions, and afflicted by hunger, thirst, and so forth—having been led into a forest filled with a multitude of evils and fears such as tigers and robbers—stood there pained by suffering, crying out and desiring liberation from his bonds; and somehow or other, he was released by a certain compassionate person.

Having reached Gandhāra itself, his own country, he became tranquil and happy; even so, for one who is truly the Self of the universe, this forest of the body—composed of fire, water, and food, filled with wind, bile, phlegm, blood, fat, flesh, bone, marrow, semen, skin, urine, and feces, and possessing many pairs of opposites such as cold and heat—is entered by him whose eyes are bound by the cloth of delusion, who is fettered by the snares of thirst for various seen and unseen objects such as wife, son, friends, cattle, and kinsmen, and who has been cast in by the thieves of merit and demerit, thinking, "I am his..."

"I have a son; these are my kinsmen; I am happy, miserable, deluded, wise, righteous, possessed of relatives; I was born, I have died, I have decayed, I am a sinner; my son is dead; my wealth is lost; alas, I am ruined! How shall I live? What is my refuge? What is my protection?"—thus crying out, possessed by a web of many hundreds of thousands of misfortunes, when by some rare stroke of merit he happens upon a certain knower of the True Brahman and the Self, who is supremely compassionate, liberated from all bonds, and most devoted to Brahman;

He attains [this state]; and by that knower of Brahman, through compassion, he is shown the path of perceiving the defects inherent in the objects of transmigratory existence. Becoming dispassionate toward the objects of the world, [he is told]: "You are not a transmigrating being possessing attributes such as being the son of so-and-so; rather, you are the True Reality—*tat tvam asi*. Thus released from the binding shroud of ignorance and delusion, like the man from Gandhāra who has reached his own true self, he becomes happy and tranquil, having attained his own Self which is Being (*sat*). It is this very meaning that is expressed in the words: "The person who has a teacher knows."

For him who possesses such a teacher and whose bonds of ignorance have been cast off, "only so long," that much time alone, is the delay—that is, the waiting—for the attainment of the true nature of the Self; this is the completion of the sentence. To the question "How long is that delay? it is said: "until I am released"—the phrase "I shall not be released" is understood through ellipsis and by implication, with the person (the verb) being shifted; the meaning is: until the fall of the body occurs due to the exhaustion of that karma by which the body was begun, through its experience.

"Then at that very moment, I shall become the Real; I shall become [the Real]"—as before. For there is no difference in time between the release from the body and the attainment of the Real, such that the word "atha" (then) would have the sense of immediate succession.

But surely, just as the fall of the body and the attainment of the Real do not occur immediately after the knowledge of the Real due to the force of residual karma, so it is with those karmas whose fruits have not yet begun to manifest.

Since there exist even those karmas accumulated in previous births prior to the arising of knowledge, another body must necessarily be commenced after this one falls, for the sake of experiencing their fruits. Furthermore, since one continues to perform prescribed or prohibited actions throughout one's life even after knowledge has arisen, another body must also necessarily be commenced for the sake of experiencing the fruits of those actions. Consequently, from those actions comes another body; thus, knowledge would be rendered useless, because actions possess the power to yield results.

If, on the other hand, the karmas of one who possesses knowledge are destroyed, then liberation would occur at the very moment knowledge is attained, because knowledge is the cause for attaining Being (*sat*). Consequently, the body would fall away, and thus there would be an absence of a teacher; this would render the statement "the person who has a teacher knows" untenable. Furthermore, it would follow that there is no liberation from knowledge, or else that the fruit of knowledge is not certain—just like the knowledge of the means to reach another country. This is not so, because a distinction is established between karmas whose fruits have already begun to manifest (*pravṛtta-phala*) and those whose fruits have not yet begun (*apravṛtta-phala*).

As for the claim that because actions whose fruits have not yet begun must necessarily bear fruit, another body must be commenced for the knower of Brahman upon the fall of the current body for the sake of experiencing the fruits of those uncommenced actions—this is incorrect. This is because of the authority of the scriptural text, "For him there is delay only so long," which pertains to the knower. [Objection: But surely the scriptural text, "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action," and so forth, also possesses authority. [Reply: True, this is so. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between actions whose fruits have begun and those whose fruits have not.

How so? Those actions whose fruits have already begun to manifest—by which the body of the knower was initiated—perish only through their experience, just as an arrow or similar object released toward a target continues its motion until its momentum is exhausted, rather than ceasing immediately at the moment it hits the mark because its purpose has been fulfilled; it is just like that.

However, other actions whose fruits have not yet begun—whether performed here before the arising of knowledge or after it, whether being performed now, or those performed in past lives—are burnt away by knowledge, just as they are by expiation; for so says the Smṛti: "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes," and the Atharvaṇa [Upaniṣad] states: "And his actions are exhausted."

Therefore, even though the knower of Brahman lacks any purpose such as living on, the enjoyment of the fruits of those actions whose momentum has already been set in motion must necessarily occur; thus, the statement "for him there is delay only so long" is perfectly appropriate, like the flight of a released arrow, and the objection regarding the aforementioned defect is untenable. Furthermore, we have already stated that for the knower of Brahman there is an absence of karma after the arising of knowledge, in the passage, "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality"; you should bear that in mind.

"My dear, when a person is afflicted by illness and his kinsmen sit around him, saying, 'Do you know me? Do you know me?', he continues to know them as long as his speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity.

"O dear one, when a person is afflicted—meaning when he is suffering from fever or some other ailment—his kinsmen and relatives surround him and wait upon him as he is about to die, asking, 'Do you recognize me? Am I your father, son, or brother? As long as his speech has not merged into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and his heat into the supreme deity—the meaning of which has already been explained—so long does he remain conscious. But when his speech merges into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and his heat into the supreme deity, then he no longer recognizes them.

The very process of death that belongs to the transmigrating soul is itself the process of merging into Being for the knower as well; this is what he says: "When one has merged into the supreme deity, into light, then one does not know. But the ignorant person, having risen from Being, enters again into the state previously cultivated—whether as a tiger and so forth, or as a god, a human, and so on. The knower, however, having entered into Being—the Self which is Brahman, illuminated by the lamp of knowledge produced by the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher—does not return; such is the process of merging into Being.

Others, however, say that having departed through the artery at the crown of the head, they go to the *Sat* (Being) by way of the door of the sun and so forth; that is incorrect, because movement is observed only when there is an intention toward place, time, cause, and fruit. For one who perceives the unity of the Self with the *Sat*, who is intent upon truth, an intention toward untruth—such as place, time, cause, and fruit—is not possible, due to their mutual contradiction. Furthermore, since ignorance, desire, and action, which are the causes of movement, have been consumed by the fire of the knowledge of the *Sat*, movement is simply impossible.

"And for one whose desires are fulfilled and who has realized the Self, all desires vanish right here"—from such scriptural passages in the *Atharva-veda*, as well as from the illustration of the river and the ocean; and [from the passage]: "That which is this subtle essence (*aṇimā*), this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self, that art thou, O Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. Thus ends the fifteenth section. (15) (3)

The passage beginning with "He who... and so forth is the same [as before]. If the merging into Being (*satsaṃpatti*) is equal for one who is dying and for one who desires liberation, then the reason why the knower, having merged into Being, does not return, while the ignorant one does return—let the Blessed One explain this further by means of an illustration. "So be it, my dear," he said. This concludes the commentary on the fifteenth section.

Listen—just as, my dear, when men have seized a person suspected of committing a theft, having bound his hands, the king’s officers bring him forward for arrest and examination; and when asked, "What has this man done?", they say, "He has stolen this man's wealth"; and they [the officers] say, "Does he deserve imprisonment merely for the act of stealing? Otherwise, there would be the consequence of imprisonment even for one who has merely given away wealth."

Having been addressed thus, they spoke again: "He committed theft; he has stolen wealth by means of robbery. While they were speaking in this manner, the other denied it, saying: "I am not the doer of that. And they said: "You have committed a doubtful theft of this wealth. And while he continued to deny it, they said: "Heat the axe for him; let him purify himself."

If he is the perpetrator of that theft and yet denies it outwardly, being thus situated, he makes himself otherwise than what he truly is by means of untruth; having thus formed a false intention and concealed himself with untruth, making himself hidden, he takes up the heated axe out of delusion. He is burned, and then he is slain by the king's men due to the fault of his own false intention.

Now, if he is not the doer of that [crime], then by that very truth he makes himself true; being one whose intention is truth, having concealed himself with truth, he takes up the heated axe. He is not burned, and then he is released. 2.

Now, if he is not the doer of that deed, then by that very fact he makes himself true. Having concealed himself within by means of truth—that is, by his non-agency in the theft—he takes hold of the heated axe. Being one whose resolve is fixed on truth, he is not burned because of the intervention of truth; thus he is released from those who made the false accusation. Even though the contact between the palm of the hand and the heated axe is equal for both the thief and the non-thief, the one whose resolve is fixed on falsehood is burned, but not the one whose resolve is fixed on truth.

"Just as there it would not be burned, so too this whole world has that as its essence; That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou, Śvetaketu. Then he understood it from him—yes, he understood it. Thus ends the sixteenth section. Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. (3)

Just as one who is truthful in his intent, in the act of grasping a heated axe, would not be scorched or burned because his palm is shielded by truth—so too, at the time of the fall of the body, when the merging into Being (*sat-sampatti*) is equal for both the knower who is intent on the Truth that is Brahman and the other, the wise man, having merged into Being, does not return again to assume the bodies of tigers, gods, or others.

But the ignorant person, identifying with the unreal modifications of nature, attains again the state of a tiger or the state of a deity, according to his karma and according to his learning. As for liberation and bondage, which are caused respectively by the realization of the Self and the failure to realize it; that which is the root of the world; that which is the abode and the support of all creatures; that of which everything consists; and that which is unborn, immortal, fearless, auspicious, and non-dual—that is the Truth, that is your Self. Therefore, Śvetaketu, you are That.

Thus has the meaning of the statement been explained more than once. But who is this Śvetaketu, the referent of the word "you"? He is the one who, having known himself as "I am Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka," and having heard, reflected upon, and understood the instruction, asked his father in order to understand that which is unheard, unthought, and unknown: "How indeed, venerable sir, does that instruction come about?"

This very one—the authorized hearer, thinker, and knower—is none other than the Supreme Deity itself that has entered the aggregate of causes and effects composed of fire, water, and food for the purpose of differentiating name and form, like a person reflected in a mirror or like the sun and other luminaries reflected in water and such. That Self, which is of the nature of pure Being and the universal Self, distinct from the body and its organs, was not previously known by him before hearing it from his father.

Now, having been enlightened by his father through illustrations and reasons with the words "That thou art," he indeed understood—that is, he realized—that what was spoken by his father was "I am indeed Being. The repetition [of the final word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.

What, then, is the fruit produced in the self here in the sixth chapter by the authority of the statement (*vākya-pramāṇa*)? The cessation of the cognition that one is qualified as an agent and an enjoyer is its fruit; this is the fruit of the realization of what was previously unknown, concerning the meaning denoted by the word "Thou," which we said was qualified for hearing and reflecting upon.

Prior to this realization, there existed in the self a cognition characterized by the sense of being an agent and an enjoyer, such as: "I shall perform these rites like the Agnihotra; I am qualified for them; I shall enjoy the fruits of these actions both here and in the hereafter; or, once the actions are performed, I shall have fulfilled my duty. This [cognition] is sublated when one is awakened by the statement "That Thou Art"—which reveals the existent root of the world, the one without a second—due to their mutual contradiction; for indeed, [the two cannot coexist].

When the Self is realized as one and non-dual—through the cognition "I am this"—then the cognition of duality, such as "this is mine," "this is other than that," "this must be done by me," or "having done this, I shall enjoy its fruit," is no longer possible.

Therefore, it is logical that when there is the knowledge of the Self as Being, Truth, and Non-dual, the knowledge of the individual self—which is a modification and unreal—is sublated. But [an objection may be raised]: in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the notion of Being (*sadbuddhi*) is enjoined with respect to the referent denoted by the word "thou" (*tvam*), just as the notion of Brahmā and others is superimposed upon the sun, the mind, and so forth, or just as in common worldly usage the notion of Viṣṇu and others is superimposed upon images and the like; it is not, however, the case that "Thou art Being itself."

If Śvetaketu were already existent as that very [Brahman], how could he not know himself, such that he would need to be instructed with "That thou art"? No, for this differs from statements concerning the sun and so forth. In passages such as "The sun is Brahman," because of the intervention of the word *iti*, the status of being Brahman is not understood directly; moreover, the sun and other such things possess form and other qualities. And in the cases of space and the mind, they are not Brahman precisely because of the intervention of the word *iti*.

In this context, however, having first shown the entry of the existent (*sat*) itself into this world, the text teaches the state of being identical with the Existent without restriction through the formula "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*). An objection might be raised: "Is not 'That thou art' like saying 'You are a lion' on account of qualities such as prowess? No, for it is taught that the Existent alone is one, without a second, and real—just as in the case of clay and other examples. Furthermore, if this were a figurative cognition, the attainment of the Existent would not be taught with the words, "For him there is delay only so long," because a figurative cognition is false, like saying "You are Indra" or "You are Yama."

Nor is it a praise, because Śvetaketu is not an object of worship. Nor can "Being" (sat) be praised by being taught as Śvetaketu—for a king would certainly not be praised by being told, "You are a slave. Furthermore, it is not logical that the all-pervading Self should undergo partial limitation, like a provincial governor being told, "You are a village headman. And no other interpretation is possible here, since the instruction is that the Self is Being.

If it is argued that here it is merely the cognition "I am Being" that is enjoined as something to be performed, and not the unknown fact "I am Being" that is being made known, [we reply: even on this view, such statements as "what has not been heard becomes heard" would be untenable. No, for the injunction to cultivate the cognition "I am Being" is intended as a glorification (stuti). No, because of the teaching: "The man who has a teacher knows; for him, there is delay only so long [as he is not liberated]."

For if it were merely the cognition "I am existent" that was enjoined as something to be performed, and not the fact that the referent of the word "thou" (tvam) is itself of the nature of existence, then the instruction on the means of knowledge—"one knows through a teacher"—would be unnecessary. It would be just like [the injunction] "one should perform the Agnihotra," where the possession of a teacher is already implied by the sense of the matter.

Furthermore, the statement "for him there is delay only so long" would not be appropriate as a provision for postponement, because if liberation were to result from the mere production of a single cognition even while the reality of the Self as Being remains unknown, that would lead to an absurdity. Nor can it be said that the cognition "I am not Being"—which arises from the authoritative sentence "That thou art"—can be subverted; nor can it be said that such a cognition has not arisen at all, since all the sentences of the Upaniṣads are exhausted solely in having that [Self] as their purport.

Just as it cannot be said that the notions of duty regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites—produced by the injunctions for those rites—are either unreal or non-existent, so it is here. As for the objection raised—that being of the nature of existence (*sad-ātman*), how could the Self not know itself?—that is not a fault, because even the cognition "I am a living soul (*jīva*), an agent, and an enjoyer," distinct from the aggregate of the body and organs, is not observed to arise naturally in living beings; how much less, then, can there be such a cognition of its being of the nature of pure existence?

How, in the absence of a consciousness distinct [from the body], could the cognition of agency and so forth regarding those [bodies] be possible? Yet it is observed. Just like that [cognition of agency], because there is also the notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth, the cognition of the true Self would not exist. Therefore, it is established that this statement, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), serves precisely to sublate the cognition of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) which is subject to modification and unreality.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixteenth section.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Govinda Bhagavat...
The sixth chapter of the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the worshipful feet [of Gauḍapāda], is completed.
"Oṃ! Teach me, Blessed One," thus Nārada approached Sanatkumāra. He said to him, "Approach me with what you already know; then I shall tell you what lies beyond that. He [Nārada] said: 1. (1)

The sixth chapter, which is primarily devoted to the instruction on the reality of the supreme goal, has served its purpose by being dedicated to the determination of the identity of Being (sat) and the Self (ātman). Since the principles characterized as modifications that fall short of Being have not yet been pointed out, [the author] begins this seventh section (prapāṭhaka) in order to point them out—beginning with Name (nāman) and ending with Breath (prāṇa)—in successive order, so that by means of them he may also point out the unsurpassed principle called the Infinite (bhūman), just like the method of pointing out the moon by means of a branch.

For someone might have the apprehension that, while the principles prior to Being (*sat*) have not been specified and only Being itself has been specified, something else might remain unknown; so that such a doubt may not arise, he desires to specify those [principles]. Alternatively, like ascending a staircase, having made known the objects of the intellect—starting from the gross and proceeding to the subtle and subtler—he desires to specify Name and the rest, intending to consecrate [the seeker] in the sovereignty that transcends them.

Alternatively, the names and so forth are presented in succession for the purpose of praising that reality called *bhūman*, which is the most excellent among the principles (*tattva*) that are progressively more distinguished starting from "Name" and so on. The narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), however, is for the purpose of praising the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). How so? Even Nārada, the celestial sage, though he had fulfilled his duties and possessed all branches of knowledge, still grieved because he did not know the Self; what then need be said of any other being of little learning who has not performed superior meritorious deeds and has not achieved his goal?

Alternatively, this narrative of Sanatkumāra and Nārada is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating that there is no means for attaining unsurpassed welfare other than the knowledge of the Self. For even though the celestial sage Nārada was endowed with the power of all means of knowledge, he did not attain the highest good; rather, having abandoned the pride caused by his excellence in lineage, learning, conduct, and capacity, he approached Sanatkumāra like a common man to obtain the means to the highest good. Thus, it is made manifest.

"Venerable sir, I study the Rigveda; the Yajurveda; the Samaveda; the Atharvana as the fourth; the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas; the science of ancestral rites; mathematics; the science of portents; the science of treasures; logic; ethics; the science of the gods; the science of sacred knowledge (*brahmavidyā*); the science of elemental spirits (*bhūtavidyā*); the science of governance (*kṣattravidyā*); the science of the stars; and the science of serpents and celestial beings—this, venerable sir, is what I study. (2)

"O Venerable One, I study [the Rigveda]"; that is, "I remember," because he is asked about what he knows. Likewise, [he mentions] the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the fourth Veda, which is the Atharvāṅgirasa—since the word "Veda" is the subject under discussion—and the fifth Veda, which is Itihāsa-Purāṇa. The meaning is that among the Vedas, with the Mahābhārata as the fifth, grammar is the Veda; for it is through grammar that the Ṛgveda and the others are understood through the analysis of words and so forth. [He also mentions] the Pitrya, which is the ritual for ancestral rites (śrāddha); and Rāśi, which is arithmetic.

*Daiva* is the knowledge of portents; *nidhi* is the science of locating treasures such as Mahākāla; *vākovākya* is the science of logic (*tarkaśāstra*); *ekāyana* is the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*); *devavidyā* is etymology (*nirukta*); *brahmavidyā*—the knowledge of the Brahman known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—is phonetics, ritual codes, prosody, and astronomy; *bhūtavidyā* is the science of spirits (*bhūtatantra*); *kṣatravidyā* is the science of archery (*dhanurveda*); and *nakṣatravidyā* is astrology (*jyotiṣa*).

"The knowledge of the snake-gods (*sarpadevajanavidyā*)—namely, the science of snakes (*sarpavidyā*), the science of the *Garuḍa* (*gāruḍa*), the science of the gods (*devajanavidyā*), and the specialized knowledges of perfumery, dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the arts—all this, O Venerable One, I have studied. Yet, O Venerable One, I am merely a knower of mantras, not a knower of the Self (*ātmavit*). For I have heard from those like your venerable self that 'the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. Therefore, O Venerable One, I am in sorrow. May the Venerable One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow. He said to him: "Whatever you have studied here, all that is merely name (*nāman*). (3)

"Thus, O Blessed One, although I know all this, I am merely a knower of mantras; the meaning is that I am one who possesses knowledge only of the literal meaning of words. For all speech is mere denotation (*abhidhāna*), and all denotation is included within the mantras. 'I am merely a knower of mantras' means 'I am a knower of mantras and a knower of rituals,' for it will be stated later that 'rituals are in the mantras. I am not a knower of the Self; I do not know the Self."

[Objection: But surely the Self is also revealed by mantras; how then can one who knows the mantras not know the Self? [Reply: No, because the distinction between the designator (the word) and the designated (the object) is a modification (*vikāra*), and the Self is not admitted to be a modification. [Objection: But the Self is also designated by the word "Self. [Reply: No, according to such scriptural passages as, "from which words turn back," and "where one sees nothing else," and so forth. [Objection: How then do words such as "the Self alone is below" and "that is the Self" cause the Self to be understood? [Reply: This is not a fault.

When a word is employed with reference to the inner self (pratyagātman) as embodied, which is the object of [apparent] difference, and once the body and other such things have been rejected as being the self, that which remains—the reality—is made known even though it is inexpressible. This is just as when an army is seen together with its king, although the king is hidden by parasols, banners, and flags and is not visible, the verbal usage "the king is seen here" occurs.

In that regard, when one seeks to determine the specific identity of a king by asking "Who is this king?", even if other kings are seen and others are excluded, the cognition of "king" would still arise even with respect to another king who is not being perceived—just like that [the notion of "I"]. Therefore, I am merely a knower of mantras and a knower of ritual action; and since all ritual action and its effects are modifications (*vikāra*), I am only a knower of modifications. The meaning is that I am not a knower of the Self, nor a knower of the true nature of the Self’s primordial matter (*prakṛti*). For this very reason it has been said: "The person who has a teacher knows," and from such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back."

Indeed, there certainly exists in me the knowledge of the path acquired through hearing, for it is said that one who knows the Self transcends—overcomes—grief, mental anguish, and the state of feeling that one's purpose has not been fulfilled. Therefore, O Blessed One, because I do not know the Self, I grieve; I am constantly tormented by the thought that my purpose remains unfulfilled.

"May the Blessed One carry me across—to the further shore, the end—of this ocean of sorrow; may he bring my intellect to fulfillment through the boat of self-knowledge; that is to say, may he lead me to fearlessness. To him who had spoken thus, [the teacher] said: "Whatever indeed you have studied here—you have learned it; by the mention of 'study,' the knowledge of its meaning is implied, meaning that you have understood it—but all this is merely a name," according to the Vedic scripture: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."

"Name indeed is the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth, the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, the science of portents, the science of treasures, the science of logic, the science of monism, the science of the gods, the science of sacred knowledge (*brahmavidyā*), the science of elemental beings, the science of weaponry, the science of the stars, and the science of serpents and divine beings—this is simply Name. Meditate upon Name as Brahman. This passage beginning with "Name indeed is the Rigveda, the Yajurveda," and so forth, means that this is simply Name. "Meditate upon Name as Brahman" means meditating on it with the thought that it is Brahman—just as one worships an image with the thought that it is Viṣṇu, in that same way.

He who meditates on Name as Brahman—so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom of movement, he who meditates on Name as Brahman. "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than Name? "There is indeed something greater than Name. "May the Venerable One tell me that. Thus ends the first section. 1. (5)

Now, hear what the fruit is for him who meditates upon *nāman* (name) as Brahman: as far as the reach of name extends, within that sphere of name, he has freedom of movement according to his desire, just as a king has freedom in his own domain. "He who meditates upon name as Brahman"—this is the conclusion. [Nārada asks: "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than name—something else worthy of being viewed as Brahman?
Sanatkumāra said: "Indeed, there is something greater than name. Nārada said: "If there is such a thing, may the Venerable One tell it to me."

Thus ends the commentary on the first section. Speech, indeed, is greater than name. Through speech, one understands the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth, the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, etymology, the science of the gods, the science of sacred knowledge, the science of spirits, the science of ruling, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings; and [through speech one understands] heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire, and the gods and humans and animals.

"Trees and grasses, forest plants, wild beasts, down to worms, moths, and ants; dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant—were speech not to exist, neither dharma nor adharma would have been known, neither truth nor falsehood, neither the good nor the bad, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant. It is speech that makes all this known. Meditate upon speech.

Speech indeed [is greater]. "Speech" refers to the organ situated in the eight locations, such as the root of the tongue, which manifests phonemes. And since phonemes constitute names, it is said that speech is greater than name. For in the world, the cause is seen to be greater than the effect—just as a father is greater than his son, so it is here. And how is speech greater than name? He says: Speech makes known the *Ṛgveda*—that "this is the *Ṛgveda*"—and likewise the *Yajurveda*, and so on, similarly. It is "heart-knowing," meaning dear to the heart.

The opposite of that is "not knowing the heart" (*ahṛdayajña*). If speech did not exist, dharma and so forth would not have been made known; for in the absence of speech there is no study, in the absence of study there is no hearing of its meaning, and in the absence of hearing it, dharma and so forth would not have been made known—that is to say, they would not have been known. Therefore, speech alone makes all this known through the utterance of sound. Thus, speech is greater than name. Therefore, meditate upon speech as Brahman.

He who meditates upon speech as Brahman—so far as speech extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon speech as Brahman. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than speech? "There is indeed something greater than speech. "May the Venerable Sir tell that to me. This is the same as before. (Thus ends the second section. 2. (2) — The rest is identical.

Thus ends the commentary on the second section. The mind, indeed, is greater than speech. Just as one’s fist encompasses two *vāmalaka* fruits, or two jujube fruits, or two *akṣa* berries, even so the mind encompasses both speech and name. When one intends with the mind, "I shall study the sacred hymns," then one studies them; "I shall perform rituals," then one performs them; "I shall desire sons and cattle," then one desires them; "I shall desire this world and the next," then one desires them. For the mind is the self; the mind is the world; the mind is Brahman. Meditate upon the mind. 1. (1)

The mind (*manas*), characterized by the function of mental reflection (*manasyana*), is greater than speech. For it is the mind, possessing the activity of reflection, that impels speech toward what is to be spoken; thus, speech is contained within the mind. And whatever is contained within something else is greater than it, because of its pervasiveness.

Just as in the world a fist encompasses two *āmalaka* fruits, or two *kola* (jujube) fruits, or two *akṣa* (vibhītaka) fruits—just as the fist pervades those fruits because they are contained within it—in the same way, the mind encompasses both speech and name, just like the *āmalaka* fruits and so forth.

When that person—at whatever time—he intends with the mind, that is, with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), "I shall study the mantras, I shall recite them"—having thus formed the desire to speak (*vivakṣābuddhi*)—then he studies. Likewise, having formed the desire to act (*cikīrṣābuddhi*), "I shall perform ritual acts," then he performs them. And having formed the desire for acquisition, "I would desire sons and cattle," then he desires them—that is, he obtains sons and so forth by practicing the means for their attainment. This is the meaning.

Likewise, one might wish, "May I obtain this world and that world by means of a method"; through the practice of the means for attaining them, one who so wishes indeed obtains them. For the mind is the self (*ātman*); since agency and enjoyership belong to the self, and these exist only when the mind exists and not otherwise, the mind is called the self. For the mind is the world; for it is only when the mind exists that there is a world and the practice of the means for attaining it. Since the mind is the world, therefore the mind is Brahman. Because this is so, therefore, "Meditate upon the mind."

He who meditates on the mind as Brahman—so far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on the mind as Brahman. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than the mind? "There is indeed something greater than the mind. "May the Venerable Sir explain that to me. This is the third section; the rest, beginning with "He who [meditates] on the mind," is the same as before.

Thus ends the commentary on the third section. Volition (*saṅkalpa*) is indeed greater than the mind; for when one wills, then one directs the mind, and one directs speech toward that [mind]. One directs that [speech] toward the name, and in the name the mantras become one. In the mantras, the ritual acts (*karman*) reside. 1. (1)

Volition (*saṃkalpa*) is indeed greater than the mind. Volition, like reflection (*manasyana*), is a function of the internal organ; it is the determination [of an object] through the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. For when an object has been determined through such distinction, the desire to act (*cikīrṣābuddhi*) arises immediately after reflection. How so? When one indeed wills—that is, when one distinguishes objects such as what ought to be done—thinking, "This is fit to be done; this is unfit to be done," then one reflects, "I shall study the mantras," and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, one impels speech for the purpose of uttering mantras and so forth. And one impels that speech by forming the intention [to speak] with respect to the name—that is, for the purpose of uttering the name. Within the name—in the general category of names—the mantras, being specific sounds, become one; that is to say, they are subsumed within it. For the particular is subsumed within the general. Within the mantras, the ritual acts become one. Ritual acts are performed as revealed by the mantras; there is no ritual act that is without a mantra.

For indeed, when an action, having acquired its existence through the manifestation by a mantra, is enjoined in the Brāhmaṇa—stating that "this must be performed by the Brāhmaṇa for such-and-such a result"—even that which appears as the origin of actions in the Brāhmaṇas is merely the clarification of those very actions whose existence was already established in the mantras. For no action unmanifested by a mantra is ever seen to originate in a Brāhmaṇa. It is well known in the world that "action is prescribed by the Trayī"; and the word *trayī* is a designation for the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
And in the Atharvaveda it says: "The sages beheld those rites within the mantras. Therefore, it is logical that the rites are contained within the mantras.

Verily, these have thought as their sole path, thought as their essence, and are established in thought. Heaven and earth were thought out; wind and space were thought out; water and fire were thought out. For the sake of the thought-out ordering of these, rain is thought out; for the sake of the thought-out ordering of rain, food is thought out; for the sake of the thought-out ordering of food, the vital breaths are thought out; for the sake of the thought-out ordering of the vital breaths, the sacred hymns are thought out; and for the sake of the thought-out ordering of the sacred hymns, ritual acts are thought out.

Through action, intentions are formed; for the formation of intentions, the world is formed; for the formation of the world, everything is formed. This is that intention (*saṅkalpa*). "Meditate upon intention," it is said. 2. (2)

Now, these things beginning with the mind have *saṃkalpa* as their single point of convergence (*ekāyana*). Those whose single point of convergence—their goal, movement, and dissolution—is *saṃkalpa* are "those having *saṃkalpa* as their single convergence. They consist of *saṃkalpa* at their origin; they are established in *saṃkalpa* during their existence. For heaven and earth—Heaven-and-Earth—appear as if they have performed *saṃkalpa*, as if they have formed a resolve; Heaven and Earth are perceived as motionless. Likewise, wind and space also appear as if they have performed *saṃkalpa*.

In the same way, water and fire resolved; they appear motionless in their own forms. Because of that, for the sake of the resolution of heaven, earth, and the rest—that is, with the intention of their formation—rain resolves, meaning it becomes capable [of occurring]. Likewise, for the sake of the resolution of rain—that is, with the intention of its formation—food resolves, for from rain food comes into being. For the sake of the resolution of food, the vital breaths resolve.

For the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) consist of food; they are supported by food, as the Śruti declares: "Food is the bond. For the purpose of their coordination, the sacred formulas (*mantra*) are coordinated. Indeed, one who possesses vital breath studies the formulas, not one who is weak. For the purpose of the coordination of the formulas, the rituals such as the *agnihotra* are coordinated; when performed as revealed by the formulas, they become capable of yielding fruit. From that, the world coordinates its fruit—that is to say, it becomes capable through its inherence in the agent of the action.

For the world’s conceptualization, the entire universe conceives itself in order to maintain the integrity of its own nature. Indeed, this entire universe—which culminates in results—is all rooted in volition (*saṃkalpa*). Therefore, this particular volition is distinguished. Having said, "Meditate upon volition," he states the fruit for the one who meditates upon it.

He who meditates upon *saṅkalpa* (volition) as Brahman attains, indeed, worlds that are fashioned, stable, firmly established, unshakable, and free from distress; he himself becomes stable and unshakable. As far as the reach of volition extends, so far he has freedom of movement. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than volition? "There is indeed something greater than volition. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. Thus ends the fourth section. (3) — 4 — (3)

He who meditates upon *saṃkalpa* (volition) as Brahman, with the understanding that it is Brahman—he, being wise, beholds these worlds fashioned by the Creator as "fashioned," meaning prepared, established, and willed; he sees them as "firm" (*dhruvān*), eternal in comparison to things that are extremely non-eternal, and he himself is also firm. For if the inhabitant of the worlds were non-firm, the fashioning of the worlds as firm would be purposeless; thus, being firm, he sees them as "well-established," meaning endowed with all necessary means and resources, as is seen from the observation that one is "established" through cattle, sons, and so forth—and he himself is likewise [established].

Established [in this state], endowed with his own implements, he—being himself unshaken and free from fear of enemies and the like—accomplishes and attains [his goal]. This means that as far as the range of his resolve extends, there he has freedom of movement according to his will; this refers to the resolve of the self (the practitioner), and not to the resolves of all others, because that would contradict the description of the subsequent fruit. "He who meditates on resolve as Brahman," and so forth, is as explained previously.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth section.

Mind, indeed, is greater than volition. For when one perceives, then one wills; then one reflects; then one utters speech; and one utters that [speech] in a name. In a name, the mantras become one; in the mantras, the ritual acts [become one]. 1. (1)

The mind (*citta*) is indeed greater than volition (*saṃkalpa*). The mind possesses the quality of being a cognizer (*cetayitṛtva*), the capacity for awareness appropriate to the time at hand, and the power to discern the purpose and nature of objects past and future; it is therefore greater even than volition. How so? When one perceives an object that has been obtained, thinking, "This has been obtained in such a way," then one forms a volition (*saṃkalpayate*) regarding its acquisition or rejection, and then one reflects upon it (*manasyati*), and so forth, as described previously.

These, indeed, have thought as their single path, thought as their self, and are established in thought. Therefore, even if a man is a man of great learning but lacks thought, people say of him, "He is nothing," because of what he knows; for even though he is learned, he would not be so if he were lacking in thought. But if a man has little learning yet possesses thought, people listen even more eagerly to him from all sides, for thought is indeed their single path, thought is their self, and thought is their foundation. Meditate upon thought. 2. (2) —-

Those [factors] beginning with volition and ending with the fruit of action have the mind as their single path, have the mind as their essence, arise from the mind, are established in the mind, and abide in the mind—this is also to be understood as before. Furthermore, what is the majesty of the mind?

Since the mind is the root of volition and the like, therefore, even if one is highly learned—possessing a thorough knowledge of many scriptures—and becomes "mindless," being devoid of the capacity for volition and so forth, the discerning people of the world say of him: "Though he exists, he is as good as non-existent. Furthermore, they declare that whatever of the scriptures and such he knows or has heard is entirely in vain for him.

Why? The meaning is that they say: "If this person were truly learned, he would not have such a mind; therefore, even though he has heard [the teachings], it is as if he had not heard them at all. On the other hand, if even one who knows little possesses a [receptive] mind, then people desire to hear—that is, they wish to listen—for the very purpose of grasping the meaning of what has been said to him. And for that reason, "the mind alone is the single path to these [functions] such as volition," and so forth, as explained previously.

He who meditates on Brahman as the mind (*citta*) indeed attains worlds that are constant, being himself constant; established, being himself established; unshakable, being himself unshakable. As far as the reach of the mind extends, there he has freedom of movement according to his desire—this is true for one who meditates on Brahman as the mind. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than the mind? "There is indeed something greater than the mind. "May the Venerable Sir tell me that. [Note: *Cittān* means "accumulated" or "built up" by the qualities of the intellect. The terms "constant" (*dhruva*) and so forth have already been explained. This is the fifth section. (5) (3)

Thus ends the commentary on the fifth section. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed greater than thought (*citta*). The earth meditates, as it were; the intermediate space meditates, as it were; the sky meditates, as it were; the waters meditate, as it were; the mountains meditate, as it were; and gods and humans meditate, as it were. Therefore, those among humans here who attain greatness become, as it were, parts of the attainment of meditation. Now, those who are insignificant—quarrelsome, slanderous, and backbiters—and those who are powerful, they too become, as it were, parts of the attainment of meditation. "Meditate upon meditation! [1] (1–2)

Meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed greater than thought. Meditation is defined as a continuous stream of cognitions that is unwavering with respect to the objects of focus taught in the scriptures—such as deities—and is uninterrupted by heterogeneous mental states; this is what they call "one-pointedness. And the greatness of meditation is seen through its results. How so? Just as a yogi becomes motionless while meditating upon attaining the fruit of meditation, so too the earth appears as if it were meditating, motionless; the atmosphere appears as if it were meditating, and so forth—the rest is the same.

"Gods and humans" (*devamanuṣyāḥ*) refers either to gods and humans, or to humans who are equal to gods; that is, humans endowed with qualities such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, who do not abandon their divine nature. Since meditation is thus distinguished, therefore those humans in this world who attain greatness—meaning the state of greatness—among humans through wealth, knowledge, or virtues, [they] obtain the cause for greatness consisting of wealth and the like. This is the meaning.

The term *dhyānāpādāṃśāḥ* means "parts of the attainment of meditation. Here, "attainment" (*āpāda*) refers to the acquisition of the fruit of meditation; a "part" (*aṃśa*) is a portion or fraction (*kalā*). The meaning is that they appear as if possessing some small fraction of the fruit of meditation. They appear as if motionless, yet they are neither dull nor inert.

Furthermore, those who are few, insignificant, and have not attained even a fraction of greatness such as wealth and so forth, are the opposite of those previously described: they are quarrelsome, having a disposition for strife; they are slanderers, exposing the faults of others; and they are revilers, being those whose habit it is to speak of another's fault as if it were imminent.

Now, those who have attained greatness through wealth and other means are "sources" (*prabhavaḥ*) because they exercise power over others—such as learned teachers, royal lords, and so forth—who are like the constituent parts of meditation. Thus, the greatness of meditation is seen by way of its fruit; therefore, [the text says] "greater than the mind," and "meditate upon that," and so forth, as previously explained.

He who meditates upon meditation as Brahman—so far as meditation extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon meditation as Brahman. "Sir, is there anything greater than meditation? "Indeed, there is something greater than meditation. "May the Blessed One tell me that. Thus ends the sixth section. (1–2) — Section Six.

Meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed greater than thought. Meditation is defined as a continuous stream of cognition that is unwavering with respect to the objects of focus taught in the scriptures—such as deities—and uninterrupted by heterogeneous mental states; this is what they call "one-pointedness" (*ekāgratā*). Furthermore, the greatness of meditation is seen through its results. How so? Just as a yogi becomes motionless while meditating upon attaining the fruit of meditation, so too the earth appears as if it were meditating, becoming motionless; the atmosphere appears as if it were meditating, and so forth—the rest is the same.

"Gods and humans" (devamanuṣyāḥ) refers to both gods and men; or alternatively, "humans who are like gods" (devasamā manuṣyāḥ), meaning humans endowed with qualities such as tranquility (śama) and so forth, who do not abandon their divine nature. Since meditation is thus distinguished, therefore those humans in this world who attain greatness—meaning the state of being great—among other humans by means of wealth, knowledge, or virtues; that is to say, they obtain the causes for greatness such as wealth and the like.

"Like portions of the attainment of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). *Āpāda* means the attainment of meditative absorption; that is, the acquisition of the fruit of meditation. A "portion" (*aṃśa*) of that is a part or a fraction (*kalā*). The meaning is: "as if they possessed some small fraction of the acquisition of the fruit of meditation. They appear as if motionless, yet they are not dull-witted (*śudra*).

Furthermore, those who are few, insignificant, and have not attained even a fraction of the greatness of wealth and so forth, are the opposite of those previously described; they are quarrelsome, having a disposition for strife, slanderous, exposing the faults of others, and abusive—those whose habit it is to speak of another's faults as if they were right before them.

Now, those who have attained greatness through wealth and other means are "sources" (*prabhava*) because they exercise power over others—such as learned teachers, royal lords, and so forth—who are like the constituent parts of the attainment of meditation (*dhyāna*). Thus, the greatness of meditation is seen by way of its fruit; therefore, it is said that [meditation] is greater than the mind, and for this reason, one should meditate upon it.
This concludes the commentary on the sixth section.

Consciousness, indeed, is greater than meditation. For by means of consciousness one knows the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaṇa* as the fourth, the *Itihāsa-purāṇa* as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, the science of the gods, the science of sacred knowledge, the science of spirits, the science of governance, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings; and [one knows] heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire, the gods and humans.

"By means of consciousness alone, one discerns domestic animals and birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey, down to worms, moths, and ants; dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant, food and flavor, this world and the world beyond. Discern consciousness; meditate upon consciousness.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is indeed greater than meditation (*dhyāna*). Consciousness is the knowledge whose object is the meaning of the scriptures; because it is the cause of meditation, it is greater than meditation. And how is it greater? He says: "By means of consciousness, one indeed knows the *Ṛgveda* [thinking], 'This is the *Ṛgveda*'; for its knowledge of the meaning serves as the cause for meditation by way of being the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Likewise [one knows] the *Yajurveda*, and so forth."

Furthermore, the meaning is that one understands through cognition alone such things as cattle and so forth, as well as merit and demerit established by scripture, the good and the bad known from worldly experience, or what is recorded in the Smṛtis, and everything within the realm of perception. Therefore, it is logical that cognition is more abundant than meditation; hence, "Venerate cognition."

He who meditates on consciousness as Brahman attains worlds that possess consciousness and knowledge; as far as the reach of consciousness extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on consciousness as Brahman. "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than consciousness? "Indeed, there is something greater than consciousness. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. Thus ends the seventh section. (2) — 7 — (2) —

Listen to the fruit of worship for one possessed of *vijñāna*. He attains—that is, he reaches—the worlds belonging to those who possess *vijñāna*, as well as the worlds of those who possess *jñāna*. Here, *vijñāna* is knowledge concerning the subject matter of the scriptures, while *jñāna* is skill regarding other subjects; the meaning is that he attains the worlds inhabited by those endowed with such qualities. The phrase "as long as there is *vijñāna*" and so forth is to be understood as before. Thus ends the commentary on the seventh section.

Strength, indeed, is greater than consciousness. For even a single strong man can shake a hundred men possessed of consciousness. When one becomes strong, then he becomes able to rise; rising, he becomes able to move about; moving about, he becomes able to approach [a teacher]; approaching, he becomes able to see, he becomes able to hear, he becomes able to think, he becomes able to understand, he becomes able to act, and he becomes able to discern. By strength, indeed, the earth stands firm; by strength the intermediate space; by strength the sky; by strength the mountains; by strength gods and humans [exist].

"By strength do beasts and birds, grasses and trees, wild animals, and all down to insects, moths, and ants exist; by strength the world stands. Meditate upon strength! He who meditates on strength as Brahman attains freedom of movement as far as strength extends—so much so for him who meditates on strength as Brahman. "Revered sir, is there anything greater than strength? "Indeed, there is something greater than strength. "May the revered sir tell me that. Thus ends the eighth section. 8.

Power is indeed greater than consciousness. For even a single powerful man can shake a hundred men possessed of consciousness. When one becomes powerful, then he becomes able to rise; rising, he becomes able to move about; moving about, he becomes able to attend upon others; attending upon others, he becomes able to approach them; having approached, he becomes able to see, able to hear, able to think, able to understand, able to act, and able to discern. By power indeed the earth stands firm; by power the intermediate space; by power the sky; by power the mountains; by power gods and humans [exist].
"By strength do beasts and birds, grasses and trees, wild animals, and all things down to worms, moths, and ants exist; by strength the world stands. Meditate upon strength! ... 1 ...

Power, indeed, is greater than consciousness. "Power" refers to the capacity of the mind for manifestation regarding objects of knowledge, generated by the consumption of food; for the Śruti says, "Because of fasting, the [Vedic] hymns and so forth do not manifest to me, O sir. This same capacity exists even in the body, as evidenced by the ability to rise up and so forth, since even a single powerful living being can cause a hundred conscious persons to tremble, just as a single rutting elephant can shake a hundred men gathered together.

Since strength has its cause in the consumption of food and other such things in this manner, therefore, when that person becomes strong—that is, possessed of strength—he becomes an "utthātā," a doer of exertion; and while exerting himself, he becomes a "paricaritā" of his elders and his teacher, a doer of service and attendance. While serving them, he becomes an "upasattā"—one who goes near them, one who is intimate and dear to them; this is the meaning.

Approaching—that is, going into the presence of—the teacher or another instructor with one-pointed concentration, he becomes a beholder of the guru. Thereafter, he becomes a listener to what has been said by him. Thereafter, he becomes a thinker through reasoning, thinking, "What has been said by these [teachers] is thus logically established. And while thinking, he becomes a knower, realizing, "This is exactly so. Then, having thus ascertained, he becomes a doer—that is, a performer—of the meaning taught by him; the sense is that he becomes a cognizer, an experiencer of the fruit of that performance.

Furthermore, as for the greatness of strength: "By strength indeed the earth stands," and so forth, which has its meaning plain. He who meditates on strength as Brahman—so far as strength extends, there he has freedom of movement according to his will—he who meditates on strength as Brahman. "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than strength? "Certainly, there is something greater than strength. "May the venerable sir tell me that. Thus ends the eighth section. (1–2) — Section 8.

Power, indeed, is greater than consciousness. "Power" refers to the capacity of the mind for manifestation regarding objects of cognition, produced by the consumption of food. This is based on the Vedic text: "From lack of food, the [Vedic] visions and so forth do not manifest to me, O sir. In the body as well, it is that very capacity for rising up and so forth, because even a single powerful living being can shake a hundred conscious ones, just as a single rutting elephant can shake a hundred men gathered together.

Since strength has its cause in the consumption of food and other such things in this manner, therefore, when that person becomes strong—that is, possessed of strength—he becomes an "utthātā," a doer of exertion; and while exerting himself, he becomes a "paricaritā" of his elders and teacher, a doer of service and attendance. While serving them, he becomes an "upasattā," one who goes near them, an intimate, and a beloved—this is the meaning.

Approaching—that is, going into the presence of—the teacher and another instructor with one-pointed concentration, he becomes a beholder of the guru. Thereafter, he becomes a hearer of what has been spoken by him. Thereafter, he becomes a thinker through reasoning, thinking, "What has been said by these [teachers] is established in this way. And while reflecting, he becomes a knower, realizing, "This is indeed so. Then, having thus reached a certainty, he becomes a doer—that is, a practitioner—of the meaning taught by him; and he becomes a perceiver, in the sense that he is the experiencer of the fruit of that practice.

Furthermore, as for the greatness of strength: "By strength indeed the earth stands," and so forth; this has its meaning explained straightforwardly. Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section. "Food, verily, is greater than strength. Therefore, even if one were not to eat for ten nights, if he should yet live—he would then become one who does not see, does not hear, does not think, does not understand, does not act, and does not discern. But by means of food, he becomes a seer, he becomes a hearer, he becomes a thinker, he becomes an understander, he becomes an actor, and he becomes a discerner. Meditate upon food. 1.

(1) Food indeed is greater than strength, because it is the cause of strength. How is food the cause of strength? It is said: since food is the cause of strength, therefore even if someone were not to eat for ten nights, he would die due to the loss of that strength which has food as its cause.

If, however, he should live—for there are indeed those seen living even without eating for a month—then even while living, he becomes one who does not see, nor hear, and so forth; everything becomes the opposite of what was previously described. Now, when, having gone without food for many days and being incapable of such activities as seeing and so on, he becomes "one whose sustenance is food" (*annasthāyī*); *āya* means arrival, that is, the acquisition of food; he who possesses this is *annasthāyī*. [The form] *āyai* is due to a transposition of syllables.

Now, even in the reading *annasyāyāḥ*, the meaning is exactly the same, because of the mention of effects such as "the seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth. For it is observed that the capacity for seeing and other such functions exists when food is consumed, not when it is not obtained; therefore, [the instruction is]: "Meditate upon food. He who meditates upon food as Brahman attains worlds full of food and full of drink. As far as the reach of food extends, there he has freedom of movement according to his desire—he who meditates upon food as Brahman. "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than food? "Yes, indeed, there is something greater than food. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. Thus ends the ninth section. 9.

(2) And as for the fruit: he attains worlds that possess abundant food, indeed worlds with plenty of food, and those possessing abundant drink, indeed worlds with plenty of water, because of the constant connection between food and drink. The rest is the same.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth section.

Water, indeed, is more than food. Therefore, when there is no good rain, living beings become distressed, thinking, "Food will become scarce. But when there is good rain, living beings become joyful, thinking, "Food will abound. Water alone is these material forms: this earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the mountains, gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses, trees, wild beasts, down to worms, moths, and ants—water alone is these material forms. Meditate upon water. 1. (1) ————-The final answer is: Water, indeed, is more than food. Therefore, when there is no good rain, living beings become distressed, thinking, "Food will become scarce. Water indeed is greater than food, because it is the cause of food. Since this is so, when—at whatever time—a good rain, a beneficial and auspicious rain for the crops, does not occur, then the vital breaths become afflicted and people become miserable. For what reason? He says: "In this year, our food will become less, that is, more meager."

Furthermore, when there is good rain, living beings become joyful, happy, and delighted, thinking, "There will be abundant food. Since material food originates from water, these very waters—having transformed into various forms of material objects—are what is meant by "the formed," such as this earth, the intermediate space, and so forth. These formed things are indeed the waters; therefore, meditate upon the waters.

He who meditates upon water as Brahman obtains all desires; he becomes satisfied, and as far as the reach of water extends, there he has freedom of movement according to his wish—he who meditates upon water as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than water? "There is indeed something greater than water. "May the venerable sir tell me that. Thus ends the tenth section. (2) — 10 —

The fruit [of this meditation]: he who meditates upon water as Brahman obtains all desires; that is to say, he obtains desirable objects that possess form. Furthermore, because satisfaction arises from water, by meditating upon water one becomes possessed of satisfaction. The rest is the same. Thus ends the commentary on the tenth section.

Fire, indeed, is greater than water. It seizes the wind and flies toward the sky. Then they say, "It is glowing; it is scorching; it will rain. Fire, having first manifested itself, then creates water. Therefore, when they see flashes of lightning, both upward and across, and hear the crashing sounds, they say, "It is flashing; it is thundering; it will rain. Fire, having first manifested itself, then creates water. Meditate upon fire. 1. (1) —-

Fire is indeed greater than water, because fire is the cause of water. How is it the cause of water?
