He says: because fire arises from water, therefore this very fire, having seized and constrained the air—having made it motionless by its own nature—and heating the ether, that is, heating while pervading the ether, then people in the world say: "It is scorching and burning the world in general; it is scorching bodies; therefore, it will surely rain."

For it is well known in the world that one who has seen a cause being exerted possesses the cognition that the effect will come to be. That fire, having first manifested itself, then immediately creates water; therefore, because it is the creator of water, fire is more extensive than water. Furthermore, that very same fire becomes the cause of rain in the form of thunder.

How so? Together with the upward-moving and upward-going lightning flashes, as well as the crosswise and crosswise-moving ones, resounds and thunders—the sounds of thundering proceed. Therefore, upon seeing that, worldly people say: "It lightens," "it thunders," "it will surely rain," and so forth, according to the meaning already explained. Therefore, "venerate the Light."

He who meditates upon Brahman as splendor (*tejas*) indeed becomes splendid; he attains splendid, radiant worlds from which darkness has been dispelled. As far as the reach of splendor extends, so far he has freedom of movement. "He who meditates upon Brahman as splendor"—"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than splendor?"—"There is indeed something greater than splendor."—"May the Venerable Sir explain that to me. Thus ends the eleventh section. (2) — 11 — (2) —

The fruit of the worship of that *tejas* is as follows: he indeed becomes radiant (*tejasvī*). And from that very radiance, he attains worlds that are luminous, shining, full of light, and with darkness dispelled—that is, with the darkness of external and internal ignorance and so forth removed. The rest has its meaning plain. Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh section.

"Space, indeed, is greater than fire. In space, indeed, both the sun and the moon exist; in space, lightning, the stars, and fire reside. By means of space one calls out; by means of space one hears; by means of space one hears back. In space one delights; in space one does not delight; in space one is born; one is born facing toward space. Meditate upon space. 1. (1)

"Space, indeed, is greater than fire," because space is the cause of fire along with wind. Since it was said, "having grasped the wind," wind was mentioned together with fire; therefore, it is not mentioned here separately from fire. For in the world, the cause is seen to be greater than the effect—just as clay is greater than jars and the like—so too, space, being the cause of fire along with wind, is greater than it. How so? Indeed, both the sun and the moon, which are of the nature of light, as well as lightning, the stars, and fire—all of which are of the nature of light—are within space.

Furthermore, that which exists within another is small, while the other is greater. Moreover, one calls out to another by means of space; being called, the other hears by means of space; one person hears back the sound spoken by another; everyone delights and sports with one another in space; likewise, one does not delight in space when separated from kinsmen and others; one is born in space, not in that which is obstructed by a material form. Similarly, sprouts and the like grow directed toward space, not in the opposite direction. Therefore, meditate upon space.

He who meditates on space as Brahman attains worlds that possess space, that possess light, that are unconfined, and that are wide-extending; as far as space extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on space as Brahman. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than space? "There is indeed something greater than space. "May the Venerable Sir explain that to me. Thus ends the twelfth section. 12. (2)

Listen to the fruit [of this knowledge]: that wise man attains worlds that possess space (*ākāśavat*), which are expansive; worlds that possess light (*prakāśavat*), because light and space are eternally connected; and worlds that are unconfined (*asaṃbādha*)—*saṃbādha* meaning confinement, which is mutual oppression, and thus *asaṃbādha* means free from that; worlds that possess wide-striding ones (*urugāyavat*), meaning worlds of vast movement and vast range. "As far as space extends," etc., has already been explained. Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section.

Memory, indeed, is greater than space. Therefore, even if many people were sitting together, if they were not mindful, they would not hear anything, they would not think, and they would not understand. But when they become mindful, then they hear, then they think, and then they understand. By memory one recognizes one's sons; by memory one recognizes one's cattle. Meditate upon memory. 1. (1) —-

Memory indeed is greater than space. Memory—meaning the faculty of recollection, which is a quality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—is to be understood as greater than space by means of a change in gender (liṅgavyatyaya). For when there is memory on the part of the rememberer, everything beginning with space becomes purposeful, since it serves as an object of enjoyment for one who possesses memory. But in the absence of memory, even though things exist, they are as if non-existent, because the effects of existence are absent. Furthermore, in the absence of memory, it is impossible to ascertain the existence of space and the other elements; therefore, memory is greater than space.

For it is observed in the world that there is a great deficiency of memory (*smara*) in this regard: therefore, even if many people were to sit together in one place, if they were not to remember what was said by one another while sitting there, they would not hear any sound at all; likewise, they would not reflect upon it, for they would reflect only if they remembered what is to be reflected upon—due to the absence of memory, they would not reflect; and likewise, they would not discern anything.

When indeed they remember that which is to be reflected upon, that which is to be understood, and that which is to be heard, then they hear it, then they reflect upon it, and then they understand it. Likewise, by means of memory one recognizes, "These are my sons," and by means of memory one recognizes the cattle. Therefore, because of its abundance, meditate upon memory. The rest has already been explained. Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth section. He who meditates upon Brahman as memory—so far as memory extends, there he has freedom of movement as he desires.

"One meditates on Smara as Brahman. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than Smara? "Indeed, there is something greater than Smara. "May the Venerable Sir explain that to me. (Thus ends the thirteenth section. "Hope, indeed, is greater than Smara. For impelled by hope, one studies the sacred hymns, performs ritual acts, desires sons and cattle, and desires this world and the world beyond. Meditate upon Hope. (Thus ends the first section.)

(1) Hope, indeed, is greater than memory. Hope is the longing for an object not yet attained; it is what they call by various synonyms as thirst or desire. And that hope is greater than memory. How so? For by means of hope residing within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one remembers what is to be remembered. Remembering in the form of an object of hope, one becomes memory itself. Therefore, kindled by hope and intensified by hope, having become memory and remembering, one studies the mantras such as the *Ṛgveda* and others.

Having studied the Veda and heard from the Brahmins its meaning and the injunctions, he performs rituals with the expectation of their fruits; he desires and longs for sons and cattle, which are the results of ritual action; it is solely out of such expectation that he undertakes the means to achieve them. Remembering this world, he desires it only through the impulse of expectation by means of causes for the maintenance of the world. And remembering the other world, he desires it only through the impulse of expectation by performing the means to attain it.

Therefore, [the world] is bound by the girdle of hope, revolving like a wheel for every living being, bestowing names such as "Love" (Kāma), "Space," and so forth. Since hope is greater even than love, meditate upon hope.

He who meditates on hope as Brahman—by means of that hope, all his desires are fulfilled; his prayers become unfailing; he attains self-sovereignty over everything as far as the reach of hope extends, provided he meditates on hope as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than hope? "There is indeed something greater than hope. "May the venerable sir tell me that. Thus ends the fourteenth section. 14.

(2) Now, listen to the fruit for him who meditates upon hope (*āśā*) as Brahman: by constantly meditating upon hope, all desires of this meditator flourish and reach fulfillment. All his prayers and aspirations (*āśis*) become unfailing; the meaning is that whatever he has prayed for, all that necessarily comes to pass. "As far as the reach of hope extends," and so forth, is as explained before.
This concludes the commentary on the fourteenth section.

Breath is indeed greater than hope. Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub, even so everything is fixed in this breath. Through breath one moves; breath gives breath; for the sake of breath one gives. Breath is the father, breath is the mother, breath is the brother, breath is the sister, breath is the teacher, and breath is the Brahmin.

That Prāṇa, from which everything—from name to hope—proceeds, which exists as cause and effect and as sign and consequence, established in an ever-increasing succession, which is bound by the snares of hope through the existence of the causes of memory, and into which all this is fastened on every side like lotus fibers with their threads; and by which, as by an all-pervading thread extending inside and out, everything is strung together and held fast like a multitude of gems upon a string—that very Prāṇa is indeed greater than hope.

"How is there a multiplicity of this? To this he replies, supporting that multiplicity with an illustration: "Just as in the world the spokes of a chariot wheel are fixed, fastened, and inserted into the hub of the chariot, even so in this vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of a collection of subtle bodies (*liṅga-saṃghāta*), which is the cognitive self (*prajñātman*), and which is the primary [breath] pertaining to the body—in that [vital breath] the supreme deity has entered by means of the individual self (*jīva-ātman*) for the purpose of differentiating names and forms, like a reflection in a mirror."

And because of the Vedic text: "He who, like the Great King, the Lord of all authorities, thought, 'Upon whose departure shall I depart? Upon whose being established shall I be established?'—he created Prāṇa"; and because he follows the Lord like a shadow, as stated by the Kauṣītakins: "Just as the rim of a wheel is fixed on the spokes and the spokes are fixed on the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed on the powers of cognition (prajñāmātrāḥ), the powers of cognition are fixed on Prāṇa; this very Prāṇa is the conscious self (prajñātman). Therefore, everything as described is thus entrusted to this Prāṇa.

Therefore, this very *prāṇa* is independent; it moves by its own power alone through *prāṇa*, meaning that its capacity for actions such as moving is not produced by anything else. The meaning of the entire section is that the whole collection of distinctions consisting of actions, instruments, and results is *prāṇa* itself, and nothing exists outside of *prāṇa*. *Prāṇa* gives *prāṇa*. That which it gives is indeed its own self; that to which it gives is also *prāṇa* alone. Therefore, even that which is designated as "father" and so forth is *prāṇa* itself.

If he speaks harshly to his father, or mother, or brother, or sister, or teacher, or a Brahmin, they say to him: "Fie on you! You are indeed a slayer of your father; you are indeed a slayer of your mother; you are indeed a slayer of your brother; you are indeed a slayer of your sister; you are indeed a slayer of your teacher; you are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin. 2. (2) —-

How is it that words such as "father" and so forth, by abandoning their well-known meanings, come to have the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as their referent? It is said: because the word "father" and so forth are applied to the father and others only when the vital breath is present, and because they are not applied when it has departed. How is that so? He says: if anyone should address one of the father or others with some speech that is quite harsh, as if inconsistent with his status, and filled with insults such as "thou," then those standing nearby who are discerning will say of him: "Shame on you! Shame indeed upon you!"—meaning, "You are a slayer of your father," and so forth.

Now, even if one were to burn these [people] while their vital breaths have not yet departed, by applying a stake all at once, people would not say of him: "You are a parricide," nor "You are a matricide," nor "You are a fratricide," nor "You are a sister-murderer," nor "You are a murderer of your teacher," nor "You are a murderer of a Brahmin.

Now, even if one were to burn these very persons whose vital breaths have departed and who have abandoned the lordship of their bodies—burning them by joining them together with a stake (*śūla*) or burning them by interchanging their limbs—even though such an extremely cruel act characterized by burning is performed upon that which is connected to the body through methods such as joining or interchanging, people would still not say of him, "He is a parricide," and so forth. Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that what is designated as "father" and so on is indeed nothing but the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed becomes all these things. He who sees thus, thinks thus, and understands thus, becomes an "over-speaker" (*ativādin*). If they should say to him, "Are you an over-speaker?", he should say, "I am an over-speaker," and he should not deny it. Thus ends the fifteenth section. (15) (4)

Therefore, Prāṇa alone indeed becomes all these things—the ancestors and so forth, both moving and stationary. He who knows Prāṇa, seeing in this manner according to the method described, experiencing it as the result, thinking thus by reflecting with logical arguments, and knowing thus by joining [the knowledge] with logical arguments—this means he forms the firm conviction that "it is exactly so. For it is through reflection (*manana*) and higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) combined that the meaning of the scripture becomes certain and clearly perceived.

Therefore, seeing thus, he becomes an "ativādī"—the meaning is that he becomes one whose habit is to speak having transcended [all things] beginning with name and ending with hope. If they should say to him—meaning, if they should say to him who declares, "I am the Prāṇa, the Self of the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass," "Are you an ativādī?"—he should say, "Yes, I am an ativādī," and he should not deny it. For why would he deny it, since he has approached the Prāṇa, the Lord of all, as his own Self, saying, "This I am"?
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth section.

"But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of the Truth. 'Venerable sir, may I speak transcendentally by means of the Truth? 'But one must desire to understand the Truth itself. 'Venerable sir, I desire to understand the Truth. Thus ends the sixteenth section. 16. (1)

"But this one indeed speaks surpassingly, whom I shall describe. One who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) does not speak surpassingly in the ultimate sense; rather, his status as a 'surpassing speaker' is dependent upon [lower categories] such as Name. But he who knows the Reality called the Plenum (*bhūman*), which transcends all and is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), is a 'surpassing speaker. Thus it is said: 'But this one indeed speaks surpassingly—he who speaks surpassingly by means of Truth, that is, by possessing the knowledge of the ultimate truth. Therefore, having approached you, O Blessed One, may I speak surpassingly by means of Truth."

The intention is: "May the Blessed One enjoin me in such a way that I may speak beyond [the ordinary] by means of Truth. When it was said, "If you thus desire to speak beyond by means of Truth, then Truth itself must first be sought to be known," Nārada replied: "So be it; O Venerable Sir, I wish to know Truth specifically—that is, I desire to know it from you.
This concludes the commentary on the sixteenth section. "When one truly knows, then one speaks the Truth; one who does not know does not speak the Truth; only one who knows speaks the Truth."
"But consciousness itself is what one should desire to understand. "Venerable sir, I desire to understand consciousness. Thus ends the seventeenth section. 17.

When one indeed understands the Truth from the perspective of the ultimate reality—thinking, "This is the Truth from the perspective of the ultimate reality"—then, having abandoned the unreal collection of modifications which are merely "the beginning of speech" (vācārambhaṇa), one speaks only that which is the one Being (sat) alone, existing as the state of all modifications, as the Truth. But is it not the case that even modification is indeed real? For another scriptural passage states: "Name and form are real; by these this vital breath (prāṇa) is concealed," and "The vital breaths are indeed real; of them, the Truth is [Being] alone."

It has been stated that reality belongs to the modification, yet this was not stated with reference to ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). What then? It was called "real" (*satyam*) with reference to its being both "existent" (*sat*) and "perceptible" (*tyat*), because it is neither a sense-organ nor an object of the senses; and by means of that [modification], the apprehension of ultimate reality is intended. This is also accepted here, as it is said: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed real, and He is their Reality. *Note: IAST diacritics have been applied to Sanskrit terms.*

In this context, however, the specific intended meaning is as follows: having raised Nārada from his conceit regarding the knowledge of the ultimate reality (paramārthasatya) concerning the vital breaths (prāṇa), [the Lord] intends to make known that which is truly existent, real in the highest sense, and called "Bhūman. One does not speak the truth without knowing it; for he who speaks without knowing speaks while imagining fire and the other elements to be ultimately real by means of words such as "fire," yet they do not exist in reality apart from the three forms.

Likewise, those forms also do not exist at all from the perspective of Being (*sat*); therefore, one who does not know [Being] does not speak the truth. Only one who knows [Being] speaks the truth. And that knowledge of truth is not known without being sought or without inquiry; thus he says: "But knowledge itself is what must be sought. If this is so, [the disciple says]: "Venerable Sir, I wish to seek to know knowledge. In this way, the fact that each preceding element among the series beginning with Being and ending with action is the cause of each succeeding one is to be explained.
Thus ends the commentary on the seventeenth section.

"When one indeed thinks, then one understands; one does not understand without having thought. Only after having thought does one understand. Therefore, the intellect (*mati*) itself is what must be sought to be understood. "Venerable sir, I wish to understand the intellect. Thus ends the eighteenth section. (1) Regarding the phrase "When one indeed thinks": *mati* means thinking, which is reasoning (*tarka*).

Thus ends the commentary on the eighteenth section. "When one has faith, then one reflects; one does not reflect without faith; only when one has faith does one reflect. Faith, indeed, is what one must seek to understand. [The student said: "Venerable sir, I wish to understand faith. Thus ends the nineteenth section. (1)–19–(1)

"Reverence for the subject to be meditated upon, the intellect of conviction, is faith (*śraddhā*)... thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth section. "When one is firmly resolved, then one has faith; one who is not firmly resolved does not have faith; only when one is firmly resolved does one have faith. But firm resolve itself must be sought to be understood. 'Venerable sir, I wish to understand firm resolve. Thus ends the twentieth section. 20.
*Niṣṭhā* is the state of being intent upon serving the teacher and so forth for the sake of the realization of Brahman.
Thus ends the commentary on the twentieth section.

"When one acts, then one attains completion; one does not attain completion without having acted. Only by acting does one attain completion. Therefore, action itself is what must be sought to be understood. 'Venerable sir, I wish to understand action. Thus ends the twenty-first section.

When one acts—action (*kṛti*) consists of the restraint of the senses and the concentration of the mind. For when that exists, the aforementioned stages beginning with "attainment" and ending with "knowledge" come to be.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-first section.

(1) The meaning is this: that effort (*kṛti*) also comes into being when one thinks, "I must attain the unsurpassed happiness that is about to be described. Just as an effort directed toward happiness with a visible result occurs, so too here, one does not act without having attained happiness. Even a future result is said to be "attained," because it is logical to engage in activity for the sake of that [result]. Now, it might follow that since Truth (*satya*) manifests of its own accord when subsequent stages such as effort (*kṛti*) are present, no separate effort need be made to realize it.

Then this is said: "But bliss indeed is what one should desire to understand," and so forth. To him who had become attentive, saying, "Venerable Sir, I desire to understand bliss," [the Teacher] spoke.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-second section.

That which is indeed the "plenum" (*bhūman*)—for "the great," "the unsurpassed," and "the much" are synonyms—is happiness. That which is less than that is "small" (*alpa*), because it possesses a higher degree [of limitation]. Therefore, there is no happiness in that smallness, because smallness is a cause for excessive craving (*tṛṣṇā*). And craving is the seed of suffering. Indeed, a seed of suffering is never seen as happiness in the world, such as fever and the like. Therefore, it is logical that there is no happiness in the small; hence, the plenum alone is happiness, because in the plenum the possibility of the seeds of suffering such as craving does not exist. Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-third section.

Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūman*). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (*alpa*). That which is the Infinite is immortal; that which is finite is mortal. "In what, O Venerable Sir, is that established? "In its own majesty, or perhaps not even in majesty. What is the defining characteristic of that Infinite? He says: "Where"—in that reality which is the Infinite—"nothing else" is to be seen by another distinct instrument as a separate seer.

He sees from the visible; likewise, he hears nothing else. Since all distinctions of objects are included within name and form, only the perception and hearing that grasp them are mentioned here, while the others are intended as illustrations. Furthermore, "he thinks nothing else" should be understood as stated here [in the context of the Self], because knowledge is generally preceded by thought. Likewise, "he knows nothing else. That which is characterized in this way is the Plenum (bhūman).

What is meant here by the passage beginning with "he does not see anything else," etc., is the absence of the perception of other things well-known in the world—that is, the state of being the "Great" (*bhūman*)—or is it that he does not see another, but rather sees the Self? What follows from this? If it is said to be merely the absence of the perception of others and so forth, then it is stated that the "Great" is distinct from the conventional dealings of duality. However, if, by the negation of the specific act of seeing another, it is said that he sees the Self, then a distinction between action, agent, and result would have to be admitted within that very same entity.

If this were so, what would be the fault? Is it not this very thing—the non-cessation of saṃsāra? For saṃsāra is indeed the distinction between action, agent, and fruit. If it is argued that the distinction between action, agent, and fruit exists within the unity of the Self alone, and is thus different from [ordinary] saṃsāra, we say no; for if one accepts the undifferentiated unity of the Self, the acceptance of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit in acts such as seeing is merely verbal.

If it is argued that even on the view that [the text] expresses the absence of seeing anything else, the two qualifiers "where" (*yatra*) and "he sees nothing else" (*anyanna paśyati*) would be redundant—[the opponent might say]: "In common worldly usage, when it is said 'in an empty house he sees nothing else,' it is understood that he does not fail to see pillars and so forth, nor himself; so it should be here as well"—we reply: No, because of the teaching of identity in the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), a distinction between a locus and a subject cannot be established. Furthermore, this has been determined in the sixth book [of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*] that Being is one alone, without a second, and is the Truth.

Based on such scriptural passages as "In the invisible, the bodiless," "His form does not stand within the range of vision," and "O, by what means could one know the Knower?", it follows that seeing and other such activities are impossible with respect to the Self. If it is argued that the qualification "wherein" (*yatra*) would thus be rendered meaningless, we say no; for it is used with reference to the distinctions created by ignorance (*avidyā*). Just as, with reference to the present context of the realization of truth, unity, and non-duality, it is said that "Being is one only, without a second"—despite Being being incapable of number and the like—so too is the qualification "wherein" applied to the "Full" (*bhūman*), even though it is a single reality.

Because, in the state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*), the intention is to describe the abundance (*bhūman*) as being characterized by the absence of that [perception] through a restatement of other perceptions, the qualification "he sees nothing else" is employed. Therefore, the collective meaning is that the worldly transaction (*saṃsāravyavahāra*) does not exist in the Abundant One. Now, where—in the sphere of ignorance—“one sees another as something else,” that is "the small" (*alpa*); the meaning is that it exists only during the time of ignorance. It is just like an object seen in a dream, which exists only prior to awakening and belongs to that specific time; so it is here.

Therefore, that which is mortal is perishable, just like the objects seen in a dream. That which is the opposite of this is the *bhūman* (the Infinite); the word "that" refers to immortality. To Nārada, who had asked, "In what, then, is that *bhūman* characterized by such attributes established, O Blessed One? Sanatkumāra replied: "In its own majesty. This means the *bhūman* is established in its own greatness, its own majesty, and its own manifestation.

"If you desire a foundation somewhere, or if you are asking about the ultimate reality itself, we say that [the Infinite] is not established even in greatness; the meaning is that the Infinite is unestablished, not resting upon anything whatsoever.

"Cows and horses are called 'greatness' here, as are elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, and dwellings. I do not speak thus," he said. "I do speak thus: for one thing is established in another. Thus ends the twenty-fourth section. (24) (2)

If the Infinite (*bhūman*) is established in its own greatness (*mahiman*), how then is it said to be "without support" (*apratiṣṭha*)? Listen: here, "greatness" refers to cattle, horses, and so forth. "Cattle and horses" (*go-aśvam*) is a dual compound used in the singular. It is well known everywhere that cattle, horses, and the like constitute greatness.

Just as Caitra is dependent on that [house] and established therein, I do not say that the Infinite (*bhūman*) is likewise dependent on some other greatness by its own nature like Caitra. Here, the reason is provided by the phrase "for one is established in another," which connects with the previously mentioned [statement]. Rather, he said, "I speak thus"—beginning with "He alone," and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-fourth section.

Why, then, is it said that he is not established anywhere? It is said: because that very *bhūman* (the Infinite) is below, and nothing else exists apart from it in which he might be established. The same applies to "above" and so forth. If there were something other than the *bhūman*, then the *bhūman* would indeed be established in it; but no such thing exists. He alone is everything. Therefore, for that reason, he is not established anywhere.

Lest anyone should suspect that the "plenum" (*bhūman*) might be something other than the seeing individual soul (*jīva*), because of the indication of a locus and a subject in the passage "where one sees nothing else," and because of the indirect reference in "that very [Self] is below," the text proceeds immediately thereafter with the "instruction by means of the ego-sense" (*ahaṃkārādeśa*). This is called the "instruction by means of the ego-sense" because it is taught through the ego-sense. It is the plenum itself that is indicated by means of the ego-sense—through such statements as "I alone am below"—in order to demonstrate its non-difference from the seer.

Because the aggregate of the body and so forth is also designated as "I" by those lacking discrimination, the following instruction is given immediately thereafter to prevent such a misconception: "Then, the Self is designated. By the Self alone—by that which is pure and whose nature is Being—it is designated. "The Self alone is everything, everywhere"—thus seeing the one, unborn, all-pervading like space, devoid of anything else, that wise person, through both reflection and higher knowledge, becomes "one who delights in the Self," meaning he whose delight and sport are in the Self alone. Likewise, he is "one who plays with the Self."

In the world, sexual pleasure (*rati*) is accomplished by means of the body alone, while play (*krīḍā*) is accomplished by external means, as is seen from the presence of women and friends. It is not so for the knower; rather, the meaning is that both of these become caused solely by the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavijñāna*). Furthermore, for that knower, even the pleasure born of the couple (*mithuna*) is independent of the couple. Likewise, the bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*) is not like the bliss of the ignorant, which is caused by sound and other sense objects.

What then? [The meaning is that] everything is always and in every way for the sake of the Self alone; that is to say, he is independent of external objects such as the body, life, and enjoyments. A wise man characterized in this way, even while living, is consecrated in self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); even when the body has fallen away, he remains a self-ruler (*svarāṭ*). Since this is so, for that very reason, he possesses freedom of movement at will (*kāmacāra*) in all worlds. In the previous stages, beginning with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), it was stated—by the words "therein his"—that his freedom of movement was limited to only those specific domains.

And the state of having another as king follows logically from this, because there is a degree of excellence [in self-rule]. By restating the attainment of one's own sovereignty (*svarājya*) and the freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) as they were previously established, their cessation is here expressed by the passage beginning with "He is his own king" (*sa svarāṭ*). Now, however, those who understand otherwise—that is, differently from the view thus described, or conversely, or even if they do know it exactly as stated, yet not correctly—become "those who have another as king" (*anyarājānaḥ*); that is, those for whom there is another, a different person, as their king or master.

Furthermore, "those whose worlds are perishable" (*kṣayyalokāḥ*) refers to those for whom the world is perishable. Because the vision of duality has a limited scope, we have already stated that such a [vision] is small and mortal. Therefore, those who perceive duality possess worlds that are perishable, corresponding precisely to the nature of their own perception; for this very reason, they lack freedom of movement in all the worlds.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-fifth section.

The phrase "of this very one" (*tasya ha vā etasya*) and so forth refers to the aforementioned knower who has attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). Prior to the realization of the Self as Being (*sad-ātman*), there occurred the origination and dissolution of everything from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) down to names, all of which were distinct from his own Self. But now that the realization of the Self as Being exists, these two have become withdrawn into his own Self alone. Likewise, every other worldly transaction of the knower proceeds from his own Self alone.

Furthermore, regarding this matter, there is also this verse, which is a mantra: "The seer does not see death. The term "seer" (paśya) means one who sees as described—the wise man. He does not see death, nor disease such as fever, nor even the state of suffering. That seer sees everything indeed—only the Self. Therefore, he attains everything in every way, through all modes. Moreover, that wise man, prior to the differentiation of creation, exists as one alone.

Being one alone, it becomes of infinite varieties through divisions such as the threefold and so forth at the time of creation; then, at the time of reabsorption, being independent, it returns to its own ultimate state of oneness, which is its very root—thus he praises Vidyā by inciting [the practitioner] toward its fruit. Now, the means for the purification of this aforementioned Vidyā—which is the cause of its perfect manifestation—is taught, just as a mirror is the cause of the clarity of the face’s reflection: "When the food is pure."

It is called *āhāra* because it is brought (*āhriyate*) [to the enjoyer]; that is, the cognition of objects such as sound and so forth is brought for the enjoyment of the experiencer. The purity (*śuddhi*) of that cognition, characterized by the perception of objects, is "purity of food" (*āhāra-śuddhi*). The meaning is that the cognition of objects is untainted by the defects of passion, hatred, and delusion. When that purity of food exists, there arises the purity—meaning the stainlessness—of the *sattva*, which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) possessing that [cognition].

And when there is purity of being (*sattvaśuddhi*), there arises a firm and uninterrupted mindfulness—that is, non-forgetfulness—regarding the Self as it has been understood. And when that mindfulness is attained, upon the acquisition of mindfulness, there occurs the complete release—that is, the specific liberation or destruction—of all the knots residing in the heart, which consist of the snares of misfortune created by ignorance, hardened by the impressions (*bhāvanā*) of experiences from many previous births.

The meaning is that since this [discipline] is the aforementioned progressively higher foundation for the purity of food, therefore it must be practiced. Having stated the entire meaning of the scripture in its entirety, the Śruti concludes the narrative: "To him whose *kaṣāya* was rubbed away"—since *kaṣāya* is of the nature of passioning the mind, it consists of defects such as attachment and aversion; like the resin of a tree, it has been washed away, rubbed away, and destroyed by the alkaline solution consisting of the practice of knowledge and dispassion—for that worthy Nārada, from whom [the darkness] of *tamas*... [has been removed].”

He shows, or has shown, the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), which is on the further shore beyond the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*). Who is he? The Blessed One (*bhagavān*), concerning whom it is said: "He who knows the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings, and who knows both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), he is to be called the Blessed One. Sanatkumāra possesses such qualities. Those who know him call that very god Sanatkumāra by the name Skanda; so say those who know him. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-sixth section.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya*), the illustrious Govinda Bhagavat...
The seventh chapter is completed in the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the worshipful teacher.

Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, in the small lotus-palace, there is a small space (ākāśa) within it; what is inside that is to be sought after, that indeed is what one must desire to understand. 1.

(1) Now, immediately following this, that which is about to be described—the small (*dahara*), tiny lotus, resembling a lotus, like a dwelling because it possesses gatekeepers and so forth—in this city of Brahman (*brahmapura*): just as a king’s city is possessed of many subjects, so too is this "city of Brahman" endowed with the various senses, mind, and intellect, which act for the sake of its Lord. Thus it is called the city of Brahman.

Just as the palace of a king is pure, so too is there a small chamber within that city of Brahman, the body; the meaning is that it is the locus for the perception of Brahman, just as Sālagrāma is for Viṣṇu. For it has been stated that Brahman, which is designated as "Being," has entered this body—which is a sprout of its own transformation—in the form of the individual soul (jīva) in order to manifest names and forms.

Therefore, the meaning of this section is that Brahman is attained within this dwelling of the heart-lotus by those who have withdrawn their senses, who are detached from external objects, and who are especially endowed with the disciplines of celibacy and truthfulness, meditating upon it as possessing the qualities to be described hereafter. It is "dahara," meaning extremely small; because this dwelling is small, that which exists within it is even smaller than the dwelling. The "interior space" (antarākāśa) is Brahman, known as Ākāśa.

For the text will say, "That which is called space. It is like space because it is bodiless, and because of its common characteristics of subtlety and omnipresence. That which is within—that is, in the middle—of that which is called space, is what must be sought. The meaning is that this very thing indeed must be specifically desired to be known; having sought it by means such as relying on a teacher and hearing [the teachings], it must be directly realized.

If they should say to him, "In this city of Brahman, there is this small lotus-palace; within it is a small space. What is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand? he should reply: 2. (2) — "As large as this space here is, so large is that space within the ether. Both heaven and earth are contained within it; both fire and wind, both the sun and the moon, and indeed all these stars. Within this very space are contained all these beings, and whatever else one might desire. They should say to him, "If everything is contained within this, then what is left over [of the body]? He should say, "It is like this: when a man is asleep, he has not seen any dream, he becomes one with this ether alone. They should say to him, "Where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 3. (3) — "There are these veins called hitā, which extend from the heart upwards toward the pericardium. As fine as a hair split a thousandfold, filled with a white, blue, yellow, green, and red liquid—through these, indeed, does he move about, enjoying himself in dreams. They should say to him, "When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 4. (4) — "Just as a cart, heavily laden, creaks along its way, so does this bodily self, having reached the state of sleep, creak along its way. When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, he has entered into those veins. They should say to him, "When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 5. (5) — "As a great fish swims along both banks of a river, the near and the far, so does this person move along both these states—the state of waking and the state of dreaming. They should say to him, "When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 6. (6) — "As a falcon, or an eagle, having flown around in the sky, becomes weary, folds its wings, and is borne down by its own nest, even so this person hastens to that state where, sleeping, he desires no desires and sees no dreams. They should say to him, "When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 7. (7) — "This person, my dear, consists of cognition, is surrounded by pleasure and pain, and has true being as his essence. Pleasure and pain do not touch him, for he is the seer of pleasure and pain. They should say to him, "He is indeed touched by pleasure and pain; for when he sees something pleasant, he rejoices. He should say: "When he is touched by pleasure, he does not know himself, 'I am being touched by pleasure,' nor does he know anything else that exists. It is because he is enveloped by consciousness that he does not know. They should say to him, "When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 8. (8) — "Just as a spider moves upward by means of its thread, or as tiny sparks leap forth from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths (prāṇas) spring forth, from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds. They should say to him, "When he is thus asleep, serene, tranquil, and conscious of nothing, where was the person who saw the dream? And from where did he come back? He should say: 9. (9) — "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form. This is the Self," he said. "This is the immortal, the fearless. This is Brahman. The name of this Brahman is ‘The True. They should say to him, "What is the meaning of ‘The True’? He should say: "When one truly knows, then that is the True. Because one truly knows, therefore it is ‘The True. They should say to him, "When a man departs from here, what does he leave behind? And what does he take with him? He should say: "He leaves behind his accumulated merits and demerits; he takes with him his knowledge and his actions. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name. Therefore, even if a man who knows dies in a foreign land, they say, ‘He exists in his sons. This is his world; this is his Brahman-world. They should say to him, "When a man dies, what is it that does not leave him? He should say: "His name does not leave him. For a father, my dear, becomes one with the sons through the name.

If the disciples should speak thus to the teacher who has spoken as above, or should challenge him—how so? They say: "In this city of Brahman, which is limited, there is a small lotus-shaped abode within; even inside that, the space (ākāśa) is exceedingly minute. What could possibly be within that very lotus-abode? What could exist within that even smaller void? Their intention is to suggest: "The space within this is small; what is there to be found here? Nothing at all is found."

"If there were indeed something [in the heart] even as small as a jujube fruit, what would be the use for the seeker of knowledge in searching for it or desiring to know it? Therefore, for one who says that there is no purpose in that which is to be sought or desired to be known," the scripture records that the teacher should say this.

"As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart. Both heaven and earth are contained within it; both fire and wind, both the sun and the moon, both lightning and the stars, and whatever belongs to him here and whatever does not—all that is contained within it.

Listen: as for what you say—that because the space within the lotus is small, that which resides therein must be even smaller—that is incorrect. For I did not say, "There is a small space within this," thinking that the space located in the abode of the lotus was smaller than the lotus itself.

What then? The lotus is small, and the internal organ (antahkarana) situated within it conforms to its shape, being delimited by the space of the lotus. When that [space] is purified, for yogis who have withdrawn their senses, the light of consciousness—which is essentially of the nature of a reflection—appears as clear as in pure water or like a reflection in a clean mirror. To that extent, Brahman is perceived; thus we said, "In this small inner space," referring to the limiting adjunct (upadhi) of the internal organ.

However, this space within the heart—in which we have said that one must seek and desire to understand—is indeed as large in dimension as this elemental space is well-known to be by itself. It is not stated to be "as large" with the intention of implying an equality of dimension with [elemental] space; rather, it is because there is no other suitable illustration for Brahman.

But how is it understood that Brahman is not merely equal to space? [This is known] from such scriptural passages as: "By which the sky, the heaven, and the earth are covered"; "From this very Self, space was produced"; and "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is space," and so forth. Furthermore, both heaven and earth are contained within—meaning properly situated and established within—the space of Brahman when it is qualified by the limiting adjunct of the intellect (*buddhyupādhiviśiṣṭe*), for it has been said: "Just as the spokes are in the hub."

In the same way, both fire and air, and so forth, are the same [as described previously]. Furthermore, whatever belongs to this embodied self by way of being its own property exists here in this world; likewise, that which does not exist by way of being its own property—namely, what has perished or what is yet to be—is said to be "non-existent. However, it is not absolutely non-existent, because if it were, its placement within the space of the heart would be impossible. If they should say to him: "If all this is contained within this city of Brahman—the entire universe, all beings, and all desires—then when this body reaches old age or perishes, what remains of it? (4) —

If the disciples should say this again to him after he has spoken thus: "In this [city], that is, in the internal space characterized by the city of Brahman (brahmapura)—meaning within the space of the heart—everything is contained, as well as all beings and all desires," [the teacher would reply: "How can the desires be mentioned by the disciples when they were not mentioned by the teacher? This is not a fault. For the desires have indeed been mentioned by the teacher in the words, "Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have. Moreover, the desires have already been included by the word "all" (*sarva*).

When—at whatever time—this body, known as the city of Brahman (*brahmapura*), undergoes old age characterized by wrinkles, grey hair, and the like, or the decay of youth; or when it is cut by weapons and the like, perishes, falls apart, and is destroyed—what remains there other than that? Just as milk, curd, oil, and so forth, which reside in a pot, perish when the pot is destroyed, the intention is that even upon the destruction of the body, that which rests within the body perishes successively due to the destruction of each preceding layer. When such destruction has occurred, what remains other than that? What remains, persists, or endures beyond what has been described? The intention is that nothing whatsoever remains.

He should say: "This does not decay with his decay; it is not slain by his being slain. This is the true city of Brahman; in it all desires are contained. This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger, without thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true. For just as here people follow according to their instructions, whatever end they desire—whether a country or a portion of land—they subsist upon that very thing.

Thus urged by his pupils, that teacher should speak, removing their misconception. How so? "By the decay of this body, this [Brahman]—which is called the internal space (*antarākāśa*) in which everything is contained—does not decay"; the meaning is that, unlike the body, it does not undergo modification. Nor is this slain by its slaying, i.e., by the striking of weapons and the like, just as the ether (*ākāśa*) is not; how much less, then, can Brahman—which is even subtler than that, soundless, and touchless—be touched by the defects of the body, senses, and so forth? This is the meaning.

How it is not touched by the defects of the body, senses, and so forth—this is what ought to be stated at this juncture; however, it is not said here so that there may be no distraction from the subject at hand. We shall explain this later, through reasoning, in the narrative of Indra and Virocana. This "city of Brahman" is true and not false; it is Brahman itself that is the city, hence "brahmapura. But the city of Brahman known as the body is [only figuratively] so called because it serves as a means for perceiving Brahman. That [body], however, is indeed unreal, according to the scriptural text: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."

Even though this sprout-like body is subject to modification and is unreal, Brahman is perceived within it; thus, it is conventionally called the "City of Brahman" (*brahmapura*). However, the truly real City of Brahman is this very Brahman itself, because it is the locus of all worldly transactions. Therefore, in this City of Brahman, characterized by the lotus [of the heart], all desires—those which you seek externally—are already contained within this very Self. The intended meaning is: therefore, practice the very means for attaining That, and abandon thirst for external objects.

This Self is your own true nature. Listen to its characteristics: it is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*), meaning that evil—consisting of merit and demerit—is destroyed in it. Likewise, it is "free from old age" (*vijara*) and "free from death" (*vimṛtyu*). This has already been stated previously: "It is not slain by the slaying of this [body]. Why is it stated again? Although it is not connected with the old age and death associated with the body, this is said to remove the doubt that there might nevertheless be some other kind of connection with them.

"Free from sorrow" (*viśoka*) means having departed from sorrow. Sorrow (*śoka*) is defined as mental anguish caused by separation from what is desired and so forth. "Free from hunger" (*vijighatsa*) means having departed from the desire for food. "Free from thirst" (*apipāsa*) means having departed from the desire for drink. Now, one might object: since he is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*), aging and the other states ending with sorrow are already excluded, because their cause has been negated. For these [states] are indeed the effects of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Alternatively, by the negation of aging and the rest, merit and demerit—being devoid of effect even if they were present—are equivalent to non-existence; thus, a separate negation would be redundant.

This is true; nevertheless, one might suspect that just as there is an intrinsic bliss in the Lord—as evidenced by the Vedic scripture, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss"—there might likewise be an intrinsic nature of suffering such as old age and so forth, even apart from the effects of demerit (adharma) like old age. Therefore, in order to preclude this, it is appropriate to negate old age and the rest separately from merit and demerit. The mention of "old age and the rest" is intended to include all forms of suffering.

However, because evil-occasioned sufferings are infinite and it is impossible to negate each one individually, the statement that He is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) is indeed appropriate for the purpose of negating all suffering. He whose desires (*kāma*) are true—that is, non-false—is "one whose desires are true" (*satyakāma*). For the desires of those in transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*) are false; the Lord’s are the opposite of that. Likewise, His volitions (*saṃkalpa*), which are the causes of desire, are also true; thus He is "one whose volitions are true" (*satyasaṃkalpa*).

The volitions and desires of the Lord are caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of pure being (*sattva*), like those of a painter; they do not arise from Himself, because He has been described as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). This Self, characterized as stated above, should be known from the teachers and from the scriptures, and through personal realization (*ātmasaṃvedyatā*) by those who desire self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). If it is not known, what fault would there be? Listen to the fault in this matter by means of an illustration: for just as in this world subjects follow and conform to their ruler's command; so do they act.

Just as here on earth, subjects who recognize another as their master enter into his service in accordance with that master's various instructions. Why is this so? Because they, being desirous and seeking wealth, settle according to their own understanding in whichever border region, frontier, or portion of land they desire, and they subsist upon those very frontiers and areas. This is the illustration regarding the defect of lack of independence in the enjoyment of the fruits of merit.

"Just as in this world the world won by action perishes, even so in the other world the world won by merit perishes. Those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is no freedom of movement in any of the worlds. But those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all the worlds. Thus ends the first section. 1. (6)

Now, there is another illustration regarding that exhaustion, beginning with "Just as here," and so forth. That is to say, just as in this world, for those very subjects who follow the instructions of their master, the world won through service and the like—which is enjoyed under the dependence of another—is exhausted and becomes finite; now he concludes the application to the case in hand: "In exactly the same way, in the other world, the world won by merit such as the Agnihotra sacrifice, which is enjoyed under the dependence of another, is indeed exhausted."

The fault of these has been stated; now he shows the subject matter with the words beginning "tad ye" (therefore, those...). There, those who here in this world, being qualified and fit for knowledge and action, depart—that is, pass away from this body—without having realized the Self as described by its characteristics through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, that is, without having made it their own personal experience according to the teaching; and those who likewise depart without having realized these aforementioned true desires, which consist of the effects of true volition and reside within one's own Self—for all of them, in all [worlds]...

In the worlds, there is a lack of freedom of will and a state of dependence—meaning, for example, like that of subjects who must follow the commands of a king. Now, however, those others here in this world who, having understood the Self through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and having brought it to the state of being personally realized within themselves, proceed [to the worlds] along with the aforementioned true desires—for them, there is freedom of will in all worlds, just as a sovereign emperor has in this world.
Thus ends the commentary on the first section.

If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere will the fathers arise for him; endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified. (1) — How does one come to have freedom of movement in all worlds? It is said: he who has realized within his heart the Self characterized as described above, being endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) to be mentioned hereafter, [realizes] the true desires residing therein.

When he has cast off the body, if he desires the world of the ancestors—where "ancestors" refers to progenitors who are called "worlds" because they are objects of enjoyment as causes of happiness—for one whose desire is for them, that is, one who has a wish for a connection with those ancestors, the ancestors arise by his mere volition and attain a state of being connected to him, because, due to the purity of their essence (*viśuddhasattva*), their resolve is true, just like that of the Lord.

Endowed with that world of the fathers and with enjoyment—that is, enriched by prosperity, which is the attainment of what is desired—he is magnified; he is honored, or he increases, experiencing greatness.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of mothers, by his mere will his mothers arise; endowed with that world of mothers, he is magnified. 2.

The rest is the same. "Mothers" refers to those who have passed away and were causes of happiness, by implication; for it is not fitting that a yogin of pure being should have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering—such as those who were the occasion for births as village pigs and the like. Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers, by his mere resolve (saṅkalpa) his brothers arise; endowed with that world of brothers, he is magnified. 3. (2–9) ————

The rest is the same. "Mothers" means those who have given birth in the past and have become causes of happiness, by implication; for it is not fitting for a yogin of pure being to have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who are causes of suffering—such as those born as village pigs and the like. Now, if he should desire the world of sisters, by his mere resolve (*saṅkalpa*) sisters arise for him; endowed with that world of sisters, he is magnified. 4. (2–9) —-

The rest is the same. "Mothers" means those who have given birth; by implication, they are past [lives] that served as causes of happiness. Indeed, it is not fitting for a yogin of pure being to have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering—such as those born as village pigs and the like. Now, if he desires the world of friends, by his mere will his friends arise; endowed with that world of friends, he is magnified. 5. (2–9) ————

The rest is the same. "Mothers" refers to those who have passed away and were causes of happiness, by implication; for it is not fitting for a yogi of pure being to have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering—such as those born as village pigs and the like.
Now, if he should desire the world of perfumes and garlands, by his mere volition, perfumes and garlands arise for him, and endowed with that world of perfumes and garlands, he is magnified. 6.

The rest is the same. "Mothers" refers to those who have passed away and were causes of happiness, by implication; for it is not fitting for a yogin of pure being to desire or to have a connection with mothers who were causes of suffering, such as those born as village pigs and the like. Now, if he should desire the world of food and drink, from his mere volition food and drink arise for him, and endowed with that world of food and drink, he is magnified. 7. (2–9) —-

The rest is the same. "Mothers" means those who have given birth; they are past and, by implication, have been causes of happiness. Indeed, for a yogi of pure being, desire for or connection with mothers who are causes of suffering—such as those who are the cause of births as village pigs and so forth—is not appropriate. Now, if he should desire the world of song and instrumental music, by his mere volition, song and instrumental music arise for him; endowed with that world of song and instrumental music, he exults. 8. (2–9)

The rest is the same. "Mothers" means those who have passed away and were causes of happiness, by implication. For it is not fitting for a yogi of pure being to have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering—such as those born as village pigs and the like. Now, if he has a desire for the world of women, women arise for him from his mere thought; endowed with that world of women, he is magnified. 9. (2–9) ————-

The rest is the same. "Mothers" refers to those who have passed away and were causes of happiness, by implication; for it is not fitting for a yogin of pure being to have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering—such as those born as village pigs and the like.
Whatever end he desires, whatever wish he wishes for, that arises for him from his mere resolve (*saṅkalpa*). Endowed with that, he exults. Thus ends the second section. (10) — 2 —

Whatever end or region he desires, and whatever object of desire he longs for—even beyond what has been described—that desired object which he wishes to attain within him arises for him by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*). Thus, being endowed with the non-frustration of his will and the attainment of his intended purpose, he exults; this is the meaning already explained. This concludes the commentary on the second section.

"These are those true desires whose covering is the unreal (*anṛta*); the unreal is the covering of those [desires] that are truly existent. For whoever departs from here, he does not obtain them here for the sake of seeing. (1)

(1) — Out of compassion, [the author] speaks in order to generate enthusiasm among practitioners for the practice of the means to meditate on the Self as described: "Alas, this is indeed a tragedy! That these true desires, though residing within one's own Self and capable of being attained, are covered by untruth. While they reside within the Self and have the Self as their very support, 'untruth' refers to the thirst for external objects—such as women, food, drink, clothing, and so forth—and the resulting state of acting according to one's own whims; because it is caused by false knowledge, it is called 'untruth'."

Because of that [untruth], there is a non-attainment of desired objects; thus, "covering" (*apidhāna*) is so called because it is like a covering. How is it that their non-acquisition is caused by the covering of untruth? It is said: for whatever son or brother is dear to this person, when he departs from here—from this world—dies, one does not obtain that dear son or brother again, even though he desires to see him here once more, even though he exists within the space of one's own heart.

Now, whatever living beings belong to him here, and those who have departed, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain—all that he finds upon going there; for here indeed these true desires of his have untruth as their covering. Just as people who do not know the spot might walk back and forth over a hidden treasure of gold and not find it, even so all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are held back by untruth. 2.

Furthermore, whatever living beings—such as sons, brothers, and so forth—of this wise person live here in this world, and whatever deceased loved ones have passed away, and whatever else he desires in this world but does not obtain, such as clothing, food, drink, or jewels; all that he finds and obtains here by going into the Brahman known as the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*), according to the method already described. For it is in this space within the heart that his aforementioned true desires exist, though they are covered by untruth.

How is it that this is unjust? It is said: Just as in that case, a "treasure" (*nidhi*) is so called because gold itself is deposited (*nidhīyate*) there by depositors for the sake of future recovery; and just as those who do not know the field—those ignorant of the science of treasures (*nidhi-śāstra*) regarding the location of the treasure—even while walking right over it, would not find that treasure deposited beneath the earth, even though it is capable of being found; in exactly the same way, all these creatures possessed of ignorance, as has been stated, [do not perceive the Self].

The "world of Brahman" (brahmaloka) is that which is called the space within the heart; it is Brahman itself as the world, hence "the world of Brahman. Although they go there day after day—that is, every single day—at the time of deep sleep, they do not find or obtain it, thinking, "Today I have attained the state of being the world of Brahman. For they are indeed "obstructed by untruth"—that is, as stated, they are driven away from their true nature and drawn outward by defects such as ignorance (avidyā). Therefore, the intention is this: it is a matter of great pity for living beings that even though Brahman is within their own control, it is not obtained.

This very Self is in the heart; its etymological derivation is this: "He is in the heart" (*hṛdi ayam*), therefore it is called *hṛdayam*. Day after day, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world.

"He indeed is that Self which is free from evil"—this is the Self under discussion; by the word "vai" (indeed), he causes it to be recalled. This very Self intended here is in the heart, designated by the word "ākāśa" (space). Of this very heart, this alone is the etymological derivation (*nirukta*), and nothing else. Because this Self resides in the heart (*hṛdi*), therefore it is called "heart" (*hṛdayam*); the intention is that through the well-known etymology of the name "heart," one should understand that the Self is in one's own heart.

Day after day, indeed, one who knows this—realizing that "this Self is in the heart"—goes to and attains the heavenly world, which is Brahman in the heart. But is it not the case that even one who does not know this attains Brahman in the heart during deep sleep, since it has been said: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being"?

"Certainly it is so; nevertheless, there is a distinction. Just as every living being—whether knowing or not knowing—is indeed the existent Brahman, yet the wise one who has been awakened by the instruction 'That thou art' knows, 'I am indeed the Existent, I am none other,' and thus becomes the Existent itself; even so, although both the wise and the ignorant attain the Existent in deep sleep, it is said that only the one who possesses such knowledge goes to the heavenly world. This is the distinction, because the fruit of knowledge is necessarily realized even upon the fall of the body."

Then, he said: "That serene being who, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form—this is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. And the name of this very Brahman is "Truth. 4. (4)

During deep sleep, being united with his own true Self, he becomes perfectly serene; thus, although the term "serenity" (*saṃprasāda*)—referring to the abandonment of the turbidity born from the contact between the senses and their objects during the waking and dreaming states—is common to all living beings, nevertheless, because it is the subject under discussion that "one who knows this goes to the heavenly world," the phrase "this serenity" refers to him specifically through the force of proximity. Then, having left this body—that is, having risen up from this body by abandoning the identification of the body as the Self—he [proceeds].

But it is not appropriate here to say that [the self] "arises as if from a seat" and so forth, because of the qualification "in its own form"—for one's own form is not something to be attained by arising from something else. If it were to be attained, it would not truly be one's own form. Rather, the meaning is: having reached the supreme light characterized as the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, and having attained well-being.

It manifests in its own inherent form. Prior to this attainment of its true nature, through ignorance, it had identified the body—which is a foreign form—with the Self; therefore, with reference to that previous state, it is said here, "in its own form. For bodilessness is the very nature of the Self. That serene being (*saṃprasāda*) attains its own supreme light as its true nature—of this the Teacher said, "This is the Self," as he was instructed by the Śruti to speak thus to his disciples.

Furthermore, this is called the immortal (*amṛta*), the indestructible, the plenitude (*bhūman*); for it has been said, "That which is plenitude is indeed the immortal. For this very reason it is fearless (*abhaya*), because in plenitude there is no second. Therefore, this is Brahman. Now, its name—that is, its designation—is "the True" (*satya*). For Brahman is indeed the True, the non-false; for it has been said, "That is the True, that is the Self. Why, then, is this name stated again? It is for the purpose of praising the injunction for its meditation (*upāsana*).

These, indeed, are those three syllables: *sa-tī-yam*. That which is *sat* is immortal; that which is *ti* is mortal; and by the *yam*, one holds both together. Because one holds both together by means of this [syllable], therefore, day after day, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world. Thus ends the third section. 3. (5)

These, indeed, are the three syllables of the name of Brahman: *sat*, *ti*, and *yam*. The letter *ī* in *iti* is an auxiliary phonetic marker (*anubandha*) for the purpose of pronunciation, because the word is subsequently referred to by its short vowel alone. Of these, that which is *sat*—the letter *sa*—is the immortal; it is the existent Brahman. Because it denotes the immortal, the letter *sa*, ending with the letter *t*, is indicated as being itself immortal. Now, that which is *ti*—the letter *t*—is the mortal.

Now, as for the syllable *yam*: by that syllable he restrains, controls, and brings under his own power both the preceding syllables called "immortal" and "mortal"—this is the meaning. Since he restrains both by means of this [syllable] *yam*, therefore it is called *yam*. For by this, the two [preceding syllables] appear as if restrained (*saṃyata*). This possession of attributes such as immortality and so forth is a great glory even of the syllable that is the name of Brahman; how much more so, then, of the possessor of the name? Thus, Brahman is praised through the etymological derivation of its name for the sake of being an object of meditation.
One who knows thus is a knower of the one possessing such a name. "Day by day, indeed, the knower of thus goes to the heavenly world"—the meaning of this has already been explained.
Thus ends the commentary on the third section.

Now, as for "that which is the Self": that state of supreme tranquility (*saṃprasāda*) whose characteristics have been described is again praised by means of qualities—both those already mentioned and those yet to be stated—for the purpose of connecting it with the spiritual discipline (*brahmacarya*) as its means. This very Self, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, is like a bridge (*setu*); it is a support, a sustainer. For by this [Self], the entire world is sustained, ordaining through the regulations of distinctions such as caste (*varṇa*), stage of life (*āśrama*), actions, agents, and fruits, in accordance with the doer.

For if this universe were not held together by the Lord, it would perish; therefore, He is the "bridge," the support. For what purpose is He the bridge? He says: for the sake of the non-confusion, the non-disruption, and the non-destruction of these worlds—beginning with the earth—which serve as the locus for the fruits of the actions of their creators. And of what nature is this bridge? He says: neither day nor night—those two which delimit everything that has birth—cross over this bridge, which is the Self.

The intention is that this one is not delimited by time in the way other transmigrating beings are delimited by time characterized as days, nights, and so forth; for another scriptural text states, "From whom the year revolves with its days. Therefore, old age does not overcome—that is, does not reach—him. Likewise, neither death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds [reach him]; "good deeds" and "evil deeds" refer to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Here, the word "overcome" (*taraṇa*) is intended to mean "reaching," not "transgressing."

For the Self is the cause. Indeed, it is impossible for an effect to transcend its cause. Day and night, and all such things, are effects of Being (sat). For the attainment or transcendence of one thing can be effected by another, but not by that very same thing itself. Indeed, clay is neither attained nor transcended by a jar.

Although the negation of evil and so forth was already stated previously in the passage beginning with "this Self is free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*), nevertheless, there is this distinction here: by the phrase "he does not cross over," the state of being an object of attainment is negated. In that previous context, the mere absence of old age and so forth was stated without qualification. Here, however, all evils—those mentioned such as day and night, as well as those unmentioned—are referred to; therefore, the meaning is that they turn back from this bridge-like Self without even reaching it. For this very one, who is free from evil, has been called the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). (2)

And because the effects of evil, such as blindness and so forth, belong to one who possesses a body and not to one who is bodiless, therefore, having crossed—that is, having reached—this very Self which is a bridge, one becomes non-blind, even though previously one was blind while possessing a body. Likewise, being pierced while possessing a body, upon the separation from the body and reaching the bridge, one becomes unpierced. Similarly, being afflicted—that is, suffering from the afflictions of disease and so forth—one becomes unafflicted.

Furthermore, because day and night do not exist on the bridge, therefore, having thus crossed and reached that bridge, even "night"—which is of the nature of darkness—even the night becomes entirely "day" for the knower.
