The meaning is that for the knower, there arises a state like day, which is the light of the nature of consciousness, eternally uniform like day. This world of Brahman is "shining once," meaning it is always shining, eternally uniform, and exists in its own true nature.

This being so, those who—through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which is the abandonment of craving for women as objects—attain this aforementioned world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) by following the instructions of the scriptures and the teacher, and bring it to the state of being directly experienced within their own selves; for those knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) alone who possess the means of celibacy, this is the world of Brahman, and not for others, even if they are knowers of Brahman, who still harbor cravings born from contact with women as objects. For them, "there is freedom of movement in all worlds," as has already been stated.
Therefore, the intention is that this celibacy is the supreme means for the knowers of Brahman.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth section.

Now, when they speak of "sacrifice," that is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*); for by means of celibacy alone does one who knows find that [Self]. And when they speak of "sacrificial offering" (*iṣṭa*), that is indeed celibacy; for by means of celibacy alone, having sacrificed, does one find the Self.

Now, that which people in the world call "sacrifice" (yajña), which the learned describe as the means for attaining the supreme goal of human life—that is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya). Even the fruit of sacrifice, one obtains by practicing celibacy; therefore, it should be understood that sacrifice itself is nothing but celibacy.

"How is celibacy (*brahmacarya*) a sacrifice? He says: Because by means of celibacy alone, the knower attains—that is, obtains—that world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), which is the ultimate fruit of the sacrifice even through a succession of causes; therefore, the sacrifice is indeed celibacy itself. Since the word "knower" (*jñātā*) follows from the preceding verse, the sacrifice is celibacy itself. Furthermore, that which they call "sacrifice" (*iṣṭa*), that too is celibacy alone.

How so? By the very means of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), having sacrificed to—that is, having worshipped—that Lord, or alternatively, having made the quest for the Self as his object, he finds that Self. Even that which is called "sacrifice" (*iṣṭa*) is indeed celibacy; for by celibacy alone one finds protection (*trāṇa*) for the existing Self. Furthermore, that which they call the "Sattra-sacrifice" (*sattrāyaṇa*) is indeed celibacy; for by celibacy alone one finds protection for the existing Self. And that which they call "silence" (*mauna*) is indeed celibacy; for by celibacy alone, having found the Self, one reflects upon it. 2. (2) ————-

Now, that which they call the *sattrāyaṇa* (the sacrificial session) is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Being thus, one finds protection and preservation for the self from the Supreme Self by means of the practice of celibacy; therefore, even the word *sattrāyaṇa* refers to celibacy itself. Furthermore, that which they call "silence" (*mauna*) is indeed celibacy; for it is only when one is endowed with the means of celibacy that, having understood the Self through the scriptures and the teacher, one subsequently reflects upon and meditates [on It]. Therefore, even the word *mauna* refers to celibacy itself.

Now, that which they call "the path of non-perishing" is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*), for this self (*ātman*) does not perish, which one finds through celibacy. And that which they call "the path of the forest" (*araṇyāyana*) is also celibacy. For in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here, there are two oceans, Ara and Ṇya; there is the lake Airammadīya; there is the Aśvattha tree Soma-savana; and there is the unconquerable citadel of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord. 3. (3) —-

Now, that which they call "the indestructible course" (*anāśakāyana*) is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*). For that Self which one finds through celibacy does not perish because it has celibacy as its means of attainment; therefore, even "the indestructible course" is nothing but celibacy. Furthermore, that which they call "the forest course" (*araṇyāyana*) is indeed celibacy. Because one who possesses celibacy goes (*ayana*) to the two "arṇavas"—that is, the two *araṇyas*—it is called "the forest course," and that is celibacy.

Because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is praised through such great means for achieving the goals of human life—as sacrifice (*yajña*) because it is knowledge (*jñāna*), as the chosen goal (*iṣṭa*) because it is seeking (*eṣaṇā*), as protection (*tāraṇa*) because it saves from existence (*sat*), as silence (*mauna*) because of its contemplative nature (*manana*), as the path of non-destruction (*anāśakāyana*) because of its non-eating (*anaśana*), and as the way of the forest (*araṇyāyana*) because of going to the two forests (*araṇya*)—it is the supreme auxiliary cause and means for knowledge; therefore, the meaning is that it must be guarded with effort by the knower of Brahman.

For there, in that world of Brahman, there are two well-known oceans, Ara and Ṇya—either actual seas or things resembling seas—and they are powerful. In the third heaven from here—that is, counting from this world, the third sky in relation to the earth and the intermediate space—there is a lake called Aira. "Aira" means made of *irā* (food); it is a lake full of *maṇḍa* (the essence of food), which is intoxicating and joy-inducing for those who partake of it.

And right there is a tree named Aśvattha, called Somasavana—meaning that which flows with *soma*, or "the immortal," thus it is "the flow of immortality. And right there in that world of Brahman is the city of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha, named Aparājitā, which cannot be conquered by others who lack the means of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) compared to those who possess such means. Furthermore, it is specially measured and constructed by the Lord Brahmā; and that golden, celestial pavilion is what is meant by the term "Prabhu-vimita" (measured by the Lord)—this is the completion of the sentence.

Now, those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy—it is theirs alone that this world of Brahman belongs; for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. Thus ends the fifth section. 5.

In that world of Brahman, those who attain through the means of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) these two oceans called Ara and Ṇya—it is for them alone that this world of Brahman which has been described exists. And for those knowers of Brahman who possess the means of celibacy, there is freedom of movement (*kāmacāra*) in all worlds; the meaning is that it never belongs to others who are devoted to non-celibacy and whose intellects are attached to external objects.

Now, some maintain that here, just as a person of great worth is praised by such statements as "You are Indra, you are Yama, you are Varuṇa," so too, by words such as "desired" (iṣṭa) and the like, it is not merely the cessation of craving for objects such as women that is worthy of praise; rather, since knowledge is the means to liberation, it is that very knowledge which is praised by words such as "desired."

No; for those whose minds are carried away by thirst for external objects such as women and the like, the discriminative knowledge of the inner Self (pratyagātman) is impossible, according to hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts such as: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self. It is indeed proper that celibacy (brahmacarya) be praised, because it must be enjoined as a means for the cessation of thirst for objects such as women—a factor that assists knowledge. But [an objection may be raised]: since celibacy is praised along with sacrifices and other rites, it is understood that sacrifices and the rest are themselves means for attaining the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).

It is true that [the goal] is reached, but here celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is not praised by means of sacrifice and the like with the intention of establishing their status as instruments for attaining the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). What then? It is in view of their well-known status as instruments for achieving human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Just as a king is said to be "with Indra and others," yet he is not present wherever Indra and others are active—that is how it is here.

Are these enjoyments—the oceans and so forth belonging to the world of Brahmā, as well as the fathers and others born of mere volition—composed of earth and water, just as they are seen here in this world, such as the oceans, trees, cities, and golden pavilions; or are they merely products of mental conviction? What follows from this? If they were composed of earth and water and were gross, their placement within the space of the heart would be impossible.

Furthermore, the statement in the Purāṇa that "in the world of Brahman, the body and other things are composed of mind" would be contradicted, as would the scriptural texts such as "free from sorrow and free from pride. [Objection: But would not the Purāṇic tradition be contradicted if they were mental, given that it says, "The oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, sacrifices, Vedas, mantras, and so forth, appearing in embodied forms, wait upon Brahmā"? [Reply: No, because it is impossible for those things with well-known physical forms to go there while retaining those very forms.

Therefore, one must postulate that the oceans and other such beings possess another form, distinct from their well-known forms, which they assume in order to go to the world of Brahman. And when two such postulations are equally possible, it is more appropriate to postulate that the mental forms are indeed those with shapes corresponding to men, women, and so forth, as these are already well-known; for this allows for the logical connection of the mental body with its corresponding shape. Indeed, we observe in dreams that there are mental forms of men, women, and so forth, which possess specific shapes.

"But surely they are indeed unreal; if that were so, the scriptural text, 'These desires are real,' would be contradicted. No, for it is possible for mental cognitions to exist as reality. For mental cognitions in the form of women, men, and so forth, are seen in dreams. "But the objects seen in dreams are merely forms of impressions from the waking state; women and the like do not actually exist there in the dream. This is a very insufficient argument.

Even the objects of the waking state are produced solely from mental cognitions, because those waking objects consist of fire, water, and food, which are themselves produced by that [mental] vision. For it has been stated that "the worlds have their root in volition" in the passage, "Heaven and earth were fashioned. Furthermore, in all the Vedas, the origin, dissolution, and abiding of the inner Self within that very [Brahman] are declared through such passages as, "As the spokes are fixed in the hub," and so forth.

Therefore, it is indeed accepted that mental and external objects stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect, like a seed and its sprout. Even though external objects are themselves mental and mental objects are themselves external, there is never any falsity in them with respect to their own nature. [Objection: But surely the objects seen in a dream become false for one who has awakened. [Reply: True, but that falsity is relative to the waking consciousness, not inherent in the objects themselves.

Likewise, the unreality of objects perceived in the waking state is relative to the awakening from a dream, not intrinsic. However, the mere aspect of particularity for all things is the cause of false cognition; thus, "modification is a mere verbal handle, a name, and is unreal; only the three forms (earth, water, and fire) are real. Even these are unreal in terms of their specific aspects, yet real in themselves as being of the nature of pure Being (*sanmātra*). Prior to the realization of the Self as Being, everything—even within one's own sphere—is indeed real, like the objects seen in a dream; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Therefore, the forests and other such things belonging to the world of Brahman are purely mental, as are the objects of desire, such as the ancestors, which arise from volition (*saṃkalpa*). Because they are free from impurity—unlike the enjoyment of external objects—they are produced by the volitions of pure being (*śuddhasattva*); thus, they constitute unsurpassed happiness and are real for the lords (the liberated ones). This is the meaning: even when there is the realization of Being, Truth, and the Self, things imagined upon it—such as snakes on a rope—attain the very nature of Being and the Self; therefore, they are indeed real as that Being-Self. Thus ends the commentary on the fifth section.

Now, those channels of the heart—those of the minute, tawny-colored [substance], as well as of the white, the blue, the yellow, and the red—[correspond to] this very sun: it is tawny, it is white, it is blue, it is yellow, and it is red. 1.

Now, these channels—which are about to be described, which belong to the heart that is shaped like a lotus and serves as the locus for the meditation on Brahman, and which extend out in all directions from the mass of the heart-flesh like rays from the solar orb—remain full of the essence of *piṅgala*, a subtle fluid characterized by a specific yellowish-brown color; that is to say, they exist having that very form.

In the same way, the phrase "filled with white, blue, yellow, and red juice" is to be supplied everywhere. Solar heat—known as *pitta* and produced through the process of digestion—becomes tawny due to contact with a small amount of *kapha*. That same solar heat known as *pitta* becomes blue when there is a predominance of *vāta*, and it becomes white when there is a predominance of *kapha*. When there is an equilibrium with *kapha*, it is yellow; and due to an abundance of blood (*śoṇita*), it is red.

Or rather, these specific colors should be sought from medical science as to how they come to be. But the Śruti says: "These specific colors belong to that light of the sun itself which has entered into the channels. How so? "That sun, indeed, is tawny by color; this sun is white, this is blue, this is yellow, this is red—the sun itself [is all of these]."

Just as a great highway, stretching out, goes to two villages—this one and that one—so too these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one. They extend from yonder sun and enter into these channels; they extend from these channels and enter into yonder sun.

Regarding how that [sun] is connected internally with the channels (*nāḍīs*), he provides an illustration here: "Just as in the world a great, wide path—a highway—stretched out and pervading reaches both villages, this one nearby and that one distant; even so, just as the highway enters both villages in the illustration, in this very way these rays of the sun enter both worlds—that solar orb and this person."

They go, having entered into both. It is like a great highway. How so? From that solar orb they extend and become continuous. They have crept—that is, gone and entered—into these internal channels (nāḍīs) of the aforementioned colors such as tawny (piṅgalā) and so forth. Having extended from these channels—that is, having set out and become a continuous stream—they reach that [solar orb]. Because the rays possess a dual nature (belonging to both), they are referred to by the pronoun "they" (te).
Now, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream, then he has entered into these channels (*nāḍī*); no evil touches him, for at that time he is endowed with light. 3.

This being so, at that time when this living self (jīva) is in this state of sleep—specified as "completely withdrawn" because sleep is of two kinds—it means that all the functions of the senses have been withdrawn. Consequently, due to the absence of the turbidity produced by contact with external objects, it becomes perfectly serene (*saṃprasanna*). For this very reason, it does not perceive—that is, it does not experience—the dream, which is a mental cognition appearing in the form of objects. This is the meaning.

When he is thus asleep, having entered—that is, having gone into—the aforementioned channels (nāḍīs) which are filled with solar radiance, he has reached the space within the heart by means of the channels acting as gateways; this is the meaning. For there is no perception of dreams elsewhere than upon attaining union with Being (sat); therefore, by implication, the locative case "in the channels" (nāḍīṣu) is to be understood as a third-case instrumental.

No one—indeed, not even anything in the form of merit or demerit (*dharma-adharma*)—touches that person who has become united with *Sat*, because at that time the Self remains in its own true nature (*svarūpa*). For it is only when the Self is characterized by the body and senses that evil touches it by producing the effects of pleasure and pain; however, no evil whatsoever dares to touch one who has become united with *Sat* and remains in their own nature, because such a one is not an object (*aviṣayatvāt*). Indeed, one thing becomes an object for another, but there is no "otherness" whatsoever for one who has become united with *Sat*.

Falling away from one's true nature (*svarūpapracyavana*), however, is the soul's transition toward the states of waking and dreaming—the awakening to external objects. We have already stated in the sixth [chapter] that this is caused by the burning of the seed of ignorance, desire, and action by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman; this should be understood here as well. When one is thus asleep, one becomes completely endowed with and pervaded on all sides by the solar light situated within the channels (*nāḍī*).

Therefore, because his instruments have not issued forth through the specific channels of the eyes and so on for the enjoyment of external objects, it is logical that he does not perceive a dream while remaining established in his own self due to the cessation of the instruments. Now, when one has reached such a state of weakness, those sitting around him say, "Do you recognize me? Do you recognize me? As long as he has not departed from this body, he recognizes them. 4.

This being the case, when at a certain time Devadatta—having been brought to, or reached, a state of weakness, a condition of frailty in the body caused by disease or old age, that is to say, a state of emaciation, meaning when he is about to die—his kinsmen sit surrounding him on all sides and say, "Do you know me, your son? Do you know me, your father?
and so forth; as long as that dying man has not yet departed from this body, has not gone out from it, he recognizes his son and the others.

Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays; he either goes forth saying "Om" or he is led away. As quickly as one could direct the mind, so swiftly does he go to the sun. This, indeed, is the door to the world, the path for those who know, and a barrier for those who do not.

Now, as for the phrase "when" and "where"—this being an adverbial modifier—when he departs from this body, then he ascends upwards by means of these very rays as previously described, and the ignorant man goes toward the world won according to his karma. But the other, the knower, endowed with the aforementioned means, meditating on the Self with the syllable *oṃ*, goes either as before or upwards if he is a knower; otherwise, if he is not a knower, he goes horizontally—this is the intended meaning. He is measured, or rather, he passes away; that is to say, he goes.

That wise person, when about to depart, goes to the sun—meaning he reaches it in as much time as it takes for the mind to move, that is, he goes quickly; however, it is not intended to mean that he arrives in exactly that amount of time. For what purpose does he go to the sun? It is said: this sun is indeed well known as the gate to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*); through that which serves as a gate, the wise person proceeds to the world of Brahman.

Therefore, it is the "resort" (*prapadana*) for the wise; it is called "resort" because by means of this gate one resorts to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). It is the "obstruction" (*nirodhana*) or "obstruction" (*nirodha*) because from this sun obstruction occurs for the ignorant; the meaning is that, being obstructed within the body itself by the solar radiance, they do not depart at all through the channel that passes through the crown of the head, as indicated by the verse beginning with "the others go in all directions."

Regarding this, there is this verse: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; one of them extends to the crown of the head. Ascending by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for departing—yes, for departing. Thus ends the sixth section. (6) ———— 6 ————

Regarding that aforementioned subject, there is this verse as a mantra: "There are one hundred and one principal channels connected to the heart, which is a mass of flesh; because the channels of the body are infinite. Of these, one has emerged upward toward the head. Traveling upward by that [channel], one attains immortality—the state of being immortal."

There are other channels that go in various directions—spreading horizontally and moving upward—which serve as gateways for wandering through *saṃsāra*; they do not lead to immortality. Rather, their purpose is solely for departing—that is, for the sake of exiting [the body]. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is intended to mark the end of the section.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth section.

"That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolve is true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand. He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," so said Prajāpati.

That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—for the purpose of meditating upon and perceiving it, the lotus of the heart has been described; in whom desires are contained as truths veiled by untruth; for whom celibacy has been declared as the means concomitant with its meditation; and for the attainment of the desires that constitute the fruit of meditation, the journey through the artery at the crown of the head has been described—that Self is to be sought.

It is to be known through the instructions of the scriptures and teachers; it is especially desired to be known, it is to be sought after, and it is to be brought to the state of being personally realized. What results from its investigation and seeking to know? It is said: he attains all worlds and all desires.

He who, having sought that Self in the manner described—namely, through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher—understands It and brings It to the state of being personally realized, for him this attainment of all worldly desires and the fruit of becoming the Self of all comes to pass; so indeed did Prajāpati say. "It is to be sought" and "It is to be understood"—this is purely a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). The meaning is that It must be sought and understood in this way, because seeking and understanding have a visible purpose.

Furthermore, he will repeatedly demonstrate its having a visible purpose through the statement, "I see nothing enjoyable here. Since the removal of erroneous apprehension is the visible fruit in the realization of the true nature of the Self—which is otherwise understood through the attributes of the body and so forth by means of another form—it is appropriate that this injunction has the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatā*); an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), such as those regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites, is not possible here.

Then both the gods and the asuras became aware of this. They said, "Come, let us seek that Self, by seeking which one obtains all worlds and all desires. Indra went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the asuras. Without communicating with each other, they both approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands.

The purpose of the narrative beginning with "Then both" has been stated. Indeed, those two groups—the gods and the asuras, collectively called "both"—heard and understood that speech of Prajāpati, which had come down through tradition and entered the range of their own ears.

And what did they do after understanding these words of Prajāpati? It is said: they, both the gods and the asuras, spoke to one another in their respective assemblies—"Come now! If you agree, let us seek out that Self spoken of by Prajāpati; let us investigate that Self, by seeking which one obtains all worlds and all desires. Having said this, Indra alone—being himself like a king among the gods—took with him the other gods and all their enjoyments and equipment.

Leaving behind his physical body alone, he set out toward Prajāpati; likewise did Virocana, the leader of the Asuras. This demonstrates that teachers must be approached with humility, and that knowledge is more precious than even sovereignty over the three worlds; for this reason, the two kings of the gods and the Asuras, though both worthy of the most excellent enjoyments, approached their teacher in such a manner.

It is said that those two, indeed being unaware of one another and not communicating with each other regarding the fruit of their knowledge, yet showing mutual envy toward one another, approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands—that is, with loads of sacrificial wood in their hands. They arrived.

The two of them lived as religious students for thirty-two years. Prajāpati said to them, "Desiring what have you lived here? They replied, "It is reported that the word of the Blessed One is this: 'That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that Self is to be sought, that Self is to be understood; he who, having found that Self and understood it, obtains all worlds and all desires. Desiring that [Self], we have lived here. (3)

Having gone there, the two of them lived as students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*), intent on service for thirty-two years. Prajāpati, knowing their intention, said to them: "Desiring what, with what purpose in mind, did you live here? Being thus addressed, the two replied: "The learned ones proclaim that which is the Self (*ātman*) and so forth according to the words of the Blessed One; therefore, desiring to know that Self, we have lived here."

Although they were previously possessed of mutual envy before approaching Prajāpati, nevertheless, out of respect for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, they dwelt as celibate students with Prajāpati, having become free from the defects of passion, hatred, delusion, envy, and so forth. By this, the greatness of the knowledge of the Self was proclaimed.

Prajāpati said to them both: "This person who is seen in the eye, this is the Self," he said; "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Then [Naciketas asked]: "Venerable sir, that which is perceived in the water, and that which is perceived in a mirror—which one is this? He replied: "It is indeed this very same one that is perceived in all these [reflections]. 4. (4)

Having observed that those two ascetics were thus purified of taints and fit [for instruction], Prajāpati said: "This person who is seen in the eye by yogis whose vision has turned inward and whose impurities have been wiped away—the Seer—this is the Self characterized by qualities such as being free from evil. This is what I spoke of previously, through the knowledge of which there is the attainment of all worlds and desires; this is the Immortal called 'the Infinite' (bhūman), and for that very reason it is 'Light' (abha), and for that very reason it is 'Brahman,' the most exalted."

Now, having heard these words spoken by Prajāpati, "The person is seen in the eye," the two of them took the person to be the form of the reflection. Having grasped it, and in order to confirm it, they asked Prajāpati: "O Venerable One, as for this person who is perceived all around in the water, and this form of one's own reflection which is perceived in a mirror, a sword, and so forth—which among these is the one spoken of by your honors? Or is it one and the same in all of them?"

Thus questioned, Prajāpati said: "It is indeed this very one whom I have described as the seer in the eye. Having kept this in mind, he said: "He is perceived within all these ends, that is, in their midst."

But how is it appropriate for Prajāpati, being a teacher free from defects, to permit two disciples to hold a contrary understanding? True, this is so; he did not actually permit it. How so? For Indra and Virocana had superimposed upon themselves scholarship, greatness, and intelligence, and were renowned as such in the world; if they had been told by Prajāpati, "You two are deluded and have grasped the matter wrongly," then there would have been pain in their hearts.

Furthermore, from the despondency of mind produced by that [previous answer], there would be a discouragement toward listening to, grasping, and comprehending further questions; therefore, Prajāpati considers that the two disciples must be protected. He thinks: "Let them grasp this much for now; I shall remove their misconception by means of the illustration of the water-cup. But is it not improper to speak falsely with the words, "This very one"? And yet, no falsehood has been spoken. How so? The person in the eye mentioned by the Self is more closely present in the mind than the shadow-self grasped by the disciples.

"He is the innermost of all," according to the Śruti; Prajāpati spoke of him alone when he said, "He indeed is this. Therefore, nothing false was spoken by Prajāpati. Thus ends the commentary on the seventh section. "Having looked at yourselves in a bowl of water, tell me what you do not understand about yourselves. They both looked into the bowl of water. Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see? They both replied, "Venerable Sir, we see our entire self here as a reflection, down to the very hairs and the nails. (1)

(1) — "Having looked at yourselves in a water-filled bowl or similar vessel, tell me, explain to me that which you do not recognize while seeing yourselves there immediately afterward. Thus addressed, they both looked into the water-filled bowl; having done so, Prajāpati said to them: "What do you see?"

"Now, tell me that," having been thus addressed, the two looked into the water-vessel but did not inform Prajāpati, saying, "This was not understood by us. And since the cause of their ignorance had not been disclosed, Prajāpati said, "What do you see? What is the intention here? It is said: they certainly did not have the apprehension, "This has not been understood by us"; rather, their conviction regarding the reflection as being the Self remained firmly established.

For he will later say, "With their hearts calmed, the two of them departed. Indeed, a state of calm heart is not possible regarding a matter that has not been ascertained as desired. Therefore, they did not say, "This is unknown to us. Furthermore, since disciples who have grasped things erroneously must not be neglected, he himself asked, "What do you see? And for the purpose of removing their erroneous conviction, he will say, "Well-adorned," and so forth.

The two of them said: "Venerable sir, we see this entire self of ours as it truly is, down to the very hairs and nails. Just as we ourselves, O venerable sir, possess hair, nails, and so forth, even so do we see this image of ours in the water-bowl, complete with hair, nails, and all."

Prajāpati said to them both, "Having adorned yourselves well, dressed in fine garments, and being well-groomed, look into a pan of water. Having adorned themselves well, dressed in fine garments, and being well-groomed, they both looked into a pan of water. Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see?

Then Prajāpati spoke to them again in order to remove their conviction that the reflection was the Self: "Having adorned yourselves well as you would at home, wearing fine garments and costly clothes, being well-groomed with hair and nails clipped, look again into a vessel of water. And here he gave this instruction: "Tell me what you do not understand."

But how, by means of this act of adorning oneself well and looking into a vessel of water, could the grasping of those two as the Self in the reflection be removed? Just as external things such as fine ornaments and beautiful garments produce a reflection in the water-vessel when attached to the body, it is understood that the body itself previously possessed the capacity to produce a reflection; and likewise, the parts of the body such as hair and nails—which were intended to be permanent and uncut—previously possessed the capacity to produce a reflection.

Furthermore, when the hair and nails have been cut, their reflection is no longer seen; therefore, it is established that like the hair and nails, the body also possesses the nature of coming into being and passing away. Thus, it is established that the body—which is perceived in a vessel of water or elsewhere, and which serves as the cause for that reflection—is not the Self. This is because it acts as a reflector in the vessel of water and so forth, just like the ornaments attached to the body. Not only this much: by this same reasoning, whatever is considered "belonging to the self"—such as pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and delusion—should be understood as non-self, because they are occasional, just like the hair and nails.

When Prajāpati had thus spoken the illustration of the well-dressed man and the ornaments for the purpose of removing all false attachments, although Indra and Virocana heard it and acted accordingly, their misconception regarding the reflection-self did not depart. Therefore, it is understood that Indra and Virocana were obstructed from discerning knowledge by some personal defect of their own. With their convictions as firm as before, he questioned them as previously: "What do you see?"

They both said, "Just as we two here, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and well-groomed, even so these two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and well-groomed. "This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. With their hearts thus pacified, they departed. (3) They accepted it exactly as it was presented—"just as we two here" and so forth, as before—thinking, "Just as we are distinguished by fine ornaments and the like, even so are these two shadow-selves. Thus, they became even more firmly convinced of the opposite [of the truth].

When the characteristic of that Self has been stated as "This Self is free from evil," and then, while the two seekers were further investigating its specific nature, the Self was directly pointed out as "this person who is seen in the eye," and even when the illustration of the water-jar, the well-dressed man, and the ornament was given to remove misconceptions contrary to that [Self], the misconception contrary to the true nature of the Self did not yet depart.

Therefore, thinking that the capacity for discriminative knowledge had been obstructed by some personal defect of theirs, Prajāpati—as before—set aside his intended [inner] Self from his mind and said, "This is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. However, they did not grasp the Self he intended. For they were merely refined by hearing the definition of the Self beginning with "the Self" and so forth, as well as by the scriptural teaching regarding the Person in the Eye and the supporting arguments concerning the water-cup and other illustrations.

Thinking that as they repeatedly remembered all his words, discrimination regarding the Self would arise by itself through the destruction of their obstacles, and wishing to avoid causing mental distress to them at the time of his instruction on celibacy (*brahmacarya*), Prajāpati overlooked them even as they were departing with the notion that they had achieved their goal. The meaning is that Indra and Virocana departed with peaceful hearts, contented hearts—that is, with the notion that they had achieved their purpose—but not with true tranquility (*śama*); for if true tranquility had arisen in them, their misconception would have been dispelled. Thus, they went forth.

Having observed them as they were departing without having perceived the Self and without having realized it, Prajāpati said: "Whichever of these—whether gods or asuras—shall have this as their secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), they shall perish. Then Virocana, with a peaceful heart, went to the asuras and taught them this secret doctrine: "The self alone is to be magnified here; the self is to be served. By magnifying the self and serving the self here, one obtains both worlds—this one and the one beyond."

Thus, fearing that those two kings, Indra and Virocana, being attached to enjoyments, might forget what had been said, and wishing to remove their mental distress by means of direct instruction regarding that which is not directly perceived, Prajāpati watched them as they went far away. Thinking that this too would come within the range of their hearing—just like the statement "That Self which is free from evil"—he spoke: "Without having apprehended the Self characterized as described, and without having realized it through direct perception of one's own self..."

Having formed these two contrary conclusions, Indra and Virocana depart; that is, they go away. Therefore, whether they be gods or asuras—what need for further specification—those who have this *upaniṣad*, meaning the knowledge of the Self which has been grasped by them from these two, are "those who have this *upaniṣad*"; the meaning is that they will possess such realization and hold such a conviction.

What will happen to them? They will be defeated; the meaning is that they will fall away from the path to the highest good (*śreyas*), become excluded from it, and be ruined. Of the two kings of the gods and the asuras who were returning to their own homes, it was Virocana, the king of the asuras, who, with a peaceful heart, went to the asuras. Having gone, he proclaimed to those asuras this very *upaniṣad*—the notion that the body is the Self—which his father had spoken: "The Self is merely the body."

Therefore, in this world, the self—that is, the body—is itself to be magnified, worthy of worship, and likewise to be served and attended to. By magnifying and serving the self—the body—here in this world, one attains both worlds: this one and the next. The King’s intention is that all other worlds and all desires are contained within these two worlds, namely this world and the world beyond. For this reason, even today, they say of one who does not give here, who lacks faith, and who does not sacrifice, "Alas, he is an Asura! for this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Asuras regarding a dead man's body: that it should be provided with alms, clothing, and ornaments.

For by means of this they fashion [the body], thinking that they will thereby conquer the other world. Thus ends the eighth section. Therefore, their tradition continues even today. In this world, people say of one who does not give—that is, one who performs no acts of charity, who is of a non-distributive nature, who lacks faith—that is, who is devoid of faith regarding meritorious deeds, and who does not sacrifice according to his ability—that is, whose very nature is not to sacrifice: "Alas, this man is indeed *āsura* (demoniac), for such is his character. Thus the learned (śiṣṭas) speak with regret. For this Upanishad, characterized by a lack of faith and so forth, belongs to the *asuras*.

Having been consecrated by that secret doctrine (upaniṣad), they consecrate the corpse—the dead body—of the deceased with alms consisting of perfumes, garlands, food, and so forth, as well as with clothing such as garments and the like, by means of covering it, and with ornaments made of banners, flags, and the like. By means of this consecration of the corpse, they consider themselves thinking, "We shall conquer that world which is to be attained after death.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth section.

Then Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this danger: "Just as indeed this [self] here, when this body is well-adorned, becomes well-adorned; when it is well-dressed, becomes well-dressed; when it is embellished, becomes embellished—even so, when this body is blind, it becomes blind; when it is lame, it becomes lame; when it is maimed, it becomes maimed. Following the destruction of this very body, it perishes. I see no object of enjoyment here.

Now, it is said that Indra, even before reaching the gods, while traveling and repeatedly recollecting the words of his teacher due to his possession of divine qualities such as lack of cruelty, perceived this following danger arising from the cause of grasping for his own self. A portion of the reasoning—which had been stated by Prajāpati using the illustration of the water-jug—flashed upon Maghavan’s intellect, whereby he saw the defect in grasping the shadow-self.

How so? Just as indeed, when this body is well-adorned, the shadow-self (chāyātmā) also becomes well-adorned; when it is well-dressed, [the shadow-self] is well-dressed; and when it is groomed, [the shadow-self] is groomed—just as when bodily parts such as nails and hair are removed, the shadow-self also becomes groomed, being deprived of those nails, hair, and so forth; even so, this shadow-self, because its status as a bodily part is equal to that of nails, hair, and the rest in this body, becomes blind when the eyes are lost through blindness, and lame when [the legs] are lame.

A *srāma* is indeed one who has only one eye, because his [other] eye has become blind; or he is called *srāma* whose eyes or nose constantly discharge [fluid]. A *parivṛkṇa* is one whose hands or feet have been cut off. When the body is *srāma* or *parivṛkṇa*, the shadow-self (*chāyātmā*) likewise becomes so. Thus, following the destruction of this body, it perishes. Therefore, I see no fruit to be enjoyed here in this perception of the shadow-self, or in this perception of the body as the self.

Having thus determined the defect in the view that the self is the shadow of the body, he returned with fuel in his hand to dwell as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*). Prajāpati said to him: "O Maghavan, since you have departed with a peaceful heart, having gone away together with Virocana, desiring what have you come back? Although He already knew, He asked again in order to make manifest Indra's intention, just as one says, "Approach me with what you already know."
And thus he made his own intention manifest, saying, "Just as this indeed," and so forth; and Prajāpati rejoiced, saying, "It is exactly so."

Now, since the hearing of the "Person in the Eye" is equal for both, why was it that Indra took the reflection in the body to be the Self, while Virocana took the body itself to be so? Regarding this, it is considered as follows: Just as in the case of Indra—who, while remembering Prajāpati’s words concerning the water-jar and other things, had not yet reached the gods—there occurred both the grasping of the reflection as the Self due to his understanding of the teacher's instruction and the perception of its defects; such was not the case with Virocana. Rather, he perceived the Self in the body itself, and no perception of defects arose there.

In the same way, Indra’s and Virocana’s grasping of the shadow-self and the body respectively was dependent on the smallness or greatness of the defects obstructing their capacity to receive knowledge. Because Indra had few defects, he accepted the literal meaning of the scriptural statement, "He is seen," out of faith. The other, however, having abandoned the body which is the cause of the shadow, grasped the meaning of the scripture figuratively, thinking, "This is what was spoken by Prajāpati," because his defects were more numerous.

Virocana’s intention was as follows: "Just as when two garments, one blue and one not blue, are seen in a mirror, that which is [actually] blue is said to be 'the precious garment' on account of its reflection, yet it is the garment itself that is so called, not the reflection—so it is here. For it has been demonstrated in another Vedic passage that the determination of the meaning of words depends solely upon the qualities and defects of one's own mind, even though the hearing of the sound is identical: from the mere hearing of the syllable *da* in the phrase "Restrain yourselves (*dāmyata*), give (*datta*), show compassion (*dayadhvam*)," different meanings are understood. Furthermore, external circumstances also become auxiliary factors only in accordance with those internal dispositions.

"Precisely so, O Maghavan, you have correctly understood: the shadow is not the Self," thus said Prajāpati. "As for this Self which I mentioned as the subject under discussion, I shall explain that very Self to you once more, even though it has already been explained previously. Since, although it was explained but once, you did not grasp it—despite its having become an object of comprehension for those free from defects—you must therefore have your capacity for grasping obstructed by some defect."

"Therefore, dwell for another thirty-two years in order to exhaust that [remaining fault]. Having said this, he spoke to him who had lived accordingly and whose faults were exhausted. Thus ends the commentary on the ninth section. "He who moves about being honored in a dream—that is the Self," he said; "that is the immortal, the fearless; that is Brahman. With a peaceful heart, he departed. Even before reaching the gods, he perceived this fear: "Even if this body becomes blind, he (the Self) remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not lame. Indeed, he is not affected by its defect. (1)

(1)—This is that very Self characterized by freedom from evil and so forth, which was explained by the passage beginning with "this one in the eye. Who is he? He is the one who moves about being honored—meaning, being worshipped by women and others—in a dream, experiencing various kinds of dream-enjoyments. "This is the Self," he said; the rest is the same as before. Having been told this, Indra departed with a pacified heart. But even before reaching the gods, as before, he perceived fear in this Self as well.

How so? Although this body may be blind, that self which exists in the dream state is not blind. If this body is lame, he is not lame. This dream-self is not defiled by the defects of this body. He is not killed when it is killed; he does not become lame when it becomes lame. They indeed kill him [in the dream], they chase him away, he experiences what is unpleasant, and even weeps—as if. [The king said: "I see nothing here that can be enjoyed. (2–4)

Nor is he killed by the killing of this [body], like the shadow-self; nor does he become weary by its weariness, like the dream-self. That which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter on the basis of scripture alone—namely, "He does not age with the aging of this [body]," and so forth—is here introduced to be established through reasoning. To begin with, this [self] is not possessed of the defects of the body like the shadow-self; however, they certainly kill him—the word *eva* (certainly) being used in the sense of *iva* (as if).

It should be understood that "some indeed seem to kill him," and not that they actually kill him, because the word "indeed" (iva) is seen in all the subsequent passages. If it is argued that [the text] implies they do indeed kill him because of the qualification "he is not killed by his killing," this is not so. For it would be impossible for Indra—who takes Prajāpati as his authority—to make Prajāpati's statement "this is the immortal" false while taking him as his authority. How could Indra, accepting Prajāpati as authoritative, render that word of Prajāpati a lie?

[Objection: But surely, when Prajāpati spoke of the "shadow-person" (chāyā-puruṣa), he pointed out its defect by saying, "When this body perishes, it perishes after it. The same would apply here as well. [Reply: It is not so. Why? Because Maghavan considers that the one Prajāpati spoke of as "this person who is seen in the eye" is not the shadow-self.

How so? If one were to think that when the Self characterized by freedom from evil and other qualities was questioned, Prajāpati spoke of the shadow-self, then how could one, having accepted Prajāpati as an authority, go again with fuel in hand to hear further instruction? Yet he did go. Therefore, one concludes that Prajāpati did not speak of the shadow-self. This has been explained thus: "The seer is seen in the eye. Likewise, [the text says] it seems to conceal, it seems to drive away; and likewise, one becomes as if experiencing what is unpleasant due to the death of a son or others.

Moreover, he himself seems to weep. Now, one might ask: "Does he not actually experience what is unpleasant? How can you say 'as if he experiences'? It is said in reply: No, because the scriptural declarations of his being immortal and fearless would otherwise be untenable, and because of another Vedic text stating, "He meditates, as it were. If it is argued that this contradicts direct perception, we say no; for such a perception is possible as an error, just like the perception of the body as the Self. Let the question of whether he experiences what is unpleasant or not stand aside for now. My intention is this: "I see nothing enjoyable here; even in the knowledge of the self in the dream state, I do not obtain any desired fruit."

"Even so, this is according to your intention"—this is the completion of the sentence, because the possession of the qualities of immortality and fearlessness by the Self is what was intended. Although [the truth] has been stated twice, he does not grasp it correctly due to his own reasoning; therefore, thinking that there is still an obstructing cause for him even now, as before, Prajāpati instructed him, saying, "Dwell for another thirty-two years in the life of a student (*brahmacarya*)," and so forth. To him who had lived accordingly and whose impurities were exhausted, he spoke.

With fuel in his hand, he returned once more. Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back? He replied: "Venerable Sir, it is because even if this body becomes blind, he [the self] does not become blind; if it becomes lame, he does not become lame; indeed, he is not affected by its defect. 3. (2–4)

Nor is he killed by the killing of this [body], like the self that is a shadow; nor does he become weary by its weariness, for he is the self in dream. That which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter on the basis of scripture alone—namely, "He does not age with the aging of this [body]," and so forth—is here introduced to be established through reasoning. To begin with, this [self] is not possessed of the defects of the body like the shadow-self; however, they do indeed kill him. The word *eva* (indeed) has the sense of *iva* (as if).

It should be understood that "some indeed seem to kill him," and not that they actually kill him, because the word "indeed" (iva) is seen in all the subsequent passages. If it is argued that [the text] implies they do indeed kill him because of the qualification "he is not killed by his slaughter," this is not so; for it would be impossible to charge Indra with speaking untruth when he accepts Prajāpati as an authority. How could Indra, accepting that statement of Prajāpati—"This is the immortal"—make it false?

[Objection: But was it not the case that when Prajāpati spoke of the shadow-person, he pointed out its defect by saying, "When this body perishes, he perishes"? The same might apply here as well. [Reply: It is not so. Why? Because Maghavan considers that the one spoken of by Prajāpati as "this person who is seen in the eye" is not the shadow-self.

How so? If one were to think that when the Self characterized by freedom from evil and other attributes was questioned, Prajāpati had actually spoken of the shadow-self, then how could he, having accepted Prajāpati as an authority, go again with fuel in hand to hear further instruction? Yet he did go. Therefore, one must conclude that Prajāpati did not speak of the shadow-self. This has already been explained: "The seer is seen in the eye. Likewise, [the text says] it seems to cover him, it seems to drive him away; and thus, due to the death of a son or others, he becomes as if he experiences what is unpleasant.

Moreover, he himself seems to weep. Now, one might object: "Does he not actually experience what is unpleasant? Why do you say 'as if he experiences'? To this it is replied: No, because the scriptural declarations regarding his being immortal and fearless would otherwise be untenable; and furthermore, there is another Śruti text stating, "He meditates, as it were. If it be argued that this contradicts direct perception, we say no, for such a perception is possible as an error, just like the perception of the body as the Self. Let the question of whether or not he experiences the unpleasant remain for now. "I see nothing enjoyable here"—the intention is that even in the knowledge of the self during the dream state, one does not obtain the desired fruit.

"Even so, according to your intention"—this is the completion of the sentence, because it was intended that the Self possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness. Although [the truth] has been stated twice, he does not grasp it correctly due to logical reasons; therefore, thinking that there is still an obstructing cause for him even now as before, Prajāpati instructed him, saying, "Dwell for another thirty-two years in the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*)," and so forth. To him who had dwelt accordingly and whose impurities were exhausted, he spoke.

"It is not slain by the slaying of this [body], nor does it waste away by its wasting away; rather, they indeed slay it, as it were, they disperse it, as it were; one becomes as if experiencing what is unpleasant, and one even weeps, as it were. 'I see nothing enjoyable in this,' said he. 'It is just so, O Maghavan,' he replied, 'but I shall explain this further to you. Dwell here for another thirty-two years. He dwelt there for another thirty-two years, and then he spoke to him. (4) (2–4)

Nor is he killed by the killing of this [body], like the reflection-self (*chāyātman*). Nor does he become weary through the weariness of this [body]; this is like the reflection-self in a dream. That which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter merely on the basis of scripture—namely, "He does not age with the aging of this [body]," and so forth—is here introduced to be established by means of reasoning. To begin with, this [self] is not possessed of the defects of the body like the reflection-self; however, they certainly do kill him. The word *eva* (certainly) has the sense of *iva* (like).

It should be understood that "some indeed kill him" means they strike him, but not that they actually kill him, because the word "indeed" (iva) is seen in all the subsequent cases. If it is argued that [the text] implies they do indeed kill him because of the qualification "he is not killed by his slaying," this is not so; for it would be impossible to charge Indra with falsehood when he accepts Prajāpati as an authority. How could Indra, accepting Prajāpati as his authority, render false that statement of Prajāpati's, namely, "This is the immortal"?

[Objection: But did Prajāpati not point out a defect regarding the shadow-person he described, saying, "When this body perishes, it perishes after it"? Would it not be the same here as well? [Reply: It is not so. Why? Because Maghavan considers that the one Prajāpati spoke of as "this person who is seen in the eye" was not the shadow-self.

How so? If one were to think that when Prajāpati was asked about the Self characterized by freedom from evil and so forth, he had actually spoken of the shadow-self (chāyātman), then how could one, having accepted Prajāpati as an authority, go again with fuel in hand to hear further instruction? Yet, he did indeed go. Therefore, one concludes that the shadow-self was not what Prajāpati spoke of. This has already been explained: "The seer is seen in the eye. Likewise, [the text says] it seems to conceal, it seems to drive away; and thus, one becomes as if experiencing unpleasantness caused by the death of a son or other such things.

Moreover, he himself seems to weep. Now, one might ask: "Does he not actually experience what is unpleasant? Why do you say 'as if he experiences'? It is replied: No, because the scriptural statements regarding his being immortal and fearless would otherwise be untenable, and because of another Vedic text stating, "He meditates, as it were. If it is argued that this contradicts direct perception, we say no; for such a perception is possible as an error, just like the perception of the body as the Self. Let us set aside for now the question of whether or not he experiences what is unpleasant. My intention is this: "I see nothing here to be enjoyed; even in the knowledge of the self during dream, I do not obtain the desired fruit."

"In this very way, according to your intention"—this is the completion of the sentence, because it was intended that the Self possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness. Although I have stated it twice, he does not grasp it correctly due to his own reasoning; therefore, thinking that even now there exists an obstructing cause for him as before, Prajāpati commanded him: "Dwell for another thirty-two years in the life of a student (brahmacarya)," and so forth. To him who had lived accordingly and whose impurities were exhausted, he spoke [the next words]. Thus ends the commentary on the tenth section.

"Now, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream—this is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. With a peaceful heart, he departed. But even before reaching the gods, he perceived this danger: "Indeed, in this state, one does not know oneself as 'I am this,' nor does one know these beings; one has gone to utter destruction. I see no enjoyment here. (1–2)

As before, having said "But him indeed, my dear," and so forth, the passage beginning with "Now, when one is thus asleep" has been explained. He who is the seer in the eye and who moves about being honored in the dream state—he is this very one who, when asleep, unified, and serene, does not perceive any dream; "This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman"—this was precisely what he intended. However, Maghavān perceived a defect even in that.

How so? It is not that this Self, even while staying in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), does not know itself at all right now—nor does it know "I am this" nor "these beings are these," as it does in the waking state or in a dream. Therefore, the phrase "it has indeed perished, as it were" is to be understood as before. It has "merged" (*apīta*)—the intention being that it has become as if destroyed. For when knowledge exists, the existence of the knower is perceived; it is not perceived when knowledge is absent.

Furthermore, no cognition is perceived in one who is in deep sleep; therefore, the intention is that he is as if destroyed. However, one who desires the authority of the scriptural statements regarding the Self being immortal and fearless does not consider the Self to be actually subject to destruction. He returned with fuel in his hand. Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back? He replied: "Indeed, O Venerable One, even now this Self does not know itself as 'I am,' nor does it know these beings; it has gone to utter destruction. I see nothing enjoyable here. (2) (1–2)

As before, having said "But him indeed, my dear," and so forth, the passage beginning with "When he is thus asleep" has been explained. He who is the seer in the eye and who moves about being honored in the dream state—this very one, when asleep, unified, and serene, does not perceive a dream; "This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. This was precisely what [Prajāpati] intended. However, Maghavan perceived a defect even there.

How so? It is not that this Self, even while staying in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), does not know itself at all right now—nor does it know itself in this way: "I am this," nor "these beings exist. This is just as in the waking state or in dreaming. Therefore, the phrase "it is indeed destruction, as it were" should be understood as before. "It has merged" (*apītaḥ*) means it has gone into [oneness]; the intention is that it becomes as if destroyed. For when knowledge exists, the existence of the knower is perceived; when knowledge does not exist, it is not.

Furthermore, no cognition is observed in one who is in deep sleep; therefore, the intention is that [the self] is as if destroyed. However, one who desires the authority of the scriptural statements regarding the self's immortality and fearlessness does not consider the self to be actually destroyed.

"So it is indeed, O Maghavan," he said. "I shall explain this further to you, but not otherwise than this; dwell [here] for another five years. He dwelt for another five years. Those [years] together with the previous ones amounted to one hundred and one. This is what is meant when it is said: "For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati. To him, he then spoke. Thus ends the eleventh section. (3) — 11 — (3) —-

Having said, "It is exactly as before," he spoke: "That which has been described by me through three stages—that alone, and not anything other than this Self, will I explain. However, a small deficiency remains in you; to exhaust that, dwell for another five years. Thus addressed, he did accordingly.

To him—Maghavan, whose defects such as the *kaṣāya* had been rubbed away—he spoke of the true nature of the Self, which is free from connection with the defects of the three states and characterized by freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and other qualities. Those one hundred and one years were completed; they came to an end. This is what the learned in the world say: "For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati. This very point, which was shown by the passage beginning with "thirty-two," is now stated by the Śruti itself, stepping aside from the narrative.

Thus, it is said that even Indra attained this self-knowledge—which is more weighty than his very status as Indra—only with great effort and through the exertion of a hundred years of practice, one year at a time. Therefore, the text praises self-knowledge by stating that there is no other human goal (puruṣārtha) higher than this.
Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh section.

O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal, seized by death; it is the support for this immortal, bodiless Self. For he who possesses a body is indeed seized by pleasure and pain. Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain. But pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless. 1. (1)

O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal and subject to death. As for what you think—that the Self described by me as characterized by the eye, the support, and so forth, and characterized by supreme serenity, has simply perished—listen to the reason for that: this body which you see is indeed mortal and perishable; and it is constantly seized and swallowed by death.

When it is said that "one dies only at some time," the resulting terror is not as great as when it is said that "one is already swallowed" or "always pervaded by death. This distinction is stated for the sake of dispassion—namely, that one has been "seized by death"—so that, becoming detached from the identification with the body, one might turn away from it. Here, the term "body" (śarīra) is used to include the senses and the mind as well.

That body of this serene being (*saṃprasāda*), which is understood to have three locations, is immortal—meaning it is devoid of the attributes of death and so forth pertaining to the body, senses, and mind. Although its bodilessness is already established by the term "immortal," the further statement "of the bodiless" is intended to ensure that it does not possess parts or material form like air and the other elements. It is the locus for the experience of the Self; or rather, it is the locus produced through the sequence of fire, water, and earth for the sake of the existing Self, the Seer.

Or, "adhiṣṭhāna" means that which, having entered in the form of the living soul (jīva), presides over this [body]. Since this body—which is of such a nature, eternally seized by death, and possessed of pleasure and pain because it is produced from merit and demerit—is its locus of presiding, the embodied one is that which is presided over by it, or that which possesses it. For the Self, whose true nature is bodiless, the state of being embodied arises from the lack of discrimination in thinking, "I am this very body," or "this body is indeed I"; thus, being embodied, it is "attained"—that is, seized—by pleasure and pain.

This is well known. For one who possesses a body and who, due to contact with external objects, considers "these contacts and separations from external objects are mine," there is no removal, destruction, or cessation of pleasure and pain—which are caused by such contact with and separation from external objects—so long as they exist in a continuous stream. However, when that person has become bodiless through the knowledge of his true nature as bodiless, which has dispelled the non-discriminative knowledge arising from the identification with the body, pleasure and pain do not touch him.

The verb *spṛś* (to touch) is connected with each [term] individually; thus, there are two statements: "he does not touch what is pleasant" and "he does not touch what is unpleasant," just as in the rule: "one should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous. For those two [barbarians and the unrighteous] are the effects of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), whereas bodilessness (*aśarīratā*) is one's true nature (*svarūpa*); since merit and demerit are impossible in that state, the existence of their effects is even further removed. Therefore, pleasure and pain do not touch him.

Now, if it is argued that even pleasure does not touch one who is bodiless, then what was said by Maghavan—that "one staying in deep sleep has indeed gone to destruction"—would follow here as well. This is not a fault, because what is intended to be expressed is the negation of pleasure and pain, which are effects of merit and demerit and are connected with the body—namely, that "pleasure and pain do not touch the bodiless."

For the term "contact" (*sparśa*) is observed to apply to things that come and go—as in "cold contact," "hot contact"—but one does not say "the contact of fire" with respect to heat and light, which are the very nature of fire. Likewise, there is no negation here of the bliss (*ānanda*) that constitutes the essential nature of fire or the sun, nor of the "dear" (*priya*); for this is known from such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānamānandaṃ brahma*) and "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*), and because it has been stated even in this context that "only the Infinite (*bhūman*) is happiness."

Now, one might object that since the plenitude (*bhūman*) is either imperceptible when singular or eternally perceptible by its very nature, it would be devoid of distinctions; yet this was not Indra’s view, for he said: "Indeed, at present he does not know himself as 'I am this'; nor indeed does he know these beings; he has gone to utter destruction; I see no enjoyment here."

For that is indeed desired by Indra—that he may know both the beings and himself, and that he may not experience anything unpleasant; and by means of that knowledge, he attains all worlds and all desires. This is true: it is desired by Indra that "these beings are other than me, all these worlds and desires are other than me, and I am their master. However, this is not for Indra's benefit. And what is beneficial for Indra must be told by Prajāpati.

The attainment intended by Prajāpati was that which results from realizing oneself as the Self of all beings and the desires of the world, through being bodiless like space; it was not intended as something distinct [from the Self], as in the case of a king’s acquisition of a kingdom. This being so, when there is oneness of the Self, how could one perceive "these beings" or "I am this"? But, [one may object: in this view, scriptural passages concerning lordly power—such as "he moves about with women or vehicles," "if he is desirous of the world of the fathers," and "he becomes onefold"—would be untenable.

No, for there is no contradiction in the fact that the one who is the Self of all is connected with all fruits—just as clay pervades all jars, bowls, pots, and the like. If it is argued that, being the Self of all, he would also be connected with suffering, we say no; since suffering too is admitted to be of the nature of the Self, there is no contradiction. Sufferings have their cause in the imagination of ignorance within the Self, just as the imagination of snakes and such has its cause in the rope.

And since that ignorance—which is the cause of suffering—is severed by the vision of the true nature of the unity of the bodiless Self, the suspicion of a connection with suffering is no longer possible. However, desires arising from the volitions of pure *sattva* constitute a connection with the body of the Lord for those mental states present in all beings. The Supreme alone is the enjoyer through the medium of the adjuncts (*upādhi*) of all beings; thus, the Supreme Self alone is the substratum of all conventional transactions created by ignorance, and there is no other—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Vedānta.

Some maintain that the person seen in the eye mentioned by Prajāpati was merely the shadow-self (chāyā-puruṣa), and that those in the states of dream and deep sleep are entirely different, not the Supreme Self characterized by freedom from sin and so forth, because of the contradiction [with those attributes]. They further explain the purpose of teaching through the shadow-self and others as follows: if the Supreme Self were taught at the very outset, since it is difficult to comprehend, there might arise confusion when hearing about such an extremely subtle reality among those whose minds are intensely attached to external objects. Thus, they say, this was done to prevent such delusion.

Just as, for instance, one who wishes to show the subtle moon on the second day first points out a certain tree directly before him, saying, "Look, this is the moon," and then another, and then yet another mountain peak situated near the moon, saying, "This is the moon," until finally he sees the moon; in the same way, what was spoken by Prajāpati in three stages beginning with "He who is in the eye" does not refer to the Supreme.

"But in the fourth stage, having risen from the mortal body and attained bodilessness, one becomes of the nature of light. That supreme person in whom one exists eating, playing, and rejoicing with women and others—that supreme person is said to be the 'Highest' (para). This they say. True, this interpretation is indeed pleasant to hear; however, the meaning of this text cannot possibly be such.

"How so? Having introduced [the subject] with the words, 'The person is seen in the eye,' if Prajāpati had taught that the reflection-self alone is what is seen in the eye, then the two disciples' grasping of it as such, Prajāpati's awareness of their contrary grasp, his presentation of the water-bowl for its removal, and his question, 'What do you see? as well as the instruction regarding the ornaments, would all be purposeless. Furthermore, if he himself had taught [it to be the self], then a reason for the removal of even that very grasp would have to be stated."

One would have expected Prajāpati himself to state the means for removing the misconception of the Self in both the dream and deep sleep states; however, he did not do so. Therefore, we conclude that the reflection in the eye was not the Self taught by Prajāpati. Furthermore, if the Seer in the eye had been intended as the one taught, then after saying "But him alone I shall explain to you," there would have been a teaching concerning the Seer even in the context of dreaming. If you argue that the Seer was not taught in the context of dreaming, we say no, because of the teaching: "He seems to weep" and "He seems to experience what is unpleasant."

Nor does anyone other than the seer move about being honored in a dream; for this has been established through reasoning and by another scriptural passage as "this person is self-luminous. Although in a dream one possesses the intellect (*dhī*), nevertheless the intellect does not function as an instrument for the perception of dream-enjoyments. Rather, like a painting on a canvas, the intellect is itself an object of sight, resting upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state; thus, there is no sublation of the seer's self-luminosity.

Furthermore, in the states of waking and dreaming, one knows both the elements and oneself—thinking, "These are the elements" and "This is I. Since this knowledge is actually present, a negation would be appropriate [only if it were absent], such as "Verily, he does not [know this]," and so forth.

Thus, having stated that for the conscious self alone, while it possesses a body due to the cause of ignorance, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant, it is logical that for that same self when it is bodiless and knowledge is present, there is a negation of those two which were previously thought to apply to the embodied state: "Verily, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who is bodiless. Furthermore, it is established in another scriptural passage that the single Self moves through the states of dream and waking without attachment, like a great fish.

As for the claim that the "supreme person" (uttama-puruṣa) mentioned as the locus in the phrase "having risen from the body, he who rejoices with women and so forth"—being distinct from the serene being (saṃprasāda)—is incorrect; for even in the fourth section, Prajāpati says, "But him indeed, I shall explain to you. If he had intended someone other than that [serene being], Prajāpati would not have said "But him indeed, I shall explain to you," as he did previously, for he would have been speaking falsely.

Furthermore, having shown the entry of the existent Being—the creator of fire, water, food, and so forth—into the sprout of its own body which is a modification [of itself], the instruction "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) would result in being false for one who has already entered. If there were a supreme Person distinct from the serene one (saṃprasāda), then the appropriate instruction would have been: "In him you will become a lover with women and so forth."

Likewise, [the scripture] would not have concluded with "All this is indeed the Self" after having taught "I am indeed [Brahman]" and so forth in the section on the Infinite (bhūman), if the Infinite were other than the individual soul (jīva); for there is another scriptural passage stating, "There is no other seer but He," and so on. Furthermore, the term "Self" (ātman) would not have been applied to the Supreme in all the scriptures if the innermost Self (pratyagātman) of all living beings were not the Supreme Self. Therefore, it is established that the Self under discussion is one and the same.

Nor does the Self possess transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), because transmigratory existence is superimposed upon the Self by ignorance (*avidyā*). For it is not the case that a snake, silver, impurity, and so forth—which are superimposed through false cognition (*mithyājñāna*)—actually belong to a rope, mother-of-pearl, the sky, or similar objects. By this, the statement that "for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain" is explained. And as for the established point that "one experiences what is unpleasant," it is proven that [the Self] is not actually an experiencer of the unpleasant.

This being the case, the statement of Prajāpati—“This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman”—found in every such passage, or rather the statement of the Śruti appearing in the form of Prajāpati, must indeed be true. It is not proper to render it false through the intellect of fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*), because no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more authoritative than that can be established.

If it is argued that the state of being a perceiver of unpleasant things such as suffering is experienced as an invariable perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no; for this is established by the very same kind of perceptual experience as "I am aged though free from old age," "I have been born," "I am long-lived," "I am fair," "I am dark," or "I am dead. If it is argued that all of this is true, [we reply] that this is indeed so, yet it is difficult to comprehend, since even the King of the Gods (*devarāja*) was utterly deluded in this matter, despite having been shown the reasoning regarding non-destruction through the example of the water-cup and so forth, [when he heard]: "He becomes merged into non-destruction alone" (*avināśam evāpīto bhavati*).

Likewise, Virocana, though possessed of great wisdom and being a son of Prajāpati, came to regard the body alone as the Self. Similarly, the Nihilists (vaināśikas) sank into the very ocean of fear regarding the destruction of the Self for Indra. Likewise, although the Sāṃkhyas understood the Seer to be distinct from the body and so forth, they remained fixed in the perception of duality within the realm of death, because they had abandoned the authority of the sacred scriptures (āgama).

Likewise, others who follow the systems of Kaṇāda and so forth have set out to purify the substance of the self—which they believe to be endowed with nine qualities—just as one might cleanse a cloth dyed with astringent dyes using alkaline substances and the like.
