Similarly, other ritualists, whose minds are captivated by external objects, even though they accept the Veda as authoritative, regard the ultimate truth of the oneness of the Self as if it were perishable, like Indra [vanquished by his enemies]; thus, like a water-wheel, they wander incessantly through various modes of ascending and descending.

What need is there to speak of other small creatures who, being devoid of discrimination, have by their very nature minds that long for external objects? Therefore, this [work] is to be known only by those wandering mendicants (parivrājakas) of the highest order (paramahaṃsa), who have renounced all external desires, who have no other refuge, who are exceedingly diligent, and who are devoted to the realization of Vedānta; it is to be honored by those most excellent ones who follow this Prājāpatya tradition and have composed it in four chapters. Thus they instruct even today: "Only these [should know it], and no others."
The wind is bodiless; the cloud, lightning, and thunder—these are bodiless. Just as these, having risen from yonder sky and having reached the highest light, appear in their own forms... 2...

In this regard, since the serene being (*saṃprasāda*), which is bodiless, has attained a state of embodiment—characterized by non-distinction from the body due to ignorance—it must be explained how it emerges from the body and manifests in its own true form. To illustrate this, the following examples are given: the wind is "bodiless" (*aśarīra*), meaning it lacks a body consisting of a head, hands, and so forth. Furthermore, the cloud, lightning, and thunder are also bodiless.

This being the case, when the purpose such as the rains has been fulfilled, just as the scriptural expression "from that" (amuṣmāt)—referring to something situated on earth—designates a region of space connected to the heavenly world; so too these [elements], having attained a form identical to space as previously described, and no longer being perceived in their own forms such as air and so forth, have reached the state of being called "space. Just as the serene being (*saṃprasāda*) attains the very nature of the body during the state of ignorance, so too those [elements], having become thus, [proceed] from that which is connected to the heavenly world.

They rise from the region of space for the purpose of bringing about rain and so forth. How so? At the end of the cold season, having reached the supreme solar light—that is, having attained the intense heat of the sun—during the summer.

Having been brought to a state of separation by the heat of the sun, they abandon their state of stillness and emerge in their own respective forms at the arrival of the rainy season: the wind in the form of the *purovāta* and other winds; the cloud also in the form of the earth, mountains, elephants, and so forth; the lightning also in its own form as flickering streaks of light; and the thunder also in its own form as rumbling and lightning-bolts. Thus they manifest in their own respective forms.

In this very way, this serene being, having arisen from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form. He is the Supreme Person. There he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen; he does not remember this body, which has been produced anew. Just as a draft animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath yoked to this body. 3. (3)

Just as in this illustration where air and the other elements attain a state of similarity with space and so forth, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), having attained a state of identity with the body during the condition of transmigratory existence through ignorance—thinking "I am the son of such-and-such," "I am born," "I have grown old," "I shall die"—is awakened by Prajāpati, like Maghavan, according to the stated sequence: "You are not the attributes of the body, senses, and so forth; *tat tvam asi* (That thou art). Then this serene being, the individual soul, having emerged from this body—just as air and the others emerge from space—realizes its own nature as distinct from the body and other such things.

"Having understood form and abandoned the notion of the body as the Self"—this has been explained previously by the statement that "he manifests in his own true nature as the Existent Self. That by which this serene being (saṃprasāda) manifests in his own true nature—just as before awakening a rope becomes a snake due to the cause of delusion, but later, once illuminated, it manifests in its own true nature as the rope—so too does that Supreme Person (uttamapuruṣa), who is both supreme and a person, manifest. He alone is that.

The Supreme Person (uttamapuruṣa). The person in the eye, the person in dream, the manifest, the unmanifest, the one in deep sleep, the one who has gathered all, the serene, and the bodiless in its own form—abiding in its own form in relation to these very states, namely the perishable and the imperishable, as well as the manifested and the unmanifested, it is called the Supreme Person; for this term has indeed been defined in the Gītā.

That serene being (*saṃprasāda*), by his own nature, abiding in himself as one who has become the Self of all, moves about; sometimes, in the form of Indra and others, he eats, laughs, or consumes various desired foods, high and low; and sometimes he plays with women and other objects produced merely by the mind—arising from mere volition (*saṃkalpa*)—whether they be worldly or non-worldly—and rejoices with them through the mind alone. "Birth" (*upajana*) does not apply here; for "birth" means that which is born from the mutual union of a woman and a man, or that which is born from the state of selfhood or in proximity to the self.

Thus, this body is a superadded [accidental] thing, and he does not remember it. For if he were to remember it, there would be only suffering, since its nature is suffering. If he did not remember what was experienced, then the liberated one would lack omniscience. This is not a fault. That which was produced by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) and so forth has been eradicated by true knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, that [body] was not truly experienced [as part of his nature], and thus there is no loss of omniscience due to not remembering it.

For indeed, what is experienced by one who is insane or possessed by a spirit need not be remembered even when the insanity or possession has ceased; likewise here, that which is experienced by transmigrating beings who possess the defect of ignorance does not touch the Self that is all-pervading and bodiless, because the cause—ignorance—is absent.

However, those desires which are experienced by those whose defects have been eradicated and whose impurities (*kaṣāya*) have been rubbed away—desires that are real in their essence but covered by untruth—are manifested through knowledge (*vidyā*). It is these very desires that are connected with the liberated one who has become the Self of all; thus they are pointed out for the sake of praising the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, it is well said to specify them as "those which are in the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*). For wherever they may exist, they exist indeed in the world of Brahman alone, and because Brahman is the Self of all, they are so described.

But how is it not contradictory that he, being one, neither sees another, nor hears another, nor understands another, yet "being the *bhūman*, he beholds and enjoys the desires belonging to the world of Brahman"? For it would be as if one who sees at one very moment did not see at that same moment. This is not a fault, because it has been resolved in another scriptural passage: "Because the vision of the seer is never lost, he is indeed seeing; yet because there is no existence of desires as something other than the seer, he does not see."

Although that was stated regarding deep sleep, the absence of a second is equally true for the liberated one because of the oneness of all; furthermore, it has already been said, "By what means could one see whom? Yet, Prajāpati asked how this person, whose nature is bodiless and characterized by freedom from evil and so forth, is seen in the eye. To that end, it is now commenced to explain how he is directly perceived in the eye.

Regarding the question, "What is the reason for [the term] 'darśana' (vision) being applied to the eye? he says: That is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Just as *prayogya* means that which is to be employed, or the word *sa-* implies that which is employed—where *prayoga* is that which is employed, such as a horse or an ox; and just as in common usage *ācaraṇa* is that by which one moves, such as a chariot or a cart—to which one is yoked for the purpose of pulling it; even so, in this body which stands in the place of a chariot, the five-fold vital breath (*prāṇa*), conjoined with the senses, mind, and intellect, is the conscious self (*prajñātman*) whose nature is a fusion of the two powers of cognition and action.

"Engaged" means appointed for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of its own actions; it has been appointed by the Lord—just as a prime minister by a king—to the exercise of vision, hearing, and movement, with the thought: "Upon whose departure shall I depart, and upon whose being established shall I be established? Of that [Self] alone, however, the eye-organ is a mere portion or part, serving as the gateway for the perception of form.

Now, where the eye is extended into this space, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing. And he who knows, "Let me smell this," he is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling. And he who knows, "Let me speak this," he is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking. And he who knows, "Let me hear this," he is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing. 4. (4)

Now, where the space characterized by the black pupil (kṛṣṇatāra) is present—pervading, adhering to, and following along with the cavity of the body—therein is that aforementioned bodiless Self, called "cākṣuṣa" because it exists in the eye; for the purpose of seeing—that is, for the perception of form—the eye is the instrument.

That which exists for the sake of the supreme Seer—who is distinct from the body and its constituents because of their composite nature—is perceived here in the eye by means of the mark of seeing. That supreme Self, who is bodiless and non-composite, is indicated by Prajāpati’s statement, "He is seen in the eye," which is intended as an illustration for all the doors of the senses, for He alone is the perceiver of all objects. However, the specific mention of "in the eye" occurs in all the Śrutis because it is the cause of clear perception, as the Śruti says: "When one thinks, 'I have seen,' that becomes true."

Moreover, he who knows within this body—"How so?—'Let me smell this, whether it be fragrant or foul; let me discern its odor'"—he is the Self; for that [Self], the organ of smell exists for the sake of odor, that is, for the cognition of odor. Furthermore, he who knows—"Let me utter this speech; I shall speak"—he is the Self; for the accomplishment of the act of uttering, the instrument is the organ of speech. Furthermore, he who knows—"Let me hear this"—he is the Self; for the sake of hearing, there is the ear.

Now, he who knows, "May I think this," that is the Self; the mind is its divine eye. With that divine eye, the mind, he indeed beholds these desires and rejoices in them, which are in the world of Brahman. 5.

Now, he who knows—"I shall think"—knowing the activity of thinking untouched by the senses as "I am merely thinking," he is the Self; the mind is for the purpose of thinking. Because of the universal application of the statement "he who knows is the Self," it is understood that knowing is his essential nature—just as when it is said, "He who illumines from the east is the sun; he who illumines from the south, from the west, from the north, and from above is the sun," it is understood that its essential nature is illumination.

The instruments, such as the eye, exist for the purpose of accomplishing actions like seeing and so forth. This is understood through the inherent capacity of this Self: the Self’s agency in knowing consists in its mere existence, not in being actively engaged in action—just as the sun’s agency in illumination consists in its mere existence, not in being actively engaged in action. Likewise, the mind is the divine, non-material eye of this Self, unique among the other senses; it is called the "eye" because one sees (*caṣṭe*) or perceives by means of it.

The sense organs have objects belonging to the present time; therefore, they are non-divine (*adaiva*). The mind (*manas*), however, is the cause for perceiving objects of all three times, and when its defects are suppressed, it is the instrument for perceiving everything—subtle, concealed, and so forth—and is thus called the divine eye. That liberated one, having attained his true nature, being separated from the body, senses, and mind created by ignorance, and having attained the state of being the Self of all, is like the pure ether, the Lord of all, possessing the mind as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Being that very Lord with the mind as his adjunct, he rejoices while beholding these desires through a vision that is eternally continuous, like the light of the sun.

He specifies which desires [he means]: "those which are in the world of Brahman, like a hidden treasure of gold, covered over by the untruth of attachment to external objects, and obtainable by mere thought"—this is the meaning.

Regarding this, Prajāpati said: "The gods indeed worship this Self; therefore, all worlds and all desires are attained by them. He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," so said Prajāpati, so said Prajāpati. 6. (6)

Since this Self was declared to Indra by Prajāpati, therefore, having heard of that Self from him, even today the gods worship it. And through that worship, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them. The intention is that the gods have obtained that very fruit for which Indra lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati for one hundred and one years.

It might be argued that this [attainment] is appropriate for the gods because of their great fortune, but it is not possible now for humans because of their short lifespan and their comparatively duller intellect. To this, the following is said: "He attains all worlds and all desires—even one belonging to the present time. Who is he? Prajāpati spoke in general terms, saying: "He who, having searched, realizes that Self"—just like Indra and the others. Therefore, the meaning is that the knowledge of the Self and the attainment of its fruit are exactly the same for everyone.
The repetition of the word is intended to mark the conclusion of the section. Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth section.

"I go from the dark to the variegated; I go from the variegated to the dark. Shaking off evil like a horse shakes its hairs, and as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu, I—having shaken off the body and perfected my self—attain the uncreated world of Brahman; I attain it.

The traditional recitation of the mantra beginning with "From the dark I go to the speckled" is purifying and intended for recitation (*japa*) or meditation (*dhyāna*). "Dark" (*śyāma*) refers to a deep color; like the dark, it is "dark"—namely, the Brahman within the heart (*hārda brahma*)—because of its extreme profundity. Having known that Brahman within the heart through meditation, one goes from that dark [Brahman] to the "speckled" (*śabala*); it is called "speckled" because the world of Brahman is mixed with various desires such as those of the forest and so forth. That speckled world of Brahman, I go to by means of the mind after the fall of the body, or upward [from this state].

"I shall go. The intention is that since I have come from the variegated world of Brahmā (*śabalo brahmalokaḥ*) for the purpose of manifesting name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), I have now entered the state of the Heart (*hārdabhāva*). Therefore, the meaning is: "Having reached that very Self, which is the primordial nature (*prakṛtisvarūpa*), the variegated one (*śabalam*)."

"How may I attain the variegated world of Brahman? It is said: Just as a horse shakes off its own hairs, removing fatigue and dust from them by shaking, and thus becomes pure; even so, having shaken off evil—namely that which is called merit and demerit—through the knowledge of the Brahman within the heart, one becomes radiant like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu when it was seized by him. Thus, having shaken off and abandoned the body, which is the locus of all misfortunes, right here through meditation...

"Having perfected my self and accomplished all that was to be done, may I attain the uncreated, eternal world of Brahman. The repetition [of the mantra] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the mantra.

Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth section. Space, indeed, is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Self. I enter the assembly hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati. May I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas, the glory of the Kṣatriyas, the glory of the Vaiśyas. I have attained glory. I am indeed the glory of glories. White, eating, not eating, white, slippery—may I not go to the slippery; may I not go to the slippery. 1.

(1) — "Or rather, space," and so forth, is for the purpose of indicating the definition of Brahman for the sake of meditation. Indeed, the Self is well-known in the Vedas by the name "space" (*ākāśa*), because, like space, it is bodiless and subtle. And that space is the sustainer, the bearer, and the differentiator of Name and Form—which reside within its own self, which constitute the seed of the world, and which stand in the relation of foam to water.

That Brahman is that which exists "between" those two—namely name and form—meaning within them, or else that which exists between name and form, meaning untouched by name and form. This Brahman is distinct from name and form and untouched by them; nevertheless, it is the very sustainer of the two. Such is the meaning: Brahman is characterized in this way. This very point has been stated in the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa: because pure consciousness (cinmātra) permeates everything, it is understood that the nature of all things is indeed consciousness; thus, there is a single coherent statement.

How is this understood? He says: "That is the Self. For the Self is indeed well-known as the inwardly conscious, self-perceived [reality] of all living beings. Having inferred it by that very nature [of one's own], one should understand that the bodiless, all-pervading Self, like space, is Brahman. And that Self is Brahman, the Immortal, whose nature is not subject to death. Hereafter follows the mantra: "I enter—that is, I go to—the assembly hall, the abode fashioned by the Lord, of Prajāpati, the four-faced one."

Furthermore, I am Yaśas; I am the Self named Yaśas for the Brāhmaṇas. For it is the Brāhmaṇas who especially worship that [Self], and therefore I become their Yaśas. Likewise for kings and Vaiśyas; since they too are entitled [to such worship], I am also their Self. Thus, "I have sought to attain Yaśas"—I desire to attain it. I am indeed the Self of those Yaśas characterized by the body, senses, mind, and intellect.

"For what purpose am I approaching this?"—to this it is said: "Śyeta" by color, resembling a ripe jujube fruit, "rohitam" (red). Likewise, "adatkam," meaning toothless, yet also "adatka" as a devourer—the female organ, which is the destroyer and annihilator of the splendor, strength, vigor, wisdom, and virtue of those who indulge in it. May I not approach, may I not go toward, that which has such characteristics, the "śyeta" (white), the "lindu" (oozing) and "picchala" (viscous). The repetition [of the negative particle] is for the purpose of demonstrating that it is the cause of extreme misfortune. Thus ends the commentary on the fourteenth section.

Brahmā told this to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu [told it] to his offspring. Having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher according to the rules, and having performed the duties for the teacher with the remainder of his time, having returned home, studying the Veda in his own household in a pure place, establishing virtuous sons, and fixing all the senses within the self, not harming any living beings except at sacred places—truly, conducting himself thus for as long as he lives, he attains the world of Brahman and does not return again, and does not return again.

This very knowledge of the Self, along with its auxiliary practices—comprising meditations such as "Om is this syllable" and so forth, together with the text that expresses them, namely the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*—was spoken by Brahmā, whether as Hiraṇyagarbha or the Supreme Lord, through him to Prajāpati Kaśyapa; he in turn spoke it to his son Manu; and Manu [spoke it] to all creatures. Thus, this realization of the Upaniṣads, having come down through the lineage of the traditional transmission of the meaning of the Vedas (*śruti*), is understood even today among the learned.

Just as the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā), revealed here in the three chapters beginning with the sixth, is understood to be fruitful, so too, when it might be concluded that there is no purpose whatsoever for ritual actions (karman), this meaningfulness of action—performed by the wise—is stated in order to avoid the contingency of its being purposeless: namely, having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher together with its meaning (*sahārthataḥ*), having performed the study according to rule, and being endowed with the observances (*niyama*) as prescribed in the Smṛtis; such is the meaning.

Although every duty prescribed by the Smṛtis must be performed by the *upakurvāṇaka* (the student), the author says the following in order to demonstrate the preeminence of service to the teacher: "Having performed whatever work for the teacher is to be done, with that remaining time which is free from [other] duties, one should study the Veda. The intention is that the Veda, when studied by one who observes such rules, leads to the attainment of the fruits of ritual action and knowledge, but not otherwise.

The meaning is: having returned [from study], having completed the inquiry into the Dharma, having retired from the teacher's house, having lawfully taken a wife, and remaining in the household stage, abiding in the duties prescribed for the life of a householder.

Even there, in order to demonstrate the preeminence of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) among the duties prescribed for the householder, it is said: sitting properly in a pure, secluded place free from impurities and the like, studying the Veda according to rule—performing both the obligatory and the additional recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas to the best of one's ability; establishing righteous sons and disciples in dharma, restraining them through righteousness; and having firmly established all the senses within the Self, that is, in the Brahman within the heart (*hārda*).

Having withdrawn the functions of the senses consisting of grasping [objects] and having renounced them, "not harming" means not causing injury—that is, not afflicting any living beings, whether stationary or moving. Lest one might think that even wandering for the sake of alms could cause injury to others, he says: "except at sacred sites" (*anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ*). A "sacred site" (*tīrtha*) refers to a matter permitted by the scriptures; the meaning is "other than that. This applies equally to those in all stages of life (*āśrama*). Others explain it as follows: except at sacred sites, there must be non-injury alone.

Performing all this within the household itself, he is indeed qualified; acting thus throughout his life, for as long as he lives, in the manner described, he reaches the world of Brahman at the end of the body. And he does not return again to assume a body, because of the prohibition against returning which would otherwise have been possible. Having reached the world of Brahman—the world of the effected (kārya) Brahman—by the path beginning with light, he remains there for as long as that world of Brahman exists; the meaning is that until then he does not return. The double repetition is for the purpose of concluding the Upaniṣadic teaching.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth section,
composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order.
The Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is complete. "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha; for one begins the Udgītha with 'Om'. Here follows its detailed exposition. (1)
